News.title: Angela Rayner: 'Andy Burnham's vow to end rough sleeping is not just a gimmick for Christmas'
News.content:
Angela Rayner: 'Andy Burnham's vow to end rough sleeping is not just a gimmick for Christmas'

EXCLUSIVE: Housing Secretary Angela Rayner said she was confident the commitment given by Andy Burnham to offer all rough sleepers an offer of a bed by Christmas would be delivered on

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Andy Burnham's promise to offer all rough sleepers a bed this winter will not just be a gimmick for Christmas, Angela Rayner has insisted.

‌



‌



The Housing Secretary, who is responsible for delivering on the Prime Minister's flagship pledge, said she was confident the commitment would be delivered on.

‌



Ms Rayner told The Mirror's new YouTube show, Sense Check: "The reason I am [confident] is because I have been incredibly proud of seeing the response by the public, by philanthropists, by local government, by mayors, to Andy Burnham's pledge to end rough sleeping.

‌



"That doesn't mean everybody will take that offer, but certainly I've been working with the community and voluntary sector, local authorities, we've put that record investment - £442 million into that."

Pressed on what happens after Christmas, Ms Rayner said: "We continue. We double down. I want people to know that their offer is there. It's not just there for Christmas, it's not a gimmick."

In total there were 4,793 rough sleepers in the autumn 2025 - a 171% hike on 2010 - according to the most recent snapshot data available.

‌



View 2 Images Housing Secretary Anglea Rayner on The Mirror's new Youtube show, Sense Check (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

But the Cabinet minister refused to be drawn on the housing benefit freeze ahead of Chancellor John Healey's maiden Budget on October 28 - but said the policy is "reviewed annually".

Asked how the freeze could be justified, Ms Rayner said: "Local housing allowance has been frozen for a period of time and it's something that is a concern alongside what was section 21 no-fault evictions that were happening at the same time. We've solved that and that and that is something that's reviewed annually.

‌



"But the challenge that we've got is we're putting more money into housing allowance and people are paying more money for rents and on housing than ever before.

"And the problem there is because we don't have the supply. We don't have council housing, we don't have social housing, and we're paying more for less in effect. So therefore we've got to fix that."

View 2 Images Angela Rayner with Chancellor John Healey and PM Andy Burnham on a visit to a homeless shelter (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Ms Rayner - a former care worker - also described being asked to attend one of the new Prime Minister's first major interventions over the summer where he delivered a speech at a care home.

The Cabinet minister said around 20 years earlier she had berated a young Mr Burnham - then the MP for Leigh - as a union rep over issues facing care workers, including short 15-minute home care visits.

Ms Rayner told Sense Check: "Anyway, so then fast forward, and Andy becomes Prime Minister. He puts me back in the cabinet, which I was really grateful for. And then he asked me to attend his announcement he was making over summer at the care home where he was talking about this national care service.

‌



"I'm sat there. And he mentions the 15 minute care calls and he makes his speech without any notes. And I just sat there and I thought, I've waited a long time for a Prime Minister to say that, I was getting emotional.

"Sat there and thinking, this feels different. It feels like he gets it. He'll finish my sentence on things like the ending rough sleeping. He really has an interest in the areas and the things I care about.

"So it's like pushing against an open door, basically. That feels really positive to me. That's different.

Article continues below

"Whereas before, it felt like you had to really fight the arguments, whereas now it just feels like, you're not arguing about what you're doing. You're arguing about how you get there."

News.title: Angela Rayner: 'I saw my premature baby fight for his life – quitting politics was never an option'
News.content:
Angela Rayner: 'I saw my premature baby fight for his life – quitting politics was never an option'

EXCLUSIVE: Senior Labour Cabinet minister Angela Rayner, who returned to government in July, opens up on the painful episode in her career on The Mirror's new YouTube show, Sense Check

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Angela Rayner told how seeing her premature baby fight for his life helped give her a new perspective as she vowed never to walk away from frontline politics.

‌



‌



Opening up about the painful episode in her career, the Labour heavyweight was forced to resign from the heart of government over her tax affairs.

‌



Ms Rayner - who returned to Cabinet in Andy Burnham's new administration in July - said the "rollercoaster of hell" experience with the traumatic premature birth of her second son at just 23 weeks had given her an "anchor".

‌



She said against the odds she had walked out of the hospital after nine months with her "miracle son" Charlie in 2008, saying to herself: "If not thing else good comes in my life, I've banked that [luck], I'm having it."

Speaking to The Mirror's new YouTube show, Sense Check, Ms Rayner described the saga over her tax affairs that brought an abrupt end to her time in Keir Starmer's Cabinet as "mortifying".

She said: "It was also to do with my son and his disability and what's going on for him - and I'm very private about my kids because they go through a lot. My son was at an age where he was 17 - just about to turn 18 - and he'd just started work and it was wall-to-wall coverage of his mum.

‌



"There was press coverage implying that I'd done something to try and take my son's money or I'd done something that was to try to set something up that was try and get around rules, which was, it just wasn't the case."

​Angela Rayner wins emotional standing ovation as she returns to limelight at Labour conference READ MORE :

View 2 Images Angela Rayner with her son Charlie

In a move that rocked the Labour Party last summer, Ms Rayner was forced to resign as Deputy Prime Minister and Housing Secretary over £40,000 in unpaid stamp duty on her second home in Hove, East Sussex.

‌



But seven months later she was cleared by HMRC of deliberate wrongdoing or carelessness over her tax affairs - paving the way for her return to the Cabinet.

Asked whether she ever thought she wouldn't come back into frontline politics or consider just walking away, Ms Rayner told presenter Nicola Thorp: "Not walking away because I think there's a lot of people....that go through a lot more hardship."

Describing her own personal hell, she added: "I remember when my son was born at 23 weeks and I was told that we need to switch the machine off because there's nothing more they can do for him. And I remember seeing on that neonatal unit, lots of families come out of there without a child. I came out of with my son, against all odds.

‌



"Compared to what happened to me or what was going on at the time, I banked every bit of luck that moment in my life. And that's where I think, you know what, people go through things like that every single day and they struggle.

"So my struggle, when you look at it like that, it puts it into perspective.

"It's like, you what, I lucked out that day. That moment, I walked out of St. Mary's [a specialist neonatal unit], I was like, you know, what, if nothing else good comes in my live, I've banked that I'm having it. And it gives you an anchor when you've been through hardship and you've being through things like that it kind of gives you a perspective especially in the Westminster side of things you know 'I've got a bad headline in the Daily Mail' it's like okay, well that's nothing."

‌



On the nine months she spent in hospital, Ms Rayner, who was a single mum with her first son Ryan, went on: "That was a rollercoaster of hell, a rollercoaster of hell."

View 2 Images Angela Rayner on The Mirror's Sense Check Youtube show with presenter Nicola Thorp (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

But she later added: "I feel like I lucked out. Because I've got three beautiful children. They're all amazing. My three Gen Zs, as I call them, my three boys. And they're all doing incredibly well. I'm very lucky."

‌



In the interview, Ms Rayner also described the "humbling" moment she returned to the limelight at the Labour conference in September as a Cabinet minister. She told delegates gathered in the conference hall at the time: "I don't often cry, but nearly. It's so good to be back".

Ms Rayner told Sense Check it was an emotional moment, saying: "You could feel the love in the room". She added: "When I went on the stage... and sat down I could hear the delegates talking about some really important issues around housing and a delegate on women's rights.

"And I was, kind of like, it was nice to be there and actually the room wasn't that full. At that point when I sat on the stage I was thinking there's not many people here and the Cabinet — we're all in Cabinet.

Article continues below

"So none of my colleagues were sat there either so I was empty chaired by the Cabinet because they were in Cabinet to be fair and then the hall wasn't as packed but then all of a sudden within like 10 minutes the hall was rammed just before I was getting up.

"So it was just like wow people have turned out to listen to me and it just was really humbling and that's when I kind of said that when I stood up and I could feel the energy in the room."

News.title: 'Loving' mum dies after flying 1,300 miles for BBL surgery - despite family's desperate pleas
News.content:
'Loving' mum dies after flying 1,300 miles for BBL surgery - despite family's desperate pleas

Jennifer Arias flew from New York to Miami for a liposuction and a Brazilian Butt Lift (BBL), but after the procedure was struggling to breathe - and eventually died

View 3 Images Jennifer Arias was 29 (Image: Jam Press)

A "loving" mum died after travelling 1,300 miles for cosmetic surgery, despite being warned by her family not to do it.

‌



‌



Jennifer Arias, who was 29, flew from New York to Miami for a liposuction and a Brazilian Butt Lift (BBL) at New Life Plastic Surgery. Hours after the procedures, however, her family was told the mother-of-one was struggling to breathe.

‌



The woman was rushed to hospital in Miami but doctors were unable to save her. Jennifer had already died by the time her devastated family made it to Florida. The Miami-Dade Medical Examiner's Office ruled her death an accident, stating she had suffered fat embolisms in both lungs as a result of the surgeries.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 3 Images Jennifer Arias had a seven-year-old daughter (Image: Jam Press)

But before she went to the clinic, Jennifer's mum, Monica Arias, had warned her against the procedures. The grandmother feared Jennifer's seven-year-old daughter would be left without a mother.

‌



She said: "I told her, don't do it, don't do it." She said she had warned Jennifer: "If something happens to you, what will happen to your daughter?"

Jennifer's sister, Erika Arias, said she received a text from her sibling at 4.18am on the day of the operation, telling her she was heading into surgery. Hours later, she received the devastating news. She said: "I couldn't believe it. That's my sister. That's my best friend."

The family said they were told by the surgeon, Julio Clavijo-Alvarez, that everything possible had been done. Her family is now demanding answers about the tragedy.

‌



Erika said: "She was a great mother. She definitely loved her child so much, so deeply." Monica added: "No-one will ever be able to give her a mother's love. My granddaughter has been left without that."

According to local media citing civil lawsuits and state and county records, Jennifer is among at least six patients to die following surgery at the clinic since 2018. One of the previous cases involved Naimy Sucetz, 41, who died in 2022 after undergoing liposuction and a tummy tuck at the clinic.

View 3 Images Jennifer Arias (Image: Jam Press)

‌



Her death was attributed to a blood clot in her lungs, and Clavijo-Alvarez was also her surgeon. The surgeon has faced at least four lawsuits since 2020 alleging inadequate medical care caused injuries or complications. He denied the allegations in court documents.

In 2024, Florida's medical board reprimanded him and fined him $15,000 (£11,200) to resolve three administrative complaints. As part of the agreement, he neither admitted nor denied the allegations.

New Life has denied responsibility in court filings relating to two previous patient deaths, arguing in part that the doctors involved were independent contractors. The Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office has confirmed that its Homicide Bureau is investigating Jennifer's death.

Article continues below

Since her sister's death in August, Erika has launched a fundraiser to help support Jennifer's daughter going forward. The page reads: "Our family recently experienced an unimaginable loss with the sudden passing of my sister at only 29 years old."

"She was a loving mother, daughter, sister, and friend, and her absence has left a pain that words cannot describe. Most importantly, she leaves behind her beautiful seven-year-old daughter, who now has to grow up without her mom.

"Our family is doing everything we can to surround her with love, stability, and support as she goes through this heartbreaking change. We created this GoFundMe to help our family with the unexpected expenses following my sister’s passing and, most importantly, to help provide for her daughter’s needs and future."

News.title: New Mirror YouTube show Sense Check hosted by broadcaster and activist Nicola Thorp
News.content:
New Mirror YouTube show Sense Check hosted by broadcaster and activist Nicola Thorp

The Mirror today launches Sense Check, a hard-hitting flagship YouTube show hosted by broadcaster and activist Nicola Thorp

View 3 Images Actor and presenter and podcast host Nicola Thorp (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

The Mirror today launches Sense Check, a hard-hitting flagship YouTube show hosted by broadcaster and activist Nicola Thorp.

‌



‌



On the show, Nicola and the Mirror team dive headfirst into the stories dominating the nation’s group chats - from breaking political news to hard-hitting social commentary.

‌



The launch episode features Angela Rayner as Thorp’s first guest. In the episode, Angela insists she didn't consider walking away from frontline politics when she was forced to resign from the heart of government over her tax affairs. She addresses those infamous vaping photos, opens up about the traumatic premature birth of her son and gives an update on the government's commitment to ensuring all rough sleepers have a bed this winter.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

Talking to Nicola, Angela said: "I know that gut-wrenching feeling when your kid's shoes are knackered and you need to buy a new pair of shoes and you've just got no money... I know how that feels for people and that never leaves you."

New episodes will be released every week, supported by a rotating panel of guest contributors and Mirror journalists.

‌



The premiere episode is available on Sense Check’s YouTube channel.

View 3 Images The new YouTube show Sense Check is hosted by broadcaster and activist Nicola Thorp

View 3 Images Talking to Nicola, Angela said: "I know that gut-wrenching feeling when your kid's shoes are knackered and you've just got no money" (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

Article continues below

Nicola Thorp, Host of Sense Check: "I’m thrilled to be joining forces with The Mirror for Sense Check. With so much misinformation and division online, we wanted to create a show that dives headfirst into the topics everyone is talking about and brings real understanding, great conversation, and a much-needed sense check to the news agenda.”

Chloe Hubbard, Editor-in-Chief, the Mirror: "We need to meet people where they are accessing their news - and today, that’s often on YouTube. Sense Check is our chance to bring our journalism directly to the audiences we know will connect with what The Mirror has to say in 2026, but who may never have picked up the newspaper.

"We’re also delighted to have the brave and formidable Nicola Thorp hosting the podcast. Her fearless, authentic approach makes her the ideal person for this exciting next step.”

News.title: Pope Leo urges Vladimir Putin for ceasefire in occupied Ukraine city days after Pontiff's lung cancer op
News.content:
Pope Leo urges Vladimir Putin for ceasefire in occupied Ukraine city days after Pontiff's lung cancer op

Pope Leo called Vladimir Putin to call for a ceasefire in an occupied town that has had no food deliveries since May, days after the Pontiff was diagnosed with cancer

View 5 Images Pope Leo in images released by the Vatican three days after his surgery (Image: Vatican Media via AP)

Pope Leo XIV has spoken to Vladimir Putin to share his "deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation" in a Ukrainian city, just three days after he underwent lung cancer surgery.

‌



‌



The Vatican, on Friday, revealed the Pontiff and Russian President spoke on the phone to call for a ceasefire in the occupied town of Oleshky, in the Kherson region. Residents in Oleshky, occupied by Russia since 2022, have had no food deliveries since May as the United Nations revealed 1,700 people remain trapped in the destroyed town.

‌



This comes after the Pope underwent a 90-minute operation to remove the lower lobe of his right lung on Tuesday, after doctors identified a suspected cancerous nodule. The surgery confirmed he had lung adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 5 Images The Vatican revealed Pope Leo spoke to Vladimir Putin over the phone (Image: Mikhail Metzel/Pool Sputnik Krem)

Volodymyr Zelensky defies Donald Trump with major attack on Russian refinery READ MORE :

A statement, released by the Vatican, on the Pope's call with Putin said: "During the conversation, the Holy Father expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky, in the Kherson region, and called for a ceasefire to allow the delivery of food and medical assistance, and the voluntary and safe evacuation of the civilian population.

‌



"Finally, the Holy Father reaffirmed the Holy See's commitment to promoting dialogue and peace." People in Oleshky face severe food and water shortages while electricity and medical care are limited. Residents have faced Russian drone attacks and escaping the city has been made near-impossible due to landmines on the roads out of Oleshky.

View 5 Images Rally in Ukraine in support of the residents of Oleshky (pictured on October 6) (Image: Ukrinform/Shutterstock)

The Kremlin said Putin wished the Pope good health and a quick recovery. In response to the Pope's concern about the plight of civilians in Oleshky, Putin gave a "detailed explanation regarding the Kyiv regime's responsibility for the difficult humanitarian situation there," the Kremlin said in a statement.

‌



Putin also voiced support for "the Vatican's intention to help create conditions for ensuring the safety of the local population and facilitating the delivery of essential supplies," and an agreement was reached to co-ordinate efforts on this, the statement said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the crisis in Oleshky was a "genocide". Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland, he said: "Now we are not talking about famine there, we are talking about genocide.

Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, on Saturday, on Telegram wrote: "The choice that Russia leaves every day to civilian residents – stay and starve to death, leave and risk getting blown on a landmine."

‌



View 5 Images The Pope lead a mass in a makeshift chapel at the Gemelli University Hospital in Rome (Image: VATICAN MEDIA/AFP via Getty Images)

Pope Leo was seen for the first time today in images released by the Vatican. They showed him celebrating mass at a makeshift altar and chapel set up for him at the Gemelli hospital, in Rome.

The Pontiff, 71, appeared relaxed as he stood over the altar in green garments. A second image showed Pope Leo holding up the Communion as his personal secretary, Peruvian priest Edgard Rimaycuna, stood by his side.

‌



Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said the Pontiff presided alone over the liturgy, distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes present and delivered a homily.

In his homily, Pope Leo thanked the hospital staff "for the work they do every day taking care of the sick in their fragility, and in a particular way what they had done for him", the spokesman said.

View 5 Images People praying under for Pope Leo outside the Gemelli hospital (Image: AP Photo/Alessandra Tarantino)

‌



A medical update, signed by the Pope's personal physician Dr. Luigi Carbone and head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli hospital, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, said: "His post-operative recovery allows him to carry out his normal daily activities completely on his own."

The Vatican also revealed the Pope was set to deliver the traditional noontime prayer on Sunday, however they did not share if this would be done in person. Vatican media personnel were seen at the Gemelli hospital installing cables for a possible live broadcast, as has happened before when past popes have been treated in hospital.

Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said a recitation of the noontime prayer on Sunday from the hospital was a possibility, but would depend on how Leo's post-operative recovery progresses.

Article continues below

On Thursday, the Chicago-born pope resumed working from his hospital room and met with his chief of staff, while continuing with respiratory physiotherapy.

His doctors said tests showed his lung had recovered well from surgery, that other post-operative tests were in the norm and that overall his recovery was proceeding as expected.

Doctors are still awaiting the results of tests to understand the precise molecular and genetic makeup of the cancer, whether it has spread beyond the lobe and whether any further treatment is necessary.

News.title: Watch: BBC follows Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi pushing Russia back on frontline
News.content:
Deep inside an underground bunker in eastern Ukraine, commanders monitor the battlefield through a live video feed as a Ukrainian drone intercepts a Russian surveillance drone.

The footage shows the Ukrainian drone hovering above its target, before dropping a net and dragging it from the sky.

The interception is part of Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counter-offensive that Kyiv says has recaptured 277 sq km (106 square miles) of territory in the eastern Donbas region in recent months.

But Ukraine says new restrictions on Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite network, are threatening its drone operations.

The technology has played a key role in helping Ukrainian forces detect and strike Russian targets. Dan Johnson reports from the bunker.

Read more about Ukraine's counter-offensive.

News.title: Man killed by tiger may have had medical records breached by NHS staff
News.content:
Medical records belonging to a man killed by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park may have been accessed "without a legitimate reason" by staff at Yorkshire Ambulance Service, a spokesperson has said.

William Chapman, 24, was mauled to death at the park near Doncaster on Saturday.

In a statement, the trust said following Chapman's death it had identified two possible incidents of staff "accessing or attempting to access incident/medical information" about the case.

It said an investigation had been launched "to establish the full circumstances surrounding these potential breaches".

Chapman died as a result of "multiple traumatic injuries and animal interaction" after entering the tiger's enclosure at the park, an inquest into his death heard on Thursday.

News.title: Nurse stole £750k from 99-year-old woman for cosmetic surgery and home improvements
News.content:
A nurse who stole Â£750,000 from a vulnerable 99-year-old and spent the money on cosmetic surgery and home improvements has been struck off.

Rebecca Louise Burwood exploited the resident who was living at Bryn Yr Haul Care Home in Mold, Flintshire, where she was deputy manager, for her own personal and financial gain.

She coerced the pensioner from 2017 to 2023 and also bought a car and campervan with the stolen money, as well as obtaining ownership of the woman's home.

A Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) hearing found Burwood's fitness to practise was impaired by reason of misconduct and imposed a striking-off order, meaning she will be removed from the nursing register.

The NMC hearing was told Burwood had a longstanding relationship with the woman before she moved into the home in 2018.

The panel heard the resident had no family members and was vulnerable after a fall. She was dependent on Burwood for friendship and social contact.

It found that, between 2017 and 2023, Burwood abused a position of trust and power, becoming the resident's lasting power of attorney, while also overseeing her care.

Burwood withdrew money from the woman's bank account, accepted ownership of her house and received thousand of pounds, which was used for her own benefit, including for building work and the purchase of vehicles.

Evidence presented showed more than Â£370,000 had left the resident's account over five years, with Â£160,000 of that from making large cash withdrawals at ATMs.

She also took the resident to the solicitors and got her to transfer the ownership of her Â£400,000 house.

The hearing was told there was "evidence to show Mrs Burwood used the funds for house improvements, utility bills and council tax", and there were "allegations that Mrs Burwood used some of the funds for personal cosmetic surgery".

She convinced the resident to pay Â£20,000 for a car and Â£9,000 for a campervan, which she said was purchased so the pair could go on days outs.

Burwood claimed the work on her home had been so the elderly woman could live with her in the event of another outbreak of Covid - however it had been paid for before any Covid lockdown in the UK.

News.title: Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car?
News.content:
A new version of Tesla's Roadster electric sports car, equipped with thrusters which apparently allow it to hover and turn in mid-air, has been unveiled in Texas.

"You're going to see some crazy stuff tonight," the car firm's CEO Elon Musk said as he presented the vehicle at a facility owned by his SpaceX company, which helped develop the model.

Musk said an audience was needed to prove the car "is not AI", before showing a demonstration of the Roadster driving up and off a steep ramp, spinning in the air, and landing using air jets.

But there are several reasons we're unlikely to see a flying car on our roads anytime soon, as the BBC's technology editor Zoe Kleinman explains.

Video editor: Serene Khalifeh

News.title: Police feared Andrew would delay search by saying King owned his home, documents show
News.content:
On 18 February, Thames Valley Police asked for permission from the Central Criminal Court for warrants to search Wood Farm in Sandringham and Royal Lodge in Windsor.

The request included the police outlining the scenarios in which they believed they would need search warrants to ensure access to the properties.

They feared that Mountbatten-Windsor or his legal team would want to see "judicial authority" before allowing the police to enter, the documents show.

The police were concerned that Mountbatten-Windsor or his representatives could argue that the Sandringham Estate was the property of King Charles - and that it would be a slow process getting a separate right of access.

Such a delay would "frustrate the nature and purpose of the search," said the police, in their application for search warrants.

There was also a concern that no one would be present at the property and that media attention could be drawn to the police presence outside while not being able to enter.

Any of those delays could have meant the police would have been unable to gather the evidence they wanted, they argued - and "given the gravity of this investigation", the police asked for search warrants.

In separate documents filed as part of Mountbatten-Windsor's legal challenge against the warrants, he said: "These assertions were no more than speculation."

The documents also detail the type of information the police were seeking inside the properties.

They say: "Paper-work, diaries, business records or other documentary evidence of AMW's [Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's] time as Special Representative for Trade and Investment.

"Further evidence as to any action, communication, comment or in relation to matters following the release of material by the FBI concerning the late Jeffrey Epstein as AMW will be aware that Thames Valley Police is conducting an assessment.

"Specifically mobile phone(s) and computer(s) [to include electronic notebooks, surfaces, iPads and any older electronic devices," which could have held information about links to Epstein at the time when Mountbatten-Windsor had been the UK's trade envoy."

The documents show the search of Royal Lodge, Mountbatten-Windsor's former home in Windsor, continued until 24 February.

They also reveal his police interview at Aylesham Police Station began at 15:00 GMT and he was released under investigation at 18:36.

The legal documents give details of why the police wanted to talk to Mountbatten-Windsor, including the claim that when he was a UK trade envoy he had forwarded Jeffrey Epstein official reports from official visits to Singapore, Vietnam, China and Hong Kong.

There was also a claim, arising from emails in the Epstein files released in the US, that Mountbatten-Windsor had briefed Epstein on investment opportunities in Afghanistan.

Also mentioned is the suggestion Mountbatten-Windsor held meetings with a private investment firm and then suggesting to Epstein that he might invest in the company.

News.title: 'Well-known' man asks court to stop publication of sexual offence allegation
News.content:
An individual described as "well-known" has asked London's High Court to prevent two media organisations from publishing "serious allegations", including of a sexual nature, against him.

The court heard he had submitted medical evidence saying that if the allegations were made public this would "almost certainly" lead to him "attempting to take his own life", and that the prospect of publication had already led to two suicide attempts.

The court was told that Independent Television News and Guardian News & Media had carried out an investigation into the individual's "conduct over a period of years".

The individual, who has been granted anonymity in the court proceedings, denies the allegations.

The court was told that following an investigation that ITN, which produces news for ITV and Channel 4, and Guardian News & Media, which publishes the Guardian, sent two letters to the the well-known individual in the spring of 2026.

As well as denying the allegations, the individual responded with medical reports stating that there was a risk to his life if the information was published.

At an injunction hearing at London's High Court, lawyers representing ITN and Guardian News & Media said that "it would be wrong" for the court to "restrain publication" when the "law provides for a detailed and well-established scheme by which the interests of those at risk of suicide is specially protected by NHS mental health professionals".

The court has also granted anonymity to other individuals in the case.

Two individuals who have agreed to be identified in any ITN and Guardian News & Media report concerning the allegations were given anonymity in the current proceedings by High Court judge Mr Justice Nicklin. The nature of the allegations or how these two journalistic sources relate to them is not known.

A third journalistic source for the ITN and Guardian News & Media investigation has also been granted anonymity in the current proceedings. She has alleged that she was the victim of a sexual offence by the well-known individual.

The court will decide whether the ITN and Guardian News & Media will be permanently prevented from naming the well-known individual and publishing the allegations against him at a trial due to be held later this month.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

News.title: Norwegian teen 'hitman' jailed over UK murder plot
News.content:
A teenager who travelled from Norway to the UK to carry out a "hit" for an organised crime group has been sentenced to 20 years' detention.

Johannes Natland, 19, was arrested in a hotel room in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, with two working guns and 19 rounds of live ammunition in March 2025, the Old Bailey previously heard.

During his retrial, a jury heard the teen was "recruited" by the Foxtrot Network, which was described as a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime.

Natland, who had admitted to possession of the firearms and ammunition, was unanimously found guilty of conspiracy to murder and sentenced at Woolwich Crown Court on Friday.

The Foxtrot Network has been sanctioned by both the UK and the US for its close links to the Iranian government, with Natland's target remaining unclear.

Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "We haven't been able to establish exactly who the intended victim was."

The Foxtrot Network is known for pioneering a relatively new phenomenon of hiring teenage killers that Europol has called "violence-as-a-service" (VaaS).

At the sentencing hearing, Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb told Natland: "The Foxtrot Network is an organised crime group which has developed an arm's-length method of recruiting young people to carry out violent crimes.

"You were recruited to travel to England to kill an unidentified target."

Natland had been offered 270,000 Norwegian Kroner, about Â£21,000, to carry out the killing.

He flew into Manchester Airport on an emergency passport on 17 March 2025, shortly after his 18th birthday.

Natland was guided by videos on the messaging app Signal to Huddersfield, where the guns, a stolen car and a stash of cash were hidden.

He was prevented from carrying out the hit after Norwegian police arrested the teenager who had recruited him for the Foxtrot Network and found messages about the UK plot on his phone.

There was then a race against time to find Natland before he located his unknown target in England.

Addressing Natland, the judge said: "At the heart of this case is a stark fact. You agreed to assassinate another human being, a stranger to you, in a foreign country.

"You knew nothing of that person's life or circumstances. You were just 18 years old when you placed yourself in readiness to murder for money."

News.title: Woman says she was left 'bewildered and confused' by alleged Russell Brand assault
News.content:
The complainant told jurors on Friday she met Brand in 2001 when she worked at MTV.

She said she recognised him straight away and said there was "banter" between them initially.

After noticing his "distinctive T-shirt" with the words "I am Spartacus", she told Brand she "loved it" and wanted it.

"He said, 'you can have it'", the woman told the jury, to which she said she replied: "Make sure it gets a good wash first."

Brand then asked her for directions to the bathroom.

The woman, who was in her thirties at the time, said she offered to show him the way because she was going in the same direction.

Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC asked her what happened next.

She said his "demeanour changed" when they got to the bathroom door.

"He grabbed my forearm, he was leaning into the door and he was quite forceful," she said, adding that it took her "unaware".

Asked by the prosecutor what she meant by his demeanour changing, the witness said: "He grabbed me by the arm, started to pull me in."

She said Brand then said to her "come on" while still holding her forearm.

The woman said while Brand was trying to pull her into the bathroom, she was trying to pull herself away.

"I said to him, 'What are you doing, are you mad, let me go'... and then he started to... plead almost," she said.

The woman told the court she managed to "wrench" herself from Brand's grip because of her own strength.

She told jurors Brand went from "jovial, affable, friendly to suddenly turning into this wild-eyed manic so I was quite confused this was happening, as anyone would be".

Asked by the prosecutor why she did not report what had happened to her employer, she said: "I was scared... I thought it would be my word against his."

But she did tell two of her colleagues, she said.

Jurors heard that she reported the allegation to the police in 2023 after watching a Channel 4 documentary about Brand.

"I thought it was the right thing to do to come forward," she told the court.

Brand's barrister challenged the complainant on the fact that she did not report Brand for what he had allegedly done until after watching the documentary.

"You didn't think there was any need to report him," Ian Winter KC said.

"It would have been my word against his," she replied. "He didn't manage to rape me. I managed to get out of the situation."

The defence barrister said: "It was only after you saw the television programme that you think he was trying to rape you in the toilet."

The woman responded: "Why else would you drag someone into the toilet if you weren't going to assault them."

Winter KC continued: "Twenty-two years before that, you hadn't thought he was trying to get you in there to rape you..."

The woman denied that, adding: "You don't grab someone by the arm. You don't grip someone and try to drag them in, that's not consensual."

News.title: Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution'
News.content:
The prime minister has invited the Scottish government to work together to put "power back in the hands" of regions - but insisted they must "move beyond" the constitutional question of Scottish independence.

Andy Burnham said he wanted to start work on a new deal for regional economic development in the next few months, including an offer of devolution from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP).

Speaking at an event in Motherwell, Burnham called on first minister John Swinney to cede further powers from Holyrood to local areas before that happened.

SNP minister Stephen Flynn said the party had asked for increased devolution since the Smith Commission report was published in 2014.

The prime minister said devolution "was never supposed to stop at the doors of the Scottish Parliament" when Holyrood opened in 1999.

He said it was meant to be the "start of something deeper" where "communities had more of a say in their own future".

News.title: Catherine says nature can help children's emotional growth
News.content:
The Princess of Wales has launched a project promoting the use of nature to help develop young children's social and emotional development.

"Nature is such an extraordinary environment for us all and, in this tech-driven, digital age, spending quality time outdoors has never been more important," says Catherine, in a social media post.

This is the latest stage in Catherine's campaign to improve the status of early years education and to find ways to improve children's wellbeing.

She says that research has shown "just how important nature is for our psychological and physiological wellbeing".

In her own recovery from cancer, the princess has spoken about the importance of spending time in nature, which she described as her "sanctuary".

She has hailed the holistic benefits of nature, which she described in almost spiritual terms, in a series of videos showing the changing seasons.

This faith in nature is now being applied to her early years project - the Royal Foundation Centre for Early Childhood.

She wants to encourage ways of using the natural world to improve children's sense of creativity and to help their emotional development - and sites for such educational visits could be provided by the Duchy of Cornwall.

A new photograph of Catherine taken on Thursday in Cornwall by Josh Shinner has been released to accompany the project.

"This project is about exploring how nature, creativity and relationships can best support the healthy development of babies and young children," says the princess.

"We believe that taking a whole-child approach is important, and nature becomes a wonderful place to explore how we can successfully nurture the social and emotional skills that underpin lifelong health and wellbeing.

"My hope is that through this practical, nature-based research, we can build supportive environments that help make nature more accessible, benefiting babies, young children and their families across the UK."

Dr Nicola Kemp of the Froebel Trust, which supports early years education research, said: "A growing body of evidence shows that regular contact with nature can support children's development in many ways, helping to foster curiosity, creativity, emotional wellbeing and social connection."

The Princess of Wales has looked for ideas for improving early years education, including her trip earlier this year to Reggio Emilia in Italy, which had developed a system that prioritised relationships and learning through play.

There is no funding announced so far for the project, but Catherine is using her profile to promote a cause that she once described as her "life's work".

The emphasis on families enjoying the natural world is also an antidote to an overload of screens and mobile phones, with Catherine having warned of an "epidemic of disconnection" from too much tech disrupting family life.

News.title: Banks expect to be hit with higher taxes in Budget
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey is planning to increase taxes on the bank sector, senior banking executives have told the BBC.

Healey has described banks as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, but leaders in the sector have said it will be "on the menu" at the Budget in two weeks' time.

The biggest four banks collectively made about Â£15bn profit in the first six months of this year, and trade unions have called for them to face additional taxes.

The trade body for the banking sector, UK Finance, warned "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode".

Shares in banks including Lloyds and NatWest fell on Friday on expectations that the sector would be hit by tax hikes. The firms were among the biggest fallers on the UK stock market, with both dropping more than 2%.

Barclays fell only slightly and HSBC actually rose as both have large international businesses and would be less affected by a hike in UK taxes.

There are a number of ways the chancellor could extract more money from the sector.

One option is for Healey is to reverse a reduction in the surcharge that banks pay on corporation tax, from 8% to 3%, introduced in 2023, by Conservative chancellor Jeremy Hunt.

Critics argue this would be unfair noting the cut coincided with a rise in corporation tax from 19% to 25%.

Healey could also raise the bank levy - a small percentage charged on loans.

The BBC understands that the Treasury is leaning towards changing the surcharge if they were to go ahead as it is easier to change an existing tax rather than impose a new windfall tax.

Reversing the 2023 surcharge rate would raise around Â£2bn. However, the last government was persuaded that adding 8% on top of corporation tax of 25% would leave UK banks struggling to compete with European and US rivals - so it may be that it is raised, but not all the way back to the 8% level.

Speaking to the press in Bangkok, Healey praised the role banks play in the British economy.

Adding that he has "decisions to take in the Budget", he said: "My observation on the banks is that people too often see âthem as big, distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future â prospects."

In the past banks have successfully argued that higher taxes would risk making the UK uncompetitive with other jurisdictions and would reduce their ability to lend, and therefore be anti-growth.

Sir Philip Augar, an author and former banker in the City of London, told the BBC's Today programme there was "room for a moderate increase" in taxes on the sector that could raise up to Â£3bn a year.

He said lenders were enjoying "booming conditions", benefiting from higher interest rates which boost their profits.

Rising interest rates have expanded the margin between the rate at which banks lend to customers and the rate they pay savers.

Sir Philip added that when the banking sector "hits really rocky times it expects the taxpayer to bail them out - when it hits boom times, it expects some kind of special treatment".

He said banks cannot simultaneously be "too big to fail and too big to tax".

Paul Nowak, general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, which represents trade unions, said Britain's four biggest banks are making a billion pounds a week, with bonuses at post-financial crash records. "These are bumper profits - driven by high interest rates and households' mortgage misery," he said.

"Now it's time to make sure banks pay their fair share," he added.

"But if the chancellor does ask the Banks to pay a fairer share of tax in the Budget, that's 100% the right call," he added.

News.title: Covid vaccine compensation scheme set for overhaul after Inquiry criticism
News.content:
The benefits of vaccination are well documented. The AstraZeneca Covid jab is credited with saving millions of lives worldwide. But some people have experienced harm.

In her fourth report, the chair of the Covid Inquiry, Baroness Hallett, called for better support for those affected.

She said while this was a minority, the way they are supported needed urgent reform.

More than 24,000 people have made Covid-related claims to the Vaccine Damage Payment Scheme (VDPS), a form of financial support paid by the government, but just over 1% have resulted in one-off tax-free awards of Â£120,000.

The report called for "urgent" reform of the scheme, saying that it is "not sufficiently supportive".

It said the current system, in which those affected must show they have been at least "60% disabled", does not work effectively for Covid vaccines.

In its response to the report, the government says, external it is committed to reviewing the scheme to ensure it is "fit for purpose and delivered effectively."

Ministers in England have promised to work closely with the other nations of the UK as well as those injured by the Covid vaccine and their families.

News.title: Police officer who raped two women jailed for 12 years
News.content:
A former police sergeant who was found guilty of a catalogue of sex crimes, including raping two women, has been jailed for 12 years.

Campbell Petrie had been convicted of eight charges involving physical and sexual abuse towards the women in Glasgow between 2006 and 2022.

Petrie, who had denied the allegations, will be supervised and monitored in the community for a further three years after his release.

He is one of four serving or former Police Scotland officers who have been exposed as rapists in the space of five months.

It has also emerged that 45 serving officers are currently suspended over allegations of violence against women and girls.

News.title: Reform councillor quits over offensive remarks
News.content:
Warning: This report contains racist and offensive language.

A Reform UK councillor filmed calling Asian homeowners "parasites" has resigned from two councils and apologised for his comments.

Alan Feeney, who has since stepped down from the party, was heard making the remarks during undercover filming for an ITV News investigation, external in the run up to council elections in May.

Feeney said he had resigned every post he held on Solihull Council and Birmingham City Council, adding that his remarks "were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable".

He has also been suspended from his job with the prison service, with the Ministry of Justice [MoJ] describing the comments captured during the documentary as "despicable".

In July, his register of interests with Solihull council recorded he was employed as a custodial manager, a position described on the HM Prison and Probation Service website as "the most senior uniformed officers in a prison".

Feeney was one of several Reform members featured in the ITV investigation, which was gathered over the course of a year.

In it, while campaigning in the run-up to May's elections, Feeney described an area as "infested" with Asian families and called them "absolute parasites".

He was also recorded saying no more than 1% of the UK population should be non-white.

News.title: Wildlife park reopens after man killed by tiger
News.content:
Yorkshire Wildlife Park has reopened for the first time since a man was killed by a tiger in an enclosure.

William Chapman, 24, was mauled to death at the park near Doncaster on Saturday. The public were evacuated after the incident with the attraction closed since then.

An inquest that opened into Chapman's death on Thursday heard of his history of mental illness and a diagnosis of schizophrenia. His family expressed concerns about his contact with mental health services leading up to his death.

City of Doncaster Council, which is responsible for licensing the park, is carrying out a health and safety investigation and said it would share the outcome with the coroner, the inquest was told.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park confirmed on Thursday it would reopen following "engagement with the relevant authorities".

In a previous statement on social media, the park said "many, many people" had contacted it about Altai, the Amur tiger involved in the incident, and it confirmed he was "safe and well" and would not be euthanised.

A spokesperson said its "Land of the Tiger" area, where Saturday's incident took place in front of staff and members of the public, was also open.

News.title: Doctor regrets not going to police earlier about Lucy Letby
News.content:
A senior doctor who raised suspicions about Lucy Letby has said he should have gone to police sooner.

Dr Stephen Brearey was the lead neonatal consultant at the Countess of Chester Hospital when the nurse murdered seven babies and attempted to murder seven others.

In his first interview since the publication of the Thirlwall Inquiry report into what happened, Brearey reflected on the effect on staff and said he had "naively" assumed senior managers would respond to suspicions about the nurse's involvement in a series of baby deaths.

The inquiry found a "toxic negativity" within the NHS that continued to discourage staff from speaking out, despite stronger whistleblowing guidance, and said regulation was lacking.

Brearey claimed his warnings about Letby were repeatedly ignored by bosses at the hospital, which is now under new management - and also fears cultural change at the NHS will take time to implement.

"I was naively thinking that raising concerns with senior managers, they had the same values that I did and, once they got it, they would be thinking the same way," he said.

The doctor led a group of seven consultants who shared the same concerns about Letby.

Hospital bosses carried out a series of internal reviews into increased infant mortality in 2015 and 2016, but Cheshire Police was not asked to investigate until May 2017.

Letby remained employed at the hospital until her arrest more than a year later.

"I think one of the reasons we got through this and ended up picking up a police investigation is that the seven of us stuck together," he said, speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

"But obviously in retrospect, clearly, if we'd known what was ahead of us, we would have gone to the police earlier."

News.title: Fabio Wardley says Anthony Joshua brings ‘aura’ to training camp ahead of Daniel Dubois fight
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Fabio Wardley has been feeding off the “aura” of Anthony Joshua as he looks to reclaim the WBO world heavyweight title from Daniel Dubois at The O2 Arena on Saturday.

Joshua has reunited with Wardley’s trainer Ben Davison ahead of his British grudge match against Tyson Fury on 11 December and the fighters have been put through their paces together at his training facility in Harlow.

Wardley insists the presence of the two-time world champion and Olympic gold medallist has provided a boost as he looks to avenge the only defeat of his career against Dubois in May.

“AJ’s been back for a good while in the gym and it’s been good to see him,” the 31-year-old from Ipswich said.

open image in gallery Anthony Joshua has been training at the same gym as Fabio Wardley ahead of his clash with Tyson Fury (Bradley Collyer/PA)

“He has a different energy and a different aura around him so when he appears it gives the gym a little buzz and a different feel.

“He’s straight back in the mix and he’s shoulder to shoulder with the boys, just like you’d expect.”

Joshua left Davison after his fifth-round knockout by Dubois in 2024 and his return is validation for a coach who has been criticised for his corner work and preparation for world heavyweight title bouts involving Joshua, Wardley and Moses Itauma.

His failure to throw in the towel as a bloodied Wardley faced a ferocious onslaught late on in first showdown with Dubois has been scrutinised – referee Howard Foster came to the fighter’s rescue – but he has the complete trust of his fighter on Saturday night.

“The whole conversation around Ben has always been incredibly frustrating,” Wardley said. “The level of criticism he gets is incredible.

“It’s so strange because the levels at which he’s said to have ‘not achieved’ or not done the right job have been at the absolute pinnacle of the sport.

“I trust these people with my life and I don’t say that lightly. I genuinely do. They know me.

“They know me well enough to know whether I’m in a fight or not and I was still very much in that first fight.

open image in gallery Daniel Dubois, left, and Fabio Wardley clash on Saturday at the O2 (Adam Davy/PA)

“I’m glad they let me carry on because I was still catching Daniel, even in the 10th.”

Dubois previously identified nerves as the reason for his pedestrian start against Wardley having come off the back of a second confidence-sapping loss to Oleksandr Usyk.

But he now accepts that tension is his default setting and will use his state of mind as a weapon for his 27th professional fight.

“I feel nervous every day,” he said. “I’m a nervous and chaotic character. I’m chaos and I’m just holding that chaos in until the fight.

“It’s a power for you if you know how to use it. It’s about harnessing it. I enjoy inflicting pain and putting that chaos on to the other guy.

“What’s inside me – the pain – I put on him. That’s what boxing is, it releases whatever you have inside you. It’s an outlet.”

News.title: El Niño rains flood South America, sending residents fleeing and cattle swimming
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Rivers swollen by heavy rains linked to El Niño continued flooding swaths of Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay on Friday, forcing thousands of people from their homes and sending ranchers scrambling to move cattle to higher ground.

In Argentina’s northeastern Corrientes province, the Paraná River rose to a dangerous 4.7 meters (15.4 feet) on Thursday in the riverside town of Ituzaingó, prompting evacuations there and in other towns across the province. Herds of cows waded across flooded pastures as ranchers guided them toward dry land. The calves struggled against a current thick with floating clumps of river plants. Provincial officials said they were digging canals and installing drains to prepare for more heavy rain.

The floodwaters come from three major rivers that start in Brazil and flow south through the region: the Paraná, the Uruguay and the Iguazú. Torrential rain has pushed all three waterways higher for days, spilling them over their banks in northeastern Argentina, southern Paraguay and western Uruguay.

This part of South America often gets heavy rain during El Niño, a natural climate phenomenon in which warmer-than-usual waters in the Pacific Ocean scramble weather patterns around the world. Forecasters say this year’s could be among the strongest on record, and its effects are already being felt across South America and far beyond, from an unusually stormy hurricane season off Mexico’s Pacific coast to the threat of severe drought in Southeast Asia.

Paraguay has seen the most evacuations from the recent floods. In the border city of Ayolas, across the Paraná River from Ituzaingó, more than 2,000 people have fled their homes, Mayor Carlos Duarte told a local radio station Friday. He said the river had reached its highest level there in more than four decades and could rise further.

The flooding has also hit one of South America’s biggest tourist attractions. At Iguazu Falls, the waterfalls on Argentina’s border with Brazil, park authorities have closed the walkway to the Devil’s Throat, the largest and most dramatic of the cascades, because of the high Iguazú River. Other trails that were shut in recent days have reopened.

In Uruguay, the Salto Grande hydroelectric dam, which the country shares with Argentina, has gradually opened its gates to relieve the rising Uruguay River, flooding parts of cities downstream. Several dozen people remain out of their homes.

More rain is on the way. Uruguayan officials have warned that the country’s drenched northwest will get its heaviest rain of the year in the coming months. In southern Brazil, where the rising Paraná, Uruguay and Iguazú rivers originate, the national weather service expects above-average rainfall through December.

___

Associated Press writers Ramiro Barreiro in Montevideo, Uruguay, and Isabel DeBre in Buenos Aires, Argentina, contributed to this report.

News.title: Caroline Dubois bidding to become biggest boxing name with brother Daniel

Daniel Dubois returns to centre stage of the heavyweight division this week but younger sister Caroline Dubois believes the world champion siblings could soon become the faces of the sport.

After months of Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua dominating the boxing agenda, Dubois’ rematch with Fabio Wardley at The O2 will turn the focus back to events inside the ring with the WBO belt on the line.

While WBC and WBO lightweight champion Caroline remains estranged from big brother Daniel, she is still thrilled to see her older sibling thriving and talked up the prospect of the family members taking over men and women’s boxing respectively.

“I like the sound of that. That would be awesome and really cool,” Caroline told the Press Association.

“I don’t know if that has ever been done before – a brother and sister as undisputed world champions and dominating in their respective weight categories and divisions.

“Obviously to say we were the face of boxing and British boxing, I’d be very happy with that.

“Yeah, it would be awesome and amazing. I’d be really happy if we could achieve that.”

Both Dubois siblings have undisputed plans on the agenda for 2027 but Wardley will try to gain revenge on Saturday.

Wardley and Dubois produced a thriller at Co-op Live in Manchester back in May in a critical fight for the latter to win after he lost comprehensively to Oleksandr Usyk last year.

For Caroline Dubois, it was no surprise to see her brother take on a big challenge and succeed, she said: “Daniel has done a really good job of rebuilding himself time and time again and being brave I think.

News.title: Fabio Wardley relishing return to underdog status for Daniel Dubois rematch
News.content:

Fabio Wardley is revelling in the freedom of being reinstated as the underdog for his bid to recapture the WBO world title lost to Daniel Dubois in May.

The British heavyweight rivals collide at The O2 Arena on Saturday in an immediate rematch of their savage first meeting that saw Dubois climb off the canvas twice to stop Wardley in the 11th round.

Having been relieved of his belt, Wardley is now back in the familiar territory of being asked to defy the odds in the latest assignment of an unconventional route to the top that began in white collar boxing.

open image in gallery Fabio Wardley (left) was stopped by Daniel Dubois (right) in their first fight (Richard Sellers/PA) ( PA Wire )

“Honestly, it’s great,” the 31-year-old from Ipswich said. “I actually really love it. It feels more natural, more weightless.

“Don’t get me wrong, it’s fantastic being a world champion and holding that belt. It was also having an undefeated record and the weight of going in with such a good fighter like Daniel.

“Now I just feel free. The talk around the fight has changed. I’m back to being expected to lose and things going worse for me.

“I’ve been proving people wrong for I don’t know how many years now. Seemingly for me, it’s better when I’m told I’m going to be the underdog and I’m going to lose, that this is a level too far for me.

“I’m the challenger and chaser and honestly for me it all just feels like, ‘this is it, this is the nice bit that I enjoyed for the past however many years on my rise and on my way up’. It feels great.”

News.title: A fight over a bandana might have led to a cold-case murder in rural West Virginia, cops say
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Read our Privacy notice

A fight over a bandana in West Virginia may have kicked off a series of events that led to a murder and now an arrest, a decade later.

Richard William Nichols, 65, was arrested in connection to the 2016 murder of Ivan “Vanya” Perlis, 25, last month. He was taken into custody in Indiana and extradited to West Virginia to face charges.

Perlis’ remains were found on November 12, 2016, after a hunter discovered them near Maysville, West Virginia. Authorities found a skull with three bullet holes in the back, West Virginia State Police wrote in a criminal complaint.

A state medical examiner determined that Perlis was killed about a month before the remains were found.

Early in the investigation, police focused on an argument between Nichols and Perlis over a bandana.

open image in gallery Richard William Nichols, 65, has been arrested in connection to the cold-case murder of Ivan Perlis in 2016. Perlis’ remains were found in rural West Virginia ( WVRJA )

In 2016, Perlis and Nichols lived on the same property but in different areas. One day, Nichols accused Perlis of taking a bandana and using his camper, police noted. That led to a fight where Nichols picked up Perlis by the neck and shook him, according to police.

Nichols, however, told authorities in 2017 that he and Perlis patched up their dispute and got along after the confrontation.

Throughout the investigation, Perlis’ story kept changing. At one point, he told troopers that he took Perlis to meet another man. He then changed his account saying that other man threatened both with a gun and demanded Nichols leave.

Nichols also wrote an apology letter to Perlis’ family and friends saying he gave Perlis a ride and the victim never returned. Nichols added that he wished he had done more to help Perlis.

Police continued to conduct interviews and the case remained open over the next decade.

In July 2024, police again interviewed the man who owned the property where both Nichols and Perlis lived. He said he saw the two leave together and Nichols returned wearing different clothes. The witness said Nichols claimed he changed because he had blood on his clothing and Perlis would not be coming back.

Police say there was a possible motive in a separate burglary where Perlis was reportedly pictured at the scene. It was speculated that Nichols might have wanted to prevent Perlis from identifying other people involved.

Nichols is now being held in a West Virginia jail until his next court appearance.

News.title: Daniel Dubois taunts Fabio Wardley before rematch: ‘He punches like a baby’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Daniel Dubois has taunted Fabio Wardley ahead of Saturday’s world heavyweight title rematch at The O2 Arena by declaring “he punches like a baby”.

The British rivals clash in a replay of their classic in May when Dubois climbed off the canvas twice to stop Wardley in the 11th round, seizing his WBO belt in the process.

Wardley was left bloodied and bruised by Dubois’ onslaught over the last five rounds yet immediately demanded they fight again, encouraged by his early success in flooring his foe.

Dubois, however, insists that he did not feel the shots as he dismissed the heavy hands that are seen as one of Wardley’s key weapons.

open image in gallery Fabio Wardley (left) was stopped in the 11th round by Daniel Dubois in Manchester (Richard Sellers/PA) ( PA Wire )

“He doesn’t have no power,” the 29-year-old Londoner said. “He punches like a baby.

“The knockdowns were early doors, whatever. I didn’t feel it. You just get up and keep fighting. You just plough through it.

“My mentality was to plough through and chip away and I did that. He doesn’t punch, so I’m just gonna land my punches and bring the pain.

“I’m gonna bash him up easy. I’ve learned what I’ve needed to learn from the first fight and I’m just ready to put it on him.

“I’m going to break him down and beat him up, like I’m his daddy.”

Wardley is convinced that he can make the technical changes needed to avenge his only defeat in another twist to a a late-blooming career that began with four white collar bouts before turning professional.

“He’s not good enough to adapt, so he’ll do the same thing as he did in the first fight,” Dubois said.

News.title: Asia’s vaccine self-sufficiency drive gets $650m boost
News.content:
An “innovative” partnership to boost vaccine security across Southeast Asia will inject up to $650 million into regional manufacturing, in a bid to reduce reliance on imported shots.

The five-year initiative, announced at the annual meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund in Bangkok on Friday, will see major lenders, non-profits, and the private sector come together to invest in the region’s vaccine industry.

Currently Southeast Asia’s production base remains limited and exposed. The majority of shots are imported, and any capacity the region does have is highly concentrated – one analysis this year estimates 60 to 90 per cent sits with a single vaccine manufacturer.

Even before Covid-19 hit, this vulnerability was recognised. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), a regional bloc of 11 countries, endorsed a vaccine security and self-reliance initiative in 2019, driven by Thailand’s National Vaccine Institute (NVI).

These concerns have mounted since the pandemic, but up until now investment as well as political will has been lacking. The partnership announced on Friday, led by NVI, hopes to remedy this, and develop a model that can be copied worldwide.

​​“If we can do it here in Asia, then that really provides a model for the world,” said Aurélia Nguyen, deputy CEO of the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (Cepi), a a vaccine research non-profit. “We can build it out in Africa, in Latin America, and that really gives us the resilience that we want the next time we have a major epidemic.”

Cepi has committed up to $20 million of “catalytic funding” for the programme, which is backed by the World Bank as well as organisations like the Singapore-based AVPN investment network.

In all, the package of loans and grants will include at least $174m in public financing, and up to $460m in private capital mobilisation for regional vaccine manufacturing. Further details, including recipients, have not yet been announced.

But Paschal Donohoe, the managing director and chief knowledge officer of the World Bank Group, told a panel in the Thai capital that “we believe this has the ability over time to mobilise up to $650m of finance”.

He added that the group would use public loans and grants alongside investments by its private-sector arm, the IFC, while its guarantee arm, MIGA, would help cover investors against risk.

“It’s really important because each element of the World Bank Group is involved in it,” Donohoe said. “We’re not just talking the talk, but walking the walk.”

Speaking to the Telegraph after the event, Nguyen added: “Innovative models and partnerships like this, where we’re each bringing a piece to de-risk scientific technology, [allow us] to leverage larger quantities of capital.

“But I think what’s also helpful in this model is, beyond the financing, [we] have a sort of coordinating umbrella through Asean,” she said. “So you can be smart and [avoid] duplicating investments, which brings commercial sustainability and resilience for health systems.”

Nakorn Premsri, the director of NVI, added that the investment model will help “build a more sustainable and resilient regional vaccine ecosystem, to meet both routine needs and the demands of health emergencies”.

News.title: Bank tax would raise mortgage costs, warns UBS
News.content:
Bank stocks have fallen on fears that John Healey will launch a tax raid on the sector in the Budget.

NatWest and Lloyds Banking Group shares were both down more than 2pc in early trading on the London Stock Exchange as investors responded to news the Chancellor is poised to raise taxes on the industry.

The banking sector has come into Mr Healey’s focus after their earnings were boosted by higher interest rates caused by the Iran war.

He is understood to be planning to target lenders despite praising banks at an International Monetary Fund (IMF) event in Bangkok on Thursday.

He said: “They’re a big contributor to the economy.

“They’re an important part of our business. They’re a part of the jewel, if you like, in the British economic crown.” Here is what you need to know.

Asian shares mostly rose a day after a tech sell-off dragged stocks lower.

South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index jumped 3.6pc, after tumbling 7.6pc on Thursday. Samsung Electronics was up 4.2pc, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix added 3.5pc.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 1.9pc to 65,658.59, after falling 4.9pc a day earlier. OpenAI investor SoftBank climbed 1.7pc. Chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron was 2.8pc higher and memory chipmaker Kioxia advanced 3.2pc.

The Asian technology stocks traded higher after losses in AI shares moderated in the US.

Kevin Warsh, the chairman of the US Federal Reserve, said Friday at the IMF and World Bank gathering in ⁠Bangkok that AI could bring about positive impacts to global economies.

He said: “I’d say, the advent of this new technology is probably the most consequential change to the U.S. and the global economy in my lifetime.

“There really is, I think, a huge benefit to the global economy, the US economy, over the horizon.”

Taiwan’s Taiex, which also benefited from the AI frenzy, was up 0.6pc. But shares of TSMC, or Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, were 0.4pc lower even as it posted record quarterly profits on Thursday and said AI demand remained very strong.

In Indonesia, the Jakarta Composite index fell more than 10pc, the lowest in years, after MSCI said Indonesia’s continued classification as an emerging market would be “no longer appropriate.”

News.title: Are my smart home devices always watching me? How to stay safe (and private) in a connected house
News.content:
The past decade has seen a huge rise in the number of smart devices in the home, from video doorbells to robot vacuum cleaners.

Smart connectivity offers many useful upsides, from letting us keep an eye on package deliveries to streamlining household chores. However, concerns remain about whether these devices are safe from hackers and how they might impinge on our privacy.

As a technology journalist for almost 20 years, I have reviewed many smart appliances and have lots of connected devices in my own home, so I’m an experienced user. To find out more about their potential downsides, and how to keep yourself protected, I’ve also spoken to an expert from cybersecurity firm Kaspersky, a board member at the Connected Standards Alliance (CSA) – which promotes openness and safety within smart-device networks – as well as other leading brands in the space.

What is a smart appliance?

A smart appliance connects to your home network, often via Wi-Fi, to allow for a wider range of interactions. That might be a washing machine that notifies you when it’s finished, or a fridge-freezer such as the Samsung Family Hub with a screen and voice controls.

But smart appliances don’t have to be huge: connected lightbulbs, baby monitors, smart plugs and more can all link up with your home network, in many cases integrating with voice assistants such as Amazon’s Alexa or Apple’s Siri.

News.title: Pierre Sage’s Lyon return ends in disappointment for Crystal Palace
News.content:
Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of Thursday night’s European football with Crystal Palace, Sunderland and Bournemouth in Europa League action, and Brighton hosting Kauno Zalgiris in the Uefa Conference League.

Palace manager Pierre Sage managed Lyon between November 2023 and January 2025, and another sub-plot is American businessman John Textor’s involvement with the French club. The former Palace shareholder was the reason the club missed out on Europa League participation last season because Lyon were in the same competition and thus Palace were considered in breach of multi-club ownership rules. Textor sold his stake in Palace, but despite the club’s best efforts they had to settle for the Conference League, a competition they subsequently won.

Palace could have been three or four down against Nottingham Forest at the weekend but fought back for a much-needed Premier League victory. They made a winning start in Europe, beating Lech Poznan 4-0 at Selhurst Park in their opening Europa League game.

Bournemouth and Sunderland also made winning starts, despite both teams’ poor form domestically. Sunderland travel to Portuguese side Torreense, while Sturm Graz are the opposition for Bournemouth’s first ever European game at the Vitality Stadium (or Dean Court if you prefer). Bournemouth continue to be without Justin Kluivert, Eli Junior Kroupi and Alex Scott because of injury.

Brighton are favourites to win the Conference League and play their first game in the competition against Lithuanian club Kauno Zalgiris. Lifting the trophy in Istanbul at the end of the season would assure Brighton of a place in next season’s Europa League, though given their Premier League form and Manchester City’s predicament, Champions League qualification could be a realistic aspiration. Brighton won with 10 men at Sunderland on Saturday, and were successful in their appeal against Pascal Struijk’s red card.

Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: Economy slows before Healey’s maiden Budget
News.content:
The Chancellor said banks are too often seen as “distant financial institutions”, in a sign he will not raise taxes on the industry in the Budget.

John Healey has faced pressure to impose a windfall tax on bank profits to help rebuild an expected decline in his wiggle room in the public finances.

John Healey said: “My observations on the banks are just that people too often see them as a big distant financial institutions when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects.

“That said, you know I’ve got decisions to take in the Budget, and I will. I’ll set those out in two weeks’ time.

“And my special responsibility as Chancellor is to protect the resilience of the British economy for the future. That the resilience that the IMF has reported on this week by upgrading our growth figures in the UK this week, that the welcome monthly growth figures published this morning reinforce, and importantly, alongside that, the IMF reports said that Britain stands out for our deficit reduction plans, and will have his forecast actually a reflection not just on forecast plans but performance over the last couple of years. You know, a consolidation plan in place and underway.

“I’ve said from day one and week one, and I’ve had Andy Burnham in lockstep alongside me, I will meet those fiscal rules in full.

“That will be part of the Budget that I set out in two weeks’ time, and I think the IMF report reinforces that that is not just a not just a reinforcing the strength of Britain’s position, but something that they say they want to see other countries doing as well.”
