Jose, from the USA, is a fan not just of the racing but also of the strategy, technology and teamwork behind F1. He visited his home race in Las Vegas last year and said: “Travelling to every race in the 2027 would honestly be a dream come true.”

Singapore GP Photo by: Colin McMaster / LAT Images via Getty Images

Picking a winner

The opportunity to travel to every grand prix opens up unprecedented access to the sport and its fans. The current ticket holder Burgess has shown just how to get the best out of the experience this season and he was on the judging panel that picked the shortlist.

Speaking before the competition began, he said: “The key thing I'll be looking for is the passion for F1, because you have to be a true fan to make the most of this opportunity. It’s going to be hard to give it up and there’s quite a lot of pressure choosing who’s next.”

The competition was open to fans aged 25 or over, with entrants asked to name their favourite team and driver and select who they would take to a future race from a list of options provided by F1 and Heineken.

Fifty entrants were then selected at random and invited to submit a 90-second video on why they should become the next ticket holder – and the final six videos are now available to watch, so fans can determine who should win the adventure of a lifetime.

Meet the final six and decide who you would like to see crowned the 2027 Heineken F1 Season Ticket holder - click here!

Sports.title: Camara over Ocon - did Haas make the correct call for F1 2027?
Sports.content:
Rafael Camara has been announced as a Formula 1 driver for the 2027 season and he will serve as Esteban Ocon’s replacement at Haas.

It will see the 21-year-old Brazilian make his F1 debut after such a rapid rise through the junior formulae.

Camara won the 2024 Formula Regional European Championship and the 2025 Formula 3 title, following that up by currently leading the Formula 2 standings by seven points.

But he is still such a raw talent as opposed to the experience and race-winning know-how of Ocon, who has endured a tough time since joining Haas at the start of 2025.

So has the American outfit made the right move? Our writers have their say.

Raw speed makes Camara a great pick

Rafael Camara, Invicta Racing Photo by: Dom Gibbons / Formula 1 via Getty Images

As the saying goes, you can make a quick driver reliable, but you can’t make a reliable driver quick.

Camara is one of the fastest drivers from the past decade in junior formulae; his qualifying record speaks for him. He took seven poles, more than anyone, on his way to the 2024 Formula Regional European Championship title; his 2025 F3 record was five poles out of nine, which is unprecedented in the current era. You’d have to go back to Luca Ghiotto’s identical feat, in the 2015 GP3 season, to find similar performance. And yet, in perhaps the most competitive title fight ever at that level, Ghiotto had narrowly lost out to Ocon in the title race.

Fast-forward 11 years, and Ocon is losing his Haas seat to Camara. Are the Frenchman’s results this season representative of his actual performance? Probably not, with the VF-26’s infamous inconsistency issue plaguing him for a long time. But it perhaps took a toll on the atmosphere within the team as frustration grew, and in that case, making a change made sense – especially with someone like Camara available.

The Brazilian has it all: backing from Haas supplier Ferrari – just like expected future Haas team-mate Oliver Bearman – obvious pace and potential back-to-back titles in FREC, F3 and F2. The Invicta racer currently leads the standings in F1’s feeder series, with five pole positions out of 13. Nobody else has taken more than two.

Of course, there have been mistakes, like his lock-up into retirement as he fought title rival Nikola Tsolov for victory in Monaco, but Camara has still taken consistent points finishes and commanding feature race wins.

Haas will miss Ocon’s experience, but Bearman can grow into the team leader role, and the decision makes sense to prepare for the future.

- Ben Vinel

Why remove a grand prix winner for a rookie?

Ocon after winning the 2021 Hungarian GP Photo by: Dan Istitene / Getty Images

Ocon was quite frank about it: he doesn't deserve this shit, he said, to be precise. And to be just as frank, I see no reason to disagree with him.

Yes, the numbers usually don't lie. And Ocon, despite being the more experienced driver, with every right to be considered a team leader, has scored fewer points so far than Bearman.

But is that really a case of him underdelivering?

Ayao Komatsu has admitted there have been issues with the car's inconsistency, and if you believe Ocon, he's only had a handful of races in which he's been able to have a proper go at it. And the last few rounds certainly suggest that, even if he's not better than Bearman, he's at least on a par with him.

Throughout its history, Haas has benefited greatly from having drivers with a wealth of experience. The likes of Romain Grosjean and Kevin Magnussen helped develop it into a credible team – and it has also failed spectacularly with rookies in the past. The choice to go with Mick Schumacher and Nikita Mazepin back in the day was a matter of survival, given the financial backing both brought. But does Haas really need to go for a rookie driver now? There's no reason to believe so.

So it appears that the Brazilian has been chosen by Haas on sporting grounds, but I can't see how he can be better right now than a proven race winner. Unless there's simply too much pressure from Ferrari to take on another junior from its Academy, I can't see Camara scoring more points for the team straight away than Ocon, with all his experience.

Ocon is still fast and reliable when the car works as it should. So why make the change? Especially if it's for another driver who can be taken away whenever Ferrari needs him.

How can you build your future around drivers who are basically on loan from a bigger team? I thought the Ocon and Bearman combination made perfect sense in that regard, as the Frenchman was the team's own driver. Now Haas gives more of an impression of becoming a Ferrari junior team rather than an independent outfit.

All of that, of course, becomes irrelevant if Komatsu has seen something absolutely special from Camara during these TPC tests – and given how Bearman has turned out, you'd argue Ayao knows what he's doing.

But still, there's a feeling that Ocon has been hard done by the team – which has almost used its underperforming car as an excuse to get rid of him.

- Oleg Karpov

This is the chance for Haas to sign a potential generational talent

Rafael Camara, Invicta Racing Photo by: Dom Gibbons / Formula 1 via Getty Images

Over recent rounds it’s been hard to feel anything but sympathy for Ocon, watching him deliver such outlandish statements in a clear desperate plea to stay on the grid. Would he have been saying such things if he weren’t up against it? No. It was clearly a tactic from him to remind people of what he’s done in the past, knowing the jury was very much out.

But like it or not, a lot of what he said was actually true. Ocon did cap off a solid junior career by winning GP3 - beating Max Verstappen in European F3 in the process - and more than held his own for a decade in F1.

His very impressive first full season in 2017 mustn’t be forgotten, scoring points in every round bar two for Force India, nor should the fact that he came very close to a career-changing move to Mercedes during its dominant years. There’s also his win at Hungary, 2021, as well as the fact that he’s one of only two drivers - Jenson Button the other - to outscore Fernando Alonso in a season as team-mates - 92 to 81 in 2022.

It is hoped that the above facts are what Ocon will be remembered for, and not his two seasons with Haas. Similarly, Daniel Ricciardo should mostly be remembered for everything but his decline at the end.

Yet there is another fact - or opinion - that mustn’t be ignored: it is time for Ocon to leave. Although results have improved of late, how much of that is down to the 30-year-old knowing he has a point to prove and a job on the line? Haas just isn’t going to get much better with the Frenchman behind the wheel, but it just might with such an exciting youngster in Camara.

Oleg talks about age and experience, but the 2026 champion-in-waiting - Kimi Antonelli - started the season as a teenager. So is that really as important in this day and age? Camara is also the same age as Bearman, and his junior record speaks for itself.

If he becomes F2 champion, he will join Charles Leclerc, George Russell, Oscar Piastri and fellow Brazilian Gabriel Bortoleto to win that and F3 as rookies. Camara will also become the only driver to win those two and FREC in consecutive seasons.

These are all the statistics of a future frontrunner and when one considers the 21-year-old’s speed as outlined by Ben, he is already F1-level. There’s no reason to believe he won’t be fighting for wins and titles in 10 years time. A chance for Haas to sign such a driver may not arise again, so this is an opportunity it must pounce on, and fair play for doing so.

- Ed Hardy

Sports.title: Camara to make F1 debut as Ocon's replacement at Haas in 2027
Sports.content:
Formula 2 championship leader Rafael Camara will make his Formula 1 debut for Haas in 2027 and is expected to line up alongside Oliver Bearman.

The 21-year-old Brazilian is replacing Esteban Ocon who will leave the American outfit at the end of 2026 after two disappointing seasons, his departure being confirmed on 30 September.

Camara has enjoyed a rapid rise through the junior ranks by winning the 2024 Formula Regional European Championship title and 2025 F3 crown, both done in dominant fashion.

So if he clinches the F2 championship for Invicta - he currently leads Nikola Tsolov by seven points - he will become the only driver to have won FRECA, F3 and F2 in consecutive seasons.

“I’m very happy to be joining TGR Haas F1 Team as a Formula 1 driver,” said Camara, who has signed a “multi-year” deal.

“It’s an important step in my career and I want to thank Gene Haas and Ayao Komatsu for the trust they have placed in me.

Oliver Bearman, Haas F1 Team, Esteban Ocon, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Mark Thompson / Getty Images

“I’m also very grateful to the Scuderia Ferrari Driver Academy for their support and for everything they have contributed to my development over the years, as well as to my family for always being there throughout this journey.

“Now my focus is on preparing myself in the best possible way for this new challenge. There will be a lot to learn, and I’m looking forward to working closely with the team, understanding the car and continuing to develop as a driver.”

Although Haas took its time in confirming this decision, it was entirely expected that Camara would be given the seat and triumph over the likes of reigning F2 champion Leonardo Fornaroli and reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa.

All three have taken part in TPC (Testing of Previous Cars) programmes for Haas, the most notable being a three-day test at Portimao in August as part of a plan to evaluate all candidates.

What also would have helped Camara's cause is him being a Ferrari academy graduate - like Bearman - and the Scuderia has a strong relationship with Haas, selling it many car parts like the power unit.

Team boss Ayao Komatsu said: “I’m really excited to sign such a young, amazing talent like Rafael Camara.

Ayao Komatsu, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

“I don’t need to tell everyone about his achievements in the junior formulas, it’s been very impressive, and in his rookie season in Formula 2, the speed he’s shown in some very difficult moments, like qualifying in Monaco and Montreal – that all goes to show the potential Rafa has.

“He showed when we had him drive in our TPC programme in Portugal that he could handle himself very well with not a huge amount of time to learn the car, he showed us more than just raw speed.

“Rafa managed to create an environment to get the best out of himself, it was very impressive and certainly the laps he completed were special.

“We’re all excited about this opportunity and really committed as TGR Haas F1 Team to nurture this talent and provide a place where he can flourish.

“We want to create an environment where he’s comfortable and supported, where he can really excel in his capabilities.”

This news means there are now just three seats theoretically left available for 2027, two coming at Racing Bulls, but it is expected to retain Liam Lawson and impressive rookie Arvid Lindblad.

The other is the seat alongside Camara, though it is an open secret that that’ll be taken up by Bearman, 21, who has highly impressed since joining as a rookie last year.

Sports.title: Mekies extends contract as Red Bull's F1 team boss
Sports.content:
Laurent Mekies has extended his contract as team principal of the Red Bull Formula 1 outfit with a new deal that takes him through until the end of 2031.

That will see the Frenchman spend at least six seasons leading the Austrian outfit after joining in July 2025 to end Christian Horner’s 20-year tenure as Red Bull team boss.

Mekies joined from sister squad Racing Bulls, who the 49-year-old took over at the start of the 2024 campaign following six years at Ferrari - first as sporting director and then racing director.

“I am incredibly proud to continue this journey with Oracle Red Bull Racing,” said Mekies.

“I would like to thank Chalerm [Yoovidhya, shareholder], Mark [Mateschitz, shareholder], and Oliver [Mintzlaff, CEO], the entire team and everyone involved for the trust they have placed in the project.

“What makes this team special is the way everyone comes together in pursuit of the same goal, and I feel privileged to work alongside such a talented and committed group every day.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, Laurent Mekies, Red Bull Racing Team Principal Photo by: Joe Portlock / Getty Images

“Together, with Pierre Wache’s and Ben Hodgkinson’s teams playing a central role in shaping our future, we have a strong platform for the years ahead.

“We genuinely believe this is only the beginning. As we look ahead, we will continue to embrace the principles that define us: being free in our thinking, fast in our actions and bold in our decisions.”

This news comes at a good time for Red Bull as it has responded to its slow start to the 2026 regulation change by fitting continuous car upgrades, leading to a late resurgence.

World champion Max Verstappen has won the last two grands prix - Malaysia and Singapore - from pole, with Red Bull now only seven points off third-placed McLaren with six rounds left.

Verstappen also recently tied his future to Red Bull in August by signing a new deal through to the end of 2030, extending on his original deal that was set to expire in 2028.

That put an end to any mounting speculation over his future and in 2027 the Dutchman will partner impressive sophomore Isack Hadjar, who was confirmed last month.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Mark Sutton / Formula 1 via Getty Images

“Laurent has demonstrated outstanding leadership since returning to the Red Bull family,” said Mintzlaff.

“He combines technical expertise, strategic thinking, and a deep understanding of what makes our team successful.

“Just as importantly, he embodies the values and mentality that define the Red Bull way: courage, teamwork, determination, and an unrelenting desire to compete at the highest level.

“Continuity in leadership is a key ingredient for sustained success, and we are delighted that Laurent will continue to lead the team through the next chapter of our journey.”

Sports.title: Five key takeaways from F1's big African Grand Prix reveal in Rwanda
Sports.content:
Tuesday's launch of the new African Grand Prix at Kigali's BK Arena in Rwanda was attended by Rwandan president Paul Kagame and both F1 boss Stefano Domenicali and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.

But following the official presentation, several key questions were still outstanding and Autosport has now heard from the key people behind the race to fill in some of those blanks.

When will Rwanda actually join?

Rwanda will officially join in the "early 2030s", leaving the door open for plenty of wiggle room to actually join the calendar. It is quite curious for a new race to be officially announced in 2026 without a clear entry point, especially when the earliest possible date is four years into the future.

But the reality is that the project hinges on a number of critical infrastructure projects to get done. The big ticket item is the brand-new Bugesera international airport, which is currently just a runway with a concrete apron while early work has started on the terminal building. The airport isn't due to open until the second half of 2028.

Then there is the ambitious 6km track itself, which runs south of the future airport up and down two steep hills and alongside a lake. The circuit design itself is finished, with the project handled by Tilke Engineering & Architects, engineering consultancy DAR and Wurz Design now entering the engineering phase, and the Rwandan government will also have to figure out how to get 100,000 fans in and out of the track smoothly.

While there is every chance of racing there by 2030, by not pinning an exact entry point on Rwanda, the local authorities have less pressure and more time to complete all the required works on time and to the right standard. With Kigali set to become F1's anchor point in Africa for at least a decade, the sport is keen for the race to be executed as well as possible, rather than as early as possible.

Rwanda African GP Photo by: Formula 1

"There aren't really limiting factors other than key milestones that we keep in mind," Jean-Guy Afrika, CEO of the Rwandan Development Board, said when asked about the flexible start date. "One of the major ones is the completion of the international airport which is set to be completed in early 2028. The other one was more to retain the flexibility to finalise what must be done in relation to the racetrack, before a final decision is made on where we would fit exactly on the calendar. That decision is driven and coordinated by F1, but it is a decision that we prefer to postpone to the future."

At the same time, after over three years of talks and planning it was still important to make a public announcement well ahead of time to get the project out of the conceptual stage and into something that will actually happen. "We needed this moment, because we were in a sort of chicken-and-egg moment," said F1 CEO and president Stefano Domenicali.

"We're talking, having everything almost ready, and I said: 'Listen, if we don't start, we're [not] going to get it [done]."

Why is it called the Africa Grand Prix and not the Rwandan Grand Prix?

Curiously, the race isn't named after its host country or city but after the entire continent, which organisers say is a gesture of goodwill towards Africa as a whole.

"Rwanda has always been a champion of regional integration," said Afrika. "We are a member of the East African Community, of the Common Market for Eastern Africa. We abolished visas on arrival for Africans. So, it's really part of that spirit to bring the sport to the continent.

"We want to make it bigger than just Rwanda. We want to make it the moment when the sport came back to Africa and then never left. So that's why we felt that calling it Kigali Grand Prix or Rwanda Grand Prix would have felt slightly exclusive. It's much easier if you call it an African Grand Prix to approach partners in this wider effort."

Afrika also believed Rwanda would open the floodgates for more races on the continent. "We foresee a future where we look back at this moment and we see a critical juncture from where multiple races eventually end up happening in Africa. You've already seen that the interest [in Africa] was very high. We weren't the only ones bidding, and we expect that after the first race, there probably would be many more races."

What kind of circuit will Rwanda get, and will it be good for overtaking?

Rwanda F1 track for African GP Photo by: Formula 1

The Rwanda Motodrome is a permanent, purpose-built facility, rather than a street or urban track. The 6km, 17-corner layout is built from the ground up to make full use of the natural features of the Bugesera site, especially the two hills the circuit will be going up and down. The total elevation change per lap is 197m, which is almost twice as much as the current number one - Spa Francorchamps (102).

As well as fast and flowing corners that will get the drivers excited, there's also a 1km back straight followed by a hairpin to promote overtaking. TILKE managing director Carsten Tilke said the site chosen for the venue was a "dream location" because the undulating topography did a lot of the heavy lifting to come up with a challenging circuit as well as an arena-like vistas for fans.

"When we design a racetrack, of course we need to always work with the site we have," Tilke said. "We were very, very lucky because it's a very hilly topography. We have a lake. We have everything you dream of when you design a track. This also gives the character of the track; very flowing, very fast. It's really shaped by the natural features and beauty of the site. And this is why we also have a lot of elevation changes. It's really is a roller coaster track with a lot of banking. It goes up and down 12% to 13%."

Wurz is perhaps in a slightly awkward position as he is also the chairman of the F1 drivers association GPDA, so there is no place to hide for him if the track isn't a big hit. But when asked about his design, the former F1 driver was bullish about its potential to be both beloved by the drivers, by the spectators and by fans watching on TV because of the overtaking opportunities baked into the design. And he revealed several current drivers and FIA world champions had already tried his design in the simulator.

"The circuit is not designed for specific rules or categories, so you will see some corner combinations, which work perfect for touring cars, for motorbikes, where you can have really sneak attacks, or if you are up on your tyre degradation and you can stay very close, even on downforce [heavy] cars, whether that's World Endurance Championship cars or Formula 1 cars.

"We will have long straights, the hairpins and all the attack corners within the simulator. We are playing heavily with slight camber changes at times where you have degradation on the front or the rear, we consider what tyre temperatures are coming into the tyres on certain corners, so that the defending driver actually is at a disadvantage for the next long straight.

"There's a lot of science as well as knowledge from the years of driving and designing tracks going in, and I hope that this circuit is the cherry on the cake on everyone's list. More than a dozen FIA World Championship titles eyes have seen the circuit, have seen the onboard videos, and I think everyone is sharing great excitement."

What does F1 get out of Rwanda?

Stefano Domenicali at African GP announcement in Rwanda Photo by: Filip Cleeren

Domenicali called Tuesday's announcement "one of the most significant days in the history of Formula 1." Even for a man who generally embraces hyperbole, that's quite a statement to make. But it's true that finally breaking into the African market could well be one of Domenicali's biggest achievements when everything is said and done.

F1 hasn't been back to the African continent since leaving South Africa after 1993, and given the impressive list of requirements for a Liberty Media era grand prix, for the longest time it has felt like it just couldn't be done.

But as pointed out by Lewis Hamilton, who was praised by Rwandan sports minister Nelly Mukazayire as a "very strong voice about F1 in Africa", F1 can't call itself a truly global championship without setting foot on African soil. The hope is that Liberty Media has now found the right, credible and stable partner to do so, one that doesn't underestimate the huge workload ahead.

Domenicali claimed Africa's rapidly growing market "is home to more than 100 million fans of Formula 1", who will now get to watch a race on their own continent.

What does Rwanda get out of F1?

Attracting the latest high-profile sporting property has landed Rwanda fresh accusations by Amnesty International of using F1 for sportswashing, drawing attention away from significant human rights issues.

Domenicali, however, called Rwanda "one of the world's great success stories" and "a nation of extraordinary natural beauty and stunning landscapes, combined with resilience and courage to overcome and be reborn from challenges of its past", referencing the devastating 1994 genocide. F1 maintains that sport can be a positive force for good.

Long-time president Paul Kagame explained hosting elite level sports on home soil was a first step towards reversing the one-way traffic of Africa delivering some of the biggest global stars in football, basketball, athletics and other sports, but not getting any economic benefit from them.

"For decades, African athletes have been a pillar of the global sports economy, adding significant commercial value to top leagues, with the continent receiving almost nothing in return. Partnerships like the one we are building help break this cycle because they serve as a catalyst for sports infrastructure development. This is not just about building venues. It's about creating a sustainable economic model where different revenue streams across hospitality, tourism, and entertainment are generated and anchored into local communities. Sports is a great equaliser, but we have to be intentional about delivering this promise."

F1 also offers the next step in Rwanda's development as a tourist destination and business hub, fresh off hosting the 2025 road cycling world championships. Unlike that one-off event, Rwanda has signed up for a 10-year period which gives it time to write off investment, which is said to be an undisclosed mixture of public and private investment.

"I think it's critical to highlight that F1 is part of a much bigger picture and long-term strategy to position Rwanda as a hub for tourism investment and services," Afrika said. "F1 was a natural continuation of this effort. The track will have a capacity of around 100,000 spectators. Over a weekend, we're talking close to 300,000 people consuming everything from retail products, restaurants, hotels, accommodation infrastructure. Massive demand that generates growth for our existing businesses. And that means more in terms of what we can collect in terms of sales taxes, increases in corporate income taxes, and so on. We also anticipate an increase in terms of investment in new businesses and that means more jobs and so on."

The Rwanda Development Board is keen to make the venue a multipurpose facility that can be used year-round for events like concerts and conferences, with a karting track, off-road facility and handling track also built in to further boost grassroots motorsports. After launching the FIA cross car at the FIA General Assemblies in Kigali two years ago, FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem vowed the governing body would step up efforts to support karting in the country.

"The arrival of Formula 1 in Rwanda will send a very powerful message to young people across the continent. It will tell them that the highest levels of international motorsport are within their reach, that Africa can not only participate in the future of our sport but help shape it," Ben Sulayem said.

Sports.title: Why McLaren cannot fix its F1 car handling until 2027
Sports.content:
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella has conceded it cannot improve its Formula 1 car handling characteristics ‘without fundamental changes’ that will not be possible until 2027.

While every F1 driver has needed to adapt to the new generation of cars and engines in order to extract the maximum performance, often applying unnatural or unusual techniques never used in their entire careers, McLaren has also been battling a car handling issue in greater depth all season.

As Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri have attempted to adapt their driving styles to suit the V6 turbo hybrids with the increased electrical power elements from this year, the added complication of car handling has hamstrung the team’s overall progress relative to its frontrunning rivals.

A problem that has seemingly struck Piastri harder than his team-mate due to their different natural driving styles, it is a matter the team cannot fully solve until it can make major technical changes with an all-new car in 2027.

Stella explained: “I don't expect that what's coming to the car will improve this characteristic. I think we need something more fundamental than simply adding some downforce to the car like it's happening in the coming races.

“Without fundamentally changing some further aspect which we are addressing longer term and at the earliest I would say with the MCL41 for 2027.”

Oscar Piastri, McLaren Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

After the Singapore Grand Prix Norris went into detail on the subject, explaining he needs to “force” his McLaren F1 car into what he wants it to do rather than finding a balance he is comfortable with.

“It's [the car] just on a knife edge on every single corner,” Norris said. “You've just got to drive it within an exact percent, and you have to force the car in every single way. You can't let the car do any work. You can't just let the front do the work, or the rear do the work. You have to force the front; you've got to force the rear.

“You've got to drive it in a way that takes so much concentration and so much ability. It's just full-on and mentally draining because of how hard you have to work behind the wheels.

“It's just too difficult and it makes it impossible to put laps together in qualifying, which just shows how good of a job we were able to do when we were getting on pole and things like that and how rewarding that felt.

“We haven't been quick enough now, it's just too difficult and you can't do anything magical because you're simply not quick enough. You have to force the car, and you can't let the car do any work because it doesn't do it on its own. And that's not what you want from a car at all.”

This driving “intensity” is a feature Stella believes has been a part of McLaren’s F1 car all season which Norris and Piastri have needed to adapt to and something the Australian’s natural smoother and gentler inputs found harder to get to grips with.

Oscar Piastri, McLaren Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

“The fact that the car needs quite a lot of effort to deliver lap time, and it requires a level of intensity in the driving input, which is much superior to last year, this is something that took some time for the drivers to understand,” he explained.

“And it's also one of the reasons why Oscar, at some stage, he almost lost like some of the competitiveness compared to Lando. And we were here discussing, what is happening with Oscar? And I've always said that that was a technical matter. Oscar just needed to understand how to force the car to do some things and sort of abandon the fact that driving fast will not necessarily mean driving clean if that makes sense.

“Which was the signature of Oscar when we have seen him fast in the past. He was like... He was clean, he was really good [with the] data to see he was very repeatable and he was fast. With this car, all these things together they don't seem to happen very often so it's a lot of work for the drivers.”

Sports.title: F1 signs historic 10-year Rwanda deal to host African Grand Prix
Sports.content:
The government of Rwanda and Formula 1 have announced a 10-year deal for a new African Grand Prix in capital Kigali, which will first be held in 2030 at the earliest.

F1 will head to a yet-to-be-built natural road course 40km south of Kigali, next to the Rwandan capital's under-construction Bugesera international airport. The first edition of the race, which is officially billed as 'Formula 1 African Grand Prix, presented by Visit Rwanda', could be held as early as 2030, depending on when construction of the track is completed.

Regardless of the start date, the deal is billed as a 10-year agreement which will see F1 head back to the African continent for the first time since the 1993 South African Grand Prix.

The deal was announced on Tuesday at a press conference in Kigali attended by Rwandan president Paul Kagame, F1 CEO and president Stefano Domenicali and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.

The Bugesera track, the result of a cooperation between Tilke Engineering & Architects, former F1 driver Alex Wurz and his design company WurzDesign, and engineering consultancy DAR, will make full use of the natural terrain, creating a natural arena for fans to watch cars tackle the 6km, 17-corner anti-clockwise challenge - with no less than a 197m change in elevation per lap. It is part of a wider investment plan by the Rwandan Development Board in tourism, infrastructure and commercial development.

Damon Hill, Williams FW15C, leads Alessandro Zanardi, Lotus 107B, Rubens Barrichello, Jordan 193, and Ivan Capelli, Jordan 193 Photo by: Motorsport Images

"Today belongs to Africa. For more than three decades, the world's premier motorsport championship has raced without this continent, and that changes with this agreement," said president Kagame. "Rwanda is proud to host the Formula 1 African Grand Prix, and to share this moment with more than 100 million fans across Africa, many of them young people who deserve to see the sport at home and to see themselves in it: as engineers, technicians, entrepreneurs and, one day, drivers.

"This 10-year partnership is also an investment in Rwanda's future. The circuit in Bugesera, alongside the new international airport, will bring jobs, skills, tourism and new business to our country and our region for decades to come, because our aim was never a single race weekend, but a lasting benefit for our people."

Domenicali said: "Today is a landmark moment for Formula 1. With Rwanda joining the calendar from the next decade, our sport will race in every inhabited continent, bringing the World Championship closer than ever to fans around the globe. Africa has always been part of Formula 1's future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact.

"This is about much more than hosting a Grand Prix. Together, we can create lasting economic and social benefits through tourism, investment, skills development and local business growth, ensuring the positive impact of this event is felt for generations. For our fans, this is an especially exciting moment. Africa is home to more than 100 million Formula 1 fans, and that number continues to grow rapidly."

FIA president Ben Sulayem added: "The return of the FIA Formula One World Championship to Africa is a historic moment for our sport and an important step in the continued global growth of motorsport. Rwanda has demonstrated a strong commitment to delivering a world-class event, and the FIA will work closely with FOM and our partners as this new circuit is developed to the highest international standards."

Stefano Domenicali at African GP announcement in Rwanda Photo by: Filip Cleeren

Talks between F1 and Rwanda over a race accelerated in 2024, with the central African nation keen to attract major sporting events to boost tourism and business. Last year Kigali hosted the UCI Road World Championships in cycling, and in 2024 it hosted the FIA's annual Prize Giving Ceremony, with Max Verstappen among the FIA world champions travelling to the country to collect his fourth F1 world title trophy.

Seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton has been a long-time proponent of an F1 return to the African continent. "For the past six years I've been fighting in the background to get a grand prix," he said earlier this year. "So, sitting with the stakeholders and asking them the question, why are we not in Africa? We're on every other continent, why not Africa? I know they're really trying.

"The ones that I've enjoyed the most so far [were] Kenya, and Rwanda was particularly spectacular - two places I felt like I could live. And South Africa. I think those are the ones that I think would be good places for us to potentially go to."

Sports.title: Singapore victory leaves Verstappen one win away from a full set – but not for long | 2026 Singapore Grand Prix stats and facts
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen’s 73rd career victory was surely one of the most overdue of his career. At his 10th attempt, the Red Bull driver finally won the Singapore Grand Prix.

He’d come close several times before. Verstappen had started second four times and converted three of those into second-place finishes. On the other occasion he was wiped out by the Ferrari drivers as they sprinted to turn one.

But after finally claiming his first pole position at the Marina Bay circuit, Verstappen never let go of his advantage, leading every lap of the race. However with other drivers switching to the preferred soft tyres over the final stint, Verstappen did not set the fastest lap, so he did not collect his seventh ‘grand slam’.

He has now won at 27 different circuits, a feat only bettered by Lewis Hamilton on 31. Verstappen has won on every track on the calendar with a single exception: the Madring, which held its first grand prix this year.

However in order to complete a clean sweep of victories at every track on the calendar, Verstappen will have to win at three new rounds next year. Two venues where he has raced in F1, but not previously won at, will return on the 2027 F1 calendar.

What’s more, another driver will be in the same position as Verstappen. This is Hamilton, the last driver to have achieved a clean sweep:

Track Verstappen’s best result Hamilton’s best result Bahrain International Circuit 1st 1st Jeddah Corniche Circuit 1st 1st Albert Park 1st 1st Suzuka 1st 1st Shanghai International Circuit 1st 1st Miami International Autodrome 1st 6th Circuit Gilles Villeneuve 1st 1st Monaco 1st 1st Autodromo do Algarve 2nd 1st Silverstone 1st 1st Red Bull Ring 1st 1st Spa-Francorchamps 1st 1st Hungaroring 1st 1st Monza 1st 1st Madring 2nd DNF Baku City Circuit 1st 1st Istanbul Park 2nd 1st Singapore 1st 1st Circuit of the Americas 1st 1st Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez 1st 1st Interlagos 1st 1st Las Vegas Strip Circuit 1st 2nd Losail International Circuit 1st 1st Yas Marina 1st 1st

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Hamilton last achieved a clean sweep when he won the French Grand Prix in 2018. He kept up the achievement over the next two seasons – even as the Covid-19 pandemic added new races to the schedule in 2020 – but his run ended when he failed to win at Zandvoort in 2021.

Achieving a clean sweep next year would arguably be a greater feat for either driver. There were 21 circuits on the calendar when Hamilton achieved it in 2018, but there are 24 on next year’s schedule.

Verstappen became the fifth driver to achieve 50 pole positions last weekend. He did so in his 250th race start and joins Ayrton Senna, who took 108 races to do the same, Hamilton (168), Michael Schumacher (177) and Sebastian Vettel (196).

This was the fourth year in a row the Singapore Grand Prix has been won from pole position. Verstappen led every lap on his way to victory, which is the fourth ‘lights-to-flag’ victory at the circuit in the last five years, along with Sergio Perez’s win in 2022 (from second on the grid), Carlos Sainz Jnr’s in 2023 and Lando Norris’s from 2024.

Red Bull was only one win behind Mercedes when the season began. However Mercedes has enjoyed such a strong season that Red Bull’s victories in the last two rounds means its is now 10 behind. However Red Bull did end Mercedes’ streak of leading at least one lap in every race this year.

Racing Bulls reached 100 points, which is more than they scored last year and their best score since 2021, when they competed as AlphaTauri.

But Alpine’s season has decidedly hit the skids as they failed to score for the third round in a row. It was a particularly frustrating weekend for Pierre Gasly, who finished one place outside the points in both the sprint race and grand prix.

Williams left Singapore point-less, too. Carlos Sainz Jnr got his car into the top 10 early on in his 250th appearance in a grand prix weekend, but slipped to 14th at the flag.

Sports.title: On This Day: Stroll wins final race before becoming a Formula 1 driver | Brief
Sports.content:
10 years ago today Lance Stroll scored his most recent victory to date, in his final race before he became a Formula 1 driver.

Just two weeks shy of his 18th birthday, Stroll’s promotion to F1 with Williams the following year had already been announced. He had clinched the European Formula 3 championship earlier in the season and won both of the preceding two races in the season-ending triple-header at the Hockenheimring.

For his last race at Prema, Stroll lined up fourth on the grid behind Joel Eriksson, Jake Hughes and Callum Ilott. Stroll wasn’t the only future F1 driver on the grid: others included Nikita Mazepin (10th), Zhou Guanyu (13th) and George Russell (15th). Anthoine Hubert, who tragically died in a Formula 2 crash in 2019, lined up seventh.

Sports.title: F1 could make call to move finale to Imola as late as ‘mid-November’ – report | Briefs
Sports.content:
Formula 1 team bosses have said they want to know where the season finale will be held by mid-October.

The series intends to run its final two races as planned in Qatar and Abu Dhabi. However ongoing disruption caused by the US-Iran war has put that in doubt and led F1 to enlist the Imola circuit as a potential alternative venue for the final race.

A new report claims F1 could wait until the middle of November before deciding its plans for the final race of the season.

“There were also rumours in Malaysia and Singapore, where the sport has spent the last fortnight, that some sort of deal had been done between Qatar, the UAE and Iran to guarantee security, giving F1 increased confidence to press ahead,” adds the report in The Telegraph.

It comes after missile strikes hit an airport in nearby Saudi Arabia, whose world championship round was cancelled earlier this year. F1 is due to return to the country in March next year.

Sports.title: Official: Camara to make Formula 1 debut with Haas in 2027 | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Ferrari junior driver Rafael Camara will make his Formula 1 debut for Haas next season.

Haas, one of Ferrari’s customer teams, confirmed the 21-year-old will take the seat vacated by Esteban Ocon at the end of the year. He is expected to partner Oliver Bearman, another member of Ferrari’s driver academy, who has driven for Haas since last year.

Camara has enjoyed a stellar rise through the junior formula series since being picked up by Ferrari in 2022. He currently leads the Formula 2 championship standings, with no indication yet whether the final rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi will be able to go ahead.

Like fellow Brazilian Gabriel Bortoleto, Camara won the Formula 3 championship at his first attempt. He also won the Formula Regional European Championship the year before.

Camara has already experienced one of Haas’s Formula 1 chassis in a Test of Previous Cars at the Autodromo do Algarve, which will hold the Portuguese Grand Prix next year. He has also tested for Ferrari.

Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu said he is “really excited to sign such a young, amazing talent like Rafael Camara.”

“He showed when we had him drive in our TPC program in Portugal that he could handle himself very well with not a huge amount of time to learn the car,” Komatsu continued, “he showed us more than just raw speed. Rafa managed to create an environment to get the best out of himself, it was very impressive and certainly the laps he completed were special.”

Camara thanked Komatsu, Haas team owner Gene Haas and the Scuderia Ferrari Driver Academy for his chance to make his F1 debut.

Sports.title: Colapinto tells his supporters to stop abusing rival drivers: “They don’t help me” | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Franco Colapinto has urged his supporters to stop abusing his rivals and others involved in the series online.

“They are thinking that they are defending me, but they are doing the opposite,” Colapinto told his followers in a video posted on social media.

The FIA and Alpine issued statements in the last two months condemning the abuse which occured following the Dutch, Spanish and Azerbaijan grands prix. Neither specifically mentioned Colapinto’s supporters but both identified the victims of the abuse, including his team mate Pierre Gasly and FIA officials. “It has become a regular occurrence in recent races and cannot be condoned,” said Alpine in a statement last month.

Colapinto told his supporters the online abuse must stop.

“I know it makes you feel very proud when I do well, when I get points, me and the whole team, and I will always be very grateful for that,” he said. “But there are times when we end up attacking other pilots, other colleagues, my team mates, my mechanics, my engineers, people I work with day by day.

“I know they are thinking that they are defending me, but they are doing the opposite. They don’t help me. And I really want you to understand that this is what we have to change, all together.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“We have to try to improve as a society, and to help me have a better performance, to help get my dream and my results, that is, to score points, I need you to help stop this, all of us together.”

Colapinto made his F1 debut with Williams in the second half of 2024, but the team had no space for him in their line-up for the following season. He joined Alpine, who promoted him to a race seat in place of Jack Doohan early in the season. Doohan later revealed he received death threats from those who wanted him out of the car.

Alpine issued the first in a series of reactions to abuse from Colapinto’s supporters this year following the Chinese Grand Prix, when Esteban Ocon collided with him. Some Colapinto supporters also accused Alpine of sabotaging Colapinto and failing to provide him with the same equipment as Gasly.

Recent flashpoints included the penalties Colapinto received for failing to slow sufficiently for yellow flags at Zandvoort, Colapinto’s brief delay behind Gasly at the Madring and the collision between the Alpine drivers and Lando Norris in Baku.

Sports.title: Social Media: Mekies extends contract to lead Red Bull until 2031 | Brief
Sports.content:
Red Bull has given a vote of confidence in its team principal Laurent Mekies by extending his contract to run the team until 2031.

Mekies took over from Christian Horner in charge of the team last year. Horner had run Red Bull since it entered F1 in 2005.

Under Mekies, Red Bull rebounded from a poor start to last season. From over 100 points behind, Max Verstappen came within two points of retaining his drivers’ championship title in one of the closest ever finishes to a world championship.

This year, in the team’s first season with its own power units designed in conjunction with Ford, Red Bull has won the last two grands prix.

Strengthening our long-term platform for success 💪 We're delighted to announce that Laurent has signed a long-term contract extension with the Team, through 2031 👏#F1 #RedBullRacing pic.twitter.com/SvEXHqyMjs — Oracle Red Bull Racing (@redbullracing) October 14, 2026

Formula 1

Sports.title: Verstappen says Red Bull’s car was “scary” to drive early in 2026 | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Red Bull has made huge progress with a car which felt “scary” to drive early in the season, says Max Verstappen.

The four-times world champion has won the last two grands prix in a row and also took victory in the sprint race in Singapore last week. The team’s form has improved significantly since the beginning of the season, when Verstappen only reached the podium once in the first seven rounds.

Verstappen spun out of the British Grand Prix suffered costly spins in qualifying at the Red Bull Ring and Hungaroring as the team struggled to get on top of its car. However their most recent upgrades have transformed its performance.

“The car definitely felt a lot nicer from Baku onwards,” said Verstappen. “It’s just been a lot more balanced. Then naturally, of course, when you can compete a bit further up front without having too many issues with the car compared to the beginning of the year, where it was actually sometimes a bit scary to drive, that makes it a lot nicer.”

Verstappen finished a close second behind George Russell in Baku. He qualified only eighth but was in contention for pole position until his final lap was compromised by a yellow flag.

He has been undefeated since then and expects to remain competitive over the final rounds. “We’re not in a championship fight, and that’s why I think ’til the end we’ll just try to have a good time and try to add more podiums and hopefully a few wins.”

It is the second time in as many years that Red Bull has made a breakthrough with a troublesome car in the second half of a season. “Two completely different cars as well, with the regulations,” Verstappen noted. “Also two completely different problems.

“We had to find lap time. Plus, of course, also this year with the engine side of things, I think for everyone it’s been sometimes a bit complicated to get the most out of it.”

Red Bull needs to ensure they begin next year in better shape, said Verstappen.

“From race one to now, I think we’ve gained a lot of experience. Of course, we’re still not where we want to be, but I guess everyone will say the same thing.

“But we have learned so much and definitely also on the car side have fixed a lot of our weaknesses. We just need to keep improving, keep learning this year that so we can apply that also into next year.”

Sports.title: Spotlight: Cadillac already has better facilities than Mercedes, says Bottas | Brief
Sports.content:
Cadillac remain yet to score a point in their first season in Formula 1 but Valtteri Bottas says their progress is clear to see.

“We are definitely seeing an improvement somewhere every weekend,” he told the Financial Times. “It’s not necessarily in the results yet, but it’s in how we operate as a team in different areas.”

Bottas scored all 10 of his grand prix victories for Mercedes. He drove for the world champions between 2017 and 2021.

Cadillac is based partly at Silverstone, a short distance from Mercedes’ Brackley factory. Asked whether his new team’s facilities are better than the world champions’, Bottas replied: “I would say so.”

Formula 1

Sports.title: Liam Paro Calls Haney and Shakur Talks Embarrassing
Sports.content:
Liam Paro calls the Devin Haney–Shakur Stevenson negotiations “embarrassing,” and the months of public bargaining have made both fighters look bad without either taking a punch.

Each wants fans to believe the other is responsible for the fight failing to happen. Instead, their arguments over weight and rehydration conditions have given fans reasons to doubt how much risk either is willing to accept. Both have taken something resembling a defeat, except the damage is to their reputations rather than their records.

“These guys obviously don’t really want to fight each other,” Paro said. “There’s always some little problems that’s not making it happen. And in a way, it’s a bit embarrassing.”

The IBF welterweight champion understands the frustration firsthand after his own unification talks with Haney fell apart. Paro denied pricing himself out of that matchup, though he withheld specific numbers during the interview.

His critique also targeted Stevenson’s conditions for jumping up to 147 pounds. In Paro’s view, Stevenson should meet Haney at the standard welterweight limit without caveats.

“Shakur is a hell of a fighter. I’ve shared the ring with him,” Paro remarked. “He’s got all the tools to be victorious against Haney. But fight him at 147, then call yourself a true 147 champion.”

Haney claimed Stevenson tried inserting a 10-pound rehydration clause after both sides settled on a 145-pound catchweight, though Paro declined to quote an exact number.

Promoters observing this saga face an uncomfortable reality about future matchmaking. Name recognition sells tickets, yet getting marquee talent to sign contracts remains a major hurdle.

Winning social media debates does nothing positive for Haney or Stevenson. Prolonging this dispute simply makes it tougher for either champion to claim he wants the challenge.

The biggest problem for both Haney and Stevenson is that neither owns the kind of explosive, crowd-pleasing style that forgives this level of nonsense. When knockout artists or charismatic brawlers play hardball, fans usually grumble, pay the pay-per-view fee anyway, and tune in for the inevitable explosion. But Haney and Shakur are safety-first purists.

The public was already skeptical about whether their matchup would turn into a low-volume chess match of feints and clinches. Piling endless, petty negotiations on top of a fight style that already tests casual fan patience is box office suicide.

Instead of looking like hungry young champions chasing greatness, they managed to make Liam Paro look like the mature adult in the room. Paro called it what it is: embarrassing. If a fighter genuinely believes he is the pound-for-pound king, he steps in the ring and proves it, rather than whining on an app about rehydration terms after already getting a catchweight concession.

Even if they sign the contracts tomorrow, the energy is completely gone. The narrative will no longer be about which fighter establishes his legacy. The narrative will be that two over-entitled divas finally ran out of excuses because the public stopped caring about their tweets.

Sports.title: Sebastian Fundora Camp Tells Ennis “50-50 Deal or Nothing”
Sports.content:
Sebastian Fundora risks pricing himself out of an undisputed title clash against Jaron Ennis before talks even get underway, courtesy of promoter Sampson Lewkowicz demanding a 50-50 split right out of the gate.

That is a big ask against the unified junior middleweight champion. Ennis brings more titles, a strong Philadelphia following, and recognition as the division’s leading fighter. Fundora brings the WBC belt, but he hasn’t established the same commercial pull.

Lewkowicz openly admitted that hammering out a deal will take serious effort, assuming Fundora defeats Ermal Hadribeaj this weekend.

“It will not be an easy negotiation,” Lewkowicz said to Sean Zitttel, expecting Ennis to seek the lion’s share. “It’ll be 50-50 or nothing.”

Ennis and promoter Eddie Hearn have zero reason to entertain that stance. Boots would surrender clear market value just to pick up the remaining hardware, giving Fundora parity he has not earned at the box office.

Fundora struck a far more reasonable tone about finding common ground.

“Of course, there’s going to be some sacrifices from both sides, but we’re going to get it done,” Fundora stated. “I tell Sampson, ‘Hey, I’m going to fight this guy.’ Sampson will do it for me.”

Demanding half the pie before serious conversations start feels like an attempt to either secure an oversized payday before Fundora takes a bad beating, or build a convenient excuse to walk away and face lower-risk opposition on PBC cards.

Calling it a 50-50 fight at the negotiating table ignores where the actual leverage sits. Ennis carries the commercial momentum, sells out arenas, holds multiple belts, and represents the clear A-side here. Fundora walking in and demanding parity looks less like an honest starting point and more like setting up a scenario where Ennis has to pay an inflated toll just to unify the division.

If Hearn and Ennis were to concede to an equal split, Ennis is essentially footing the bill for the WBC belt rather than sharing revenue based on merit. The style matchup also explains why Sampson Lewkowicz might be shooting for the moon right now. Fundora is an anomaly at 6’6″, but he notoriously gives up his height, fights on the inside, and absorbs heavy punishment in almost every outing.

Against an elite, sharp counterpuncher and fluid switch-hitter like Boots, those defensive flaws are a disaster waiting to happen. Ennis has the speed, punch placement, and inside combinations to exploit Fundora’s wide frame all night.

Sports.title: Jacob Bank Gets Janibek Alimkhanuly At Home January 23
Sports.content:
Jacob Bank meets Janibek Alimkhanuly on January 23 in Horsens, Denmark, for the vacant WBO super middleweight title. That placement gives the younger contender home-turf momentum against an older veteran returning from an extended layoff.

Both camps reached terms earlier this month. These updated details lock in the date and venue for Bank (20-0, 11 KOs) to test himself against the former unified middleweight champion.

Hamzah Sheeraz vacated the belt after being directed to face Janibek, clearing the path for Bank. The WBO promptly ordered talks between the pair of undefeated fighters.

At 25, Bank brings youth, current ring sharpness, and familiarity with the 168-pound limit. He has stepped inside the ropes three times in 2026, entering this contest with no ring rust. Meanwhile, the 33-year-old Janibek spent the entire calendar year idle before stepping up in weight.

Bank gained his strongest validation by stopping William Scull in the 12th round this past January. He stopped the Cuban survivor who previously lasted the full distance against Canelo Alvarez, staying on the hunt until he finally broke through.

The contrast goes beyond the finish. Bank appeared bigger, fresher, and physically stronger against Scull than Alvarez looked. He tackled the task like a true super middleweight, eager to assert his presence and refusing to let Scull’s tentative approach slow the action.

The Kazakh southpaw brings championship rounds alongside sharp counterpunching, yet neither fighter has built an extensive resume against upper-echelon rivals. Janibek’s tight points victory over Denzel Bentley proved that his feared reputation will not intimidate a gritty challenger.

Bank’s amateur pedigree pales in comparison to Janibek’s world-class amateur foundation, but elite pedigree matters far less when a physical, aggressive fighter turns a bout into an ugly high-volume battle. Denzel Bentley proved in 2022 that Janibek doesn’t handle persistent, physical inside pressure cleanly. Bentley’s pressure left him looking exhausted by the eighth round.

At 33, coming off a twelve-month layoff, spending that much energy in the early going is dangerous. The legs are the first thing to go when fatigue sets in. If Janibek’s mobility fades by the middle rounds, he will be forced to stand flat-footed along the ropes against a much younger super middleweight who fights three times a year and is accustomed to that grueling pace.

Sports.title: Devin Haney Claims Shakur Stevenson Wanted Rehydration Clause
Sports.content:
Update: Devin Haney fired back at Shakur Stevenson, stating he initially accepted 145 pounds before Stevenson vanished for days and tried sneaking in a rehydration clause.

“You’re cap.. I agreed to 145 u went missing for days. Tried to put a rehydration clause on me. I wasted 6 months negotiating with you,” Haney posted on X. “I been negotiating with u since i was gonna sign to Zuffa. Yall did every thing for this fight not to happen even tried to throw Keyshawn in my way.”

Haney brings a crucial detail into public view. His original stance was 145 pounds with zero weight limits on fight morning. If Stevenson demanded a ceiling on Haney rehydrating after the weigh in, that altered the deal completely.

That explains Haney shutting down the catchweight talk. Trimming down two extra pounds while keeping the freedom to bulk back up on fight night is completely separate from accepting strict secondary limits. Haney skipped over Stevenson’s claim that an attorney formally demanded 147 pounds, but his message makes his anger obvious.

For Haney, who already had to dry himself out to shave two pounds off the 147 welterweight limit, that restriction is brutal. Capping Haney at 155 on Saturday morning prevents him from drinking freely, forces him to go to bed dehydrated, and leaves him depleted inside the ring.

That is why Haney walked away. Offering the two-pound concession at 145 was already a compromise.

Devin Haney Has Reasons to Reconsider Shakur Catchweight

Shakur Stevenson claims Devin Haney pulled out of their agreed 145-pound catchweight to demand the full 147-pound welterweight limit, blowing up a deal that looked locked down earlier this month.

Shakur has plenty of reason to be furious. Still, Haney can always rethink whether draining himself below welterweight makes sense against a slick target who rarely gets hit cleanly.

“At the 11th hour, after agreeing to 144 and then 145, DeeHoe had his lawyer email and say that he would only fight at 147. Big waste of everybody’s time,” Shakur posted on X.

Haney originally offered 145 with no rehydration limits, which Shakur took on October 8 with a quick reply: “145.0 U GOT A DEAL.” If Stevenson is telling the whole story, Haney backed off the exact compromise he put on the table.

Fans will call him out for it, but Haney does not have to sign off on terms that leave him depleted in the ring. Two extra pounds below welterweight might sound like nothing from the couch, but that extra pull can easily ruin a camp.

Stevenson is stepping up from 140 to take a shot at Haney’s WBO welterweight belt. Haney can legitimately question why he should drain his body for a challenger whose defensive mastery already makes for a nightmare night at the office.

Haney holds the chips here. He carries bigger commercial pull, so Stevenson is hardly his only ticket to a monster bag. Sitting back to see what happens between Ryan Garcia and Teofimo Lopez gives him another massive payday with far less hassle.

Nobody has seen the lawyer’s email yet, and Shakur never explained what prompted the change. His anger makes complete sense after shaking hands on a public deal, but Haney has to protect his physical edge while weighing the bigger options waiting for him.

Once a fighter shows weakness on the scales, the other camp smells blood and starts picking at the money.

Catchweight concessions always shift the psychological leverage. If Haney drops down to 145 just to accommodate Shakur moving up from 140, Shakur immediately feels like the A side dictating terms. From that vantage point, Shakur starts pushing for an even split or demanding parity he has not earned at the box office.

Sports.title: William Zepeda Replaces Shakur Stevenson Atop Ring Rankings
Sports.content:
Stripping Shakur Stevenson of the top spot at lightweight was long overdue. The Ring finally bumped William Zepeda to number one, updating the board to reflect reality since Shakur departed for junior welterweight.

Shakur hasn’t stepped into the ring at 135 pounds since his 2025 scrap with Zepeda. He snatched the WBO junior welterweight belt off Teofimo Lopez in January. Keeping him perched above fighters who actively compete in the weight class makes zero sense.

Leaving a division means stepping aside for the next man up, whether Shakur likes it or not. He got the official win over Zepeda, sure. That win shouldn’t grant him lifetime ownership over a division he completely walked away from.

That bout was much tighter than the lopsided scorecards indicated anyway. Zepeda relentlessly marched forward for twelve complete rounds, pressing Shakur hard without offering any real breathing room. On my scorecard, that fight was a draw. Shakur landed cleaner single shots, but those flashes never created the massive margin the judges turned in.

Now Zepeda sits atop an exciting lineup featuring Abdullah Mason, Floyd Schofield, plus Andy Cruz. This crew brings serious offensive firepower, giving 135 pounds a fresh identity beyond Shakur’s ultra-defensive fencing routine.

Every single one brings a distinct look. Zepeda drowns opponents in relentless volume. Mason pieces together crisp, heavy combos. Schofield loves trading shots in the pocket. Cruz flashes elite technical timing, bringing an offensive arsenal that belongs against the division’s best.

Getting these contenders inside the ropes together is the real challenge now. Deep rankings do not mean much when promotional walls keep top talent apart.

Shakur earned his respect at lightweight, but holding the crown requires actually fighting there. The 135-pound scene has plenty of momentum to move forward, giving Zepeda the green light to take over the division.

Sports.title: Liam Paro Wanted $1.73 Million for Devin Haney
Sports.content:
Liam Paro’s reported $1.73 million asking price was more than Devin Haney wanted to pay for a welterweight unification. The figure offers an explanation for why talks failed to produce a fight between the two champions.

Paro would have brought his IBF belt into a contest with WBO champion Haney. That gave Haney an opportunity to collect another title, but the sides still needed to agree on the cost of making it happen.

Australian journalist Peter Badel described Paro’s financial expectations in comments reported by EverythingBoxing, which credited @JaiMcAllisterx.

“Liam Paro — a little bit has gone quiet there. Look, I’ve been talking to his team. They’ve been a little bit frustrated. They’re trying to get the right fight at the right price for Liam,” Badel said, as quoted by EverythingBoxing. “I’m told he was seeking around 2.5 million Australian dollars [$1.73 million US] for a fight against Haney. Haney didn’t want to pay him that amount.”

EverythingBoxing identified the comments as being eight days old. Badel’s account gives Paro’s reported asking price without revealing Haney’s offer or how far apart the sides were.

Haney’s position involves more than choosing his next opponent. He operates Devin Haney Promotions and has worked through co-promotional agreements, giving him a business interest in the cost of putting a fight together.

Another championship gives Haney something to pursue, but his side must also decide whether an opponent’s price fits the event’s budget. Paro has his own title to bring to negotiations and a financial return he wants from risking it.

The reported $1.73 million request alone does not establish that Paro priced himself out. Equally, declining that figure does not establish that Haney wanted to avoid him.

The missing piece is the counteroffer. Without knowing what Haney’s side offered, it is difficult to judge whether Paro’s expectations prevented an agreement or whether the available money simply fell below his price.

Sports.title: Rico Verhoeven Accepts Deontay Wilder Fight Offer
Sports.content:
Rico Verhoeven has accepted an offer to fight Deontay Wilder on December 11, potentially adding another heavyweight bout to the Tyson Fury–Anthony Joshua undercard in Cardiff.

Wilder’s response is still outstanding, and the terms need to be negotiated. However, Verhoeven has made his willingness clear as he looks to continue boxing after his stoppage loss to Oleksandr Usyk.

“I can’t confirm just yet,” Verhoeven told talkSPORT. “What I can tell you is that they offered me the fight. They offered me Deontay Wilder. I said yes.” “The details need to be talked about still. But for that, I’m waiting on a response. So, if there’s a yes from the other side, it’s going to happen.”

Verhoeven did not identify who made the offer. His comments introduce another possible opponent for Wilder, who had been linked with a fight against Jai Opetaia on the same card.

Wilder would give Verhoeven an opportunity to turn the praise he received against Usyk into a victory over an established heavyweight. Going deep into a fight with Usyk earned him attention, but beating Wilder would give him something firmer to build on.

There is an obvious danger in treating Wilder as a faded name to collect. His right hand still gives Verhoeven a reason to be careful. Yet Wilder’s reduced activity and hesitant offense in recent performances could allow the Dutchman time to settle into the fight.

Verhoeven also made clear that he intends to remain in boxing after considering several offers.

“I want to make a statement,” he said. “I want to show that … I am able to transition into the sport of boxing.”

Peter Fury remains in his corner, and Verhoeven is already looking beyond the proposed December appearance. He hopes Joshua beats Fury because he wants that fight himself.

“I hope that Anthony Joshua’s winning that fight because then I’m next for him.”

Beating Wilder would give that ambition a stronger foundation. First, Wilder needs to accept.

Putting Wilder against Verhoeven spares Jai Opetaia a bizarre heavyweight detour that threatened to derail his cruiserweight meeting with David Benavidez. That alone makes it slightly more tolerable than the initial rumor, but it remains a carnival booking.

Wilder has looked completely spent for years. At 40, his trigger is hesitant, his balance is compromised, and the reflex to pull the trigger on his right hand has eroded. Grinding past an aging Derek Chisora by a 12-round split decision did not erase the one-sided beatings he took against Joseph Parker, Fury, or Zhilei Zhang.

Verhoeven, 37, proved his toughness by surviving into the eleventh round against Oleksandr Usyk, but surviving is not contending. He is an elite kickboxer with a tiny boxing resume, still learning basic ring craftsmanship under boxing rules.

Sticking two aging names together with mismatched pedigrees belongs on the preliminary streaming portion of the broadcast, not sharing equal billing right beneath Fury against Joshua. It caters to novelty rather than sport.

Sports.title: Frank Warren Rates Dubois Wardley Rematch Even
Sports.content:
Frank Warren still views Daniel Dubois against Fabio Wardley as a 50-50 fight heading into Saturday night at the O2 Arena in London. Even though Dubois won their violent clash in May, Wardley dropped him in the first and third rounds, proving his power can alter the course of the bout instantly.

Dubois weathered that storm to secure the stoppage, yet those early visits to the canvas give Wardley massive confidence that he can flip the script. The real challenge for Wardley will be finishing the job if he gets Dubois in trouble again.

“I just feel that either of them can win. I think it’s still an even-money fight,” Warren told talkSPORT. “Daniel will go as favorite because he’s probably … got more experience as amateur as well as pro.”

Surviving clean bombs once does not guarantee Dubois can take them a second time. At the same time, reckless aggression could cost either man dearly.

“You’ve got to remember he called for this rematch,” Warren said of Wardley. “It was a brutal fight in May, and here we are now, and it’s on, and he believes that he can win it.”

Warren believes victory hinges on establishing the jab instead of hunting for wild knockout blows right away. For Dubois, a sharp jab keeps Wardley on the outside and stops him from landing cold early.

“For me, the key to this fight is getting behind the jab,” Warren said. “Not looking to lead with big punches, to actually go out and try and … jab and then let your shots go.”

Both heavyweights know what to expect after their first battle. The winner will be the man who made the right adjustments and capitalizes on them first. Neither fighter is built to play it safe, which is why Warren expects another explosive finish before the final bell sounds. Dubois proved his resilience, Wardley proved his firepower, and both step into the ring knowing one clean shot can end it.

When promoters preach boxing fundamentals and patience for a high-profile rematch, they are usually trying to protect their fighters from another grueling brawl. The problem is that fans are paying for fireworks, not a tactical chess match.

“They know each other’s strengths and weaknesses,” Warren said. “It’s who’s learned from the last fight and who can exploit what he’s learned.”

If Dubois and Wardley actually listen to Warren and spend 36 minutes trading cautious jabs from ring center, public reaction will be brutal. Paying premium pay-per-view prices on DAZN just to watch two sluggers neutralize each other behind the lead hand is the exact opposite of what made their May fight thrilling.

“I don’t think the fight’s going to go the distance, whatever happens.”

The thin undercard makes that risk even worse. Here, there is zero safety net. If the headliner devolves into a safety-first sparring session, the whole broadcast will disappoint, and the backlash from paying customers will land squarely on Warren.

Ghana News.title: Vice President arrives in China for Global South Academic Forum
Ghana News.content:
Vice President Professor Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang has arrived in Shanghai, China, to participate in the Global South Academic Forum.

The Forum serves as an important platform for dialogue, knowledge exchange, and cooperation on issues shaping the development trajectories of countries across the Global South.

In a statement upon her arrival, the Vice President said she looked forward to engaging stakeholders and exploring opportunities for stronger partnerships.

“Over the coming days, I look forward to a series of engagements to strengthen partnerships and explore opportunities for collaboration in areas that contribute to our national development,” she stated.

Professor Opoku-Agyemang is expected to participate in discussions and meetings aimed at fostering cooperation, sharing development experiences, and promoting mutually beneficial partnerships among countries of the Global South.

Ghana News.title: Ghana Armed Forces receives 45 utility vehicles to boost troop mobility
Ghana News.content:
The Ghana Armed Forces (GAF) has received 45 military utility vehicles under the government’s ongoing retooling programme to improve troop mobility and strengthen operational readiness.

The vehicles were received on Friday, October 16, 2026, as part of efforts to equip the military to effectively discharge its constitutional mandate.

The fleet comprises 15 KIA utility vehicles, 15 four-by-four vehicles and 15 six-by-six Troop Carrying Vehicles (TCVs).

The vehicles are expected to improve troop transportation, facilitate movement across difficult terrain and enable the Army to respond more swiftly to operational demands.

The acquisition forms part of the government’s broader efforts to modernise the Ghana Armed Forces, strengthen national security and enhance the military’s capacity to protect Ghana’s territorial integrity.

The latest delivery follows other acquisitions by the military this year aimed at strengthening the capabilities of the various services.

The Ghana Navy commissioned the Ghana Navy Ship (GNS) PRU on February 10, 2026, while the Ghana Air Force took delivery of an Airbus H175 helicopter from France on March 5, 2026.

Ghana News.title: 20% VAT on digital services punishes Ghanaians abroad, favours foreigners – Boako
Ghana News.content:
Tano North MP Dr Gideon Boako has criticised the 20% Value Added Tax (VAT) on cross-border digital transactions, arguing that the policy could unfairly penalise Ghanaians living and studying abroad while allowing some foreigners residing in Ghana to avoid the charge.

In a Facebook post on Friday, October 16, 2026, Dr Boako said Ghanaian students in countries such as the United Kingdom and the United States could be charged VAT when purchasing digital services with their parents’ Ghanaian bank cards, despite consuming the services outside Ghana.

“It will affect lots of Ghanaian students who use their parent’s Ghana bank card to purchase digital services abroad,” he wrote.

He contrasted this with a hypothetical situation involving a UK or US diplomat living in Ghana who purchases digital services using a bank card issued by their home country.

According to the MP, such a transaction could escape the VAT, creating what he considers an unfair difference in how the tax applies.

“A UK or USA diplomat who lives in Ghana and procures digital services in Ghana using his home country bank card will avoid the VAT,” he stated.

Dr Boako argued that the arrangement risked placing an additional burden on Ghanaians while giving some foreign residents an advantage.

“We have just introduced a tax to punish even Ghanaians living abroad while letting foreigners living in Ghana to go free,” he wrote.
