The administration will also coordinate media activities, organize public forums and undertake measures intended to promote reconciliation, rebuild public confidence and prepare residents for reconstruction and development.

The government said the caretaker administration must base its activities on Ethiopia's national interests and territorial integrity, as well as the fundamental interests of the people of Tigray.

Its authority will be limited to providing routine regional services and creating conditions for the next election. It will not undertake matters with longer-term strategic implications, the government said, and will operate under the direction and supervision of the federal government.

The administration's senior officials are Asefa Abraha Hagos, chief executive for administration and public services; Tewodros Aregay Woldeselassie (PhD), chief executive for the economy and reconstruction; Gebre Egziabher Beyene Hailu (Brig. Gen.), chief executive for security and peace; and Redae Hailuom Woldeselassie, chief executive for political affairs and public organization.

Shishay Amare (PhD) was appointed mayor of Mekele, the regional capital.

The federal government will provide direction, support and oversight for the officials' activities, according to the announcement.

World.title: Malawi: Gold Rush or Gold Bust? Malawi's Smuggling Crackdown Faces Credibility Test
World.content:
Malawi's latest bid to turn gold into a lifeline for its struggling economy is facing uncomfortable questions about the evidence on which it has been built.

A state-backed scheme designed to intercept gold before it is smuggled out of the country rests on a headline-grabbing claim that $100 million worth of the precious metal is lost annually through illegal trade. Yet, according to an analysis by Collins Mtika for the Mail & Guardian and the Centre for Investigative Journalism Malawi, the figure has never been publicly explained.

The programme, spearheaded by the Malawi Mining Investment Company (Mamico), aims to buy gold from artisanal miners operating at roughly 100 sites nationwide, funnel it through buying centres in Lilongwe, Kasungu and Nkhotakota, and ultimately sell it to the Reserve Bank of Malawi (RBM).

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

But a closer examination of the numbers reveals a troubling inconsistency.

Earlier this year, Mamico reported findings from a month-long assessment which estimated that more than $700 million worth of gold was being lost each year through illicit activity and identified 81 illegal mining sites.

The latest estimate is seven times lower. At the same time, the number of mining locations linked to the programme has increased to around 100.

The analysis asks a simple question: which number is accurate?

Without a published methodology, there is no way to test either claim. For a project requiring hundreds of billions of kwacha in public and private financing, that gap matters.

Mamico says it will need K85 billion to fund its first three months of operations and around K300 billion annually thereafter. The company has enlisted FDH Bank and NBS Bank as partners, but key parts of the commercial framework are still unresolved.

Most notably, the arrangement depends on an offtake agreement with the RBM that has yet to be concluded.

The uncertainty extends beyond the figures.

The analysis points to potential duplication between Mamico's planned operations and an existing RBM gold-purchasing initiative run through the Export Development Fund.

By September, that programme had already acquired about 1.63 tonnes of gold, raising questions about whether the government is creating parallel structures within the same market.

There is also a more fundamental challenge. Artisanal miners will only sell through official channels if they can secure competitive prices and prompt payment.

If unofficial traders offer better deals, the incentive to bypass the formal system remains intact, regardless of how many buying centres are established.

Close 

Yet the pressure to make the project work is immense.

Malawi's foreign exchange position remains fragile. Official reserves stood at $600.6 million in September, enough to cover just 2.4 months of imports, below the internationally recognised three-month benchmark.

Gold has emerged as one of the few commodities capable of generating substantial foreign currency earnings. In April alone, the RBM exported 589.95 kilogrammes of locally purchased gold valued at $75.09 million.

For ministers and policymakers, the allure is obvious: bring more gold into formal channels and bolster dwindling reserves.

But as Mtika's analysis suggests, the success of the strategy may hinge less on ambition than on transparency.

Until Mamico discloses how it calculated its smuggling estimates, clarifies how it will coexist with existing state-run gold programmes, and produces verifiable data on production, purchases and exports, the initiative will continue to face a credibility problem.

For now, the government's gold rush is asking the public to trust numbers it has yet to prove.

World.title: Somalia: Somalia's Govt Welcomes Election Timetable and Urges Political Dialogue
World.content:
Mogadishu — Somalia's federal government on Thursday welcomed an election timetable announced by the Independent National Electoral and Boundaries Commission, covering elections for both houses of parliament and the president.

In a statement dated October 15, 2026, the government described the timetable as an important step towards implementing the electoral process and strengthening democracy in the country.

The government said it had spent the past 18 months offering opportunities for consultation and negotiations aimed at helping Somali political stakeholders reach agreement on key national issues, particularly the electoral process.

It said the consultations would continue, adding that it remained committed to securing a broad-based understanding among the country's political actors.

The government described its support for the election timetable and its continued commitment to dialogue as complementary efforts that would help preserve stability, strengthen national unity and safeguard citizens' constitutional rights.

It called on all political stakeholders to engage in consultations in good faith and with a sense of national responsibility, urging them to work together to ensure peaceful elections that strengthen public confidence and Somalia's state institutions.

The statement comes amid political differences over Somalia's electoral process, including disagreements over the proposed arrangements and calls for an inclusive political agreement.

World.title: South Africa: Masemola Back As Police Commissioner After Ramaphosa Lifts Suspension
World.content:
Masemola was placed on precautionary suspension in April 2026 after appearing in court on charges linked to a R360-million police health services tender.

Lieutenant General Puleng Dimpane has served as acting National Police Commissioner, and Ramaphosa says she served with distinction.

President Cyril Ramaphosa has lifted the suspension of National Police Commissioner General Fannie Masemola, who will resume his full duties on Monday, 19 October.

The Presidency made the announcement on Friday.

Ramaphosa and Masemola agreed in April 2026 that Masemola would be deemed to be on precautionary suspension. This followed his appearance in the Pretoria Magistrate's Court on charges of contravening the Public Finance Management Act. The charges were linked to a R360-million police health services tender awarded to Medicare24.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

National Director of Public Prosecutions Andy Mothibi ordered the charges to be withdrawn after a review found no reasonable prospects of a successful prosecution on 15 September. The Pretoria Magistrate's Court formally withdrew the charges on 22 September.

Lieutenant General Puleng Dimpane, the police's chief financial officer, was appointed acting National Police Commissioner when Masemola was suspended.

Ramaphosa thanked her and said she served with distinction in the interim.

"The President welcomes the National Police Commissioner on his return to his full duties," presidential spokesperson Vincent Magwenya said.

The South African Policing Union had urged Ramaphosa to lift the suspension after the charges were withdrawn. After the withdrawal, Masemola told the media that he had not heard from the president.

The National Prosecuting Authority has also referred the case to the oversight judge of the Investigating Directorate Against Corruption, to look into whether there was any malice behind the original charges.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 16, 2026
World.content:
UK Threatens Visa Ban on Eritreans Over Deportation Dispute

UK Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has threatened to ban all Eritrean nationals from entering the UK unless the East African country agrees to accept more of its citizens facing deportation, including foreign national offenders. Initial measures, which took effect, restrict Eritrean diplomats from travelling more than 60km outside London without permission. The UK will also stop fast-track visas for VIPs. Eritrea has condemned the move as a political gimmick, accusing the UK of failing to engage in meaningful dialogue and disputing claims about cooperation on returns. The UK government maintains that Eritrea withdrew its cooperation earlier this year. However, migration experts have questioned whether the restrictions will be effective. They said that many Eritrean asylum seekers qualify for protection because of repression and forced military conscription in their home country.

DR Congo Ebola Outbreak Response Progresses in Bunia





Efforts to contain the Democratic Republic of Congo's worst-ever Ebola outbreak are showing progress in Bunia, Ituri province, where health workers are intensifying community awareness campaigns and home visits to encourage residents to seek medical care. The outbreak has reportedly killed more than 4,000 people in five months. It was declared a public health emergency of international concern by the World Health Organization. Fear of infection and misinformation have disrupted healthcare services, particularly maternity care, with maternal deaths in Bunia rising from an average of three to almost five a week, according to health officials. UNICEF has established 12 nurseries linked to health facilities to care for children separated from parents receiving Ebola treatment. Survivors are helping support vulnerable children. Despite improvements in community trust and healthcare attendance, the outbreak continues in other areas, where armed-group activity and insufficient humanitarian funding are hampering response efforts.

China Outlines Four Principles to Resolve Conflicts Across Africa

Chinese President Xi Jinping has outlined four principles for resolving conflicts in Africa. He has called for African-led solutions, respect for national sovereignty, an end to hostilities and efforts to address the root causes of insecurity. Speaking during a meeting with Togo's President of the Council of Ministers, Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, in Beijing on October 13, Xi said African people should remain central to decisions affecting the continent. He urged parties involved in conflict resolution to respect the United Nations Charter, pursue dialogue and compromise, and combine immediate security measures with long-term development planning. His remarks come as several African regions, including Sudan, the Great Lakes region and the Horn of Africa, continue to face conflict and security challenges. The two leaders also agreed to strengthen China-Togo relations through cooperation in trade, infrastructure, renewable energy, digital technology and industrialisation. Xi encouraged Togo to take advantage of China's zero-tariff arrangements for African products.

Kenya Reflects on Raila Odinga Legacy One Year After His Death

One year after former Kenyan Prime Minister Raila Odinga's death, his legacy continues to shape debates about democracy, constitutional reform and the future of opposition politics. Odinga spent decades campaigning for multiparty democracy and played a significant role in Kenya's political reforms, including the adoption of the 2010 Constitution. His supporters credit him with promoting reconciliation and institutional change. His political alliances with former foes, critics said, diluted the opposition's ability to hold the government to account. His Orange Democratic Movement (ODM) party's future has also been in the spotlight, with party leaders warning it is in danger of losing its identity and support among ordinary Kenyans. His daughter Winnie Odinga has declared interest in the Nairobi Senate seat in the upcoming 2027 polls. As younger generations reflect on his contribution, questions remain over whether Kenya's political institutions and opposition parties will uphold the democratic principles associated with his legacy.

Close 

Nigerian Gospel Singer Toluwanisings Dies at 41

Nigerian gospel singer Olayemi Bayonile Bolaji, popularly known as Toluwanisings, has died at the age of 41. In a statement shared on his Instagram account, the family asked fans to remember his wife, children and relatives in their prayers. Toluwanisings was known for his powerful vocals and energetic praise performances, with popular songs including Unreserved Praise, A Very Big God, Onibuore, E Lagbara and Owo Re Meji Meji. News of his death prompted an outpouring of tributes from fans, fellow musicians and public figures, including lawyer Pelumi Olajengbesi and comedian Woli Agba, who had previously called for prayers for the singer. His death comes months after he was involved in a road accident alongside members of his band. The family said funeral arrangements would be announced in due course.

World.title: Jerry Seinfeld turns tables on radical anti-Israel agitators after chaotic Chicago stunt backfires
World.content:

Comedian Jerry Seinfeld turned the tables on anti-Israel hecklers who attempted to derail his Chicago performance last Friday, mocking the protesters as security removed them from the venue.

Viral video from the confrontation shows activists shouting at Seinfeld at the Chicago Theatre, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" in Gaza and alleging that American taxpayer dollars are funding the deaths of thousands of civilians.

"Twenty-two thousand Palestinians who are children now are killed with our taxpayer money, and you’re making jokes!" a woman shouted in clips posted online.

JERRY SEINFELD GIVES BLUNT THREE-WORD RESPONSE TO INFLUENCER ASKING FOR A 'FREE PALESTINE'

Seinfeld then dances on stage and mocks the protesters with sarcastic remarks, calling himself "racist" and saying, "It’s a genocide. I’m into it." He also joked that he would find out how much the protesters paid for their tickets and send the money directly to Israel.

As security personnel escorted the demonstrators out of the auditorium, one audience member shouted, "Rough her up!"

The Anti-War Committee Chicago and the Chicago branch of the US Palestinian Community Network have taken credit for organizing the disruption, writing on Instagram, "Friday’s disruption sent a clear message: Those who defend Israel’s genocide and ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in Gaza and throughout Palestine will be met with protest and are not welcome on Chicago’s stages without opposition."

COMEDIAN DECLARES JERRY SEINFELD 'UNCANCELLABLE' DESPITE 'WOKE' ANTI-ISRAEL FESTIVAL BOYCOTT

Fox News Digital reached out to Seinfeld’s team for comment but did not hear back.

The altercation is the latest in a string of protests targeting the 72-year-old Jewish comedian over his staunch defense of Israel.

ANTI-ISRAEL PROTESTERS LABEL MAMDANI A 'TRAITOR,' ACCUSE HIM OF 'GENOCIDE' OUTSIDE OCT 7 VIGIL

Comedian and media analyst Tim Young told Fox News Digital he believes protesters are paying top dollar to hijack comedy shows for viral attention rather than political discourse.

"They know that once they start yelling, everyone will whip their cameras out, and it is a very direct interaction and maybe one of the only direct interactions protesters get to have with celebrities and with the internet," Young said.

"If you are in a very intimate environment where everyone is quiet, listening to one person, you will be heard. And, so, that's what they're taking advantage of here."

Young compared the disruptions at Seinfeld's shows to protests at political rallies, arguing that some activists are willing to pay steep ticket prices to confront the comedian.

"It seems like people are going to Jerry Seinfeld's shows like they're going to a Trump rally to protest," Young said. "They wanted to get Jerry's attention. They want to, for some reason, they're very, very adamant on getting him to react to the Israel-Palestine conflict."

Young also linked the disruptions to Seinfeld's past criticism of performing at universities.

30% OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE ACCEPTABLE WAY TO STOP SPEAKERS ON CAMPUSES, SURVEY FINDS

"It's why Jerry doesn't like to go and perform at college campuses. And he said he hates performing at college campuses specifically for that reason," Young said.

"He doesn't want to get into the political thing. He doesn't want to have protesters yelling back and forth with him. It's a waste of the rest of the audience's time, and he knows that."

In May 2024, dozens of students walked out during Seinfeld's commencement address at Duke University, some holding Palestinian flags.

Seinfeld returned to the university in September 2025 to introduce freed Israeli hostage Omer Shem Tov at a campus event, where he addressed anti-Israel protests, saying, "Free Palestine is, to me, just — you’re free to say you don’t like Jews. Just say you don’t like Jews."

QUIET PART OUT LOUD: ANTI-ISRAEL MOBS WANT ONE STATE CALLED 'PALESTINE,' ERASING ISRAEL

"By saying ‘Free Palestine,’ you’re not admitting what you really think," he said. "So, it’s actually — compared to the Ku Klux Klan, I’m actually thinking the Klan is actually a little better here because they can come right out and say, ‘We don’t like Blacks, we don’t like Jews.’ OK, that’s honest."

Seinfeld also faced controversy overseas last month when several European acts withdrew from the inaugural MEO Commedia a La Carte Fest in Lisbon, Portugal, where he is scheduled to headline later this year.

The acts did not name Seinfeld directly in their withdrawal statements, but some cited concerns about the Israel-Gaza conflict. One performer said someone involved in the festival defended ideas they considered indefensible.

Young, who previously dismissed efforts to cancel Seinfeld over his support for Israel, argued that protesters target the billionaire comedian because of his influence and celebrity status.

World.title: Lawyers for girl alleging sexual assault by trans wrestler fire back at Washington officials in SCOTUS appeal
World.content:
A Washington high school wrestler who alleges she was sexually assaulted by a transgender opponent during a girls’ match is asking the Supreme Court to intervene before her next season begins, and her attorneys are firing back after the defendants tried to write off her claimed harm as "manufactured."

In an Oct. 15 filing, her attorneys at Alliance Defending Freedom accused the three defendants, the Puyallup School District, Washington’s Office of Superintendent of Public Instruction and the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association, of shifting responsibility for providing those protections.

"Defendants’ briefs mostly point the finger at each other, trying to pass the buck for the harm inflicted," Alliance Defending Freedom (ADF) attorneys wrote in an Oct. 15 reply supporting the girl, Kallie Keeler and her mother, Stephanie Brown.

WOMEN WHO FACED BIOLOGICAL MALES IN GIRLS' SPORTS AND LOCKER ROOMS SPEAK OUT AHEAD OF WASHINGTON STATE VOTE

"Exit isn’t accommodation. It’s the injury, and Brown and K.M.K. are suffering it now," the attorneys added, rejecting the argument that withdrawing from competition adequately addresses the family’s concerns.

Keeler, identified in court as K.M.K., alleges a transgender opponent sexually assaulted her during a girls’ wrestling match in December 2025. Pierce County prosecutors declined to file criminal charges. Her family is seeking protection against being matched with male opponents while its lawsuit proceeds.

The reply follows opposition briefs from the Puyallup School District, Washington’s Office of Superintendent of Public Instruction and the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association.

"The ‘irreparable’ nature of Applicants’ claimed harm is manufactured," the state argued, challenging the asserted emergency and likelihood of future injury. The statement addressed the justification for immediate court intervention, rather than characterizing the alleged assault as fabricated.

The district said Brown could decline matches without district-imposed penalties. It also cited supportive measures, an expedited school transfer and an ongoing independent Title IX investigation. The defendants raised concerns about their authority to control matchups, competition rules and other students’ privacy.

ADF countered that the defendants collectively control eligibility, participation and competition rules.



"Defendants each disclaim full power, but in so doing, they ignore that together they hold it all," the reply states.

The attorneys also challenged the suggestion that the family should await the ordinary appeals process. The district’s appellate answering brief is due Nov. 19, three days after wrestling practices begin, according to its opposition and WIAA’s calendar. ADF said the extension was granted over the family’s objection.

Alongside its Title IX request, ADF outlined an alternative accommodation based on parental rights: Officials would withdraw Keeler, or notify her mother so she could withdraw her, when they know or have reason to know an opponent is male.

Under that proposal, Keeler would receive treatment comparable to the most favorably treated forfeiture allowed by the rules, such as a medical forfeiture. In a tournament, her opponent could advance while she continued in the applicable consolation bracket.

"Her opponent advances, and she stays in the tournament," ADF wrote.

The district court and Ninth Circuit previously denied temporary relief. The Supreme Court application remained pending Friday, with the docket listing the family’s reply but no ruling.

World.title: Pope Leo XIV seen for first time since lung cancer surgery amid major recovery milestone
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Pope Leo XIV is up and moving after having part of his lung removed.

After undergoing thoracic surgery Tuesday, during which surgeons removed the lower lobe of the pope’s right lung, examination of the tissue confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, or lung cancer, according to the Vatican.

The pope, 71, has spent four days recovering at Gemelli Hospital in Rome, Italy, after the successful procedure.

DR MARC SIEGEL: POPE LEO'S LUNG SURGERY PUTS MODERN MEDICINE ALONGSIDE FAITH

On Friday, the Vatican released the first photos of Pope Leo after the operation.

The pope is pictured standing at an altar in green vestments, celebrating Mass in a makeshift chapel at the hospital where he distributed communion.

According to a Holy See Press Office statement, several members of Gemelli’s medical and nursing staff and members of the Vatican City State Gendarmerie Corps attended the service.

POPE LEO'S LUNG TUMOR RAISES QUESTIONS ABOUT CANCER RISK FOR NONSMOKERS

"In his homily, the Pope thanked all the staff — doctors, nurses and orderlies — for the work they do every day caring for patients in their frailty and especially for what they have done and continue to do for him," the statement said.

The Vatican also confirmed on Friday that the pope’s recovery continues with "steady improvement in his overall condition."

Dr. Luigi Carbone and professor Stefano Margaritora added that the pope’s "post-operative recovery allows him to carry out normal daily activities entirely independently."

Pope Leo plans to make his first public appearance since the procedure on Sunday during the noon Angelus, which he normally leads.

NEVER SMOKED A CIGARETTE? YOU COULD STILL BE AT HIGHER RISK FOR LUNG CANCER

Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel said the pope’s procedure included a small incision with VAT (video-assisted thoracoscopy), which involves less pain and has a quicker recovery.

The pope was in good health "to begin with" and is highly active, which plays a "major role in recovery," Siegel, who has not treated the Pope, told Fox News Digital.

"Since he wasn’t a smoker and likely had very good underlying lung function, loss of a lobe, when there are three total on the right, shouldn’t have a major impact on daily activity, especially with pain controlled," the doctor added.

CLICK HERE TO 

In a separate Fox News Digital interview, Lary Robinson, an oncologist at Moffitt Cancer Center in Tampa, Florida, shared his surprise regarding the pope’s health status.

About 80% of lung cancers occur in people who smoke or have smoked, said Robinson, who has not treated the pope. However, he noted that lung cancer also occurs among never-smokers, including an estimated 10% of male patients and 25% of female patients.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"But [the pope] had surgery and had a lobectomy, so this is usually only done with people who have localized disease, and presumably he had localized disease. And hopefully that's a Stage 1 cancer," the doctor added.

If the pope’s cancer is Stage 1, there is a "high chance" of cure — about 90% — depending on the size of the tumor, the oncologist said. The fact that he went straight to surgery suggests there was likely no evidence that the cancer had spread.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"We'll have to wait for the pathology to determine … whether he needs any additional treatment afterward," Robinson said.

World.title: NBA and many sportsbooks agree to ban multiple types of bets due to recent betting scandals
World.content:
The NBA has been rocked with scandal over the past year as it pertains to sports betting. Sports betting is now integrated into almost every broadcast. It's ingrained in the game from the weekly talk shows to the pregame coverage. Now the NBA is putting some guardrails on multiple bets within some of the most prominent sportsbooks. Apparently, having players allegedly help bettors cash massive parlays wasn't exactly great for business.

According to ESPN, the league is banning several types of bets this season, including same-player parlays involving multiple statistical unders — the very wagers at the center of recent gambling scandals involving Jontay Porter and Terry Rozier.

If you haven't seen the videos of Terry Rozier allegedly botching plays, shooting wild shots, and turning the ball over in ridiculous ways, check it out here.

NBA GUARD TERRY ROZIER MAY GET HIT WITH NEW CHARGES IN ALLEGED GAMBLING SCHEME

These are also getting the boot in sportsbooks:

Bets on opening tip winners

Players to miss specific shots

Unders involving players expected to play fewer than 12 minutes

MALIK BEASLEY INDICTED ON FEDERAL CHARGES FOR ALLEGEDLY FIXING HIS OWN NBA PERFORMANCES FOR BETTORS

World.title: Man who confronted Oregon elementary school gunman identified by brother
World.content:
Kaylub Giamanco was driving home from lunch when he heard gunshots and saw a gunman entering the Oregon elementary school his two young daughters attend. Armed with a long gun, the 36-year-old carpenter ran into the school and killed the teenage suspect.

Kyle Giamanco identified his brother as the bystander who intervened in the Thursday afternoon shooting. He recounted to NBC News on Friday what he was told happened.

Officials have not named the community member who killed the shooter, but said the person’s actions prevented further loss at Silver Rail Elementary School.

Kyle Giamanco said his brother told him he was headed home after grabbing a bite to eat when he saw the gunman entering the school. Police have said that the suspect, identified by three senior law enforcement officials as John J. Griffin, 16, gained entry to the building by firing through locked doors.

Two of the officials said the gun used in the shooting was purchased by the suspect’s mother around the time of his birthday in August.

Kaylub Giamanco. via Facebook

Kyle Giamanco said his brother has a concealed-weapon permit “and decided to go in after” the shooter. Kyle Giamanco and several parents told NBC News that the shooting happened in a special education room.

A teacher and three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, were killed. Two other people, a 7-year-old and another teacher, were critically injured at the Bend, Oregon, school.

Kyle Giamanco said his brother is a hero, but said Kaylub Giamanco does not want to speak out right now because he feels guilty that he could not save more children.

Kaylub Giamanco wasn’t the only person to try to stop the gunman. The first 911 call was placed by a person who reported that a gunman had shot at his vehicle. That call and the dozens of others that police said were placed to 911 reporting that a gunman had entered the school enabled police to arrive on scene just three minutes after the first call, according to police.

Justin Penfield, whose son is in kindergarten, said that when he got to the school the class was already outside. As he walked back to his car with his son, Penfield said he saw a man standing next to a pickup truck with “seven or eight gunshot holes in his truck.”

Penfield said the man told him that he was driving back from lunch when he saw someone throw what appeared to be a shotgun over the fence and then jump into the school’s playground.

The man said he yelled to ask the guy what he was doing, and the person opened fire on his truck, Penfield said, recounting his conversation with the man.

According to Penfield, the man said he sped off and called 911.

The names of those killed and injured have not been released.

One parent recalled getting an automated phone call from the school about a lockdown, followed by a text message from her son saying that there had been a shooting.

“Mom there was a school shooting we’re ok tho,” the fifth grader wrote.

Jenn Johnston said she and her husband rushed to the school but were rerouted to a nearby church. They waited hours with few updates from police or school officials before she was reunited with her son.

“My son came running to me in tears,” she said.

World.title: Trump looms as tensions flare in final Maine Senate debate
World.content:
BANGOR, Maine — The marathon of debates in the Maine Senate race has ended, but there is still one unanswered question: Just how large will President Donald Trump loom in November?

That question was at the center of the clashes between Democrat Troy Jackson and longtime GOP Sen. Susan Collins as they faced off in four debates over the last two weeks, including a finale Thursday hosted by Maine Public Broadcasting Network, the Portland Press Herald and NBC affiliate WCSH of Portland.

Jackson is betting voters’ views of Trump, who has never won Maine, will dominate their views of this Senate race, which could determine which party controls the chamber next year.

He repeatedly tied Collins to Trump throughout all four debates. Collins, meanwhile, tried to appeal to Mainers who want a senator willing to break with his or her party.

“I voted against my own party more often than any other senator on either side of the aisle,” Collins said during the final debate. “That is not something that Troy could ever say. He’s going to be an automatic vote for the Democratic position, no matter what. We have lost a lot of the centrists, and one reason I’m running again is we need people who will work across party lines.”

Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson debate Thursday in Bangor. Gregory Rec / Portland Press Herald via Getty

Jackson countered: “The reality is that 100% of the time, when Donald Trump needs her, Susan Collins is going to be there. That has happened time and time again.”

Trump’s policies were intertwined with the major topics covered in all four debates, including high costs, the war in Iran, immigration enforcement and an ongoing trade war with Canada, which Maine borders.

On Thursday, Collins was also pressed about her support for some Trump Cabinet officials, including Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. She said she didn’t regret having voted to confirm him while noting that she disagrees with Kennedy’s vaccine skepticism. Collins said Kennedy has helped release more funds from a program to help low-income Mainers buy heating oil amid soaring prices.

Jackson, meanwhile, said he would vote to convict Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on impeachment charges.

“But that’s not my focus,” he quickly added. “My focus is delivering healthcare, prescription drugs, child care, the things that Mainers need right now more than ever, and getting out of the Iran war so we can stabilize prices.”

Tensions were high after four debates in rapid succession. This one was the first in front of a live audience, with roughly 200 people gathered in a theater at Husson University.

Around 20 minutes into the debate, a young man stood and shouted about his concerns about data centers, exclaiming that he was scared for the future.

“Thirty years for what?” the protester shouted as he was escorted out of the theater, referring to Collins’ time in the Senate.

Collins claimed the protester was a Jackson supporter, and Jackson remarked, “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.”

While the protester questioned her decades in the Senate, Collins has argued that her seniority makes her an effective advocate for Maine. She often touts her role as chairwoman of the powerful Appropriations Committee, arguing she has helped bring home huge sums of federal money to fund projects in the state.

Collins stressed that she has broken with Trump on some key issues, noting she voted against Trump’s sweeping “big, beautiful” tax and spending law last year, though she did vote to allow the measure to proceed on the floor.

“I nevertheless voted against the bill, even though it was the president’s top legislative priority. I’ve also voted nine times against the president on the Iran war,” she said.

Jackson has argued that Collins could have done more to oppose the military action.

Asked where he would break with his own party, Jackson pointed to his pledge not to accept donations from corporate political action committees.

“I think the Democrats are still too close to that,” Jackson said. “I don’t accept corporate PACs. I don’t accept corporate money. This is a campaign about fighting for everyday working-class people, and that’s one thing that I’ve been consistent on.”

Collins tried to undermine that argument, using her one question to ask Jackson about ads run in coordination with the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which does accept corporate PAC money.

Jackson countered that he doesn’t approve those ads. While he acknowledged he has had some support from billionaires, he said his campaign is powered by small-dollar donors.

Jackson raised more than $20 million from July through September, according to a fundraising report filed Thursday. That is nearly four times Collins’ $5.2 million haul over the same period.

Jackson, a former state Senate president and logger, then pressed Collins about her claims that he couldn’t be effective in the Senate.

“I have the experience fighting for working-class people, and they deserve a senator that respects them. Is it just me that you look down on, or is it working-class people overall?” he asked.

“Troy, I do not look down on you or on anyone. I grew up in Caribou. My first job was picking potatoes,” Collins countered, saying she has “literally” worked since she was 10 years old.

“I have supported all the social safety net programs,” she said later.

Collins’ experience in the Senate is a major reason her supporters are backing her for a sixth term.

“He is just not strong on the mechanics of government,” Collins supporter Mary Ann Lynch said of Jackson. Lynch is a lifelong Democrat but is backing Collins. And she said in a phone interview Wednesday that the debates hadn’t changed her mind.

“Just watching the debates, it’s hard for me to say that if we sent Troy Jackson to Washington, he would ever be able to cut a path of leadership,” said Lynch, 71, a former member of the Cape Elizabeth Town Council.

But Jackson’s push to tie Collins to Trump does resonate with voters leaning toward supporting him, like Dan Tremble.

Tremble, a Penobscot County commissioner, said he was “pretty solid” in his decision to support Jackson as he entered the theater in Bangor on Thursday night.

“Susan Collins has done a lot for the state of Maine,” Tremble, 61, a Democrat, said when he was asked why he wasn’t certain he’d support Jackson. “But I think having her in the Senate, I think, would still leave a majority for the president in the United States Senate, and that’s very worrisome with this president.”

“He says, ‘Vote like I’m on the ballot,’” Tremble added, referring to Trump. “I will.”

CORRECTION (Oct. 15, 2026, 10:17 p.m. ET): A previous version of this article misidentified the Cabinet secretary Troy Jackson said he’d vote to convict on impeachment charges. It was Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, not Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

World.title: Alaska Senate candidates clash over the Iran war, high prices and their times in office
World.content:
The two major candidates vying for an Alaska Senate seat squared off Thursday night over issues ranging from the war with Iran to controversies during the Democratic nominee’s time in Congress in a debate that at times flared into personal attacks.

Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan described Democratic challenger Mary Peltola as someone who sought a lobbying paycheck after her time serving in the House ended in 2025, pointing to recent reporting on the tumult in her congressional office during her tenure.

Peltola sought to tie Sullivan’s support for the war in Iran to the increase in the cost of living at home, pointing out Sullivan’s own increase in wealth while in office.

The race between Sullivan and Peltola, which NBC News rates as a toss-up, is one of a handful that could determine control of the Senate in November. Democrats have targeted the seat as one of five potential pickup opportunities, despite the fact that Donald Trump carried Alaska by double digits in 2024.

When asked what he thought of the White House’s recent announcement that it would allow the release of Russian diesel fuel onto the global market, Sullivan drew a distinction between himself and the Trump administration, a tack other Republicans in tight races have taken in recent debates.

“I just led the effort on a Russia sanctions act that passed the Congress, so I’m opposed to that,” Sullivan said.

The senator then pivoted to his opposition to the Pentagon’s now withdrawn announcement that it would livestream the execution of convicted terrorist Nidal Hasan.

“Certainly he needs to be executed, but if you have a livestreaming of this terrorist, you are going to create more terrorists,” Sullivan said.

Asked about the war with Iran, both candidates said the conflict should end soon.

Peltola attributed the increase in prices at home to the ongoing conflict — issues that polling has shown have become a drag on Republicans heading into the midterms.

“There does not appear to be a peace deal on the horizon, and I think it’s so important that our military be removed and protected,” Peltola said when asked whether she would support ending the war without a peace deal.

Sullivan said he supported President Donald Trump’s war powers in Iran because “the largest state sponsor of terrorism should not have nuclear weapons.”

“But it needs to end soon. The energy costs from this war are too high,” Sullivan continued, adding that boosting domestic energy production would bring down costs.

In another exchange, Sullivan leveled criticism of Peltola’s lobbying work after losing her the state’s at-large House seat in 2024.

“Mary, you’re walking through the revolving door so much you must be getting dizzy up here,” Sullivan said.

Peltola responded by noting the increase in Sullivan’s net worth during his two terms as a senator.

“Dan’s been in D.C. for 12 years and has gotten richer every single one of those years,” Peltola said.

Sullivan shot back, referring to a recent New York Times article that described turmoil in her congressional office and campaign, including angry outbursts and offensive language.

“Twenty-five staffers quit on Mary Peltola because she abused them physically and emotionally, and then she slanders every other group, African Americans, special needs individuals. It is a character flaw on my opponent,” Sullivan said, referring to the Times’ reporting on her time on Capitol Hill.

Peltola was later asked directly about the Times’ reporting.

“I don’t think this election is about me on my worst day,” Peltola said, calling the stories “allegations” and “mass exaggerations of the truth.”

Thursday’s debate comes just days after Trump visited Wasilla, Alaska, to hold a rally in support of Sullivan amid his multistate blitz to shore up Republican candidates, and Vice President JD Vance visited Fairbanks earlier this month.

The subject of Trump, however, was largely absent from Thursday’s debate, a departure from other high-profile races.

Alaska last elected a Democrat to the Senate in 2008, when Sen. Mark Begich ousted incumbent Republican Ted Stevens.

Peltola finished ahead of Sullivan in August’s all-party primary, with Peltola receiving 49.5% of the vote and Sullivan taking 41.4%.

A second Republican candidate also named Dan Sullivan — who has denied Republican accusations of being a ploy to confuse voters — received only 2.5% of the vote. Dan J. Sullivan did not participate in Thursday night’s debate, although he will be on the ballot in November.

World.title: Trump says Ukraine resuming strikes on Russian oil sites is a ‘disgrace’
World.content:
President Donald Trump has labeled Ukraine’s resumption of strikes on Russian oil refineries a “disgrace,” the latest salvo in his campaign to pressure the U.S. ally over rising gas prices that could cost Republicans in next month’s midterm elections.

Kyiv said Thursday that it would no longer abide by Trump’s “energy ceasefire,” citing Russia’s refusal to halt its own attacks on Ukraine’s power grid. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy angrily accused the U.S. of costing civilian lives by striking deals with Moscow and withdrawing support that is crucial to Kyiv’s defense against the invasion launched by President Vladimir Putin.

Ukrainian officials had raised alarm after gaps in intelligence sharing left Kyiv vulnerable to Russian attacks and restrictions on the Starlink satellite service disrupted military operations. Zelenskyy said Friday that the technology was still not fully restored.

With Ukraine defying his demands to halt strikes, Trump responded late Thursday.

“If you tell me that Zelenskyy is again shooting at refineries, all he’s doing is making the world oil price higher,” Trump told Newsmax’s Rob Finnerty. “I think that’s a disgrace. There’s plenty of other targets; they don’t have to hit,” Trump said.

“Zelenskyy is not a good guy for us to deal with” on the war, he said, adding that “I think they actually both would like to see it end, but I think I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult to deal with than Putin.”

As his clash escalated with Trump, Zelenskyy was in Brussels on Friday to shore up support from European allies, whom he called “real leaders” as they gathered for a crucial summit.

Ukrainian President Zelenskyy in Brussels on Friday. Geert Vanden Wijngaert / AP

Ukraine hit a Russian oil refinery Thursday after Zelenskyy said he was “done” with the truce, which Trump had announced to the apparent surprise of both sides in the war. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv reported any new strikes on Russian refineries Friday.

Trump has sought to blame Ukraine’s strikes for destabilizing the price of diesel globally, despite the impact of his own war with Iran.

But this campaign of attacks deep inside enemy territory has given Ukraine crucial leverage, sparking a major fuel crisis inside Russia.

Kyiv hoped this would give it a stronger hand at the negotiating table, but as Washington pushes for an end to the conflict it has taken a series of steps that have caused surprise and alarm among Ukraine and its backers in Europe.

Fires at an oil refinery in Moscow following a reported Ukrainian drone strike, on Sept. 20. Reuters

Last week, Trump announced a deal to buy diesel from Russia, an apparent attempt to relieve pressure at the pump for American consumers ahead of the midterm elections but which reversed years of U.S. policy. Trump then called for Kyiv to stop all strikes on Russian oil infrastructure and said Zelenskyy had to be replaced as Ukraine’s leader.

It comes amid mounting questions about whether the U.S. is still sharing critical military intelligence with Ukraine after a pair of major strikes earlier this week that Kyiv said came without a usual advance warning from its partners.

Ukraine also reported a slowing down of the Starlink satellite terminals, which are critical for its army’s communications, drone missions and aerial defenses.

Kyiv said that Starshield, the military version of the technology that is used by Ukraine’s troops, had been limited without any warning.

SpaceX chief Elon Musk, the billionaire Trump ally, said that such decisions were up to the U.S. military and ultimately Trump.

After repeated requests for comment about Musk’s statement, a senior U.S. official told NBC News that “no such request was ever made by the president.” Trump has also denied restricting military intelligence for Ukraine.

Kyiv said Thursday the Starshield service was being restored, but the episode only added to the mounting suspicion in Ukraine that the U.S. was willing to cut it off from battlefield support in order to exert pressure for a peace deal. Asked about the service on Friday, Zelenskyy said that issues were ongoing. “Has the speed been fully restored to what it was? No. Is the speed returning? Yes,” he told reporters in Brussels.

European and Ukrainian officials told NBC News they believed that the moves, coming only days after Trump eased sanctions on Russia’s diesel exports and railed against Zelenskyy, were most likely aimed at pressuring Kyiv into making concessions at the negotiating table amid the stalemate in peace talks.

The Kremlin agreed with Trump on Friday, with spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying it was clear that “Zelenskyy doesn’t want to take responsibility and move toward a peaceful resolution.”

Russia has always stated it’s open to a peace settlement but only on its own hard-line terms, which would see Ukraine ceding significant territory.

World.title: Amber Guyger, ex-police officer convicted of murder, is released on parole
World.content:
DALLAS — Amber Guyger, the former Dallas police officer who fatally shot a Black neighbor after mistakenly entering his apartment in 2018, was released from a Texas prison on parole Friday.

Guyger, 38, served seven years of the 10-year sentence handed down in October 2019 for the murder of Botham Jean 26.

She left the Christina Melton Crain Unit in Gatesville on Friday. She will spend the rest of her sentence in the community, the Texas Department of Criminal Justice said.

Robert L. Rogers, one of Guyger’s attorneys during the trial, could not be reached for comment this week. He told WFAA-TV of Dallas this month that she has a place to live and work upon her release.

“She’s been remorseful. She’s stayed remorseful. She’s still remorseful,” Rogers told the station.

Jean, an accountant at PricewaterhouseCoopers in Dallas, was watching television and eating ice cream in his living room the night of Sept. 6, 2018, when Guyger entered, prosecutors said.

A demonstrator holds a sign for Botham Jean in Revere, Mass., in 2020. Erin Clark / Boston Globe via Getty

Jean, 26, lived one floor above Guyger, who testified that she parked on the wrong floor and mistakenly entered his apartment instead of her own. Guyger said that she tried to use her key but that the door pushed open. She said she shot Jean, who she believed was a burglar, out of fear for her life.

Guyger, a four-year Dallas police veteran, was in uniform but off duty at the time. She was fired.

The shooting sparked protests and renewed discourse about racial bias in policing and the use of excessive force. Guyger is white and Jean was Black.

Guyger apologized during the trial and was hugged by Jean’s teenage brother, Brandt Jean, who said he forgave her.

Botham Jean's younger brother, Brandt Jean, hugs Guyger at the Frank Crowley Courts Building in Dallas in 2019. Tom Fox / The Dallas Morning News via Getty

Guyger’s release comes about two weeks after the Texas Board of Pardons and Paroles granted it Oct. 1. She was previously denied parole in September 2024.

Her parole was approved because she “maintained a satisfactory institutional adjustment” and participated in programs that would enhance the chances that she can keep a full-time and stable job after her release, the Board of Pardons and Paroles said in a statement. It also cited her lack of a “documented pattern of violent or assaultive arrests/convictions.”

The Dallas County District Attorney’s Office, which opposed Guyger’s release in 2024, had no comment Thursday on her parole.

A representative for the Dallas Police Department on Friday declined comment and referred to the force’s statement made Oct. 1 when the former officer was granted parole.

“The Dallas Police Department understands this decision may bring renewed attention and emotion surrounding the tragic death of Botham Jean,” the agency said then. “Our thoughts remain with the Jean family and all those impacted by his loss.”

Lee Merritt, an attorney for Jean’s family, said in an Oct. 1 statement that Guyger’s sentence “was already a fraction of what was lost.”

“Releasing Ms. Guyger after seven years makes that loss feel even smaller in the eyes of the system. It is not smaller,” Merritt said.

After the news of Guyger’s expected release emerged, Jean’s family asked for privacy in a statement through the Botham Jean Foundation.

Jean was originally from the Caribbean country of St. Lucia. In 2021, the street where the shooting happened, which is home to Dallas police headquarters, was renamed Botham Jean Boulevard.

World.title: Elon Musk shows off ‘flying’ Tesla Roadster after years of delays
World.content:
Elon Musk showed off a new vehicle prototype Thursday that can briefly launch itself into the air using rocket-inspired thrusters. The Tesla Roadster made its debut eight years after it was first announced.

The company has yet to announce a price or release date, though the Tesla and SpaceX CEO said production would not begin until 2028.

In a stunt-filled demonstration at a SpaceX testing facility in Texas, Musk told the live audience that what they were about to see “was not AI or SI.”

The vehicle, a collaboration between Tesla and SpaceX, then slowly drove up a curved ramp shaped like half of a roller coaster loop before accelerating and launching itself off the ramp, hurdling over five other Tesla vehicles and bringing itself to a soft landing in a cloud of condensation using cold-gas thrusters.

“Well, it worked!” Musk said after the stunt, adding that “it’s not necessarily a safety-optimized car.”

Tesla

Tesla says a fan-based suction system creates downforce to hold the vehicle against the road’s surface, while self-refilling cold-gas thrusters power its airborne maneuvers.

Musk quipped, “This car really sucks.”

Moments later, the car accelerated toward the same five cars and jumped 27 feet in the air, according to Tesla, while performing a barrel roll. It again brought itself down gently.

Minutes later, it sped away with a 0.81-second 0-60 mph time, according to Tesla, which is more than a second faster than the company’s current fastest time with the now-discontinued Model S Plaid. Tesla plans to offer three versions of the vehicle.

The base Roadster car, Performance, will be “road-ready,” featuring the suction system but no thrusters; the “race-ready” Thrust version will add rear-mounted thrusters for acceleration. Lastly, the “air-ready” Rocket version will be invite-only; it will seat one person and contain the cold-gas thrusters along the perimeter of the car, making it capable of the acrobatics shown in the live demonstration, according to Tesla.

The flying features raise questions about where and how customers would be allowed to use the vehicle. Musk acknowledged the Roadster might not be legal in every jurisdiction, while Tesla says the Rocket version is not approved for public roads.

The Tesla prototype leaped over a series of cars in a demonstration. Tesla

The second-generation Roadster was first unveiled in 2017, with Musk initially promising production in 2020. The company has repeatedly pushed back that timeline while continuing to accept reservations from prospective buyers.

Musk said that, when it releases, he wants it to “crack halfway to the speed of sound,” or about 383 mph, more than 150 mph faster than the current announced top speed. According to Musk, when it is released, it will be able to go 300 miles on a single charge, less than half of what he had originally promised when he announced the car.

Prospective buyers can reserve the base model for an initial deposit of $50,000, or $250,000 for the Thrust augment.

World.title: Oregon school shooter ID'd, used shotgun bought by mother, sources say
World.content:
The 16-year-old gunman who shot and killed three children and one teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday has been identified as John Griffin, two law enforcement sources briefed on the investigation told CBS News. Police say he was shot and killed by a bystander at the school.

The attacker used a shotgun purchased by his mother, law enforcement sources told CBS News.

A motive for the attack has not been provided. The suspect was from Bend, but police have not said if he had a connection to the school.

Law enforcement sources told CBS News that investigators are combing through his computer, phone, social media, search history and other online activity. They are probing whether the shooter may have been obsessed with violence, including prior mass shootings. The sources emphasized that the investigators are in the preliminary stages of their investigation.

The children killed in the shooting were ages 5, 8 and 11, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said during a news conference Thursday night.

The 5-year-old victim has been identified as Rhoam Summer, according to fundraisers and a social media post from his father.

Two other people — a 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher — were hospitalized with critical injuries.

Krantz said the gunman entered the school by "shooting at locked doors." He was pursued by a bystander, who engaged the shooter and shot and killed him, Krantz said.

The family of the bystander issued a statement Friday identifying him as Kaylub Giamanco, a Bend resident with two daughters who attend Silver Rail Elementary School.

"He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support," the family said.

Police said they responded within minutes to the 911 calls from the school and found the deceased shooter and other victims inside.

World.title: Katie Zacharia out as White House press secretary after first week
World.content:
Washington — Katie Zacharia, President Trump's new White House press secretary, is being removed from the role after her first week on the job, two U.S. officials told CBS News on Friday.

Some White House staff learned about the change from news coverage. The New York Times first reported that she had been fired.

One aide said Zacharia spent the week unusually isolated and didn't function as a press secretary.

"No one thought she was sticking around long enough to even involve her in actual decision-making," the aide said.

CBS News has reached out to Zacharia for comment but she did not immediately reply. She was seen at the White House as recently as Friday morning.

Leaving the White House shortly before news of Zacharia's departure broke, the president signaled that she might not be in the role for long, saying he told her he would "reconsider" taking the job if he were in her shoes.

"They've been so nasty to her," Mr. Trump said, referring to the press. "I said, to her, 'Honestly if I were you, I'd reconsider. You think about it. But I would reconsider. You got a beautiful husband and family.' I met the family yesterday. Beautiful kids. It's like from a picture postcard. I said, 'You should reconsider. Because you don't want to go through this.'"

The abrupt shift came one week to the day since Mr. Trump announced Zacharia as his pick to replace Karoline Leavitt, who stepped aside in August. The White House has not yet indicated who may replace Zacharia.

Zacharia's qualifications and background quickly came under scrutiny as questions arose over her resumé.

CBS News and other outlets reported that Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer over the years. She graduated from Pepperdine Law School but failed the California bar exam in 2011, a fact she acknowledged on Thursday. She told the New York Times that the president of Pepperdine University advised her at one point that she could call herself a "lawyer" but not an "attorney."

Zacharia told conservative commentator Jack Posobiec that she never described herself as an "attorney at law," and said there's a "lot of misinformation around the fact that I labeled myself a lawyer."

"I was very careful how I executed this. I never came across as someone who was an attorney at law," Zacharia said.

Zacharia's abrupt departure was reminiscent of the tenure of Anthony Scaramucci, who survived just 11 days as White House communications director during Mr. Trump's first term.

"Records are made to be broken," Scaramucci said in a post on X. "But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."

World.title: Who would oversee a flying car? We asked the DOT.
World.content:
Who has oversight of a car that flies, hovers or otherwise defies gravity? We asked Department of Transportation officials, and the answer isn't readily clear.

Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk unveiled Tesla's new Roadster Rocket, which he called a "flying car" equipped with "ultra high-pressure air tanks" — describing it as "what happens when you have a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company." The car — about a decade behind schedule — would go into production in 2028.

Technical and regulatory challenges have so far prevented the much-hyped flying car sector from getting off the ground, and Tesla's website notes that the flying model isn't approved for public road use. There's a non-flying version of the car, which would-be buyers can reserve online with a $5,000 deposit, but the Tesla website says the Rocket model with the "full flight system" will be offered by invitation only.

So, who will decide whether the Roadster is safe? There's time to work that out, but a senior Department of Transportation official, who expressed skepticism that the vehicle will actually be able to take off, acknowledged there's no clear answer.

Tesla unveils its long-delayed Roadster at a launch event in Waco, Texas, Oct. 15, 2026, in this still image taken from a handout video. Tesla/Handout via Reuters

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration typically has regulatory oversight of vehicles — though it delegates safety certification to the automaker. NHTSA has not yet responded to our request for comment.

If the Roadster is going to enter the public domain with the ability for off-ground "driving," that would seem to shift to the FAA, which regulates aircraft. The FAA tells CBS News: "The Tesla vehicle does not meet the FAA definition of an aircraft."

Thursday's Roadster demo showed the car launching from a ramp that curled over so the vehicle was upside down, appearing to defy gravity by clinging to the surface before flying off the end, and then rolling over 180 degrees midair to land on its wheels.

CBS News reached out to Tesla to ask which agencies the company is working with. We will update if we hear back.

World.title: With Tesla Roadster debut, Elon Musk shows "flying cars are real"
World.content:
Tesla CEO Elon Musk unveiled what he described as a "flying" car, equipped with thrusters, during a livestreamed event at his SpaceX rocket company's facility on Thursday.

Technical and regulatory challenges have so far prevented the much-hyped flying car sector from getting off the ground.

Musk revealed Tesla's new Roadster sports car during a launch event at a SpaceX test facility in Texas.

During the demo, which was livestreamed on Tesla's X account, the car launched from a ramp that curled over so the vehicle was upside down, appearing to defy gravity by clinging to the surface before flying off the end, and then rolled over 180 degrees midair to land on its wheels.

Tesla unveiled its long-delayed new Roadster — which took flight using high-pressure gas boosters — at a launch event in Waco, Texas, Oct. 15, 2026. Tesla/Handout via Reuters

"Flying cars are real," Musk said during the event, adding that the vehicle's "success is not guaranteed" but "it will probably work."

Musk said the car was equipped with "ultra high-pressure air tanks" to propel itself into the air.

The tech billionaire described the development as "what happens when you have a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company," referring to Tesla and SpaceX.

The vehicle would go into production in 2028, he said. Prices were not announced.

Tesla's website notes that the planned flying model is not approved for public road use.

Would-be buyers can place a reservation online, with a $5,000 deposit, for a non-flying model of the Roadster. A limited-edition Thrust model is also promised online but cannot be reserved. Tesla's website says the Rocket model, with its "full flight system," will be offered by invitation only.

"The Roadster will not move the volume or revenue needle, with production likely limited, and investors should not model it as a growth driver," Wall Street analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said in a research note. "What it does is restore the brand halo at the top of the market and put a spotlight on the engineering stack a week before the FY3Q26 print on October 21st."

Tesla unveils its long-delayed Roadster at a launch event in Waco, Texas, Oct. 15, 2026, in this still image taken from a handout video. Tesla/Handout via Reuters

It wasn't immediately clear what government agency would have oversight of the vehicle, CBS News senior transportation and national correspondent Kris Van Cleave reports. A senior U.S. Transportation Department official expressed some skepticism to CBS News that the vehicle will actually be able to take off, but acknowledged there wasn't a clear answer.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration typically has regulatory oversight of vehicles but delegates safety certification to the automaker. NHTSA didn't immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.

The Federal Aviation Administration told CBS News the vehicle doesn't meet the agency's definition of an aircraft.

The concept of flying cars has been around almost as long as motor vehicles themselves, with American aviation pioneer Glenn Curtiss debuting the first flying car prototype in 1917. But successful designs have been pursued more seriously only in recent years as electric motors and high-performance batteries have advanced.

Ives said the Roadster shows how Tesla and SpaceX can collaborate. The new vehicle "puts the Tesla and SpaceX relationship on the table in a tangible way, with propulsion, pressure-vessel, and control hardware developed at the rocket company sitting on a Tesla product, which in our view strengthens the case for the two companies operating as one engineering platform over time," he said.

Musk — a major GOP political donor known for an often close but sometimes tumultuous relationship with President Trump — has thrust his companies to the forefront of several major industries, and he continues pushing into new ones.

SpaceX announced a week ago that it had agreed to buy licenses for radio airwaves that will enable its Starlink Mobile satellite business to provide cellular service inside buildings, a move the company said would allow it to "become a major mobile carrier in the U.S."

"This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America," Musk said in an Oct. 8 social media post.

World.title: Looking for a pay bump? A "nondegree credential" can help.
World.content:
You don't have to switch jobs or earn a promotion to get a pay bump.

So-called nondegree credentials (NDCs), such as professional certifications and licenses, can boost earnings, particularly for workers without college degrees, according to research from the U.S. Census Bureau.

These credentials, which demonstrate that a worker has completed training or developed a specific skill, can pay off in the job market. NDC holders had median earnings that were 16% higher than those of workers at the same level who lacked the credentials, the Census data shows.

Stacie Haller, chief career adviser at ResumeBuilder.com, said she's steering more job seekers toward alternative credentials as some employers stop requiring that candidates hold college degrees. Such certificates or licenses demonstrate "specific skills that will put you ahead of other candidates," she told CBS News.

NDCs are certificates or licenses that signal that a worker possesses a particular qualification or competency. They include vocational and educational certificates awarded by technical colleges or trade schools that focus on job skills and career preparation.

Workers can earn certificates in a variety of fields, from food service to healthcare, according to the Census Bureau. For some people, NDCs can also offer an alternative to pursuing a college degree.

Workers with job-specific knowledge and skills can also take exams to earn certifications and licenses, which usually expire and must be renewed. Boards and associations, such as the American Nurses Association, can issue certifications, as can private firms like Google. Licenses are required for certain professions, such as cosmetologists and barbers.

Roughly 40% of workers in healthcare support, food service, farming, fishing, forestry, construction and repair occupations hold NDCs.

"This is not surprising given the extensive credentialing requirements for healthcare workers and information technology-related certifications for various software, programs and equipment," Census Bureau researchers wrote. "Farm and craft trades, like agriculture and plumbing, similarly require credentialing to work with hazardous chemicals, heavy machinery and complex systems."

Just under 40% of workers in professional occupations, including management, STEM jobs, education, legal and other roles, hold NDCs.

Haller said determining which type of credential is most valuable in a given field can require extensive research. But there's one type of qualification she recommends that every job seeker obtain — a certificate or badge that demonstrates AI competency.

"Every company is figuring out how to use AI, and if you have that experience and know how to use it in a business setting, you'll be valued," she said.

World.title: Trump casts doubt on press secretary's future
World.content:
Trump casts doubt on press secretary's future

toggle caption i Win McNamee/Getty Images

President Trump on Friday cast doubt on the future of his new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, on Friday, saying he had a discussion with her just before leaving for a campaign rally in Georgia.

"I just spoke to her about it. I said, 'Katie, is this for you?'," he told reporters. "She's been treated, I would say, pretty nastily. And I said to Katie just two minutes ago, I said, Katie, you know, you don't have to do this if you don't want."

He said he was leaving the decision up to her.

Zacharia's first official day on the job was Monday and her first briefing was Tuesday morning. She faced scrutiny both over her performance – during which she delivered a lengthy and halting opening statement read from notes and called on only three reporters – and her legal credentials.

World.title: Hot flashes, night sweats, insomnia – OB-GYNS set new rules for menopause treatment
World.content:
Hot flashes, night sweats, insomnia – OB-GYNS set new rules for menopause treatment

toggle caption i BSIP/Universal Images Group/Getty Images

For the first time since 2014, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists has updated its guidelines for the treatment of symptoms commonly associated with menopause. The doctor's group, known as ACOG, recommends hormone replacement therapy alongside certain antidepressants, nonhormonal medicines, and other treatments to address symptoms like hot flashes, insomnia and mood swings.

"What's changing is the breadth of options that we now have … And the benefit of that is that we are better equipped to be able to take an individualized approach for patients," said Catherine Cansino, MD, MPH, an obstetrician/gynecologist, chair of ACOG's Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines and co-author of the new guidance.

Sponsor Message

The guidance, released Thursday, focuses on specific menopausal symptoms and underscores that the safety of hormone replacement therapy is now "well-established," Cansino said.

In 2002, the Women's Health Initiative suggested that hormone replacement therapy increased the risk of heart disease, breast cancer, stroke and pulmonary embolism.

However, as researchers revisited that data years later, they noticed certain limitations, (including that a majority of participants were 60 years or older) making it difficult to generalize the findings to younger women experiencing menopause or perimenopause.

With more and better quality studies, physicians are able to review the evidence and make better-informed recommendations, Cansino said.

"Hormone therapy is probably the best option for symptomatic, newly menopausal women within 10 years of the final menstrual period or before the age of 60," said Robert Kauffman, MD, MSCP, a co-author of the guidelines, during a press briefing on Thursday.

In addition to hormone replacement therapy, the guidelines highlight new nonhormonal options for treating menopausal symptoms, including the drug fezolinetant, brand name Veozah, which the Food and Drug Administration approved to treat hot flashes in 2023 and elinzanetant, brand name Lynkuet, which was approved in 2025.

"What's so exciting about these treatment options is they were specifically studied based on the understanding that we have of the physiology of thermoregulation and sleep," Cansino said.

The medications work by blocking certain chemical messengers in the part of the brain that regulates body temperature and manages sleep/wake cycles, according to the guidance.

About 2 million women begin menopause each year. The average age of a woman experiencing menopause is 49.9 years, according to the guidelines. However, symptoms of menopause can begin years before a woman's final menstrual period.

Sponsor Message

The new recommendations support the use of systemic hormone replacement therapy, or HRT, with a combination of estrogen and progestogen in women with a uterus who have no contraindications to hormones.

Reasons to avoid hormone therapy include undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding, and current or past histories of certain gynecologic cancers, blood clots, stroke, heart attack, liver disease or a known or suspected pregnancy.

The reason progestogen is recommended in women with a uterus is because estrogen can stimulate growth of the uterine lining and increase the risk of endometrial cancer. Progestogen therapy helps mitigate that risk, Cansino explained.

Around half a million women have hysterectomies each year, and for women without a uterus, ACOG recommends estrogen alone.

As an alternative to estrogen-progestogen therapy, ACOG also recommends a pill, sold under the brand name Duavee, that combines estrogen and a drug called bazedoxifene. Bazedoxifene is a "selective estrogen receptor modulator," which blocks the estrogen from working in certain areas of the body, such as breast tissue, while mimicking estrogen's benefit for bone density, for instance.

Another drug recommended in the new guideline is gabapentin, an anticonvulsant typically used to treat seizures. It can also manage menopause symptoms for people who can't tolerate hormones or the other new medicines.

Cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness-based interventions, exercise, clinical hypnosis, and acupuncture can all improve some symptoms, ACOG says, however the guidelines also note that the evidence for these interventions is weaker than the evidence for HRT.

Still, patients may have their own preferences and goals, Cansino said.

"I live in California, and I have a practice where many patients don't necessarily want pharmacologic therapy," Cansino said. So, she tends to have a lot of conversations about non-pharmacologic treatment options with her patients.

"A healthy diet and regular physical exercise is going to go a long way. So let's start with that," and then discuss what other interventions to add to the regimen, she said.

Sponsor Message

Asked, in a follow-up email, whether Cansino recommended one medication or tool over another, she warned against "over-simplifying treatment based on tiers."

Just like with contraception, she noted that patients may choose a certain method, knowing that it's less effective. "As long as they understand the pros and cons, such a decision is perfectly OK."

Meanwhile, demand for HRT is already rising. Last year, the FDA scrapped the "black-box warning" on labels for certain estrogen therapies.

In recent months, estrogen products like transdermal patches have been hard for pharmacies to keep in stock.

"I think the shortage of transdermal estrogen therapy highlights the fact that we have all of this attention about hormone therapy, and not necessarily enough about other treatment options," Cansino told NPR.

She also stressed the need for patients to talk to trusted clinicians about the pros and cons of treatments and to avoid having "tunnel vision" about a single option.

The level of care that OB/GYNs provide by helping individual patients find the right treatment is one of the most important aspects of the new guidance, Cansino said.

"There's a lot of misinformation out there and exaggerated claims about hormone therapy, and so some people end up taking risks when they shouldn't," she added.

World.title: Amid talk of public execution, public opinion on death penalty is split
World.content:
Amid talk of public execution, public opinion on death penalty is split

toggle caption i Paul Hennessy/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images

U.S. public sentiment about the death penalty has come to the forefront after President Trump gave his blessing, then backtracked, to livestreaming an execution via firing squad.

That planned execution comes after two botched Tennessee lethal injections this year, where the state struggled to find veins to administer death-inducing drugs to Christa Pike and Tony Carruthers.

Speaking at a press conference a day after Pike's failed execution, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said Tennesseans were disappointed about what happened.

"The people of Tennessee have determined that the death penalty is an appropriate penalty for the most heinous crimes in this state," he said. "The people of Tennessee make that decision and my job is to make sure that those sentences are carried out."

Those Tennesseans join some two-thirds of Americans who support the death penalty for people convicted of murder, according to a Pew Research Center poll from this summer. According to PRRI, a nonpartisan nonprofit, people that favor the punishment tend to be Christian, white and vote Republican.

Sponsor Message

Daniel LaChance, a history professor at Emory University, says the overall numbers mask a wide range of opinions.

" Support for the death penalty in the United States is a mile wide and an inch deep," says LaChance, who also wrote the book "Executing Freedom: The Cultural Life of Capital Punishment in the United States."

That's because the polling is incredibly nuanced, LaChance said. When polls offer more variance in the questions, such as life without parole, 60% of Americans support that over the death penalty. The number drops even further when monetary support to the victims' family members is an option.

And separate 2025 polling from Gallup — which has been tracking support for the death penalty since 1937 — shows that 52% of Americans support the death penalty if a person is convicted of murder, the lowest share in more than 50 years.

The change in public opinion

The Death Penalty Information Center, a nonprofit that tracks the use of the death penalty but does not take a position on it, has counted 203 people since 1972 who were exonerated after being wrongfully convicted and sentenced to death.

"Those are just the ones we know about," says Robin Maher, the nonprofit's executive director. "We don't know how many innocent people were executed before we learned about their claims."

Sponsor Message

The wrongful death sentences, plus the moral efficacy, are what is swaying the public's opinion, Maher said.

"For the public to realize that the death penalty system was fallible, that it made serious mistakes, raised a lot of issues in people's minds about whether this very costly public policy, that was nonetheless rather inaccurate and unfair, should be used," Maher said.

The Pew Research Center study from July also found that while most people support the death penalty for crimes like murder, some 59% of respondents in the survey said the death penalty does not deter people from committing serious crimes – versus 39% who believe it does.

Six states were responsible for the 31 executions in 2026 — even though 27 states still legally allow the most severe form of punishment in this country. Florida led the way, with more than half of the executions this year.

Maher says that the fact that more than half the states allow capital punishment, but are issuing fewer death sentences, shows that the American people are disenchanted with the use of the death penalty.
