" More often than not, they are finding it is not the right answer to violent crime," she says. "Executions on the other hand, are the result of what a handful of elected officials in just a few states are doing."

Texas accounts for the most executions since the 1970s, while Michigan holds the title for the longest-running death penalty abolition in the U.S., after banning the practice in 1847.

Out of public sight

The planned execution by firing squad is of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist stationed at Fort Hood, Texas, who killed 13 people and wounded 32 in 2009. It's slated for December but appeals could delay it further.

While 52% of Americans support Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan's execution, 80% say his death should not be livestreamed, according to an October poll from ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos.

When Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced earlier this month that Hasan would be executed publicly, the U.S. also hadn't conducted a high-profile public execution in 90 years.

Sponsor Message

In certain parts of America, quasi-public executions drew up to 10,000 viewers in the past, said LaChance, the Emory history professor. But the growing use of medicine such as anesthesia began a negative shift in public executions.

" Pain, especially in public spaces, starts to seem scandalous," LaChance says. "It's preventable now. It starts to seem barbaric."

LaChance also said the public, especially in immigrant communities, would turn the executed into heroes. "They would claim the body and conduct little parades in Lower Manhattan, celebrating the life of the person who had been put to death," he said.

One U.S. official who spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity out of fear of retribution said President Trump was talked out of a livestream execution because it was against American values — but also because there was concern the tape would show up on Jihadi websites, leading to an increase in recruits and possible danger to U.S. forces in the Middle East.

" That's the story of the death penalty," LaChance says. "People didn't want public executions to disappear when they did. Elites did because they were becoming embarrassing carnivals."

World.title: Israeli settlers beat Palestinians and a U.S. photojournalist in West Bank attacks
World.content:
Israeli settlers beat Palestinians and a U.S. photojournalist in West Bank attacks

toggle caption i Ahmad Gharabli/AFP via Getty Images

Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians as they were harvesting olives in the occupied West Bank on Friday, injuring several people including an American photojournalist.

The Washington Post said photographer Heidi Levine was reporting in the West Bank, wearing a protective vest clearly marked as "press," when she was beaten.

"Today I was brutally attacked," Levine said in a video filmed at a hospital. "We saw in the distance, in the hilltop, I would say at least 50 masked men, slingshots. And when they came running down, I was attacked, pushed to the ground." She said "they just kept kicking me and kicking me." They also tore her cameras and phone off her.

Sponsor Message

She said medical workers rushed her in an ambulance to a hospital. Washington Post Executive Editor Matt Murray said in a statement Levine has received medical care and is safe.

"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," Murray said.

toggle caption i Leo Correa/AP

Israeli police issued a statement acknowledging reports that a foreign journalist was injured and said it would investigate the incident and "bring those involved to justice."

The U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem said it was aware and monitoring the situation. Without mentioning Levine's attack specifically, it said in a statement, "We are in regular dialogue with partners about improving stability and security in the West Bank. We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests, and convictions, of those responsible."

The Washington Post said the attack happened when Palestinians were trying to gather their olive harvest. It said settlers set Palestinian olive groves on fire and hurled stones using slingshots.

toggle caption i Ahmad Gharabli/AFP via Getty Images

There were two dozen settler attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters Friday, leaving 20 people injured, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent Society.

The attacks came as groups of Israeli settlers have stepped up their assaults on Palestinians in the West Bank. They also follow another attack earlier this month, when Israelis beat Agence France-Presse photojournalist Jaafar Ashtiyeh, as he was covering settler violence against Palestinian olive farmers in the West Bank.

Sara Qudah of the Committee to Protect Journalists said Levine's beating was not an isolated incident for journalists covering the West Bank olive harvest. "It's part of a disturbing pattern of violence and harassment against journalists regardless of their nationalities," she said. She added that the attackers have no reason to fear consequences because Israeli authorities have failed to stop them.

Sponsor Message

Palestinian Journalists Syndicate also condemned the attack as an "assault on press freedom" and violation of rules protecting journalists during conflicts.

Nuha Musleh contributed reporting from Ramallah, West Bank.

World.title: Crowds throng New Delhi and wave Indian flags amid escalating protests
World.content:
Crowds throng New Delhi and wave Indian flags amid escalating protests

toggle caption i Vipin/AP

NEW DELHI — Thousands of Indians thronged a bustling thoroughfare in the heart of the capital, waving the national flag and demanding the resignation of the country's election chief, the latest show of public dissent against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.

The protesters rallied in Connaught Place, one of New Delhi's busiest commercial districts, responding to a call by the youth "Cockroach" movement, whose leader Abhijeet Dipke was detained by police ahead of the demonstration. Protesters spanning generations joined the rally, reflecting broad public anger and intensifying pressure on the country's top election official.

Protests by the youth and opposition parties have intensified over an ongoing review of voter lists that has removed more than 130 million names since last year. Critics say the exercise is politically motivated, threatens to disenfranchise millions more, and has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims. They have demanded the resignation of election chief Gyanesh Kumar.

toggle caption i Prabhat Mehrotra/AP

The Election Commission and Prime Minister Narendra Modi's administration deny the allegations and say the revision is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries.

Sponsor Message

Friday's protest was part of a growing campaign that has put Modi's government under pressure and comes a week after a police crackdown on protesters in New Delhi.

The demonstrators vastly outnumbered the security personnel lining the road, while columns of riot police stood watch.

Police had earlier asked people not to join the rally and offered to let a small group gather to wave the national flag and sing the national anthem. In anticipation of the protests, authorities also closed Central Park, a green space surrounded by Connaught Place's white colonial-era buildings, on Friday and Saturday.

Modi has not publicly commented on the protests. Some of his party leaders have dismissed the demonstrators as "anarchists" and suggested, without offering evidence, that they are backed by foreign powers.

Police detained Dipke, the founder of the "Cockroach" movement, ahead of the demonstrations. He had urged supporters unable to travel to New Delhi to raise the flag and demonstrate in their own communities.

toggle caption i Channi Anand/AP Photo/Channi Anand/AP

A live video posted on the movement's Instagram account showed Dipke leaving a house and heading toward the street, where police officers intercepted him. After a brief exchange, officers hauled him into a police vehicle and drove away.

"Waving the tricolor (Indian flag) is not a crime," he told reporters Thursday.

Sponsor Message

The "Cockroach" movement began as an online satirical campaign this summer after India's chief justice compared unemployed young people to parasites. Many young Indians embraced the remark, adopting the cockroach as a symbol of resilience. It has since expanded into a nationwide protest movement of young people. Protests led by the group forced the resignation of Modi's education minister in July, a rare setback for the prime minister, who has been in power for more than 12 years.

It remains unclear whether the protests will grow into a wider political movement. Modi's government remains electorally strong, and anger over voter lists may not necessarily translate into support for the opposition, which has used the issue to criticize his Hindu nationalist government.

World.title: Sally Rooney's books will no longer be sold in U.K. after Palestinian Action support
World.content:
Sally Rooney's books will no longer be sold in U.K. after Palestinian Action support

toggle caption i Kin Cheung/AP

Irish author Sally Rooney has long been described as "the voice of a generation" for her best-selling novels that are ostensibly about millennial relationships but also explore deeper questions of class, gender and politics.

Now the 35-year-old writer's books will no longer be sold in the UK because of her own closely-held political beliefs. She had promised to donate the revenues to a pro-Palestinian group that the UK has designated a terrorist organization.

In a statement this week, her publisher explained:

"Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher."

Sponsor Message

"As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format," Faber said.

The move comes after Rooney — who has said she believes Israel is committing genocide in Gaza — announced last year she would be donating funds from the proceeds of her books to Palestinian Action, which was controversially banned in the U.K. under terrorism legislation.

Israel vehemently denies allegations of genocide.

UK-based Palestinian Action says on its website it uses "disruptive tactics" to target "corporate enablers of the Israeli military-industrial complex and seeks to make it impossible for these companies to profit from the oppression of Palestinians."

It has targeted facilities linked to an Israeli weapons manufacturer and, in a major security breach, last year managed to break into Britain's largest air force base. The activists spray-painted two aircraft at the base blood red, in what the group said was a protest against Britain's military support for Israel.

Palestinian Action was also responsible for vandalizing one of President Trump's golf courses in Scotland in March last year, when activists painted the course with the words "Gaza is not 4 sale." Reacting on social media , Trump called those responsible "terrorists."

toggle caption i Richard Shotwell/Invision/ AP

When the British government banned the group in July last year, it said it was on the grounds that Palestinian Action is responsible for "serious damage to property." It was the first time a terrorist designation had been given to an organization that does not call for violence against people.

Sponsor Message

"Its activity has increased in frequency and severity since the start of 2024 and its methods have become more aggressive, with its members demonstrating a willingness to use violence," the British government said at the time.

The government also said that the group's "activities meet the threshold of being concerned in terrorism as set out in the Terrorism Act 2000.," adding that it assessed "that Palestine Action commits and participates in acts of terrorism."

Free speech concerns

But critics questioned this assessment, saying it raised concerns about freedom of speech.

U.N. Human Rights Chief Volker Türk urged the U.K. government to rescind the decision, saying it "appears disproportionate and unnecessary."

"It limits the rights of many people involved with and supportive of Palestine Action who have not themselves engaged in any underlying criminal activity but rather exercised their rights to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and association," Türk said.

Amnesty International UK also raised concerns, saying "the UK has a deeply flawed and overly broad definition of terrorism."

Under the U.K. law, anyone who provides financial assistance to the group could face up to 14 years in prison.

For fear of arrest, Rooney says she has stopped traveling from her home in Ireland to the U.K. to attend award ceremonies and other events since the law came into force.

But the novelist has defended her support of Palestinian Action, saying in an opinion piece in The Irish Times last year: "if this makes me a 'supporter of terror' under UK law, so be it."

It was in that op-ed that she announced she would use the British proceeds of her work "as well as my public platform generally, to go on supporting Palestine Action and direct action against genocide in whatever way I can."

Now however, her books won't be sold in Britain at all, so there will be no further proceeds.

Sponsor Message

The Normal People author was undeterred, saying in a statement shared with NPR: "I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences."

Since the ban on Palestinian Action, several thousand people in the UK have been arrested for supporting them, mainly for carrying placards and wearing T-shirts.

The ban has been challenged in the courts, with the UK's high court ruling against it in February. A court of appeal later overturned that decision. Next month, the case heads to Britain's highest court.

World.title: Teen kills 4 at Oregon school. And, DOJ sues California over alleged noncitizens
World.content:
Teen kills 4 at Oregon school. And, DOJ sues California over alleged noncitizens

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

A teenager opened fire at an elementary school in Bend, Ore., killing three children — ages 5, 8, and 11 — and a teacher, officials confirmed. A 7-year-old and a 54-year-old were hospitalized. A bystander killed the 16-year-old suspected shooter after following him into Silver Rail Elementary School, according to local officials. The suspected shooter has not been identified. Officials say he was a resident of Bend. He used a "long gun," which is similar to a rifle or shotgun, during the attack. His connection to the school — if any — remains unclear.

toggle caption i Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty Images

🎧 The teenage suspected shooter was able to enter the school by firing at locked doors, according to the Bend Police Department. NPR's Arezou Rezvani tells Up First that something she found interesting on the Bend-La Pine Schools website was its emphasis on security protocols. They said they have secure vestibules for sign-in, ID checks for visitors and electronic buzz-in systems, but none of these measures stopped the gunman. Rezvani says police arrived at the school within minutes after the shooting started, but an unidentified community member shot the alleged shooter soon after the officer arrived.

Sponsor Message

The Justice Department is suing California to stop the state from counting ballots that the government claims are from noncitizens. Three weeks before Election Day, the DOJ provided a flash drive containing the names of 20,000 people it suspected of being noncitizens on California's voter rolls to Los Angeles County's top voting official. The DOJ gave him 48 hours to investigate the names or face a lawsuit, which was filed yesterday.



🎧 California and many election experts doubt the administration's noncitizen voting claims, citing President Trump's history of misinformation around the topic and flawed data analysis that can produce false positives, NPR's Miles Parks says. With vote-by-mail ballots already sent out for upcoming elections, the DOJ is seeking to segregate ballots linked to these claims for investigation so they don't get counted. Parks says it would be surprising if the DOJ succeeds in this lawsuit, as the Constitution clearly states that states manage elections.

Trump administration lawyers will argue today at a federal appeals court that White House papers belong to Trump rather than the American people. The case could end up in front of the conservative-leaning Supreme Court. The White House's claim comes after a series of actions during Trump's second term that challenged the limits put on the president after the Watergate scandal. For some 200 years, presidents could personally decide what to do with the papers they created in office. Then, Congress established the Presidential Records Act following disputes with Richard Nixon. Until this year, every president has followed this records law. Six months ago, the Trump administration moved to invalidate it. The move came after Trump was indicted on obstruction-of-justice charges for allegedly possessing classified documents at Mar-a-Lago, although a federal judge dismissed the case for technical reasons and the Justice Department later dropped it after Trump won reelection.

Sponsor Message

Behind the story

by Monika Evstatieva, senior producer on NPR's Investigations team

toggle caption i Collage by Jackie Lay/NPR

It all began with a tip. A colleague of mine had a friend in Ann Arbor who needed help. When I called her, she told me her elderly mom had been walking through a mall when a salesperson approached her with an eye cream sample. She went into a store called Beauty Essentials in Ann Arbor, Mich., and came out with $5,000 in skincare products she didn't want, tried to refuse, and couldn't return. But, she said, it wasn't an isolated incident. She posted on Facebook and connected with more than 30 people with complaints about the store. She asked me to look into it.

And so began an investigation that took place over more than a year. My reporting partner, Caley Fox Shannon, and I found similar complaints all over the country. We followed the trail, and found a network of mall skincare stores that systematically targeted older adults and people with disabilities across the United States. There was a link between them: one company, the California-based Mazal Group.

Over the past year, we spoke with more than 50 people, including customers who say they were taken advantage of, their family members and former employees. We looked at state and federal court lawsuits, hundreds of online reviews and nearly 500 consumer complaints we got through Freedom of Information Act requests. We went to stores selling products from Mazal Group in Virginia, Maryland and California, as well as the company's Chatsworth, Calif., headquarters.

You can read about what we found in NPR Investigations' whole report here, watch our documentary or listen on Consider This.

Weekend picks

toggle caption i Nintendo

Check out what NPR is watching, reading and listening to this weekend:

🍿 Movies: Other Mommy, starring Jessica Chastain, follows a 7-year-old who is visited by a mysterious entity that takes the form of her mother. Pop Culture Happy Hour describes it as an intense horror film filled with dark family secrets.

Sponsor Message

📺 TV: The Lowdown is back for its second season, featuring Ethan Hawke as a freelance investigative reporter entangled with a prominent Tulsa family.

📚 Books: The Two Saddest Kitchens is a comic conversation between cartoonists Roz Chast and Jason Adam Katzenstein about their fear and shame over their apartment kitchens and their disinterest in cooking.

🎵 Music: Remi Wolf's new album, Mud, emerged from a period of significant personal change, including a breakup and becoming sober. Watch her talk about it and perform some songs on World Cafe.

🎮 Gaming: NPR's James Perkins Mastromarino got to play The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time early, ahead of its Nov. 5 release. He says, "The game's poised to ensnare old fans and entice new players."

❓ Quiz: This week featured changes at the White House, a child reality star's comeback and Elon Musk. If you kept up, you might score perfectly.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Mario Tama/Getty Images

The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating suspicious mailings, some of which contained a white powdery substance, to state election officials and congressional offices. Trump has canceled the livestream of Nidal Hasan's execution. The former Army psychiatrist killed 13 people and wounded 32 at Fort Hood, Texas. The Smithsonian National Zoo welcomed five cheetah cubs this month. You can watch them grow and snuggle with their mom on a 24-hour livestream cheetah cam.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: What this bankruptcy says about AI startups
World.content:
What this bankruptcy says about AI startups

You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.

After you win the economics Nobel, what would your first act be? Buy a Corvette? Gloat to your childhood bully? For co-winner Michael Woodford, his first act was … proctor an exam. The DAY that Columbia professor Michael Woodford found out that he and Robert Hall won the economics Nobel, he returned to his class with the pithy title "Cognitive Mechanisms and Economic Behavior" to administer an exam. He was welcomed to the classroom with cheers and applause. He held up his arms in triumph.

toggle caption i Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Coming up:



Character.ai is going through bankruptcy. What can we learn from the AI startup's decline?

Why President Trump wants to import diesel fuel from Russia

Why stagflation was John Maynard Keynes' Achilles' heel

News We're Watching

When AI startups get vacuumed up, what's left behind?

What to know: Character.ai is a company that allows you to speak with a "companion" — an AI-powered fictional character, historical figure, or whatever you decide to build. It came out just before ChatGPT and quickly went viral in part thanks to its adoption on TikTok. It hit 28 million monthly active users at its peak.

Sponsor Message

Character.ai had a lot of engagement, a big customer base, lots of talent … and Google promptly picked 'em up for $2.7 billion back in 2024. But Google didn't buy the company and absorb it! No, that traditional "acquihire" model would require all sorts of legal and regulatory approvals. Instead, they hired away the founders (and other big hitters on the team) and bought the nonexclusive license to the technology, leaving the company itself behind. That's called a "reverse acquihire," and it's happened at least six times in the past two years with AI startups. Now this week, Character.ai is filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy.

toggle caption i Gabby Jones/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Why it matters: A "reverse acquihire" doesn't leave a company in the greatest position. After the Google deal, Character.ai had to change its business model away from the quite costly LLM training and toward developing AI characters. Its founders were gone. Sure, the shrunken company had $2.7 billion in the bank, but leadership was still looking to raise money as they struggled to monetize their user base.

So is the "reverse acquihire" what caused the pain? Or was it a symptom of a larger issue? Character.ai faced a mountain of litigation over alleged harm to minors plus copyright concerns from Disney. So what's left behind? A once very promising company, which Disney is very excited to pick over for parts of it for $20 million.

Sponsor Message

Will this Russian diesel deal affect price?

What's going on: President Trump signed a deal last week to get diesel from Russia in an effort to lower fuel prices ahead of the midterms. Two weeks ago, we talked in the newsletter about the potential of a diesel export ban to lower prices. It didn't happen. One week ago, we talked again about Trump issuing an executive order to defer a tax from diesel. Now, this!

It's safe to say people were surprised by the move, given Trump signed a Russian sanctions law just last month that looked to tamp down on their energy revenues. Beyond surprise, a bipartisan group of senators is openly calling for the president to rescind the deal. They said it gives Putin the funds to power his war machine and "enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians."

Will this do anything? The same bipartisan group of senators said this deal will mean "limited to no relief to Americans." Goldman Sachs estimated the release of Russian oil would affect wholesale prices by $1 to $2 per barrel. The price of a barrel of diesel is around $200. So a $1 to $2 impact? Neil Atkinson, an independent energy analyst, says, "Frankly, [it's] a rounding error. It makes no fundamental difference to the global diesel market."

What's weirder to Atkinson, though … Russia hasn't really been exporting diesel. Its refineries have been damaged, and it's literally been importing diesel to make up for shortfalls. " So where these barrels of Russian diesel are going to come from to go either to the United States or elsewhere in the global market is a bit of a mystery," said Atkinson.

Today's Indicator

The Nobel Prize that wasn't

If you HAVEN'T listened: Reporter Greg Rosalsky opens the piece describing WHAT exactly Michael Woodford and Robert Hall won the economics Nobel for. They helped shape what's known as NEW Keynesian economics by bringing microeconomic principles to the traditional models of John Maynard Keynes. BUT THEN, Greg goes on to explain that the Nobel Prize did not initially include an economics award. No, that changed when the Swedish Central Bank, the oldest central bank in the world, wanted to celebrate its 300th anniversary with a bang. They would fund a new award for economics. It's a fascinating story which you can listen to below.

Sponsor Message

If you HAVE listened: A leading philosophy of John Maynard Keynes is that governments could fight recessions by boosting spending, and deal with inflation by holding spending back. In the initial draft that didn't make it into the final episode, Greg touched on how STAGFLATION was a central thorn in the side of this concept. Specifically, back in the 1970s, during the Arab oil embargo, the U.S. dealt with the one-two punch of high unemployment and high inflation, bringing about stagflation. It challenged the Keynesian idea that when lots of people are out of work and spending less, inflation comes down. Because at that point, unemployment and inflation rose together. Isn't that nice? Greg Rosalsky writes Planet Money's newsletter … you can catch that here.

Rest of the week



In Our Spare Time

Producer Cooper Katz McKim is reading The AGI Chronicles

Man oh man, this is the page-turniest nonfiction book I've read in a while. Kevin Roose, co-host of the upcoming NPR podcast Machine Gods, formerly The New York Times' Hard Fork, tracks the handful of characters racing to make AI a commercial reality. It is far from a clear-cut story. There's no one character who came up with the idea and executed it … the existence of AI today comes down to many papers, many individual discoveries, and a whole lot of obsession. I didn't realize how much progress had been made in AI prior to 2020 and how concerned many industry leaders were about even creating AI (looking at you, Amodei) for fear of creating a super-intelligence that moves outside of human control. It's gossip-y, it's matter of fact … I would recommend.

World.title: Police release more details on fiery, fatal bus crash in Calgary
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Calgary police released more details on Friday about a fiery bus crash and explosion that resulted in three deaths.

Just after 1 p.m. on Thursday, a collision involving a Calgary transit bus in the city’s northeast Saddle Ridge neighbourhood led to a fire. Three people were declared dead at the scene, and 16 were injured.

The bus was travelling north in the 800 block of Saddletowne Circle N.E., toward 80th Avenue, near the neighbourhood's fire station. Police said they believe the bus struck a truck driving in the same direction. The truck then entered an adjacent lane, sideswiped an SUV and struck the rear of a box truck.

Meanwhile, the bus continued north and struck the rear of a sedan, pushing the car through the intersection, where it hit a truck. The bus then struck the rear of another transit bus, which continued forward itself before hitting another sedan.

During the collision between the two buses, the natural gas tanks on the second bus ignited. Police said the fire intensified within seconds, leading to an explosion and a significant fire inside the bus.

Police found three passengers dead on the second bus. While two have been identified, police said they’re still working to identify the third.

The driver of the first bus was transported to hospital with life-altering injuries. The driver of the second bus was able to exit the vehicle.

WATCH | Details on crash involving Calgary city buses: At least 3 dead in fiery crash involving 2 Calgary city buses, other vehicles | Duration closed caption 2:02 At least three people were killed, with several more injured after a chain-reaction crash involving two city buses and several other vehicles. One of the buses, which was powered by natural gas, burst into flames with over a dozen people on board.

Overall, 10 people were transported to hospital via ambulance after the crash, with one in life-threatening condition. One police officer is recovering at home from minor injuries.

Police said the other drivers in the collision were either uninjured or sustained minor injuries.

It’s too early to determine whether impairment, speed or distraction contributed to the collision, police said, but each factor remains under investigation.

World.title: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia leaving her role a week after starting it: official
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump's press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving her role a mere week after he put her in it, a White House official confirmed to CBC News.

The news broke on Friday, shortly after Trump signalled to reporters that Zacharia may be on her way out.

Trump said he'd spoken to Zacharia and that he felt she didn’t deserve what he called negative media coverage.

"I told her, 'I think you're better off being happy,'" Trump said while speaking to reporters on the White House lawn as he left for a rally in Georgia.

"I want her to have a good life. I don't want her to have a life like she's led the last three days," Trump said.

WATCH | Katie Zacharia's first briefing: New White House press secretary stumbles in first briefing | Hanomansing Live | Duration closed caption 4:00 Donald Trump's new press secretary Katie Zacharia took only three questions in her first briefing.

Trump added, "I said, 'Katie, do you need this? I don’t think you need this.'"

The president initially said he'd make a final determination later — perhaps after his campaign travel.

"When I get back, we're going to talk," he said.

Trump also said, "I told Katie, in my opinion, she was treated very unfairly," Trump said, noting that Zacharia has been "brutalized by the media."

Zacharia's short tenure has been defined by questions about her professional background and lack of polish in fielding questions from journalists.

She was a surprise choice when Trump announced her appointment on Oct. 9. She was the successor to Karoline Leavitt, the youngest-ever White House press secretary who had been part of Trump’s inner circle for years.

Zacharia came under immediate scrutiny when she appeared uncomfortable during her inaugural briefing, delivering halting remarks touting the president and his accomplishments.

She took questions from just three reporters, all from conservative-leaning or Trump-friendly outlets, and left after only about 14 minutes.

World.title: Ottawa youth accused of anti-Jewish terror plot guilty of 2 of 3 charges
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A young person charged as the alleged "co-conspirator" of a planned terrorist attack against Jewish people was found guilty Friday of two of the three charges against him.

He's convicted of committing a terrorist offence by conspiring to commit murder in late 2023 and facilitating a terrorist activity by seeking to acquire a prohibited firearm in December 2023.

Justice Kerry McVey told the Ottawa court that she was satisfied that the teen had joined a conspiracy, and that his discussions about obtaining a firearm were sincere.

"I find nothing in [the teen's] communications that reasonably suggests he was anything other than serious," she said.

He was found not guilty on a different count of facilitating terrorist activity by making available and exchanging instructional material and propaganda in late 2023.

McVey said she was not convinced beyond a reasonable doubt that the teen knew the person he was sending "unquestionably disturbing" material to was contemplating a terrorist attack.

"The issue before me is not whether the content was offensive, alarming, or extremist in nature," she said. "The question is whether the Crown has established beyond a reasonable doubt that [the teen] transmitted it for the purpose of assisting a terrorist activity."

The Crown told court they will be seeking an adult sentence.

The Ottawa resident was 15 when he was arrested in February 2024.

A second Ottawa teen was found guilty of four charges in April after an unusual one-day trial that preserves his rights to appeal.

Neither teen's name can be published due to a routine ban preventing the identities of charged youths from becoming public.

World.title: Winnipeg zoo's newest orphaned polar bear cub now has a name: Mantayo
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The first polar bear cub to arrive at Winnipeg's Assiniboine Park Zoo in nearly a decade now has a name.

The bear, believed to be about 10 or 11 months old, is now called Mantayo, zoo officials announced via social media posts on Thursday.

It's derived from Mantay-sîpî, the Cree name for the Churchill River, which literally translates to "river of strangers."

"It feels like the [name] most connected to the north in a lot of ways. So I think it's a really good choice," Lindsay Hughes, a spokesperson for the Assiniboine Park Conservancy, said Friday.

Mantayo arrived in late August, shortly after being found near his dead mother just outside Churchill. (Submitted by Assiniboine Park Conservancy)

Mantayo's name was chosen in a public poll from a list that also included Duke, Marly, and Fletcher — all names related to places in or near Churchill. They were shortlisted by students from Churchill's Duke of Marlborough School and other town residents.

"Duke" and "Marly" honoured the school, while "Fletcher" was a nod to Fletcher Lake in Wapusk National Park.

Over 12,000 votes were cast in an online poll to name the bear — "the highest number that we've really ever seen in one of our naming polls," said Hughes, noting such polls typically get about 5,000 votes.

"There was a lot of attention and a lot of love for the little cub."

The public can see Mantayo in the zoo's old bear enclosures, at the Leatherdale International Polar Bear Conservation Centre. Staff will decide if he can move into the zoo's Journey to Churchill exhibit. (Submitted by Assiniboine Park Conservancy)

Mantayo arrived in late August, shortly after being found near his dead mother just outside Churchill. T he province is still investigating how she died.

He underwent a quarantine period at the zoo's Leatherdale International Polar Bear Conservation Centre, where his care team has been building his trust, helping him adjust to his new home and being around people, Hughes said.

Mantayo made his public debut last week but remains a t the Leatherdale's cub care centre, on view in the zoo's old bear enclosures.

"He is going to stay there for a little while. He's still at a point where he has growing to do before he can meet big, grown bears," Hughes said.

Since t he zoo underwent a massive renovation, replacing those old enclosures with the Journey to Churchill exhibit and the Leatherdale centre , it has welcomed 12 bears.

The majority were found orphaned in northern Manitoba, although brothers Hudson and Humphrey were born in captivity in Toronto, and later returned to that zoo.

The only others that were not orphans were Storm — who was shipped out of Churchill after attacking a man and arrived in 2013 as a three-year-old adult — and Agee, who came to the zoo from British Columbia in 2022 as a 26-year-old retired film star . She died in 2025.

Two other orphaned bears from Manitoba, Baffin and Siku, were transferred to the Calgary Zoo in 2023 after being in Winnipeg for six years.

Baffin died in 2024 after some roughhousing with Siku crushed his trachea.

Transition needs to be 'carefully managed'

Journey to Churchill is currently home to five bears: Storm, Nanuq, York, Kaska and Willow.

"The hope is that one day [Mantayo] will be able to move in, but there's a lot of decisions to be made about which bears he might meet first and who's the best fit for him," Hughes said.

"That transition process is super, super carefully managed, so we're just taking it one day at a time at this point."

The conservation team has researched polar bear personalities, which helps identify which might be the best for Mantayo's initial greeting, she said.

Polar bears are also naturally solitary animals that come together only for breeding and when the mothers are raising cubs, so "introducing polar bears is not an easy process," Hughes said.

Another bear, Star — who arrived with her brother Blizzard in 2014 — never took to group life and now lives at the Leatherdale centre, where visitors can see her in one of the old bear enclosures.

"She really showed a bit more of an independent lifestyle … and demonstrated she was not necessarily comfortable in that space with the big bears," Hughes said.

"So the decision was made back in 2018 that she would be better off on her own with an independent home."

Blizzard lived with the large group of bears until his death in 2019.

Hudson, who was born at the Toronto Zoo in 2011 but was rejected by his mother, was the first bear to call the Journey to Churchill exhibit home. He arrived in 2013, before it was open to the public.

Humphrey followed in 2015.

Aurora was the first orphaned polar bear cub to live there. She arrived shortly after Hudson and died in 2022 following a dental procedure.

World.title: He followed a debunked conspiracy theory to claim a tax refund. So why did the CRA agree to a $40M payout?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In the summer of 2023, northern Ontario ironworker Jonathon Pearce filed bogus tax returns to the Canada Revenue Agency, falsely claiming he was owed refunds going back several years totalling more than $40 million.

Internal records obtained by CBC's the fifth estate show the agen cy did not check the veracity of the returns and two weeks later began sending out the refunds in instalments to Pearce's bank account, including a $10-million deposit on Aug. 8, 2023.

Pearce, a longtime resident of Temiskaming Shores, 500 kilometres north of Toronto, initially declined an interview.

But when fifth estate co-host Steven D'Souza knocked on his door recently, Pearce said he was as surprised as anyone when the millions landed in his personal bank account.

"I thought [the CRA] would turn around and say, 'I'm sorry, sir, this doesn't work that way.' Next thing you know, [I was] getting a refund," he said. "Well, this is an easy way to create money."

WATCH | Explaining his perspective: CBC interviews man who received more than $10M in CRA refund | Duration closed caption 1:28 When the fifth estate knocked on his door, Jonathon Pearce was initially reluctant to talk but spent more than an hour explaining his perspective as hidden cameras rolled.

A fifth estate investigation has found that Pearce is one of a growing movement of so-called "sovereign s" who believe Canada as a country does not exist. Following debunked online conspiracy theories, they have successfully duped the CRA into repeatedly handing over millions in bogus refunds, taking advantage of massive gaps in the agency's fraud detection systems.

A CRA affidavit obtained by the fifth estate shows that Pearce himself contacted the agency's call centre 10 days before he got the refund. An agency investigator who later listened to the recording stated that Pearce outlined the tax "scheme" and his conspiracy beliefs.

Despite Pearce's phone call, the agency still deposited millions in his bank account.

Watch the full documentary, "The Sovereign Swindle," from the fifth estate on YouTube or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m .

After the agency looked into how Pearce got his refund, leaked records show it identified that between May 2023 and January 2024, nearly $300 million in bogus claims were linked to the same tax scheme as Pearce. It is unclear how much was paid out.

One auditor later wrote there was no validation process in place to "verify the legitimacy" of the requested refunds before they go out.

Heather Evans was appointed commissioner of the Canada Revenue Agency on July 13, 2026. Evans declined an interview with the fifth estate. (Canadian Revenue Agency)

In a recent stateme nt to the fifth estate, the CRA said it is "unable" to know how much money in total the agency has paid out in bogus returns to sovereign citizen groups, also known as "tax protesters," because it does not track fraudulent returns by "personal views or intent."

The commissioner of the Canada Revenue Agency, Heather Evans, declined an interview.

The minister responsible for the agency, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, told the fifth estate he was unaware of the specific allegations.

"We have a robust process to make sure of the integrity of what we do at the CRA, but we'll be looking into that," he told co-host Steven D'Souza outside a recent cabinet meeting.

An in-depth review of Pearce's Facebook profile shows he follows a debunked online conspiracy theory falsely claiming that every Canadian has a secret trust set up for them when they are born worth millions. According to the fallacy circulating online, only people with specialized knowledge are able to unlock the funds.

Former CRA investigator Shawna Roy says the theory is ludicrous and that there is no pot of money assigned at birth.

"That is not a thing," she said.

The government does "not have a trust assigned to you" when you are born, Roy told the fifth estate.

Former Canada Revenue Agency investigator Shawna Roy thinks there needs to be more checks and balances at the CRA to stop bogus refunds from being sent out. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

Pearce, however, said he believes more strongly in the debunked conspiracy theory than ever because the CRA did, in fact, give him the money.

"If the CRA gives me money, who are you to f–king question it?" Pearce told D'Souza.

"As far as I'm concerned, it was between me and CRA. If CRA had a problem, they wouldn't have given me the money."

In his return, Pearce filed T4A slips, which are typically used to report extra income. In his case, Pearce did not report any income, but erroneously stated he had paid millions in taxes since 2016 and wanted it refunded.

CRA's conduct 'enraging,' says former investigator

Roy told the fifth estate Pearce's views are not based on fact or law and that he clearly filed a bogus tax return at the expense of the public purse. She said it is concerning that three years later he appears not to have been charged with tax fraud.

"I can't comprehend it, I can't make sense of it."

Roy said if the agency had done even a little due diligence, it would have known that a factory worker requesting a $40-million refund would probably not qualify for one.

"I think it's enraging."

If you have tips on this topic please email, in confidence, Harvey.Cashore@cbc.ca or fifthtips@cbc.ca or call or text 416-526-4704.

During an hour-long interview on his front porch, Pearce remained unapologetic about getting the refund, echoing anti-government and anti-tax videos he frequently reposts on his public Facebook page, including conspiracies that Western democracies are illegitimate.

The conversation took place only a few metres from Pearce's Ford F-250 truck, which he says he purchased after receiving the CRA refunds and which he then made his profile picture on Facebook.

Pearce said everyone could do what he did if they just knew how.

"If you really want to know this stuff, you really got to dig deep."

Pearce said he learned those secrets through online "sovereign" gurus who provide seminars on how not to pay tax and still get a refund from the CRA.

The CRA alleges in court documents that Teresa Wallace, left, Angela Bowolin, Bernard Yankson and Pearce are linked to bogus tax refunds. (Daniel Rofusz)

In a statement, Dave Conabree, the CRA's assistant commissioner of security, said that while he could not comment on specific cases, they were aware of schemes "promoted by individuals who reject or challenge Canada's tax system."

"The CRA takes these activities very seriously and has measures in place to detect, prevent and address fraud and non-compliance."

Still, those public court documents obtained by the fifth estate detail how the agency was aware of the ironworker's conspiracy beliefs in advance of paying the bogus refunds.

An affidavit filed in early September 2024 by the CRA in Ontario Court of Justice states that Pearce contacted the agency's call centre on July 21, 2023 — more than a week before the CRA began sending Pearce the money.

According to the affidavit, Pearce discussed "matters relating to the alleged scheme for a majority of the [July 21] call" and told the call centre "he shouldn't be paying taxes."

Yet 10 days later, on July 31, the CRA deposited the first instalment of refunds into Pearce's account for slightly less than $500,000.

Instalments stopped after bank alert

On Aug. 8, Pearce received a further $10 million. Two more scheduled instalments of $10 and $20 million for later in August were stopped after Pearce's bank alerted the agency to the unusual payments, according to internal CRA documents.

In a followup email to the fifth estate, the agency said it would not answer questions about why it began depositing millions into Pearce's account despite knowing about his conspiracy beliefs beforehand.

Despite having filed a lengthy affidavit in public court about Pearce's tax details, the media office said that the CRA itself cannot disclose individual taxpayer information and would therefore also not provide the fifth estate with recordings of Pearce's conversations with the agency's call centre.

Former CRA investigator Roy said the whole story is discouraging for honest Canadians who pay their fair share of taxes and that the $10 million-plus refund should never have been paid in the first place.

"We're paying what we're supposed to pay and then you have people who can make a complete mockery and joke out of the system and then still get away with it."

Canada is a 'corporation'

According to Carmen Celestini, a lecturer at the University of Waterloo in Waterloo, Ont., who studies conspiracy theories and disinformation, so-called sovereigns believe Canada is not a country, but rather a "corporation" — and that they can opt out.

A sovereign is "somebody who sees themselves separate from society," she told the fifth estate. "They are not part of our nation. They can create their own nation. They are not beholden to our laws."

WATCH | An inadvertent effect: Carmen Celestini responds to what the fifth estate uncovered | Duration closed caption 0:17 University of Waterloo lecturer Carmen Celestini says bogus payouts by the CRA inadvertently validate anti-democratic conspiracy theories.

Leaked internal CRA records say that, in addition to Pearce, there were 19 social insurance numbers representing other individuals involved with the specific scheme he used.

Facebook conspiracy theories

The fifth estate has learned there are networks of "sovereign" online forums, websites and social media apps, many of which sprang up after the 2020 COVID-19 lockdowns. For a fee, some of them actively instruct followers how to become "sovereign" and claim tax refunds from the CRA.

One "sovereign" website promising tax refunds is run by Angela Albright Bowolin in Kaslo, in B.C.'s southern Interior.

In her online videos, she promises to unlock sovereign secrets to members who make a "donation." On her personal Facebook page, she said "not paying taxes" is possible, and that she is "leaving that system" and that "You can, too!"

The fifth estate has learned that one of her followers is Teresa Wallace, from Silverton in B.C.'s Interior, who the CRA now alleges received a bogus $5-million tax refund in 2024. Court records show the agency is attempting to get the money back.

In an audio recording posted on Bowolin's website, Wallace and her partner, Peter Gay, who also goes by Peter Carson, credit Bowolin and her colleague, Bernard Yankson, with helping them out.

Wallace and Gay did not respond to calls and emails from the fifth estate.

Pearce, however, credits Vancouver-based sovereign guru AJ DeSwart for helping him achieve his refund fr om the CRA.

DeSwart, who has their own public Telegram channel, posted voice memos in June that there are "billions and billions" available. "I knew about this shit a long time ago."

WATCH | Following a sovereign guru: Following a Vancouver-based sovereign guru | Duration closed caption 0:13 Jonathon Pearce says AJ Deswart looked over his CRA documents before he sent them in.

Raids 'across the country'

The fifth estate has learned that after paying out tens of millions in bogus refunds, the CRA is scrambling to undo the damage — and has launched criminal investigations into at least two sovereign gurus in the Vancouver area.

DeSwart has raised concerns about those CRA investigations on Telegram.

"There are raids happening across the country with 16-plus f–king agents and a bunch of RCMP officers," DeSwart said in a Telegram voice note in June.

DeSwart declined an on-camera interview, but told the fifth estate they did not help Pearce.

Still, court records obtained by the fifth estate back up their claims about criminal investigations.

A search warrant dated May 23, 2026, authorized a CRA search of Yankson's home, alleging he and Bowolin had engaged in tax fraud by counselling "others to make false statements … on tax returns" and to "obtain refunds that they are not entitled to."

According to internal records, the CRA scrambled to recover the millions it paid Pearce, but was still searching for more than $1 million that had been spent or gone missing. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

The fifth estate reached out to both Bowolin and Yankson.

Bowolin declined to speak to the fifth estate. In an e-mail to the CBC, Bowolin says she hasn't been charged with any offence and denies any criminal wrongdoing.

In an email, Yankson said he "categorically rejects any allegation" that associates him with fraud, unlawful activities or anti-government movements, or hostility towards government institutions, including allegations made by the CRA.

Yankson has filed a lawsuit concerning the raids in Federal Court, arguing his Charter rights were violated. No court date has been scheduled.

Back in Ontario, Pearce told the fifth estate the CRA searched his home two years ago and is garnishing his wages, but believes he will never be charged.

According to internal agency records, the CRA scrambled to recover the millions it paid Pearce, but was still searching for more than $1 million that had been spent or gone missing.

"I know I haven't done anything wrong," Pearce said.

World.title: Nova Scotia to host massive data centre to power artificial intelligence
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A massive data centre to provide computing power for artificial intelligence is under pre-construction just outside Port Hawkesbury in Cape Breton.

EverWind Fuels said it will build the facility in two stages, with the first phase to come online by the end of 2027 and the second in 2028.

The company, headed by Australian-American private equity veteran Trent Vichie, had previously confirmed it has data centre ambitions, but said little else.

On Friday, EverWind released more information about its plans.

The company is building the facility and has signed an agreement with an as-yet unnamed AI company to lease the first phase for a term of at least 20 years.

The first phase would have a capacity of 95 megawatts and the second, 325 megawatts, for a total of 420 megawatts. Nova Scotia’s current electrical generating capacity is close to 3,000 megawatts.

EverWind raising $8 billion for project

EverWind said it will pay for any required upgrades to Nova Scotia’s electricity system.

“Nova Scotians should expect us to demonstrate that we can protect ratepayers, safeguard local resources and deliver lasting community benefits, and we intend to be accountable for those commitments,” Vichie said in a news release.

EverWind said it is raising $8 billion in private capital to fund the project and an additional $2 billion for four of the onshore wind farms it is planning to build.

It said those wind farms would eventually support the data centre’s electricity needs, but existing generation on the provincial grid would be the primary supply to begin. Company officials said the provincial grid operator has done a system-impact study that indicates the grid can support the first phase.

EverWind's data centre will be in Point Tupper, just outside Port Hawkesbury. (Tom Ayers/CBC)

EverWind has been trying to develop renewable energy projects in Nova Scotia for several years. It says those plans remain unchanged.

The data centre is to be built at the same site as one of EverWind’s other proposed projects — a green hydrogen and ammonia facility — in the industrial park at Point Tupper, Cape Breton.

Data centre controversies

Data centres have become a flashpoint across Canada, especially those that power AI, because they can have huge footprints and require vast amounts of energy and water for cooling. Concerns about AI’s potential impacts on jobs and dire warnings about risks to human existence also have some people pushing back.

There are some proposed data centres that would dwarf this one in size, including the Wonder Valley data centre in Alberta — the first phase of which is meant to be more than a gigawatt — but this project is still on the larger end of facilities that have been recently announced in Canada .

EverWind said it has signed on to Ottawa’s responsible data centre development principles — a set of non-binding guidelines the federal government released last month .

Trent Vichie, CEO of Everwind, spoke at the event. (Tom Ayers/CBC)

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston recently laid out similar guidelines. Both levels of government say they expect any data centre to have local benefits, minimal environmental impact and minimal water use, and for there to be no resulting power rate spikes.

“We applaud the federal and provincial governments for setting high standards for responsible development,” Vichie said in the release. “And we will continue to work with communities to ensure that our work meets their expectations.”

WATCH | Prime minister's parliamentary secretary speaks at announcement: $10 billion private investments in Nova Scotia to include AI data centre | Duration closed caption 1:03 The prime minister's parliamentary secretary, Kody Blois, says $10-billion investments in an AI computing data centre and wind projects to help power it show that Nova Scotia has set the 'conditions' to draw private sector development.

EverWind said it will use a closed-loop water-glycol system. The company’s preliminary estimate for water usage is an average of 100,000 litres per day for the first phase and 500,000 litres of water per day including both phases.

Water would be drawn from nearby Landrie Lake. The provincial regulator has approved the Landrie Lake Water Utility to withdraw 34 million litres from the lake each day, which would make EverWind’s daily requirements about one per cent of the total safe withdrawal volume.

The company promised the data centre would come with a community benefit program worth tens of millions of dollars. A specific dollar figure was not provided. Local communities and the data centre’s unnamed customer would consult on how to spend the money.

A consortium of Mi’kmaw communities, fronted by Membertou First Nation, is negotiating a nine per cent equity stake in the project.

Nova Scotia's Ecology Action Centre said the Cape Breton data centre project poses more questions than it answers.

It raised concerns about the project's scale, pointing to the province's high electricity rates, limited groundwater supplies and reliance on coal for one-third of its grid power.

"I think we have some questions about how it's going to work," said Thomas Arnason McNeil, policy advocate on grid decarbonization for the centre. "What's going to be done potentially to protect and insulate ratepayers in this case, what this could mean for grid stability and water usage — and we don't have the answer to all those questions yet."

McNeil added that while the group is reserving judgment for now, thorough impact assessments are essential before moving forward.

MORE TOP STORIES

World.title: Danielle Smith has said no to a second referendum. But that decision might not be hers to make
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Premier Danielle Smith has drawn a line in the sand, saying that she will not hold another referendum on Alberta separation should the majority of her province vote to remain in Canada.

But her statement raises questions about the fate of the original citizen’s initiative petition that called for a vote on separation — one of the first falling dominos to put Alberta on the referendum path — that remains stalled before the courts.

Should an appeal by the Alberta government and a separatist group be granted, that petition could again move forward, potentially reviving the referendum conversation, legal experts say, whether Smith wishes it to be or not.

"When it comes to the prospect of a government referendum (on holding another referendum) and a citizen’s initiative coexisting in the world, “nothing like this has happened before,” says Kathleen Mahoney, professor emerita of the faculty of law at the University of Calgary.

“We're in uncharted waters,” added Gerard Kennedy, a constitutional law professor at the University of Alberta.

The potential quagmire dates back to January, when separatist group Stay Free Alberta began gathering signatures for its petition, which wanted an unabashedly-separatist question put to the province in a constitutional referendum. The petition asked: “Do you agree that the province of Alberta should cease to be a part of Canada to become an independent state?”

But that effort was quashed by a judge who found the group had failed to consult with First Nations, a decision sharply criticized by Smith. She would ultimately announce the government would pose a referendum question of its own on the province’s relationship with Canada, on which Albertans will vote next week.

Cross Country Checkup is asking: What’s at stake for you in the Alberta referendum? What conversations are you having with friends and family? What questions do you have? Leave your comment here and we may read it or call you back for Sunday's show

Both Stay Free Alberta and the provincial government appealed the court decision that put the first petition on hold. In June, Court of Appeal Justice Alice Woolley granted a partial stay, which allowed the signatures to be counted while the appeal continued.

In July, Elections Alberta confirmed that the first petition met the bar for a successful petition, having amassed roughly 220,000 verified signatures. But it’s not clear when a final decision is expected on the appeal.

If it is ultimately allowed to proceed, “the government could find itself legally required to deal with it,” Mahoney said.

“Whether that obligation would actually force a second referendum, and how quickly, remains an open legal question.”

In an email, a spokesperson for Elections Alberta said that the government has the ability to make the final decision on most citizen’s initiatives. But the exception is proposals for constitutional referendums, such as the petition from Stay Free Alberta.

The legislation says that, should the proposal be successful, the minister “shall refer [it] to the Lieutenant Governor in Council for the purpose of a constitutional referendum.”

But even if that happened, many wild cards remain. There are still unresolved questions about when Alberta would be required to consult with Indigenous people on a proposed referendum that could affect treaty rights, Mahoney said.

The government has made recent changes to the legislation, including removing rules against having two referendums on the same topic and requiring a referendum to be held within a certain time period after a successful petition.

That means the government would have a lot of control over the timing and form of such a referendum, Kennedy says. There are also restrictions on proximity to an election, he added.

A government spokesperson declined comment, referring CBC News to the premier’s previous comments.

When asked whether his group would continue to pursue another vote even if most Albertans vote to remain next week, Jeffrey Rath, counsel for Stay Free Alberta, responded “yes” in a text, before adding four cry-laughing emojis.

World.title: U.S. Coast Guard rescues 16 people floating in the Pacific, including one with a suspected shark bite
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

At least 16 people seen floating in the Pacific Ocean off Mexico's Baja California coast were rescued in the predawn hours Friday, and authorities were searching for several others in an area frequented by smugglers transporting migrants by boat to the U.S.

Those rescued were being taken to San Diego hospitals. One person was being treated for a suspected shark bite.



The Coast Guard responded to a report of a vessel in distress at around 1 a.m. local time, authorities said.

People were found floating in the water about 225 kilometres west of Ensenada, said Petty Officer Chris Sappey. Several smuggling boats have capsized over the years in fatal accidents in the area.

"There was no sight of a vessel in the water, just straight people in the water," he said.

U.S. Coast Guard personnel work near a helicopter at Coast Guard Station San Diego on Friday. (Denis Poroy/The Associated Press)



One person rescued said as many as 27 people had been on board a boat, Sappey said. It was unclear how the people ended up in the water, and Sappey had no further details on what they were doing.

Three of the people rescued were taken to Scripps Mercy Hospital San Diego including the person with a suspected shark bite and two people treated for cold exposure, said hospital spokesperson Janice Collins.

The U.S. Coast Guard was assisting Mexican authorities in the search efforts with a helicopter, a fixed-wing plane and a cutter, Sappey said.

Messages seeking information were left for San Diego's Fire-Rescue Department.

Migrants are increasingly turning to the risky alternative offered by smugglers to travel by sea to avoid heavily guarded land borders. Small boats called pangas leave Mexico in the dead of night and sometimes travel hundreds of kilometres north.

There have been several incidents in recent years of migrant vessels capsizing en route to California.

In May 2025, at least three people died when a panga flipped off the coast, about 56 kilometres north of the U.S.-Mexico border. In 2023, eight people were killed when two migrant-smuggling boats approached a San Diego beach in heavy fog and one of them capsized in the surf. It was one of the deadliest maritime smuggling incidents in waters off the U.S. coast.

A federal judge sentenced a San Diego man to 18 years in prison in 2022 for piloting a small vessel overloaded with 32 migrants that smashed apart in powerful surf off the coast, killing three people and injuring more than two dozen.
