World.title: De la Espriella announces “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella announced an “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism” as part of his “cultural counterrevolution.”

During a visit to the Culture Ministry, De la Espriella described wokeism as “an ideological paradigm that aims to transform moral, cultural, and social foundations in the West, perverting values, family tradition, and national identity.”

According to the president, Culture Minister Paola Holguin was a general in the “cultural counterrevolution.”

Culture has an enormous capacity to shape society, and that is why the State has a moral, inescapable, and political duty to prevent cultural spaces from being taken over by social communism, which is atheist and an enemy to the fundamental values upon which the nation of Colombia is built. This is where that cultural counterrevolution will begin. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that Holguin, the daughter of a reported money launderer, would lead the “Culture War” against the “extreme left,” which has “permeated all parts of society, particularly the cultural and academic spheres.”

I want to be clear about this: we are going to wage an open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism, which is nothing more than an ideological movement that aims to transform the moral, cultural, and social foundations of the West, corrupting values, family tradition, and national identity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Earlier in the day, the National Museum removed all references to members of the exterminated Patriotic Union party, slain guerrilla leader and presidential candidate Carlos Pizarro, and the struggle for the rights of Colombia’s LGBT+ community.

References to Colombia’s former guerrilla movements was “terrorism apology, which is “exactly what we have come to confront” in an attempt to “recover pride for Colombian culture.”

Atheists, the Pizarro family and gay rights activists rejected the president’s attempts to remove them from mainstream culture.

World.title: Colombia’s first lady promises transparency over earthquake donations
World.content:
Colombia’s first lady, Ana Lucia Pineda, vowed to reveal how much money she collected and spent in response to the August 10 earthquake that affected hundreds of thousands of people.

Amid mounting public pressure about where the money had gone, Pineda went on the morning program of public television channel Nuestro Caribe to promise that her foundation, Luz y Sonrisas, will take its finances public on Friday.

Carrying a white folder, the wife of President Abelardo de la Espriella stressed that “in the foundation’s accounts rest all, absolutely all of the monies from the donations we received during the ‘Colombia One Single Heart’ campaign” that was announced on August 12.

“A lie is not going to tear down the truth of who I am or what I represent, or how my children recognize me,” said Pineda.

Luz y Sonrisas was one of three NGO’s that were promoted by the De la Espriella government to collect contributions for victims of the earthquake.

Pineda’s foundation was the only one that could receive contributions from abroad.

Earlier in the week, news program Noticias Uno revealed that her foundation that was founded on July 7 lacked the tax exemption that would allow it to accept donations, a process that usually takes months.

In a press statement, tax office DIAN subsequently said that it had granted the tax exemption to the first lady and that she could legally accept financial contributions.

Pineda did not say how much money she had received, but said that she stopped supporting the initial relief efforts “because the humanitarian aid was sufficient, it was huge.”

The first lady vowed she had saved the donations for the reconstruction phase “because I have also taken the initiative to build and return to the victims a house that is durable for the families who lost everything.”

World.title: Colombia’s opposition takes to the street to protest De la Espriella
World.content:
Despite intimidation attempts by the national government and the police, tens of thousands of people took to the streets throughout Colombia to protest the far-right government of President Abelardo De la Espriella.

The protest had been organized by social organizations, labor unions and the country’s largest opposition party, the Historic Pact.

Opposition leader Ivan Cepeda, who joined the protests in Bogota, told a reporter that the government is “exercising a mafia-style rule in the service of the worst elements of Colombian politics—the drug trade.”

Contrary to what De la Espriella is saying, this is not a government that opposes drug trafficking; it is a government that supports the drug trafficking cartels, the paramilitaries, and the ultra-conservative forces that want to destroy people’s rights, the democratic advances made by President Gustavo Petro, and the progress achieved by the popular movement over the past four years. Senator Ivan Cepeda

“That’s why we’re here; we won’t allow people’s rights to be violated or trampled upon,” said the senator.

Hours ahead of the protest, the president signed off on a decree that changed the police response to protests and accused the organizers of being “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

Human rights organizations denounced that the security forces put snipers on the roofs of buildings in Bogota and in Cali, a helicopter flew over the heads of the protesters.

The protests sought to test the waters for an even larger “national strike” that is set for November and shut down parts of the country in 2021.

“We are only warming up,” warned Cepeda, who has yet to recognize De la Espriella as Colombia’s legitimate president after losing the elections in July.

World.title: Colombia’s national strike organizers “are instigators of evil,” claims De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called labor unions and social organizations who organized anti-government protests for Wednesday “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that the security forces were instructed to allow peaceful protests, but warned the protesters that “if they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is lawfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians.”

Wednesday’s protests are a preparation for a national strike that is set to take place in November and is supported by the country’s political opposition to the far-right government.

According to the president, “those who are promoting the strike and seeking to use it to once again cause chaos and destabilize the government are the very same people who left the country bankrupt, on the brink of a blackout, with the healthcare system in intensive care, energy sovereignty compromised, and public resources plundered and looted.”

“They are instigators of evil, not fighter for freedom,” said De la Espriella.

If they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is rightfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president stressed that he would be signing a decree that regulates public protests in an attempt to avoid the chaos that erupted during massive strikes in 2019 and 2021 an killed 80 people.

De la Espriella additionally is expected to present an “anti-terrorism stature” to Congress, which could see the prosecution of protest organizers on terrorism charges, according to opposition leaders and security experts.

World.title: Colombia declares official start of El Niño, warns of strong impacts
World.content:
Colombia’s meteorological institute IDEAM officially declared the arrival of El Niño, and warned that the climate phenomenon could trigger water shortages and forest fires.

In a press statement, the IDEAM said that its “confirmation reflects the sustained warm conditions in the Pacific Ocean, which, according to the latest measurement, broke records, reaching a sea surface temperature anomaly of +3.49°C.”

The meteorological institute said it expected that this year’s “Godzilla El Niño” could continue to disrupt local climate patterns until March next year.

Initially, the weather phenomenon is expected to reduce rainfall between October and December, which is normally the rainy season in large parts of the country.

“Given this situation, and in light of the alerts issued since the beginning of the year, the national government launched an interagency response,.. with specific instructions for the responsible agencies to have their contingency plans formulated and activated by November 30 at the latest,” said the President’s Office in a statement.

The National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) coordinates response capabilities across the country and enhances the monitoring of wildfires using satellite technology. For its part, the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development is taking steps to protect strategic ecosystems, water sources, and the most vulnerable areas. President’s Office

The Mining Ministry “is implementing an emergency plan aimed at ensuring the country’s energy security by strengthening thermal power generation, securing fuel supplies, and implementing efficiency and conservation measures,” according to the President’s Office.

EPM, the local utilities firm in Medellin, has been testing the effectiveness of water rations as they fear the lack of rain could affect the hydro-electric power plants that provide the northwest of Colombia much of its energy.

Before leaving office on August 7, former President Gustavo Petro ordered the mass purchase of solar panels to reduce the pressure on the electric grid.

World.title: Colombia’s draft counterterrorist statute “creates foundations of dictatorial and inquisitorial regime:” opposition
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella’s antiterrorist statute would criminalize political opposition, social movements, and social protest, and essentially form a dictatorial regime, said opposition leader Ivan Cepeda on Wednesday.

In a video, Cepeda said that the true purpose of the bill that was leaked earlier seeks “to advance in the formation of essentially a dictatorial regime,.. which, moreover, has such a regime prostrate to drug trafficking.”

“The true objectives of this statute are to wage a crusade against the political opposition, social movements, and social protest, which is a legitimate right of citizens,” said the Senator of the Historic Pact party.

“Most of the articles in this draft are devoted to provisions that seriously undermine civil liberties, human rights, and the right to protest—not to illegal armed groups,’ according to Cepeda.

The broad legal definition of the word terrorism would allow the government to prosecute protest organizers on terrorism charges if any clashes occur between protesters and police.

This law could serve to intensify the persecution already underway in Colombia against journalists, judges, students, teachers, union members, peasants, indigenous people, people of African descent, LGBTIQ+ individuals—in short, any person or group that criticizes the citizen Abelardo de la Espriella, his government, law enforcement, or any state institution. Such a person could be taken to prison—without even prior warning—and subjected to abuse and torture. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Furthermore, the creation of a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors would allow the government to criminalize citizens based on an administrative rather than a legal basis, and “grants extraordinary powers to the president to regulate a statutory judicial procedure, specifically the expedited preventive detention proceeding,” said the opposition leader.

The aim is to criminalize social protest; the alleged crime of “manipulating the civilian population” punishes anyone who promotes, finances, organizes, or leads crowds—this is the language of the draft statute—and this is nothing less than the institutionalization of political persecution and the criminalization of free speech. Senator Ivan Cepeda

The antiterrorism statute will be facing opposition when the government tries to push the legislation through Congress, Cepeda said.

“The Historic Pact rejects this and will do whatever is necessary to ensure that the opposition’s rights and guarantees are respected,” said the opposition leader.

World.title: De la Espriella announces first $309M in aid for earthquake reconstruction
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella announced that his Miracle Fund received COP1 trillion ($309 million) for the reconstruction of western Colombia, which was hit by a 7.4M earthquake on August 10.

The announcement followed announcements by the press, which reported that the Finance Ministry allocated ($192 million) COP625 billion to the fund almost two months after the disaster.

Thank you for your patience, but please understand that the government’s bureaucratic inertia and the situation we’ve inherited are extremely complex. However, we’re working to resolve the issue, and the Milagro Fund is now up and running, thanks to God and the efforts of all the officials in this administration. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“In November, the government will move forward with contracting another COP2.7 trillion ($835 million),” Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo told Caracol Radio.

The money is the first of an estimated COP30 trillion ($9.3 billion) that would be needed to rebuild the damage to airports, roads, hospitals and other public works.

The fund will be managed by De la Espriella’s general secretary, Carlos Rios, and a handful of businessmen with ties to the administration.

The announcement followed increased unrest about the government’s lack of response to the earthquake, which affected more than 400,000 people in the Valle del Cauca and Choco province, and the coffee region.

The government’s initial response was delayed because De la Espriella suspended the process to transfer power a month before he took office on August 7.

World.title: Colombia seeks to expand definition of terrorism in draft “counterterrorism statute”
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella will present Colombia’s Congress with a comprehensive “counterterrorism statute,” which would give authorities enhanced powers to fight designated terrorist organizations.

A 116-page draft bill, which was leaked to Caracol Radio, would facilitate a military approach to combat illegal armed groups and organized crime groups, for example through air strikes.

The Antiterrorism Statute would additionally create a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors, which would make it easier to freeze the assets of suspected terrorists and their financiers.

Last but not least, the bill creates a presidential Terrorism Commissioner and a special prison regime for leaders of designated terrorist organizations.

Broader definition of terrorism

The bill seeks to change Colombia’s criminal law and define terrorism as any individual or collective conduct that produces “fear, panic or terror, creating risks, threats or the use of violence.”

A technical body of the National Security Council (NSC) will advise the council on the inclusion of organizations or individuals that ought to be included to its public National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors.

Anyone who believes he was falsely put on the terror list can challenge this decision before the NSC and the Council of State, Colombia’s top administrative court.

The bill additionally seeks that “the Council of State shall hear, in the first instance, constitutional protection lawsuits filed against the President of the Republic or against defense authorities for acts or omissions related to operations by law enforcement agencies to preserve national security.”

This would make the suspension of military operations more difficult for citizens, who now can seek legal support to protect their constitutional rights at lower courts.

The bill also creates new crimes and modifies the penalties for conduct related to “terrorism,” such as the use of drones, illegal mining, oil theft, the extraction and sale of gold, kidnapping, smuggling, human trafficking, drug trafficking, extortion, cybercrimes, election crimes, riots, and attacks on critical infrastructure.

In the case of riots, “the penalty shall be increased by up to double when the riot is directed against law enforcement units conducting operations; or is carried out in conjunction with listed terrorist organizations.”

The bill also allows Colombian authorities to investigate and prosecute terrorism, terrorism financing or providing material support for terrorist organizations abroad.

High Counterterrorism Commissioner

The bill additionally seeks to expand presidential powers to create the Office of the High Counterterrorism Commissioner.

The expanded power would additionally give De la Espriella six months to regulate the powers of this new advisory office and to appoint its first commissioner.

World.title: Royal Navy urged to replace defective Ice Patrol HMS Protector
World.content:
Royal Navy urged to replace defective Ice Patrol HMS Protector

16th Friday, October 2026 - 13:59 UTC Full article

HMS Protector role helped to maintain a sovereign, reassuring, and versatile presence in the South Atlantic and the British Antarctic Territory

The Royal Navy's only ice patrol vessel has been towed into Devonport, reportedly with a double engine failure, raising fresh concerns over how the news will be interpreted by Argentina. HMS Protector fulfils an icebreaking role to monitor the demilitarized Antarctic and support safe navigation for scientific research in challenging conditions.

According to the UK’s Defense Investment Plan and the Royal Navy, she is due to be replaced by a more modern variant.

However, the document also highlighted the importance of the military's now-missing ice patrol capability to “maintain this essential presence and support Government activities in the Arctic and around the British Antarctic Territory”.

Speaking to BFBS Forces News, retired Royal Navy Commodore Steve Prest assessed the geopolitical significance of the vessel's woes given Argentina's continued claim to the Falkland Islands.

“In those territories down in the South Atlantic, there is still some contestation over their sovereignty, and we've seen a resurgence of some of those claims from Argentina in recent weeks and months, emboldened by the political situation in America,” he said.

“Let's not forget that it was the withdrawal of one of the previous ice patrol ships that was down there, HMS Endurance that was one of the precipitating factors of the invasion of the Falklands in 1982.

”It was seen as a signal that the British weren't interested in the South Atlantic in quite the way they previously had been. So these things are important, not only in terms of the work that they do, but also the signaling that they send geo-strategically.“

Considering the international discourse, the timing of HMS Protector's defect, as described by the Royal Navy, demands new context applied to any concern over South Atlantic security.

The withdrawal of the previous icebreaker in the 1980s was seen as a retreat of the UK from some of its overseas territories and interests, Cder. Prest explained.

”I don't think we're in that situation at all now,“ he said. ”I think we're absolutely crystal clear in terms of the UK Government's policy around the sovereignty of the British South Atlantic territories, the Falkland Islands and so on.

“We have significant military assets down there, not least fast jets and air defense teams and infantry companies. So the Islands are well defended, far better defended than they were in 1982.”

He added: “I don't think we should be too alarmed. The diplomatic and Foreign Office signaling is unambiguous with regard to sovereignty of the Falkland Islands. So I don't think there's going to be the same miscalculations.

”I don't think we need to worry about that. But these ships, HMS Protector and her predecessors, had a job of work to do down there. And that job of work will need to be done.

“And we should, in my view, both for reasons of doing that job of work, but also signaling that we still take our maritime responsibilities in that part of the world seriously, replace the ship as quickly as possible.”

A Royal Navy spokesperson said: “HMS Protector has returned to her home port of Devonport while investigations into a defect take place.

”As part of the Defense Investment Plan, HMS Protector will be replaced with a more modern variant to maintain the ice patrol capability. She remains part of the fleet, and any decisions on her immediate future will be made in due course.”

World.title: The Falklands dispute threatens Argentina’s bid to join the trans-Pacific trade pact
World.content:
The Falklands dispute threatens Argentina’s bid to join the trans-Pacific trade pact

16th Friday, October 2026 - 10:07 UTC Full article

The possibility was raised in the House of Commons by Conservative MP Wendy Morton, who urged the government to prepare to oppose Argentina’s application if threats over the islands continue

The escalating dispute between Argentina and the United Kingdom over the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands has spilled into trade: London, a member of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, has not ruled out using its position to stall Argentina’s bid to join the pact, which requires the consensus of all its members. The British government says Buenos Aires’s conduct raises “very serious questions about its reliability as a partner”.

The possibility was raised in the House of Commons by Conservative MP Wendy Morton, who urged the government to prepare to oppose Argentina’s application if threats over the islands continue. Overseas Territories Minister Uma Kumaran replied that the UK does not comment publicly on accession discussions and does not speculate on possible sanctions, though it will continue to consider “all appropriate measures”. She added that Argentine attempts to obstruct economic activity in the archipelago “damage legal certainty”.

Argentina submitted its accession request on June 2. The pact brings together Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Peru, Singapore, Vietnam and the United Kingdom, the only country to have joined since its creation. Opening accession talks and issuing the final invitation both require the consensus of all members, so any one of them can block the process. Uruguay, which applied in December 2022, has been in formal negotiations since November 2025 in a working group chaired by Chile.

According to Argentina’s foreign ministry, the country’s exports to the bloc’s members reached US$16.329 billion in 2025, with a surplus of US$8.93 billion. Staying out would not halt that trade but would deprive exporters of the pact’s tariff preferences and common rules. The separate bids by Argentina and Uruguay have also caused friction in Mercosur, where Brazil has questioned their departure from joint negotiations with third countries.

The warning caps a week of escalation. On Tuesday, Argentina asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea to order a halt to Sea Lion, after the United Kingdom on October 11 rejected its claims and refused to adopt the measures it had demanded. The tribunal has yet to set a hearing date. The same day, London announced it would use its protection of trading interests legislation to prevent British companies and citizens from having to comply with Argentine sanctions; according to the British press, the measures would be in force before the end of the year. Navitas Petroleum, the project’s operator, welcomed the British backing and has said it is replacing two contractors that withdrew under Argentine pressure.

The Argentine government rejects the reliability argument. “Reliability is shown by honouring the international commitments one has undertaken,” Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno said earlier this month, arguing that the United Kingdom is exploiting disputed resources in breach of UN resolutions calling on both countries to negotiate.

World.title: Inter-American Court hears case over the April 11, 2002 killings in Caracas
World.content:
Inter-American Court hears case over the April 11, 2002 killings in Caracas

16th Friday, October 2026 - 09:59 UTC Full article

The only people convicted over the events were Metropolitan Police officers, released this year, and police commissioner Iván Simonovis, who escaped house arrest in 2019 and lives in exile

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held this week in San José, Costa Rica, the first public hearing in the case over the killings of April 11, 2002 in Caracas, when an opposition march came under gunfire near the Miraflores Palace. Nineteen people died and dozens were wounded that day, in the run-up to the coup that removed then-president Hugo Chávez from power for two days.

The case, known as Trujillo et al. v. Venezuela, was brought before the inter-American system that same year by lawyers Alfredo Romero and Gonzalo Himiob of the NGO Foro Penal. The Inter-American Commission referred it to the Court on July 9, 2024, after concluding that the Venezuelan state had violated the rights to life, personal integrity, assembly, and judicial guarantees and protection, and had not shown that the use of lethal force was legitimate, necessary or proportionate. The Court has yet to rule.

Testifying before the court, journalist Delvalle Canelón, who witnessed the shooting from a rooftop and was a witness at the trial held in Venezuela, said she had been threatened during that process by two of the men who fired from the Llaguno bridge and who were later acquitted. “There has been no investigation in Venezuela into these events. There is total impunity that persists to this day,” Romero said. Mohamed Merhi, father of Jesús Capote, an 18-year-old shot in the head, said impunity “is the result of a system that has protected those responsible”.

The only people convicted over the events were Metropolitan Police officers, released this year, and police commissioner Iván Simonovis, who escaped house arrest in 2019 and lives in exile. Although Venezuela denounced the American Convention on Human Rights in 2013, the Court retains jurisdiction over events that occurred before that date.

The parties have until November 13 to submit their final written arguments, which may include alleged victims left out of the initial file and the request for reparations.

World.title: Uruguay signs a US$5.7 billion data centre investment with Spain’s Solaria
World.content:
Uruguay signs a US$5.7 billion data centre investment with Spain’s Solaria

16th Friday, October 2026 - 09:52 UTC Full article

The project, under a free-trade-zone regime, will allocate US$5.5 billion to the data centres and US$200 million to a 350-megawatt solar plant to supply the complex

Uruguayan President Yamandú Orsi on Wednesday signed an agreement with Spanish company Solaria Energía y Medio Ambiente to develop a data centre campus of up to 500 megawatts with its own solar generation, a US$5.7 billion investment the government described as the largest in the country’s history. The opposition has demanded explanations about the company’s financial capacity and the jobs the project will create.

The project, under a free-trade-zone regime, will allocate US$5.5 billion to the data centres and US$200 million to a 350-megawatt solar plant to supply the complex. It will be built in two phases: the first, with 200 megawatts of data centres in Canelones and the solar plant in Florida; the second, with a further 300 megawatts in San José. Construction would begin in 2027. The planned 500 megawatts are equivalent to almost a tenth of Uruguay’s installed power capacity.

In a filing with Spain’s securities regulator, Solaria said the memorandum provides for a power purchase agreement of up to 40 years with state utility UTE, and that the company will develop and operate the free zone and its connection to the transmission grid. The campus, initially geared to cloud services, will use low-water cooling systems. The listed company has operated in Uruguay for almost a decade. Orsi called the agreement “a signal from Uruguay to the world” and credited state policies maintained by successive governments.

According to the government, the project will create 3,100 jobs during construction and 1,500 permanent posts. The opposition National Party said it will summon Industry Minister Fernanda Cardona to Parliament. “There is not a single private analyst, of the 10 I consulted, who tells me Solaria is in a position to take on a US$5.7 billion investment,” said Senator Sebastián Da Silva, who also questioned the employment figures.

UTE’s opposition board member, Darío Castiglioni, has requested the agreement’s documentation and the technical and legal reports supporting it. The utility’s vice president, Roberto Bentancor, said confidentiality had been maintained because Solaria had “other offers” that could have led it to drop Uruguay, and pledged to provide the information.

World.title: Argentina abstains on a Russian UN resolution on colonialism and draws criticism
World.content:
Argentina abstains on a Russian UN resolution on colonialism and draws criticism

16th Friday, October 2026 - 09:40 UTC Full article

Several speakers questioned Russia’s credibility in presenting it given its invasion of Ukraine. Brazil, Uruguay and Mexico were among the countries that voted in favour

Argentina abstained on Thursday in a vote by the UN General Assembly’s Fourth Committee on a Russian-sponsored draft on “contemporary forms of colonialism”, a decision that Buenos Aires province’s government minister, opposition figure Carlos Bianco, linked to President Javier Milei’s alignment with the United States and to Argentina’s strategy over the Falklands.

The text was approved by 85 votes to 49, with 23 abstentions, and will go to the full Assembly. According to the UN statement, it recognises that colonialism persists in contemporary forms that may be expressed through unilateral economic, financial or trade measures not in accordance with international law, a point aimed at sanctions applied by the United States and its allies. Several speakers questioned Russia’s credibility in presenting it given its invasion of Ukraine. Brazil, Uruguay and Mexico were among the countries that voted in favour.

The vote did not concern the question of the islands. Bianco argued, however, that the draft reaffirmed the 1960 Resolution 1514 on decolonisation, on which Argentina bases its sovereignty claim. “The Malvinas Question deserves a diplomacy that is not on its knees,” he wrote. “Abstaining on colonialism is not just an embarrassment. It is an act of irresponsibility.” He also asked whether it was “necessary to point out that abstaining so as not to upset Washington weakens the coherence of our position”.

The Argentine government has not explained its vote. On October 1, at the opening of the debate on eradicating colonialism in the same committee, the Argentine delegation reaffirmed its commitment to its elimination “in all its forms and manifestations” and described the case of the South Atlantic islands as a “special and particular” colonial situation.

The abstention comes amid an escalating dispute with the United Kingdom over the Sea Lion oil project, which Argentina took this week to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea. Milei called at the General Assembly in September for the resumption of sovereignty negotiations, in the same speech in which he reaffirmed his alliance with the United States.

World.title: Argentina’s bill toughening sanctions over Sea Lion stalls in Congress
World.content:
Argentina’s bill toughening sanctions over Sea Lion stalls in Congress

15th Thursday, October 2026 - 20:59 UTC Full article

The bill, sent to Congress in September, has 133 articles. The first 40 repeal the 2011 law penalising hydrocarbon exploration not authorised by Argentina and create a broader regime with fines

The National Sovereignty Defence bill, with which Javier Milei’s government seeks to toughen sanctions against those involved in exploiting resources in the Falklands, failed to secure committee approval in the Chamber of Deputies and will not reach the special session planned for October 21, according to the Argentine press. The opposition is demanding that the text, which besides sanctions reforms security, defence and intelligence, be split.

The fourth joint meeting of the Defence, Criminal Law and Foreign Affairs committees ended on Wednesday without agreement, on the same day Argentina asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea to halt the Sea Lion oil project. The ruling La Libertad Avanza party refused to break up the bill.

The bill, sent to Congress in September, has 133 articles. The first 40 repeal the 2011 law penalising hydrocarbon exploration not authorised by Argentina and create a broader regime with fines, disqualifications, a public register of offenders and prison sentences of up to 20 years. According to the British newspaper The Guardian, it extends sanctions to affiliates, financial intermediaries, shareholders and suppliers of the companies involved, and includes clauses that could reach the islands’ fishing industry. The Presidency’s Legal and Technical Secretary, María Ibarzábal Murphy, told Congress that current legislation “does not provide for fishing-related offences”.

That first part has partial opposition support, but the rest of the text is contested: the creation of a National Security Council chaired by the head of state and a protocol authorising, as a last resort, the shooting down of aircraft or sinking of vessels deemed hostile. Several blocs propose approving separately only the sanctions linked to resource exploitation.

The United Kingdom announced on Tuesday measures under its protection of trading interests legislation to prevent British companies and citizens from having to comply with Argentine rules outside Argentina’s jurisdiction.

World.title: Brazil approves a 40-hour week and two days off ten days before the runoff
World.content:
Brazil approves a 40-hour week and two days off ten days before the runoff

15th Thursday, October 2026 - 20:54 UTC Full article

Lula’s campaign hopes the reform will help him overturn the nearly two-point deficit with which he ended the first round

Brazil’s Senate on Wednesday approved, by 75 votes to one, a cut in the maximum working week from 44 to 40 hours with no reduction in pay, ending the so-called 6x1 schedule of six working days and one day off and extending to two the days off for formal-sector workers. The reform, which according to Reuters benefits some 37 million people, comes ten days before the presidential runoff between Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro.

“The end of the 6x1 schedule is more than a change in working hours. It is more time to live, to rest, to be with family, to watch your children grow, to take care of yourself,” said Lula, who made the shorter working week one of his legislative priorities and a pillar of his campaign. The measure will take effect 60 days after its promulgation.

Bolsonaro, who had expressed reservations and whose Liberal Party backed an alternative proposal, voted in favour remotely from Porto Alegre, where he was attending a campaign event. His party, the largest in Congress, has not ruled out making changes in the next legislature. The only vote against came from senator and retired general Hamilton Mourão, vice president under Jair Bolsonaro.

The initiative, championed in the lower house by deputy Erika Hilton of the Socialism and Liberty Party, began in 2023 with a TikTok video by Rick Azevedo, then a pharmacy worker, complaining about the exhaustion of working six days a week. Azevedo founded the Life Beyond Work movement and was elected a federal deputy on October 4.

Lula’s campaign hopes the reform will help him overturn the nearly two-point deficit with which he ended the first round. The latest Quaest poll gives Bolsonaro 47% and Lula 45%. The two candidates will face each other on Sunday in the campaign’s first debate, hosted by the Band network, the same day Bolsonaro has called his supporters to São Paulo’s Avenida Paulista. Lula, for his part, has promised 5,000 reais to every micro-entrepreneur.

World.title: Badenoch accuses Farage of trading Chagos for Trump’s silence on the Falklands
World.content:
Badenoch accuses Farage of trading Chagos for Trump’s silence on the Falklands

14th Wednesday, October 2026 - 22:05 UTC Full article

“There is no pride in our country in the way he talks about us. This is careless, loose talk from a man who wants to be responsible for Britain’s national security,” added Badenoch

British Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has called “humiliating” a proposal by Reform UK leader Nigel Farage to offer US President Donald Trump the Chagos archipelago in exchange for him to stop talking about the Falklands. “Giving away British territory in return for someone keeping quiet is not a deal. It is humiliating,” she told The Telegraph.

“There is no pride in our country in the way he talks about us. This is careless, loose talk from a man who wants to be responsible for Britain’s national security,” added Badenoch, who said it was “mad for someone who wants to be prime minister to say we should give away one piece of British territory just to stop an American president talking about another”. “The Chagos Islands are British. And the Falklands are British and will remain British, irrespective of what the American president says. When Donald Trump is right, we should say so. When he is wrong, we should have the confidence to tell him.”

On the US podcast The Benny Show, Farage had suggested offering Trump Diego Garcia “in perpetuity” in return for his silence on the Falklands. “I give him something. I ask for something back. He’d get that. He’s a businessman,” he said. A Reform UK spokesman said he was referring to US use of the base, “not the Chagos Islands as a whole”, and noted that Farage has opposed handing the archipelago to Mauritius.

The deal to transfer sovereignty over Chagos to Mauritius while retaining the joint Diego Garcia base was paused in April following opposition from the US administration, although Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will try to see it through. According to The Telegraph, the White House even considered buying the archipelago as an alternative.

The same newspaper notes that Trump said in August he was reviewing the US position on British sovereignty over the Falklands, amid a dispute over defence spending. Burnham assured him in September in New York that the United Kingdom would defend “the right of the Falkland Islanders to self-determination and to remain British”.

World.title: MND Local San Miguel de Allende: New forum, migrant aid and local honors
World.content:
Collaboration is on the agenda for a new community organization, a local NGO recommends ways to help migrant children, a photography exhibit from Cervantino is in town, and the city and a local Red Cross team recently won major awards.

Here’s the latest on some of the many community activities happening in and around San Miguel de Allende.

San Miguel Forum aims to link philanthropy, NGOs

A new community organization focused on addressing challenging social issues by enhancing collaborative efforts held its bilingual inaugural event Oct. 6-9 at the Instituto Allende in San Miguel.

The San Miguel Forum drew 88 invited attendees evenly split between foreigners and Mexicans, said Larry Cooley, one of the group’s cofounders. Participants included international philanthropists, implementers and policy-makers interested in scaling solutions to societal challenges in six areas.

These areas — dropout prevention, hospice/palliative care, girls’ empowerment, youth employment, and water and watersheds — were joined by the overarching issue of community cohesion, which Cooley said turned out to be the most popular theme.

“It seemed important (due to) the gentrification of San Miguel, so some sense of belonging and some sense of community identity didn’t get lost in the shuffle,” he said. “It has different manifestations in different places. With people from outside, it was different than within San Miguel.”

According to a media release issued after the inaugural event, the forum’s goal “is not simply to identify problems, but to connect people and resources around solutions that can grow to match the scale of the need while remaining locally appropriate and sustainable.”

Cooley said foreigners who attended the inaugural event had an interest in scaling efforts, as well as an interest in Mexico, and that organizers wanted to focus on issues that were “really topical for Mexico now.”

Private philanthropy is being called upon to do a lot more these days, he said, and it needs to find ways to collaborate with government and the private sector to solve societal problems at scale.

“Mexico is ahead on many, many things but is behind on that part,” Cooley said. “Philanthropy’s role at scale is trying to find ways to influence what governments are doing but doing it better and include people who are not being included.”

The San Miguel Forum is planning a second gathering in San Miguel in November 2027. For more information, contact info@sanmiguelforum.org.

Ways to help migrant children, courtesy of local NGO

The San Miguel-based Latin American Relief Fund (LARF) is recommending a number of ways to assist migrant children in both Mexico and the United States. As the group’s October newsletter discusses, thousands of children have been separated from their families when parents are either detained or deported from the U.S.

LARF recommends supporting the ABBA migrant shelter in Celaya, which will celebrate its 11th anniversary next month. ABBA provides children with education, rehabilitation and therapy, while helping them acquire the documents required to enroll in school or access other services in Mexico.

LARF also recommends these U.S. organizations that help migrant children:

The Young Center for Immigrant Children’s Rights, which supplies trained staff and volunteers to act as independent child advocates.

The Acacia Center for Justice , which provides lawyers for unaccompanied children.

Each Step Home , which funnels donations to a commissary account for families held in a Dilley, Texas, detention camp.

Centro gallery hosts photography exhibit from Cervantino

The 54th annual Cervantino Festival in Guanajuato, held Oct. 3-18, is again sharing artistic offerings with other cities in Mexico. Last year, San Miguel was a host city for live music performances and film screenings from the festival’s Cervantino Circuit schedule.

This time, a photography exhibit called “Habitando la imagen” (“Inhabiting the Image”) features the work of Yolanda Andrade Salas. Her photography reveals “the complexity of urban life, popular culture, diverse identities, and the everyday gestures that construct collective memory.”

The exhibit will be shown through Jan. 10, 2027, at Galería Meridiana 101º inside the Instituto Allende, Ancha de San Antonio 22 in Centro.

Condé Nast Traveler readers rate San Miguel 4th-best city

The 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards from Condé Nast Traveler magazine ranked San Miguel No. 4 on the list of the 10 Best Small Cities in the World. It was rated No. 5 last year.

Victoria, Canada, was No. 1 on this year’s list, followed by Puerto Vallarta; Florence, Italy; San Miguel; Lucerne, Switzerland; Dubrovnik, Croatia; Porto, Portugal; Amalfi, Italy; Venice, Italy; and San Sebastian, Spain.

San Miguel did much better in Travel + Leisure magazine’s 2026 World’s Best Awards, coming in at No. 1 for the second year in a row.

Local Red Cross team shines in national competition

Cruz Roja Mexicana, the local Mexican Red Cross organization in San Miguel, was recently named No. 7 across the country in a National Vehicular Rescue Competition. The competition tested emergency rescue team members on their rapid response, technical skill and preparedness.

Team members were challenged with a timed simulated motor vehicle accident and had to use extraction equipment, apply patient care techniques and work together to achieve the desired results. They were congratulated by municipal and community leaders for the impressive national achievement.

Cathy Siegner is an independent journalist based in San Miguel and Montana. She has journalism degrees from the University of Oregon and Northwestern University.

World.title: How one elotero’s 40-year journey reflects Mexico City’s economy
World.content:
For roughly four decades, Don Pedro’s alarm has gone off at 3 a.m., Monday through Friday.

Aiming to leave his home in Atlacomulco, in northwestern México State, by 4:30 a.m., that’s just enough time for the 54-year-old elote vendor to get ready and pack up his car before making the three-hour commute to Central de Abasto in Mexico City’s southern Iztapalapa borough.

Here, Don Pedro stocks up on everything he needs to operate his traditional elote cart for the day: mayo, grated cheese and ground chili peppers — both hot and mild.

With his ingredients in tow, Don Pedro drives, on average, another hour to the corner of Avenida Ámsterdam and Avenida Michoacán in Mexico City’s well-to-do Condesa neighborhood, the same corner he’s operated on for 40 years.

A family business

Don Pedro always knew he wanted to be an elotero, a traditional corn vendor in Mexico City. Like his father before him, he wanted to be an entrepreneur — specifically in the Condesa neighborhood, back before it was trendy.

“I arrived here at age 13 to help my dad, and now, the business is mine,” Don Pedro tells me.

Together with his nephew, Jorge, the second-generation elotero spends about three hours cooking the day’s corn, setting up his stall and chopping limes, all the while watching passersby stroll along the sidewalk.

Sometimes, José, his only son, comes along. Just as Don Pedro inherited the corn-selling business from his father, he hopes José will similarly follow in his entrepreneurial footsteps.

For now, the family wants for nothing. Since Condesa became fashionable, the business “has grown a lot,” Don Pedro says proudly. When asked exactly how much, he laughs, avoiding specifics with a simple, “We’re doing very well.”

Condesa has long been considered the “darling” of Mexico City’s Cuauhtémoc borough. Even so, it’s vastly different from when Don Pedro started selling on his corner in 1985.

“It used to be pretty quiet,” he explains. “Now, I always have customers.” He pauses for a moment to sell a cigarette to a woman. She pays him 10 pesos and leaves.

On a good day, a steady stream of customers waits to buy prepared corn, esquites and his fantastic Dorilokos — the perfect blend of various Doritos flavors, mayo, spicy sauce and corn kernels.

Although Don Pedro has his regulars, the crowds visiting Parque México just a few blocks from his stand constantly bring new faces. Even foreign customers try hard to make themselves understood, usually in the universal language of gestures and pointing.

“They even ask for the spicy chili,” Don Pedro says with a laugh.

Two economies inextricably linked

Don Pedro is just one of thousands of other street vendors who make the daily, round-trip six-hour commute from México State into Mexico City for work.

Together, they make up what’s called the “informal economy,” a hodgepodge of businesses and sectors that operate on the periphery of Mexico’s formal economy.

The International Labour Organization (ILO) recently defined the informal economy as “part of the market economy because it produces (legal) goods and services to be sold or for which another form of remuneration is received.”

But the organization added an important caveat: “They are not recognized or protected by legal and regulatory frameworks.”

The distinction has led some critics to accuse vendors like Don Pedro of evading taxes and state regulations, largely because they operate cash-only enterprises.



However, that glosses over a much larger issue.

According to an economic census produced by INEGI, Mexico’s national statistics agency, informal retail businesses in Mexico City account for 62.7% of commercial establishments, which in turn made up roughly 25% of the country’s national GDP last year. Likewise, more than 55% of Mexico’s entire workforce is employed in the informal sector.

“The informal and formal economies are part of the same mechanism,” says Dr. Yerko Castro, coordinator of the graduate program in social anthropology at the Universidad Iberoamericana (CDMX).

Put another way, they are not strictly separated, despite what Mexico’s tax system might suggest. Rather, “one feeds the other,” as Castro describes it.

The murky legality of the informal sector

It’s true that Don Pedro, like so many others in his industry, doesn’t accept bank transfers or card payments, meaning he doesn’t pay income or value-added taxes.

But that doesn’t necessarily mean it’s illegal.

According to the Federal Consumer Prosecutor’s Office (PROFECO), businesses may choose not to accept card payments or bank transfers. The office states that it is illegal to charge an additional percentage for transactions made via payment platforms, primarily because the “provider is required to clearly and visibly disclose the final price of the goods, products, or services offered to consumers.”

Viewed this way, operating a cash-only enterprise like Don Pedro’s is a strategy to save a percentage of sales that would otherwise be lost entirely.

What’s more, Don Pedro needs cash.

At the Central de Abasto, his suppliers don’t accept card payments or bank transfers, either. Consequently, he needs cash to purchase his supplies early in the morning.

This, despite the fact that Central de Abasto is one of the largest wholesale markets in Latin America — and certainly one of the most important in the capital — handling a daily volume of roughly US $24.6 million, according to Deutsche Welle.

It’s a self-perpetuating cash-only cycle that runs Mexico City.

More broadly, PROFECO does not classify the country’s informal economy as illegal in the strictest sense.

After all, street vendors like Don Pedro — or entrepreneurs selling clothing and other goods at street markets — are not selling illegal products. Serving food, offering cleaning or repair services, and not accepting bank transfers or card payments are practices permitted by Mexican authorities.

All told, it may constitute an administrative or tax violation, but does not rise to the level of a criminal offense.

At the same time, the worker does not enjoy any of the legal protections that would come with operating a formal business. To combat irregularities and provide some security for workers, the Mexico City government doles out permits for conducting business on public streets.

In practice, though, the application process, which moves through the authorities in each individual borough, is often restricted, subject to availability and a patchwork of regulations depending on location.

Between the system’s complex bureaucracy, the murky legal ground, and frankly, minimal knowledge that such permits even exist, many informal economy vendors continue to operate without one.

‘Ya nos la sabemos’

While carrying cash is becoming increasingly less common, people are willing to withdraw money to buy elotes and other Mexican street antojitos. That’s because the informal economy is stitched into the fabric of Mexican culture and everyday life.

“Ya nos la sabemos,” as we locals like to say. “We know the drill by now.”

Born and raised in Mexico City, I can confidently say that few pleasures compare to heading out just after nightfall to buy esquites for dinner. In fact, it is a quintessential experience for anyone living in the Mexican capital.

If it isn’t esquites, it’s tamales, pan de dulce de canasta, prepared potato chips from a street cart, or the countless other treats that make up the city’s informal food sector.

These are the experiences that carry significant emotional weight and form core memories, and the impact of businesses like Don Pedro’s cannot be overstated.

Aside from propping up the wider economy, as evidenced by the INEGI survey, these vendors are the glue that holds entire communities together. Come rain, thunder, lightning or wind, Mexico City’s informal retail trade supports a vast number of Mexican families, whether they be vendors or customers.

Simply put, these businesses are an integral part of the capital’s soundscape and cultural fabric, regardless of the moralizing debate over their formality.

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: US sanctions horse racing network tied to the Northeast Cartel
World.content:
In a new round of sanctions, the U.S. Department of the Treasury has targeted a horse racing enterprise allegedly run by the Cartel del Noreste (Northeast Cartel) as well as the group’s broader criminal network.

Treasury announced on Tuesday that its Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) had sanctioned four individuals and eleven entities connected to the Cartel del Noreste (CDN), a Nuevo Laredo, Tamaulipas-based criminal group that was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the U.S. government in February 2025.

“Those designated include individuals and businesses involved in quarter horse racing, construction, trucking, and the oil and gas sector, highlighting the cartel’s diverse commercial footprint,” Treasury said in a statement.

“… CDN has a long history of money laundering through the American Quarter Horse racing industry,” the department said.

“Between 2008 and 2012, Z-40 and Z-42 bought and sold racehorses with drug money and trained and raced them in the United States,” Treasury said, referring to Miguel Angel “Z-40” Treviño Morales and Óscar Omar “Z-42” Treviño Morales, brothers and founders of the CDN, which grew out of the notorious Los Zetas crime group.

“Over a 30-month period, Zetas-affiliated front persons and shell companies spent $16 million in New Mexico, Oklahoma, California, and Texas to support the operation and laundered upwards of $22 million for the cartel,” Treasury said.

“In June 2012, the U.S. Government seized 455 horses at an Oklahoma horse farm, racing venues, and training farms. CDN’s involvement in horse racing continues to this day.”

One of the 11 sanctioned entities is Club La Molienda, described by Treasury as “a horse racetrack, restaurant, and bar located on the outskirts of Nuevo Laredo that is controlled by CDN.”

“As the most prominent racetrack in Nuevo Laredo, La Molienda generates revenue for CDN, charging entrance fees for those racing their horses at the track as well as for spectators,” the department said.

“CDN leaders and members purchase horses, including many from the United States, to race at La Molienda. La Molienda is controlled by Z-40 but is ultimately overseen by various CDN leaders and associates while Z-40 is incarcerated in the United States.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by LA Molienda Race Track (@clublamolienda)

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that the sanctioning of individuals and entities connected to the CDN “exposes Cartel del Noreste’s exploitation of the horse racing sector to launder illicit proceeds and finance cartel operations.” “This action marks Treasury’s most significant effort to date to disrupt Cartel del Noreste’s financial infrastructure,” he said. Treasury said on Tuesday that “as a result of today’s action, all property and interests in property of the designated or blocked persons described above that are in the United States or in the possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to OFAC.” It noted that “OFAC coordinated on this action and previous actions against CDN with the Government of Mexico’s Financial Intelligence Unit [UIF].” OFAC has previously sanctioned individuals and entities linked to various Mexican criminal groups, including the CDN, the Jalisco New Generation Cartel and the Sinaloa Cartel.

A ‘horse racing enthusiast’ and ‘a current CDN plaza boss’ among the 4 sanctioned individuals

The four individuals sanctioned by OFAC on Tuesday are:

Gamaliel Garza García , described by Treasury as “a Mexico-based businessman, horse racing enthusiast, and an associate of CDN.” Treasury said that Garza García is involved in horse racing in both Mexico and the United States, noting that his horses race at “some of the most prestigious tracks in California and New Mexico,” and at Club La Molienda.

, described by Treasury as “a Mexico-based businessman, horse racing enthusiast, and an associate of CDN.” Treasury said that Garza García is involved in horse racing in both Mexico and the United States, noting that his horses race at “some of the most prestigious tracks in California and New Mexico,” and at Club La Molienda. Gamaliel Garza Elias , Garza Garcia’s son. Treasury said he was being designated for his involvement in CEGESA, a construction company owned by Garza García that has allegedly “been utilized by CDN to funnel money to election campaigns of CDN’s preferred political candidates.” Treasury said that Garza Elias has “delivered cash to fund election campaigns for CDN’s preferred political candidates in Mexico.”

, Garza Garcia’s son. Treasury said he was being designated for his involvement in CEGESA, a construction company owned by Garza García that has allegedly “been utilized by CDN to funnel money to election campaigns of CDN’s preferred political candidates.” Treasury said that Garza Elias has “delivered cash to fund election campaigns for CDN’s preferred political candidates in Mexico.” Pablo César Guajardo Álvarez , identified by Treasury as “a current CDN plaza boss of Nuevo Laredo and former leader of CDN’s sicarios.” Treasury said that Guajardo was arrested in 2020 for his connection to the January 4, 2017, assassination of Ricardo Martínez Chávez, a high-ranking law enforcement official in Tamaulipas, and four other public servants, “but has since been released.” It also said he has “been involved in arms trafficking on behalf of CDN.”

, identified by Treasury as “a current CDN plaza boss of Nuevo Laredo and former leader of CDN’s sicarios.” Treasury said that Guajardo was arrested in 2020 for his connection to the January 4, 2017, assassination of Ricardo Martínez Chávez, a high-ranking law enforcement official in Tamaulipas, and four other public servants, “but has since been released.” It also said he has “been involved in arms trafficking on behalf of CDN.” Francisco Javier Inzunza Partida, described by Treasury as “a dispatcher for Tamex.” Treasury said that Tamex Leasing (or Tamex Logistics) is a “Tamaulipas-based trucking company involved in the smuggling of narcotics into the United States.”

Like Club La Molienda, Tamex is one of the 11 entities sanctioned by OFAC, most of which are located in Tamaulipas.

The other nine are all owned, controlled or otherwise linked to Garza García. They include various construction and fuel and gas companies as well as a concrete company and a “Quarter Horse racing barn” in Nuevo León.

In addition to allegedly funneling money to “election campaigns of CDN’s preferred political candidates,” CEGESA has “corruptly obtained government contracts and then sub-contracted that work to CDN-affiliated individuals,” according to Treasury.

“CEGESA is a major recipient of government contracts in the north of the country, including from the governments of the municipality of Nuevo Laredo and the state of Tamaulipas,” the department said.

Treasury said that Garza Garcia also controls Cuadra San Dibanh, “an Anahuac, Nuevo León-based Quarter Horse racing barn.”

“Cuadra San Dibanh frequently races at La Molienda and other major racetracks throughout Mexico,” the department said.

With regard to Tamex, Treasury said that the company’s truck yard in Nuevo Laredo “has been the originator of at least two cocaine shipments bound for the United States.”

In its statement, Treasury also said that “CDN’s stronghold sits directly across the border from Laredo, Texas, the busiest port of entry (POE) on the southern border, where nearly 40 percent of all commercial traffic between the United States and Mexico crosses.”

The U.S. department said that the cartel’s “deep entrenchment in cross-border industries, combined with CDN’s ability to infiltrate local governments, steer public contracts, and manipulate regional elections, undermines legitimate authority and destabilizes communities on both sides of the border.”

World.title: A Tamaulipas teen built a fire extinguisher that puts out flames using sound
World.content:
A 17-year-old from the northeastern state of Tamaulipas is competing at an international science fair in Indonesia this week with a device she spent a year developing — a fire extinguisher that snuffs out small flames with sound instead of water or chemicals.

Ángela Karime Venegas Hernández is representing Mexico at the International Science and Invention Fair with Vortex Tech, a prototype developed with the help of her uncle, José Arturo Hernández Muñoz.

Her school, CETis 78 in Altamira, Tamaulipas, announced her participation in the fair being held this week at the University of Indonesia in Depok, near Jakarta.

Photographs shared by Mexico’s federal technical education agency showed Venegas wearing traditional Mexican clothing at the fair.

Venegas told the newspaper El País that a video of a large, roughly 4-meter (13-foot) sonic cannon extinguishing a flame — with air movement, not water or chemicals — inspired her to investigate whether she could build a smaller device.

She and her uncle, who holds a master’s degree in science, according to the Tamaulipas Education Ministry, spent about a year developing five prototypes, building on earlier experiments by others.

Just to create the first prototype — one that could extinguish a candle — took two months, not including preliminary research, she told the newspaper.

Vortex Tech uses a 12-volt battery, a frequency generator set to 30 hertz, an amplifier and a speaker. A modified bucket channels the output toward a flame.

According to Venegas’ explanation, the sound generates swirling rings of air that disrupt the oxygen supply sustaining combustion, extinguishing small flames within seconds.

The technology remains experimental. The newspaper El Universal reported that it works on small, nearby flames and does not replace conventional extinguishers for large fires.

Tamaulipas education officials said the project also includes thermal sensors designed to detect a developing fire and automatically activate the sound-based extinguishing system.

The state Education Ministry said Venegas advanced through regional, state and national competitions before qualifying for Indonesia. It also pledged support for her and her uncle/adviser’s participation.

With reports from El País, El Heraldo de México and El Universal

World.title: 2,500-year-old astronomical observatory in Puebla confirmed to be the oldest in Mexico
World.content:
A pre-Hispanic solar observatory in the municipality of Teteles de Ávila Castillo in the Sierra Norte region of Puebla has been confirmed to be the oldest in Mexico, dating back more than 2,500 years.

According to research carried out by the National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), a monumental architectural complex named “Grupo E” functioned as a solar astronomical observatory and is the oldest of its kind in Mexico.

Researchers believe the settlement’s inhabitants incorporated astronomical observations into the planning of their ceremonial buildings more than two millennia ago.

Heritage Daily —a digital publication specializing in archaeology, anthropology and palaeontology — says the discovery “provides remarkable evidence of sophisticated astronomical knowledge among ancient Mesoamerican civilizations.”

INAH says it is the first discovery of its kind outside the Maya region and is comparable to the observatory at the archaeological site of Uaxactún in Petén, Guatemala, which has been identified as the first and defining archetype for ancient Maya astronomical observation complexes.

While both the Uaxactún and Teteles complexes are believed to date to the Middle Preclassic (from 1200 to 400 BCE.), the Uaxactún structure is approximately twice the size of the one in Puebla.

Researchers have confirmed that the original layout of the “Group E” settlement (also known as Tetelihtic) and the orientation of its pyramidal structures are based on an understanding of celestial bodies.

Archaeologist Alberto Diez Barroso said the ancient settlement is an outstanding example of pre-Hispanic urban planning — shaped by the observation of the surrounding landscape, such as the nearby mountain peaks, as well as the astronomical horizon — making it “a significant point of reference for Mesoamerican studies in this field.”

Tetelihtic consists of a quadrangular courtyard flanked by two platforms at its eastern and western ends. The eastern platform is elongated (90 m from south to north by 40 m from east to west), while the western structure is smaller (46 m from north to south by 27 m from east to west) and served as an observation point.

The elongated platform does not mark the equinoxes at its center, however.

“It apparently served to establish the beginning of the pre-Hispanic Mesoamerican calendar in February and the harvest period in October, making it a complex and unique feature,” Diez said.

However, the eastern platform did function as a solar calendar; observations have confirmed that, from its front, one can track the sun’s path at dawn during the equinoxes and solstices.

Archaeologists believe the finding could provide insights into the cultural relationship between the Huastec and Maya groups during the early stages of human settlement in the Sierra Norte as it serves to confirm the Maya ethnolinguistic roots of the Huastec groups.

A Maya presence at Teteles may date back as far as 3,000 years — a possibility suggested by the Puebla observatory.

With reports from INAH, Heritage Daily and Ambas Manos

World.title: Mexico targets cheap Chinese bicycles with six-month anti-dumping duty
World.content:
Mexico has imposed a provisional anti-dumping duty of US $68.60 per unit on adult bicycles originating from China, after the Economy Ministry preliminarily determined that Chinese bicycles were being sold below fair market value, harming domestic manufacturers.

The measure, which took effect on Oct. 13, will remain in place for six months and will apply to adult bicycles with a wheel size larger than 20 inches, including urban and mountain models, with or without gears, as well as unassembled units. Electric bicycles and racing or road bikes are excluded from the measure.

The decision traced back to an anti-dumping investigation requested in April 2025 by the National Association of Bicycle Manufacturers and the companies Mercurio, Veloci, Benotto and Línea Siete. The investigation formally began in August of that year.

According to preliminary results, Chinese bicycles accounted for 95% of Mexico’s imports of adult bicycles in 2024. Apparent national consumption of Chinese bicycles rose from 53% in 2022 to 61% in 2024, while the average price of imports fell 35% during that period.

In 2024, Chinese bicycles cost 27% less than their domestic counterparts. According to the Economy Ministry, this difference pressured the Mexican industry to reduce prices by 4% to stay competitive.

As more low-cost Chinese bicycles entered the country, Mexican manufacturers saw a significant drop in business. The Economy Ministry found that between 2022 and 2024, adult bicycle production fell by 34% and domestic sales declined by 32%. Meanwhile, employment dropped by 29%.

Sales revenue in the domestic market fell by 36% in the same period, while the industry’s operating profits swung into the red, a 111% drop. These figures led investigators to conclude that low-priced Chinese imports caused material harm to Mexican manufacturers.

During the six months that the preliminary duty will remain in effect, interested parties may submit evidence for or against the measures, while the investigation continues to determine whether to establish more permanent duties.

The provisional anti-dumping duty is part of a broader trend toward increased trade protection in Mexico. According to data from the Economy Ministry, imports falling under the 1,463 tariff classifications subject to new levies — approved in December 2025 — declined by 23% between January and May 2026, compared to the same period the previous year.

China, the primary supplier of the goods subject to duties, was the hardest hit, as its tariffed goods fell by 28% — from $10.1 billion to $7.2 billion.

With reports from Milenio and Diario de Tabasco

World.title: American Airlines is the latest carrier to drop service to Tulum
World.content:
American Airlines is dropping flights from Miami to the Yucatán Peninsula destination of Tulum as part of its cutback of several international routes, including its Charlotte-Los Cabos service.

American (AA) — the largest U.S. airline by passenger numbers — joins other major carriers, including Aeroméxico and Volaris, in dropping or pausing routes to the resort town on the state of Quintana Roo’s Caribbean coast.

AA had already announced that its Miami-Tulum route would be on seasonal pause through Nov. 19, after which it would continue again until Dec. 1. The current plan is to then resume service one last time from Dec. 17 to January 5, 2027, before stopping it completely.

Los Cabos is also slated for service cuts

AA ended its service to Tulum from Charlotte, North Carolina, in February, 2025, less than a year after its launch. Next year, the only AA route from the U.S. to Tulum will be from or through the Dallas/Fort Worth hub.

American has also announced plans to remove its Charlotte-San José del Cabo route from its future schedule, after its current seasonal pause. The route was originally planned to return to normal operations in November, but the schedule now reportedly shows only sporadic operations.

That limited service will end in August of 2027. A possible motive for the discontinuation is that the route’s flights on average were just 73.69% full between June 2025 and June 2026.

With reports from Simple Flying

World.title: Rachel death toll rises to 8 in Baja California as newly formed Hurricane Trudy heads for Jalisco coast
World.content:
Listen to this article

While Pacific Coast residents are still reeling from the passage of Polo, Rachel and Simon, the newly formed Hurricane Trudy threatens to bring more chaos and disruption to the region.

Eight deaths have been attributed to Hurricane Rachel, while at least four people remain missing and the military has been actively carrying out search and rescue operations. And Simon, lurking near the Jalisco coast south of the tip of the Baja California Peninsula, is expected to remain a Category 1 hurricane through Friday.

In light of the devastation, President Claudia Sheinbaum on Thursday activated the Defense Ministry’s DN-III emergency protection plan and the Navy’s “Plan Marina.”

Sheinbaum also ordered the Interior Ministry to stay in close contact with the Baja California governor in order to provide any support that may be needed, especially as Simon is expected to move toward the peninsula on Saturday.

Last month, Polo — the second most-intense Pacific hurricane on record — made consecutive landfalls on the peninsula and then mainland Mexico on Sept. 29.

Now comes Trudy, which became a hurricane before dawn Thursday.

The storm system was located about 300 miles (480 kilometers) southwest of Acapulco and 445 miles (720 km) south-southeast of Manzanillo, Colima, while registering maximum sustained winds of 75 mph (120 km/h), with gusts of 93 mph (150 km/h).

According to the U.S. National Hurricane Center (NHC), Trudy is undergoing a period of rapid intensification as it moves northwest at 9 mph (15 km/h) and is expected to bring heavy rains to Oaxaca and Guerrero today (Thursday).

Forecast models project it will become a major hurricane as it approaches the coast of southwestern and west-central Mexico this weekend, bringing rainfall of 4 to 8 inches (101 to 203 millimeters) through the weekend across Colima and Jalisco states.

Meanwhile, Simon remains virtually “frozen” a few hundred kilometers west-southwest of Cabo Corrientes, Jalisco, and is expected to continue orbiting in place with sustained winds of 75 mph (120 km/h) and gusts of 95 mph (150 km/h).

Sustained winds were about 130 miles (210 kilometers) per hour as the week began, and the storm’s inner core was brushing up against the Jalisco coast.

The topography of the Sierra Madre mountains appeared to temper Simon’s intensity and shrink the size of its wind field, the NHC said. Still, as the storm system weakened from a Category 4 to Category 1 it delivered heavy rain and flooding to coastal areas, including the port city of Manzanillo, Colima.

With reports from La Jornada, The Associated Press, El Economista, Meteored and CNN en Español

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Brazil’s president, and Flávio Bolsonaro, senator for Rio de Janeiro, are tied at 50% of valid votes each in a new PoderData/Aya poll released on Friday, 16 October. The poll lands in the final stretch of the Brazil election 2026, with the runoff on Sunday, 25 October.

From Six Points to Zero in Eight Days

On 8 October the same poll had Flávio ahead 53% to 47%, CNN Brasil reported. On 13 October it was 51% to 49%, and on 16 October it is 50% to 50%.

Both candidates sit well inside the 1.8-point margin of error, so the poll cannot say who is ahead. Terra noted that the Senate approved a constitutional amendment ending the 6×1 work schedule, under which many employees work six days and rest one, while the interviews were running, though the poll does not show whether it moved voters.

Other pollsters still show a small Flávio edge. A CNT/MDA poll published the same Friday had him at 50.5% to Lula’s 49.5%, and Datafolha had him at 51% to 49% on 15 October.

What It Means for US Readers

A dead heat means Brazilian stocks, the real and US-listed shares of Brazilian companies can swing on each new survey until 25 October. Our tracker lets you compare pollsters in one place.

For US trade and politics, the winner sets Brazil’s course with Washington for the next four years. A tie inside the margin of error leaves both outcomes open.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, an online prediction market, bettors give Flávio Bolsonaro a 76.6% chance of winning the 25 October runoff and Lula 22.5% (16 October, 2:47 p.m. ET). The “Brazil Presidential Election” market has drawn about US$184.8 million in total bets, and we track it on our Brazil election odds page.

What Is Not Known

Terra reported at 7:30 a.m. ET that Poder360’s text did not include total votes, meaning the shares of blank, null and undecided voters. We therefore report valid votes only.

It is also not known whether the Senate vote moved any voters during the interviews. A poll measures opinion on the days of fieldwork and does not forecast the result.

On 8 October Flávio led 53% to 47%, and on 13 October 51% to 49%. His lead has gone from six points to zero.

The margin of error is 1.8 percentage points at a 95% confidence level. The survey interviewed 3,000 voters by telephone on 13 to 15 October.

What are valid votes?

Valid votes leave out blank and spoiled ballots. The electoral court reports results this way, so pollsters publish it too.

When is Brazil’s runoff?

Brazilians vote on Sunday, 25 October, nine days after this poll was published. The winner serves a four-year term as president.
