World.title: Belize participates in Small States Forum at World Bank Group and International Monetary Fund Annual Meetings
World.content:
Belize participates in Small States Forum at World Bank Group and International Monetary Fund Annual Meetings

By Zoila Palma: Today, Prime Minister John Briceño and Minister of Economic Transformation Dr. Osmond Martinez participated in the Small States Forum in Thailand, as part of the World Bank Group and International Monetary Fund (IMF) Annual Meetings.

The Forum serves as a vital platform for small nations like Belize to champion greater access to development financing, strengthen climate resilience, advance economic transformation and promote sustainable growth.

“Belize remains committed to amplifying its voice internationally, building strategic partnerships and unlocking opportunities that pave the way for a stronger, more resilient, and prosperous nation,” the Ministry noted.

World.title: Young talented performer Khaylin Reynolds who died while performing on stage to be laid to rest
World.content:
Young talented performer Khaylin Reynolds who died while performing on stage to be laid to rest

By Zoila Palma: Young performer Khaylin Reynolds, whose life was tragically cut short after she collapsed while performing on stage in Copper Bank Village, Corozal District, will be laid to rest on Sunday, October 18, in Esperanza Village, Cayo District.

On Saturday night, Reynolds reportedly collapsed while performing with the band during a live event.

The Youth Connection Band has since extended condolences to her family and friends.

“Thank you K, for everything….

Last night we had the opportunity to see you perform with us and give your all, not knowing it was your last performance,” the band said.

The music community has also extended sympathies on Reynolds passing.

“On behalf of the Gilharry 7 Band, we join in mourning the passing of Khaylin, a talented singer whose life and gift of music deserve to be remembered with love and respect. It is heartbreaking to know that someone who once shared her voice with the world is no longer with us,” Gilharry 7 expressed.

Reynolds’ funeral service is scheduled for 11:00 a.m. on Sunday, October 18, at the church next to the Reynolds residence in Esperanza Village.

A wake will be held at the family residence, located next to Joan Garbutt Stadium in Esperanza, on Saturday night, October 17.

Family and friends are expected to attend, and contributions toward the funeral arrangements will be appreciated, the family said.

World.title: Over 15,000 pounds of beef and pork worth $80,000 lost as truck goes up in flames in Sandhill
World.content:
Over 15,000 pounds of beef and pork worth $80,000 lost as truck goes up in flames in Sandhill

By Zoila Palma: Reports to Breaking Belize News indicate that more than 15,000 pounds of beef and pork were lost this morning after a truck transporting the meat caught fire in Sandhill Village.

The incident reportedly occurred along the Philip Goldson Highway.

The meat is valued at more than $80,000, while the damage to the truck and trailer is estimated at an additional $50,000, bringing the reported total losses to approximately $130,000.

World.title: Minister of Agriculture highlights Innovation, Food Security and support for farmers on World Food Day
World.content:
Minister of Agriculture highlights Innovation, Food Security and support for farmers on World Food Day

By Zoila Palma: Minister of Agriculture and Food Security Rodwell Ferguson is calling for greater investment in agricultural innovation, sustainable farming and stronger food systems as Belize joins the international community in observing World Food Day.

Speaking at the World Food Day celebration at Chunox St. Viator Vocational High School, Ferguson highlighted this year’s theme, “Innovate Today. Nourish Tomorrow,” emphasizing the need to ensure that agricultural technologies and proven solutions are accessible, affordable and suited to the needs of local farmers.

Ferguson pointed to the global hunger challenge, noting that approximately 645 million people faced hunger in 2025, while about one in three people worldwide could not afford a healthy diet. “Hunger is not inevitable,” the Minister said.

However, he noted that many small-scale producers, particularly women and young people, continue to face barriers to financing, technology, infrastructure, information and markets.

Ferguson highlighted innovations that can help farmers make better decisions and use resources more efficiently, including digital services that provide weather forecasts and market prices, animal disease surveillance systems, soil sensors and precision irrigation.

Ferguson also reiterated the importance of sustainable agriculture, protecting the environment and ensuring access to safe, nutritious and affordable food. He said the Ministry continues to work with development partners and social partners while reaching out to rural and urban communities, particularly vulnerable populations, to improve food security and food quality.

The Minister of Agriculture recognized farmers and food suppliers for their essential role in bringing food from farms to consumers, even amid global crises.

He encouraged continued support for agriculture, emphasizing that decisions and innovations made today will influence food security for future generations.

World.title: Chunox St. Viator Vocational High School hosts World Food Day celebration
World.content:
Chunox St. Viator Vocational High School hosts World Food Day celebration

By Zoila Palma: Chunox St. Viator Vocational High School hosted World Food Day celebration today bringing attention to the importance of food security, sustainable agriculture and innovation in ensuring a better food future for all.

This year’s theme, “Innovate Today. Nourish Tomorrow,” highlights the need to embrace agricultural technologies, promote environmentally responsible farming practices and improve access to safe, nutritious and affordable food.

The observance also recognized the essential contributions of farmers and food suppliers who help ensure food reaches communities across the country.

Minister of Agriculture Rodwell Ferguson, addressed the gathering, emphasizing the need for greater adoption of agricultural innovations and stronger support for farmers.

He noted that in 2025, approximately 645 million people worldwide faced hunger, while about one in three people could not afford a healthy diet. Ferguson stressed that governments, communities, businesses and agricultural institutions must work together to strengthen food systems and ensure innovations reach those who need them most.

Minister Ferguson also commended St. Viator for its commitment to agriculture and encouraged the school to continue involving students in the sector. “I am also happy to see St. Viator seems to be keen on transforming lives by continuing the practice of agriculture within its curriculum,” Ferguson said.

He further expressed hope that infrastructure investments made by his Ministry would be properly maintained, stating, “I hope to see the infrastructure investments my ministry has made in the same or better condition than today in the next 6 months, and even next year.”

World.title: Agriculture Minister commends Belize’s farmers for keeping food on the table
World.content:
Agriculture Minister commends Belize’s farmers for keeping food on the table

By Zoila Palma: Minister of Agriculture Rodwell Ferguson has recognized Belize’s farmers and food suppliers for their continued efforts to ensure food reaches consumers despite global crises and challenges affecting the agricultural sector.

Speaking during the World Food Day celebration at Chunox St. Viator Vocational High School this morning, Ferguson said farmers play a vital role in strengthening national food security, supporting livelihoods and protecting the environment.

He emphasized that the work of agricultural producers remains essential to getting food from farms to consumers.

“On the topic of agrifood systems, today it is just as important to recognize our heroes: farmers and food suppliers who labor throughout the food system – who ensure that food makes its way from Farm to table even amidst the dangers of the world’s crises,” Ferguson said.

“Farmers keep on providing food and we ought to recognize them,” he added.

He also stated, “It is their actions that shape our future by producing nutritious foods and securing our environment for a better life.”

The Minister concluded his recognition of the sector with the words, “Thank you, farmers.”

Ferguson said the Ministry of Agriculture continues working to improve food security, food quality and affordability while conserving the environment.

He noted that the Ministry pursues these goals through collaboration with development partners, engagement with social partners and outreach to rural and urban communities, with priority given to vulnerable populations.

World.title: Minister of Agriculture urges greater use of Agricultural innovation during World Food Day event
World.content:
Minister of Agriculture urges greater use of Agricultural innovation during World Food Day event

By Zoila Palma: Minister of Agriculture Rodwell Ferguson is calling for greater adoption of agricultural innovations to strengthen food security and improve access to nutritious food in Belize and around the world.

Speaking at the World Food Day observance at Chunox St. Viator Vocational High School, Ferguson highlighted this year’s theme, “Innovate Today. Nourish Tomorrow,” emphasizing the importance of investing in sustainable food systems and ensuring that proven technologies reach the farmers and communities that need them.

“Hunger is not inevitable,” Ferguson said.

He noted that in 2025, approximately 645 million people faced hunger, while about one in three people worldwide could not afford a healthy diet.

“The challenge is not a shortage of innovation, but a shortage of adoption on the scale,” the Minister said.

He also noted that “Digital advisory services can give farmers access to weather forecasts, market prices and tailored guidance,” while “Soil moisture and nutrient sensors and precision irrigation can help farmers use resources and inputs more efficiently.”

Ferguson stressed that small-scale producers, particularly women and young people, continue to face barriers such as limited access to financing, technology, infrastructure, information and markets.

He said stronger collaboration among governments, scientific institutions, private businesses, producer organizations and communities is necessary to ensure agricultural innovations become affordable and practical solutions for local farmers.

World.title: UN Caribbean: 645 million people faced hunger in 2025 despite global food production
World.content:
UN Caribbean: 645 million people faced hunger in 2025 despite global food production

By Zoila Palma: The world produces enough food to feed everyone, yet an estimated 645 million people faced hunger in 2025, while nearly one in three people could not afford a healthy diet, UN Caribbean noted.

On World Food Day, observed on October 16, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) is highlighting the role of innovation in addressing food insecurity and building sustainable food systems.

This year’s theme, “Innovate today. Nourish tomorrow,” emphasizes how science, technology and traditional knowledge can help improve food production and distribution. Innovations range from digital tools and improved seed varieties to farming practices and the knowledge of farmers, fishers and Indigenous communities.

The FAO noted that innovation can transform how food is produced, stored, transported and marketed. The organization stresses that combining scientific advances with local expertise can help make agrifood systems more stable, inclusive and resilient, while preventive measures can reduce risks before food crises occur.

The FAO also emphasizes that addressing global hunger requires collective action, investment and partnerships among governments, businesses, research institutions and communities.

World.title: ‘Deeply troubling’: JTA alarmed as 15 Kingston High teachers get termination letters
World.content:
LaSonja Harrison, JTA President

More than a dozen teachers at Kingston High School have been issued termination letters by the institution’s Board of Management, a move described by Jamaica Teachers’ Association (JTA) president La Sonja Harrison as “deeply troubling” and “extremely egregious”.

Observer Online understands that 15 teachers, some of whom have been employed at the institution for more than a year, received the letters following a recent board meeting. The letters were signed by the chairman of the school board Carlton Brown and Acting Principal Sashauna Gordon.

Brown told Observer Online that the separations were based on assessments and the performance of the teachers.

“We had a situation where we did have some separations based on assessments, outcomes, and performance, and it’s not fully completed yet. That’s as much as I can say right now,” he said.

However, the school’s principal, Jermaine Loutin, described the affected educators as excellent teachers who deserved permanent appointments, also pointing to the performance of one teacher whose subject area, he said, recorded a 100 per cent pass rate over the past three years.

Loutin, who is currently on vacation leave, said he had recommended that approximately 32 teachers be granted permanent appointments at the board’s last meeting in June. He said he subsequently learnt that the board had met and issued termination letters to some teachers.

“Most of these teachers, when I say most, 99 per cent of them are excellent teachers who are due their permanent appointment,” Loutin said. “I have seen some of the letters that teachers have sent to me, but I would have expressed to them that I have nothing to do with this.

“My recommendation for them was for them to be made permanent, so I cannot say why the board would have made that decision,” the principal said.

He further alleged an ongoing challenge of recommendations submitted by the principal to the board being disregarded.

“I cannot say why the board would have made that decision. But I know that the matter has been reported to the JTA, and the matter has also been reported to the Ministry of Education, and they are conducting their investigation,” Loutin shared.

Termination letters seen by Observer Online were all dated October 6, 2026 and stated that the teachers’ employment would end on October 21.

The letters, issued by the school’s Board of Management, said the decision followed a review of the teachers’ personnel file, appraisal records, attendance and punctuality, as well as assessment outcomes for classes taught between December 2025 and June 2026.

The board said the school’s administration would discuss arrangements for ending the teachers’ employment, including outstanding compensation, applicable benefits and the return of school property.

JTA president La Sonja Harrison said the association became aware of the matter last Friday after the affected teachers lodged complaints with its South-East Regional Office.

She said the association has since raised the issue at its monthly meeting with the Ministry of Education and is awaiting the outcome of a meeting between the ministry and the school’s board chairman scheduled for next Wednesday.

“To our understanding, the teachers would have been engaged for more than a year, and so, having received the letter, the situation is very concerning, egregious to our mind in some case, but as we said, we are awaiting to see what are the outcomes, deliberations, talks, what is coming out of those conversations with the board, and then the association will take it further,” she said.

“It is a very deeply troubling matter, extremely egregious if you ask me, but we are awaiting since the ministry assured us that they will be having a meeting on Wednesday concerning the same,” she continued.

The JTA president further pointed to provisions under the Code of Regulations for Teachers governing the termination of teachers’ services.

“Just as when persons complain that the teachers leave and should give at least three months’ notice. The teachers should receive notice, and the teachers have to receive notice at a particular time because the code tells you that the teacher is engaged and, over a period of a year, three terms, we would carry out the necessary supervisory matters and then engage in an appraisal and terming before the end of the third term, if it is that the school will continue with the services of the teacher or not,” Harrison said.

Minister of Education and Youth Senator Dana Morris Dixon told Observer Online that she had been informed of the matter and has since instructed Permanent Secretary Dr Kasan Troupe to investigate the development.

She said an update will be provided after receiving the investigation report.

World.title: JCF will not be intimidated, Blake declares after deadly Sligoville attack
World.content:
Police Commissioner Dr Kevin Blake

ST CATHERINE, Jamaica — Commissioner of Police Dr Kevin Blake has vowed that the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) will not retreat in its fight against criminal gangs following Friday morning’s deadly gun attack on police personnel in Sligoville, St Catherine, which left one officer dead and another critically injured.

In a strongly worded statement, Blake condemned the attack, declaring that the police would intensify their efforts to dismantle criminal networks responsible for violence across the island.

“Let there be no misunderstanding. The Jamaica Constabulary Force will not be intimidated. We will not retreat and we will not relent,” Blake declared.

“Those responsible and the criminal networks that enable them will be pursued, dismantled and be brought to justice. There can be no community ceded to gunmen, no safe haven for gangs, no territory beyond the reach of the law,” he added.

The deceased officer has been identified as Corporal Trevoy Shaw, who was attached to the JCF’s Special Operations unit.

Another policeman, who sustained gunshot wounds to the head, is undergoing surgery, while several other police personnel and a young girl were also injured during the confrontation.

The girl is reportedly in serious but stable condition.

READ: UPDATE: Two men killed after gun battle with police in Sligoville

Reports are that about 5:15 am, a team from the JCF’s Special Operations unit was conducting an operation in the Five Miles area of Sligoville in search of wanted men.

The officers were reportedly clearing a building on a premises when they came under heavy gunfire from two men who had barricaded themselves inside a house with other occupants.

Both gunmen were subsequently killed during the confrontation.

According to Blake, the officers were pursuing a high-risk target linked to violent crime when they came under sustained gunfire.

“This tragedy lays bare the brutal conditions our officers confront daily, pursuing the most violent elements in our society, so that Jamaicans can live without fear,” the commissioner said.

“We expect every officer we deploy to return home safely. Today, that expectation was shattered,” he added.

Blake also expressed condolences to the family of the fallen corporal and pledged the force’s support for the injured officer and his relatives.

“We mourn with the family of our fallen colleague and stand firmly with the family of our injured member,” he said.

Despite the tragedy, the police commissioner maintained that the JCF remains resolute in its efforts to confront violent criminals.

“Our resolve is undiminished, our duty unchanged. We grieve, but we will act,” Blake declared.

World.title: Court injunction blocks PNP bid to take control of Clarendon Municipal Corporation
World.content:
CLARENDON, Jamaica — An interim injunction has blocked the People’s National Party’s (PNP) bid to take control of the Clarendon Municipal Corporation, following a Supreme Court order presented during a special meeting of the council on Friday.

The court order barred the council from debating or voting on key agenda items relating to the proposed removal of Mayor Joel Williams and Deputy Mayor Clivalee Mundle.

The development comes amid political tensions at the municipal corporation following the announcement by Councillor for the May Pen North Division, Tanya-Lee Williams that she intends to leave the Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) and join the PNP.

Williams reportedly attempted to cross the floor during Thursday’s sitting of the municipal corporation. However, the move was ruled inadmissible after she failed to follow the correct procedure under the council’s standing orders, resulting in the adjournment of the meeting.

In a statement on Thursday, the JLP said it had taken note of Williams’ announcement but had not received a formal resignation letter from the councillor.

The party said processes had been activated to facilitate her expulsion.

READ: JLP moves to expel councillor after announced defection to PNP

World.title: No final for JC as ISSA upholds Walker Cup ban
World.content:
Jamone Lyle (second right) and his Jamaica College teammates celebrate a goal in their Walker Cup semi-final against Mona High on Saturday, October 10, 2026. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The Inter-Secondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) has upheld its ban on Jamaica College (JC), rejecting the school’s appeal after it was removed from the Walker Cup for using an ineligible player.

ISSA imposed the sanctions over the eligibility of footballer Jamone Lyle on October 13, days before the Walker Cup final set for Friday, October 16.

The decision was shared via press release Friday morning, with ISSA indicating the Executive Committee has upheld all decisions made by the disciplinary committee.

JC Board of Management Chairman Lance Hylton said the appeal had been lodged within 24 hours of the ruling, describing the penalties as “unsupportable, extreme and excessive”.

READ: JC appeals ISSA sanctions over Jamone Lyle, says procedure was unfair

The sanctions followed a ruling that JC fielded an ineligible player after Lyle was found to have a professional contract with Waterhouse Football Club, making him ineligible for schoolboy football under ISSA regulations.

JC was subsequently removed from the Walker Cup, banned from next year’s competition and ordered to forfeit its Manning Cup second-round match against St Catherine, which it had won 3-2. The game result was reversed to a 3-0 victory for St Catherine.

The decision also paved the way for Kingston College (KC) to face Mona High in Friday’s Walker Cup final, after Mona lost to JC in the semi-final on penalties.

World.title: UPDATE: Two men killed after gun battle with police in Sligoville
World.content:
ST CATHERINE, Jamaica — The two men who barricaded themselves inside a house with other occupants and engaged policemen in a gun battle in Sligoville, St Catherine, on Friday have been killed.

The morning shoot-out left one policeman dead and several other police personnel and a young girl injured.

The deceased officer has been identified as Corporal Trevoy Shaw, who was attached to the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s (JCF) Special Operations unit.

Another policeman, who sustained gunshot wounds to the head, is undergoing surgery. The injured girl is reported to be in serious but stable condition.

The confrontation began about 5:15 am when a team from the JCF’s Special Operations unit carried out an operation in the Five Miles area of Sligoville in search of wanted men.

The cops were reportedly clearing a building on a premises when they came under gunfire from the two men, who had barricaded themselves inside the house with other occupants.

A strong police presence remains in the area as investigations continue.

READ: Cop killed, others injured in Sligoville gun battle

— Llewellyn Wynter

World.title: Cop killed, others injured in Sligoville gun battle
World.content:
ST CATHERINE, Jamaica — An ongoing gun battle in Sligoville, St Catherine, has left several cops injured and at least one lawman killed, according to reports reaching Observer Online.

The Observer understands that the incident began about 5:15 am on Friday when a team from the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s (JCF) Special Operations unit was conducting an operation in the Five Miles area of Sligoville in search of wanted men.

The cops were reportedly clearing a building on a premises when they came under gunfire from two men who had barricaded themselves inside the house among other occupants.

During the exchange, a young girl who was inside the building reportedly sustained gunshot injuries. It is understood that she managed to escape from the house and was taken to hospital by a police team.

Sources described her condition as serious but stable.

Members of the JCF’s SWAT Team, Area 5 Area Fugitive Apprehension Team (AFAT), the Jamaica Defence Force (JDF) and other police personnel are on the scene as the operation continues.

More information to come.

— Llewellyn Wynter

World.title: DOMESTIC DISPUTE TURNS FATAL
World.content:
Nesta Anderson, a window maker and disc jockey who reportedly committed suicide after stabbing his wife who was taken hospital where she is said to be battling for life.

SAVANNA-LA-MAR, Westmoreland — The usually quiet community of New Market Oval in Savanna- la-Mar has been left in shock following a violent family dispute that left a nurse battling for life in hospital and her husband dead.

The husband, Nesta Anderson, a window maker and disc jockey, was from a neighbouring community. Police report that the couple had been involved in a dispute at their home when the woman was allegedly stabbed by Anderson.

Following the attack, Anderson used a ratchet knife to inflict stab wounds to his abdomen about 10:30 am Thursday.

He was rushed to hospital where he was pronounced dead. The Jamaica Observer was told that the couple, who had been together for more than a decade, has three young children.

Unconfirmed reports suggest the children witnessed the incident. When the Observer visited the community, police were processing the scene, while residents shied away from speaking publicly about the matter.

President of the Cooke Street Benevolent Society Bishop O’Neil Russell said he spoke with Anderson just a few days ago and that the incident came as a complete shock as the family was known to be quiet.

“We had a conversation because, you know, there were some things that the benevolent society was supposed to do for him.

We are always in constant dialogue, but he had not shown any sign of depression. It is so shocking. It comes as a shock to see really what took place,” stated Russell.

Councillor Julian Chang (Jamaica Labour Party, Savanna-la-Mar Division), who visited the scene, expressed sadness over the tragedy.

“It’s not anything to rejoice over. We all have issues, and we all have problems. We all go through things,” stated Chang.

She noted that the community, which was devastated by Hurricane Melissa last October, is already under stress and attempting to rebuild.

“We understand the constraints, but you know, we have to deal with our problems better than this, instead of taking our own lives or taking the lives of others,” stated Chang, who joined Russell in calling on people having problems to seek help.

Domestic violence, it can affect anyone regardless of our income, education, or social status. It stretches across all socio-economic backgrounds. We just have to understand that it is right in our midst and we should not be ashamed of it.

We should seek help. And I implore the persons in the Savanna-la-Mar Division, or anywhere for that matter in Jamaica, to seek help because I’m sure there are telltale signs even before it occurs,” Chang said.

She also emphasised the need for community sensitisation to stop judging victims and instead offer support, “because we all deserve to be safe in our own homes”.

World.title: Protecting Palisadoes
World.content:
An overhead shot of the Palisadoes Peninsula.

SPURRED into action by the warning from Hurricane Melissa which lashed sections of the island last year, the Cabinet has approved a US$56-million ($8.9 billion) coastal protection system for Palisadoes main road in Kingston which leads to Norman Manley International Airport and Port Royal.

The Category 5 storm, which hit Jamaica on October 28, 2025, reached wind speed of up to 190 miles per hour and devastated sections of the island’s southand north-western coasts, leaving several communities inaccessible.

With the pain from Melissa still fresh in Jamaicans’ minds, Minister of Energy, Telecommunications and Transport Daryl Vaz on Wednesday told a post-Cabinet media briefing that the Government is moving to provide even more protection for Palisadoes, the narrow approximately 14.2-kilometre strip of land that serves as a protective barrier for Kingston Harbour.

“The Government is advancing efforts to strengthen coastal protection along the Palisadoes Peninsula and Port Royal, safeguarding the Norman Manley International Airport, the main road that links from Harbour View to Port Royal, and surrounding communities against coastal erosion and storm surges,” Vaz said.

“The initiative represents a coordinated effort to protect critical transportation infrastructure, preserve access to Port Royal, and strengthen Jamaica’s resilience to coastal hazards.

So this is a far-reaching project that is going to once and for all protect the airport and access all the way to Port Royal,” added Vaz.

He underscored that over the last few years the Government has made efforts to protect the strip, which included approximately 4,500 metres of revetment work.

“We started back in 2007 when we did all of those boulders on the stretch.

As a result of Melissa and realising that, had Melissa come closer to Kingston, the access to the airport and, of course all the way to Port Royal, would be non-existent…

and seeing the work that has been done and what needs to be done, the Government has completed a comprehensive shoreline protection project [study] covering approximately 14.2 kilometres,” added Vaz.

He explained that proposed works will include strengthening revetments, rehabilitating dunes and mangroves, revegetation, and 12.1 kilometres of dunes [while] improving vulnerable road sections and installing coastal monitoring systems.

Underscoring that the country’s airports must also be built with resilience, Vaz noted that this project will be undertaken by the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authorities (NaRRA) under its work programme, with funding expected from its designated project pool.

He said with the project being under NaRRA, the Government will ensure that the procurement process is fast-tracked, which will result in it being completed in a timely manner.

“I just want to impress again, with all the noise that is being said about NaRRA, here is a project out of my ministry which has been approved by Cabinet as a NaRRA project.

Just to indicate that the noise is not always what you must listen to; you must watch the sale.

Here is a good sale.

Money that is going to be well spent [so] that if we have another catastrophe, God forbid, and it comes closer to Kingston, we will be able to respond how we responded to Melissa to get all the flights in with relief within hours,” Vaz told the media briefing.

The revetment work on Palisadoes came after Hurricane Ivan passed close to Jamaica’s south coast on September 10, 2024, leaving behind a trail of destruction not seen in the island since the passage of Hurricane Gilbert in 1988.

Ivan generated storm surge that caused the sea level to rise pushing mountains of sand and stones on the Palisadoes, leaving the vital roadway impassable.

The sand had also formed what was later referred to as the Palisadoes New Beach, essentially strips of land on the Kingston Harbour side up to 50 metres wide.

In 2007, sea water from storm surges associated with Hurricane Felix, which passed south of the island on September 3, flooded a section of the Palisadoes, making it impassable for several hours.

World.title: 21 things we learned at the EU leaders’ summit
World.content:
1) Energy stole the show right out of the gate

The summit’s first major clash came Thursday morning, with EU leaders split over whether to delay ETS2, the bloc’s second phase of carbon pricing, to address high energy prices, triggering a three-hour-long standoff.

Italy and Greece joined the Visegrád Four — Czechia, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia — in calling for a delay, a push rejected by the majority of countries.

The debate dragged on, delaying lunch (spare a thought for our hungry leaders!) and leading to the cancellation of a press conference on Thursday night.

2) Budget negotiations are a marathon…

Negotiations on the bloc’s next long-term budget were expected to be one of the summit’s most contentious topics. But they were a nothingburger, with most leaders repeating positions they have held for months. The summit brought them no closer to a breakthrough.

Many countries, of course, want a smaller budget, with Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson telling reporters that his country is “not an ATM for the EU.”

Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, meanwhile, said he had no choice but to be frugal at the European level, arguing he is used to tightening his belt at home because his wife is Dutch. Think of Bart next time your Dutch friends ask you to pay them back for that coffee.

World.title: In Europe’s tech capital, Irish labor unions are booming amid AI-driven layoffs
World.content:
Ireland's lucrative tech sector has been rattled by waves of AI-driven layoffs — and the country's fledgling tech union has seen an exponential spike in sign-ups from workers who are worried about their future.

There’s an “awakening” happening right now among workers in Ireland’s tech sector, and a growing “awareness that they’re not bulletproof,” said Sinéad Gibney, a social democrat lawmaker who previously worked for Google.

“I do think what we will see is that parts of roles will be automated, which means that people will be competing more heavily for the same roles," she said. "They won't have the same labor power and therefore we're going to see a drop in quality of work, we're going to see more zero-hour contracts, in more places than we already see it.”

The labor movement brewing in Ireland, where many of the world's tech giants have their EU bases, is part of a wider trend among tech workers globally, who have seen their work disrupted by rapidly evolving AI.

Rise in layoffs

Ireland’s dedicated union for tech workers, the Digital and Techworker Alliance (DATA), has seen a five-fold increase in membership since it was first founded in 2023.

In its first year and a half of existence, membership hovered around 270 people. In the past year-and-a-half, it's jumped to more than 1,350 members, DATA organizer John Bohan told POLITICO. He added that this number tends to spike around layoffs and other actions.

World.title: Scottish government set to drop opposition to new oil and gas fields
World.content:
The Scottish government — led by the SNP since 2007 — released a draft energy strategy in 2023 which set out its “presumption against” new oil and gas fields in the North Sea.

That draft strategy is “out of date,” one senior Scottish government official said. They said a new strategy, expected by the summer, will not contain this wording. A second person with knowledge of the policy said the new strategy will “reflect the world as it is.”

The shift in policy comes with the U.K. government widely expected to give the go-ahead to the Jackdaw gas field next week.

While the Scottish government has little power over the granting of new licenses for projects such as Jackdaw or the Rosebank oil field — where a decision is expected to come separately and at a later date — it has an important symbolic role, and can apply pressure to the U.K. government to approve licenses.

SNP politicians at the party’s conference in Aberdeen privately admitted the stance on Jackdaw has hurt the party electorally.

The party passed a resolution at its conference Friday which stated that the “utilisation of domestic production” of oil and gas is “clearly preferable to importation”. This was seen as a further softening of the position of the SNP — which governed in a quasi-coalition with the anti-exploration Scottish Greens until as recently as 2004.

World.title: Zelenskyy warns 20M Ukrainians could flee to Europe if Russia wins war
World.content:
The stark warning comes as Kyiv heads into a brutal winter and faces a cash crunch.

BRUSSELS — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Friday that as many as 20 million Ukrainians could be forced to flee to Europe if his country falls to Russia.

“Russia is killing us,” Zelenskyy told reporters at a press conference on Friday during a summit of European Union leaders, adding Ukrainians were being “pushed” out of their country. “They [Russia] don’t want to stop.”

In the early days of Russia’s full-scale invasion, millions of Ukrainians fled their homes in Europe’s fastest and largest refugee crisis since World War II. Today, over 4 million Ukrainians live in EU countries under temporary protection status, with the largest populations in Germany, Poland and Czechia, according to Eurostat.

Zelenskyy’s stark warning comes as Ukraine heads into a brutal fifth wartime winter under Russian bombardment. Kyiv faces a budget shortfall of $30 to $35 million next year, according to projections from the International Monetary Fund — even accounting for a €90 billion loan Brussels agreed to provide last year.

The Ukrainian president traveled to Brussels to meet with European leaders and shore up financial support for his embattled country. While the EU is Ukraine’s staunchest backer, the bloc’s list of priorities is stacked with rising energy costs, looming elections, geopolitical crises and an impasse over its €2 trillion budget.

World.title: Denmark, Italy, Poland urge EU leaders to harden stance on irregular migration
World.content:
The bloc’s 27 leaders were due to discuss migration during a special session on Thursday requested by Meloni and Frederiksen following a tense back-and-forth with Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez in June.

Tensions have risen further after Spain’s Ceuta exclave was overwhelmed by migrants during the summer and as far-right parties have made gains around the bloc.

The draft also “calls the Commission to explore [a] possible consultation mechanism to encourage coordination on national measures potentially affecting other Member States while respecting national competencies.”

While the last phrase does not name any one country, Sánchez has clashed with Meloni over his handling of the Ceuta migration crisis as well as Spanish measures to regularize around 1 million migrants.

However, language discussing the impact of migration on social housing was removed from the draft over concerns that it could be perceived as provocative toward Spain.

One of the diplomats — who, like the others, was granted anonymity to discuss confidential information — said the updated draft was unlikely to win unanimous support from all the leaders, but had been proposed to bring the language closer in line with political sentiment and spark debate.

World.title: Spanish opposition leader Feijóo calls for navy to be deployed to Ceuta
World.content:
Feijóo’s calls for a “firm response” are the latest in a wave of criticism of Sánchez’s government after more than 70,000 migrants arrived in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta on the Moroccan border in late July. Migration ministers across the European Union have in recent months repeatedly demanded tough new EU migration policies.

His comments also come after unconfirmed reports that a Moroccan patrol boat remained in Spanish waters off the coast of Ceuta for hours Thursday, which the Spanish Civil Guard has denied. Moroccan warships also allegedly entered Spanish waters in July, though a European Commission spokesperson told Spanish press agency EFE Wednesday that it was “up to the Spanish and Moroccan authorities to clarify the facts.”

Feijóo spent Thursday morning at a summit of the center-right European People’s Party — of which the PP is a member — in Brussels, during which the EPP lashed out at the Spanish government over the Ceuta crisis in its closing statement, according to POLITICO’s Madrid Playbook. Conservatives have said they will implement measures to curb immigration if the government swings to the right after the snap election.

“Europe as a whole must recognize the failure of the Spanish government and exert the necessary pressure to prevent this crisis from becoming entrenched, spreading, or happening again,” Feijóo said in an opinion piece earlier this month.

Tensions over Ceuta and Melilla — which Morocco considers occupied territories — are becoming increasingly strained: A POLITICO poll earlier this week revealed that 58% of respondents believe an armed conflict between Madrid and Rabat is “likely” within the next decade.

In a landmark visit to the exclaves also this week, King Felipe VI said that Ceuta and Melilla were “an inalienable part of the political and national reality that is Spain. The sovereignty and territorial integrity of our country are not negotiable.”

The last time a Spanish head of state visited the territories was in 2007, when former King Juan Carlos I traveled to Ceuta and Melilla amid a diplomatic spat with Morocco.

World.title: EU prosecutors asked to investigate advisory body
World.content:
The EPPO did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“The EESC was informed by OLAF yesterday that this case has been transmitted to the EPPO,” an EESC spokesperson told POLITICO.



“Under these circumstances, the EESC cannot comment further except to re-confirm that when these matters first arose, the EESC president immediately and proactively referred the allegations to OLAF. The EESC will continue to respect fully the independence of this process.” Séamus Boland of Ireland was elected president in October 2025.

“The EESC and its senior leadership take this matter very seriously and remain fully committed to integrity, transparency and accountability,” the spokesperson added.

The EPPO has significantly stronger enforcement powers than OLAF. Whereas OLAF conducts administrative investigations, the EPPO investigates crimes against the financial interests of the EU, and can search private homes or seize evidence.

OLAF has also been investigating a report that EESC executives tried to smoke out a staff whistleblower who raised the alarm about the funding concerns, the EU Ombudsman told POLITICO.

Anonymous letters, seen by POLITICO, say that IT workers at the EESC were asked by senior managers to identify which staffers had connected to the OLAF website in previous weeks.

The EESC said those anonymous letters contained “serious personal threats” and added that they were not made through the EESC’s “robust formal whistleblower process.”

World.title: France, Germany strike bargain on Made in Europe, car emissions
World.content:
France and Germany now want to soften the 2035 target to 90% but without having to offer investments in alternative fuels to compensate the remaining 10%, as proposed by the European Commission.

“This balanced approach will enable the European Union to pursue its climate objectives while strengthening the technological sovereignty, industrial base and international competitiveness of its automotive industry,” the two countries said in a joint statement.

The agreement, first reported by POLITICO in July, was due to have been announced Thursday, during a meeting of EU leaders in Brussels. But it was held up at the last minute by disagreements within Germany’s governing coalition.

“We hope that this Franco-German dynamic can swiftly lead to an agreement with our partners, for our jobs and our industry,” French President Emmanuel Macron said in a post on social media.

An Elysée official on Friday made clear that, under the Franco-German deal, the scope of Made in Europe for automotive can be extended to the U.K. and Switzerland under certain conditions. — addressing a key concern of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government ahead of a Nov. 20 U.K.-EU summit in Brussels.

The agreement was reached after the German Social Democratic Party, the junior partner in Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s coalition government, dropped its opposition.

World.title: Romanian president calls for greater NATO oversight in the Black Sea in Euronews interview
World.content:
Romanian President Nicușor Dan has said the Black Sea would only become safe after Russia’s war in Ukraine ends, as he called for greater NATO oversight in the region following drone strikes on commercial vessels in an interview with Euronews.

 

“I’m very optimistic that we’ll have the support and the capabilities in order to be better protected, because it’s an important economic question for Ukraine and for the whole region,” he said on the sidelines of an EU summit in Brussels held Friday.

The Romanian leader said frequent drone incursions into his country’s territory had begun roughly a year and a half ago, and that Bucharest had been “not prepared”. The country now faces a similar lack of preparedness to its east, Dan said.

“At the Black Sea, we are in the same situation,” he said, adding: “We have to protect the water under our territory.”

He also expressed confidence in continued support from US President Donald Trump, both for security in the Black Sea and for Romania’s position within the NATO military alliance.

“On defence, I think it’s a mutual benefit between us because we have an excellent position to project force towards other parts of the world,” Dan said.

The confidence comes amid bellicose statements from US President Donald Trump regarding Ukrainian and European security, such as troop cuts and a force posture review.

The president was in the Belgian capital for a quarterly summit attended by EU heads of state to discuss support for Ukraine, the bloc’s long-term budget and its growing trade deficit with China.

However, the increasingly hostile security situation in the Black Sea pushed the Romanian leader and his Bulgarian counterpart, Prime Minister Rumen Radev, to bring security threats higher up the agenda.

Dan told reporters after the summit that France had pledged “necessary equipment” and to “better understand our specific requirements in the Black Sea”.

“There are always new challenges, but fortunately, Romania has allies,” he said.

The escalating situation also prompted a meeting between the two leaders and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte to discuss stronger support. Bulgaria requested combat aircraft and anti-drone systems during the talks.

Rutte said afterwards that NATO would continue to strengthen its posture along the eastern flank, including by expanding its counter-drone capabilities.

“NATO will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed,” he said in a statement on the social media platform X.

Russia has repeatedly attacked Ukrainian ports along the Black Sea and the Danube River, leaving the war-torn country dependent on alternative routes to sell its grain to African and Middle Eastern markets.

However, this has exposed Europe’s shipping lanes to attacks.

Drones have damaged commercial vessels in the Black Sea off the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania for three consecutive days leading up to the meeting in Brussels, as well as during the previous week. At least one vessel sank after being attacked by drones last week, killing two seafarers.

Neither Sofia nor Bucharest has definitively blamed Russia for the attacks. However, Radev told reporters earlier in the week that “logic” would suggest the Kremlin stood to benefit from the deadly incursions.

“The problem is that we cannot prove it,” he said.

Investigations into all the incidents are ongoing.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said at a press conference after meeting European leaders on Thursday that “you do not need a ground war for an invasion to occur”.

He added that Russia was testing Europe’s response to the attacks, referring to incidents in the Black Sea as well as an explosive-laden drone found at an airport in Leipzig.

“Violating another country's airspace is already an incursion,” Zelenskyy said.

“We have seen drones cross airspace and borders in Romania, Poland and Germany. A corresponding drone was found in Germany, by the way. Moldova and Bulgaria have also been affected. A great deal is happening today.”

Zelenskyy and other senior Ukrainian officials have publicly blamed Russia for some of these incidents, most notably a deadly drone attack that struck a vessel carrying Ukrainian grain off the Bulgarian coast.

World.title: Budget, Ukraine, migration: Five takeaways from the EU leaders’ summit
World.content:
EU leaders gathered in Brussels on Thursday and Friday with a packed agenda, from the long-term budget and financial support for Ukraine to migration, energy and China.

 

The summit alternated between entrenched positions on the bloc’s budget, a warm welcome for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and clashes over energy and migration policies.

Here are the five highlights.

Rallying behind Ukraine

The bitter row between Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump dominated the second day of the summit.

Leaders closed ranks behind Zelenskyy and promised to keep sanctions in place for as long as Russia pursues its full-scale invasion. They also condemned the diesel deal struck by Trump with Russian President Vladimir Putin, although the Bulgarian prime minister broke ranks to support it.

The reception gave Zelenskyy a moment of diplomatic relief as Trump doubled down, claiming Zelenskyy was “more difficult” to deal with than Putin and demanding new elections in Ukraine. Trump also called Kyiv’s strikes on Russian oil refineries, its main leverage, a “disgrace”.

“I defend the interests of Ukraine and the Ukrainian people exclusively,” Zelenskyy said in a defiant tone. “We were attacked, occupied, and our people were killed. It is only logical that we have the right to defend ourselves.”

“We will keep living, fighting, and most importantly, living with dignity,” he added.

In his address, Zelenskyy asked leaders for an additional €70bn in financial and military support next year to counter Russia’s escalation.

The request upends the bloc’s plans, which assumed last year's €90bn loan would cover both 2026 and 2027. EU leaders tasked the Commission to come up with a proposal on how to address Kyiv's financial needs.

Filling the gap will be anything but easy. Soaring borrowing costs make joint debt unpalatable. The immobilised Russian assets, which Zelenskyy raised again, remain politically divisive. And bilateral contributions risk leaving the burden on a handful of wealthy countries.

EU budget

On Thursday, leaders debated the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) at length but, as expected, made little headway, as the “frugal” net contributors and the southern and eastern “Friends of Cohesion” dug in.

One thing is clear: the negotiating box tabled by the Irish presidency just days ago, which proposed slashing €141bn from the overall budget to appease the frugal, is now officially dead.

European Council President António Costa will take over the talks. He is due to present a new compromise in the coming weeks, which many expect to come before the special summit he has called for 26 November, just days before the Spanish elections.

Costa is expected to pursue three main lines: keep national contributions as low as possible, rework the package of EU-wide taxes, including by drawing on European Parliament proposals, and restore the flexibility instruments the Irish presidency ruthlessly cut.

That Costa would sooner or later step in was always on the cards. More worrying is that leaders on both sides now openly say they feel no pressure to close the deal by the end of the year.

Seasoned negotiators know that deadlines force concessions. Member states may be playing with fire: a no-deal in December would raise the prospect of talks slipping until after an electoral season that could reshape Europe’s political landscape.

Migration

Migration proved once again among the most contentious issues, after the last discussion, in June, descended into a shouting match between Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez on one side and Italy’s Giorgia Meloni and Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen on the other.

This time, Rome unexpectedly extended a hand to Madrid just before the dossier reached the table on Friday. Italy and Spain reached what appears to be a first step towards ending their border dispute, after a string of tit-for-tat checks introduced in the wake of the Ceuta crisis.

Italy’s temporary border controls were due to expire on Thursday evening. They were extended by a week to align with Spain’s, which expire on 22 October. The two interior ministers are due to agree on replacement measures by then.

But while Meloni opened the summit in a conciliatory tone, Sánchez’s other main European nemesis, Frederiksen, did not spare her fellow social democrat over his plan to regularise the status of 600,000 migrants.

“I have asked the European Commission to examine what happens when a country does almost the exact opposite of what the rest of us are doing,” Frederiksen said, referring to Spain in all but name.

Meloni, Frederiksen and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten hosted an informal breakfast before the discussion with 17 other EU leaders to explore “innovative solutions” on migration. Support is growing for emergency measures allowing asylum applications to be suspended during crises.

Tensions between the migration hard-liners and Spain and France came to the fore as the Italian, Danish and Polish governments pushed to rewrite the conclusions to call for avoiding “measures that could create incentives for illegal migration.”

By contrast, the final text merely urges the Commission to coordinate with the member states "on all types of instrumentalisation."

China

On “macroeconomic imbalances”, EU jargon for avoiding naming China, leaders held their course despite the deal between the European Commission and Beijing to curb hybrid car imports.

Over lunch on Thursday, they pressed the Commission to prepare a toolbox of new trade defence instruments, including safeguards with quotas and tariffs, to shield the chemicals and machinery industries from Chinese competition.

China loomed large as the bloc faces a trade deficit of about €360bn with Beijing. Chemicals and machinery, among the sectors hardest hit by cheap Chinese imports, were singled out as the next industries needing urgent protection after the hybrid car quotas.

While the car quotas were negotiated with Beijing, leaders called on Thursday for unilateral safeguards to be introduced “without delay”, according to officials.

The Commission presented last week’s deal as the first phase of negotiations launched in June. But time is running out: the EU’s trade deficit with China keeps widening month after month, and Chinese customs data show Chinese exports to the EU up 25% over the past year.

The EU’s strategy is to keep talking as long as dialogue delivers concrete results, while strengthening its trade defences. France and Germany last week urged the Commission to develop a new instrument to respond swiftly to market disruptions caused by China, which has been accused of unfair trade practices.

“The competition must be fair. We will create instruments against leveraging capacities, against high subsidies, against undervalued currencies. And there will be a toolbox for that. The toolbox will be bigger. It will also be applied as necessary,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said.

Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told leaders her institution would begin work on such a tool, though it remains unclear whether it will be ready before the end of the year.

Other instruments are in the pipeline, including a diversification tool to encourage EU companies to diversify their suppliers of strategic products such as critical raw materials, and a solidarity mechanism to help member states hit by possible Chinese countermeasures.

Energy

On Thursday, leaders were dragged into an interminable discussion on energy. The Visegrád Group (V4) and Italy asked to amend the summit conclusions to call on the Commission to propose new measures to curb short-term swings in electricity prices and to reassess the proposed Emissions Trading System (ETS).

The V4, Italy and, to a lesser extent, Greece led the push because they face some of Europe’s highest energy costs, a concern largely shared by other member states, which ultimately called for a coordinated European response to the ongoing energy crisis.

The attempt to reopen the ETS, however, triggered an ideological backlash from Finland, Denmark and Sweden. The system makes companies pay for their emissions and encourages investment in sustainability.

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš, by contrast, lashed out at the carbon tax, accusing it of wrecking Europe’s competitiveness by fuelling soaring energy costs for the benefit of market speculators.

“We’ve been engaged in a drafting exercise all day at the leaders’ level about something technical,” an EU official vented at the margins of the summit. “It’s not resulting in any new measures or new policies that actually help EU member states in their problems.”

Rome and the V4 know they lack the qualified majority to reopen the EU’s carbon market rules. The aim was rather to signal to domestic audiences that they are doing what they can to contain the surge in energy prices.

World.title: Albanian PM blames 'foreign hands' for escalating anti-government unrest
World.content:
Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama called for calm on Friday, blaming unnamed "foreign hands" for the unrest as protesters demanded his resignation for a fourth consecutive day.

 

"These are foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace," he said in a Facebook video.

"All of this is the work of the very same hand, the hand that has gripped the Albanian opposition by the throat, the hand that has burned and destroyed Albania more than once."

Thousands of young protesters took to the streets of Albania’s capital, also demanding education reforms, with some smashing windows and damaging traffic lights.

"The government's indifference and arrogance since the beginning of our movement have been unbearable and have made the situation worse," said the high school student, who asked to be identified only by her first name.

Protesters set rubbish bins on fire to block roads and threw stones at police, who responded with tear gas and water cannon.

"We are not criminals. We simply want a better life for our parents and ourselves. We do not want to leave Albania," 18-year-old Ledia told AFP.

Riot police fire tear gas at protesters during an anti-government demonstration in Tirana, Albania, Friday, 16 Oct., 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

The demonstrations, which began on Tuesday, have since spread beyond Tirana to other Albanian cities, with students boycotting classes amid growing anti-government unrest.

This week's escalation comes after months of anti-government protests in the Balkan nation, including demonstrations against a luxury tourism project linked to Donald Trump's daughter Ivanka and son-in-law Jared Kushner, which has become a symbol of alleged corruption and inequality in Albania.

On Wednesday, the European Union delegation in Albania called for a proportionate response from authorities, expressing concern over “the violent escalation at the protest in Tirana.”

Rama's Socialist Party won a fourth consecutive election victory last year, with the next parliamentary elections not scheduled until 2029. His government is aiming for Albania to join the European Union by 2028.

World.title: Global timekeeping rules change: leap second scrapped from 2027
World.content:
The world’s official time standard will stop adding leap seconds from 20 May 2027. The General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) decided to end the practice on Thursday 15 October 2026.

 

The resolution was adopted at the conference’s 28th meeting in Versailles, where delegates discussed the future of world time.

Until now, leap seconds have been added from time to time to keep atomic time in line with the Earth’s rotation. But from 20 May 2027, Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) will run continuously, with no interruptions.

Why the leap second is being scrapped

The old rules were meant to keep two different ways of measuring time in step. UTC is based on extremely precise atomic clocks. Astronomical time depends on the Earth’s rotation, and that rotation speed varies slightly.

To keep the gap between the two time scales small, 27 leap seconds have been added since 1972. The most recent was at the end of 2016. As a result, one minute could exceptionally last 61 seconds.

These corrections are barely noticeable for people, but they can cause technical problems. Computer systems, telecoms networks, satellite navigation and power infrastructure all depend on precise, reliable time synchronisation. Past leap seconds have already disrupted computer systems and online services.

Earth’s rotation makes new rules necessary

One reason for the decision is the way the Earth’s rotation is evolving. A negative leap second raised new risks.

Over very long periods, tidal forces slow the planet down, but in recent years it has at times been spinning slightly faster.

That raised the possibility that, for the first time, a so-called negative leap second might be needed, with a second removed rather than added. Because this has never been done, it is uncertain how reliably technical systems would cope.

The international expert community therefore chose to end the existing rules ahead of schedule. Under the new regime, the gap between UTC and astronomical time will be allowed to grow, potentially reaching 3,600 seconds, or one hour.

Experts believe, however, that it will still be some time before such a gap would actually require any correction, so the measure is essentially precautionary.

The CGPM: little known, but many member states

The CGPM brings together representatives of member states and of associated states and economic areas and usually meets every four years.

According to the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM), it currently has 69 member states and 34 associated states and economies.

In Europe, they include Germany, Austria, France, Italy, Spain, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, Poland and Ukraine.

The Americas are represented by the United States, Canada, Brazil, Argentina, Mexico and Peru, Asia by China, Japan, India, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand, and Africa by South Africa, Egypt, Morocco, Tunisia and Kenya. Australia and New Zealand are also represented.

What does this mean for the UK?

For everyday life in the United Kingdom, the decision will not bring any immediate change.

Scrapping the leap second is a technical adjustment to the international time reference and must not be confused with the familiar switch between summer time and winter time.

According to the GOV.UK Clock Change Guide, the clocks go back one hour on Sunday, 25, October, 2026, at 2:00 AM.

The statue of Winston Churchill stands in Parliament Square, backdropped by the Elizabeth Tower, commonly known as Big Ben, in London, Wednesday, June 3, 2026. (AP Photo/Alber AP Photo

As such, the local clock time in the UK will still follow Greenwich Mean Time (GMT), which is UTC+0 in winter, and British Summer Time (BST), which is UTC+1 in summer. Seasonal time changes will be unaffected.

A step towards more stable world time

The impact will be felt more strongly in specialist fields that need exceptionally precise alignment with the Earth’s rotation. These include astronomy, geodesy (the science of measuring and mapping the Earth and determining its shape, size and gravitational field) and certain satellite-based applications.

For these disciplines, accurate knowledge of the Earth’s rotation will remain crucial. Because leap seconds will no longer tie world time to that rotation, they will have to account separately for the growing gap between clock time and astronomical time when necessary.

In principle, the aim of the new rules is to make international timekeeping simpler and more reliable in the long term. In particular, digital systems will no longer have to cope with extra seconds being inserted at irregular intervals.

World.title: Commission and Ukraine launch joint task force over EU accession
World.content:
The European Commission announced on Friday a joint task force with Ukraine to speed up accession work, after Hungary lifted its veto on opening further negotiating clusters.

 

EU and Ukrainian officials will sit on the task force, which is meant to help Kyiv complete its accession homework. Earlier this week, member states agreed to open two more clusters. The remaining two are now expected by the end of the year.

“Ukraine is among the countries making most progress towards EU membership. Following the opening of two more negotiating clusters this week, I discussed the next steps with PM Serhii Koretskyi. We agreed to launch a joint Task Force,” Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said on X.

The task force will focus on the so-called interim benchmarks, the mid-process targets a candidate must meet before it can start closing negotiating chapters.

It will work through a list of outstanding requirements under the benchmarks on the fundamentals of accession, namely the rule of law and anti-corruption reforms.

“This is an important step to have a joint task force that will be meeting in fact twice a week over the next several months to really try to accelerate the work,” Katarína Mathernová, the EU ambassador to Ukraine, told Euronews.

Hungary’s veto was lifted only after Kyiv agreed on an education law for the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia. The Ukrainian parliament passed the law with a broad majority, and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy swiftly signed it.

The vote raises hopes that Ukraine’s political elite will keep up the broad consensus needed to adopt the reforms required for EU membership.

"The task force follows the model used for Montenegro and Moldova," a Commission official told Euronews, adding that it gives Ukraine’s accession process new momentum.

Kyiv is also due to receive a roadmap breaking up the main steps, and an indicative timeline to complete the accession process as part of a broader enlargement package expected at the beginning of November.

“This step shows our commitment to supporting Ukraine’s path to EU membership. Our success will require unity and commitment from all involved Ukrainian partners,” Kos said.

Sasha Vakulina contributed to the reporting.

World.title: EU–Turkey summit in October aims to restart Cyprus talks
World.content:
A high-level meeting between the European Union and Turkey is expected to take place in October, focusing on efforts to restart talks on the Cyprus issue and the future of EU-Turkey relations, Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides said on Friday.

 

Speaking to journalists, he said he had been informed of the planned meeting following recent discussions in New York with UN Secretary-General António Guterres, as well as talks between Guterres and EU leaders. The meeting, being organised at the request of the UN Secretary-General, aims to explore ways to create the conditions needed to resume negotiations on the Cyprus issue.

“I am pleased, I repeat, because from the briefing I had yesterday from the heads of the institutions, such a meeting will be held in October, following a request by the UN Secretary-General himself, so that we can see how conditions are created for the resumption of negotiations,” the President said.

Christodoulides stressed that progress in EU-Turkey relations depends on the resumption of negotiations on Cyprus under the agreed framework.

“Any progress in EU-Turkey relations depends on the resumption of talks on the basis of the agreed framework,” he said.

He also mentioned the expected visit to Cyprus by the UN Secretary-General’s personal envoy in late October, saying these developments could help create conditions for progress.

"Our clear political will is a given and I repeat that the EU can play a leading role," he said.

Christodoulides recalled that his administration had prioritised greater EU involvement in efforts to restart negotiations from the outset. He also welcomed the appointment of a senior European Commission official, saying it reflected the EU's approach to the Cyprus issue.

EU contacts with Turkey over UN Climate Conference COP31

Asked whether the European Council's conclusions would refer to the UN Climate Conference COP31, Christodoulides said the issue had been discussed on Thursday and that he had briefed his European counterparts on the latest developments.

He said that following a statement by the Turkish Cypriot leader, the EU had contacted the Turkish government on behalf of its 27 member states and received written responses.

"If these replies are implemented in practice, then we will be satisfied," he said, adding that Cyprus was prepared for any eventuality.

Migration: "No clashes between member states"

Referring to discussions on migration, Christodoulides warned that disagreements between EU member states could send the wrong message to citizens.

"A clash is certainly not the most appropriate or the best message we can send to European citizens, especially on an issue we know concerns all member states," he said.

Despite the challenges, he pointed to progress in managing migration across the EU, citing a 90% drop in arrivals in Cyprus and a 180% increase in returns compared with 2022.

He said talks should focus on identifying gaps and considering further measures, including a possible EU mechanism to respond to the use of migrants as a tool of political pressure.

Energy costs and ETS2 dominate EU talks

Nikos Christodoulides described Thursday’s discussions on energy costs and rising prices as extensive, noting that some member states initially reluctant to support proposals from Mediterranean and Central European countries, as well as the Balkan B4 group, had now recognised the need to adopt them.

On the EU’s second Emissions Trading System (ETS2), Christodoulides welcomed the wording agreed in the European Council’s conclusions.

"As it stands at the moment, as agreed last night, the wording satisfies us," he said.

He added that the European Commission appeared to recognise the need to further delay the system’s implementation, warning that it could place an additional burden on households and businesses already struggling with high energy costs. He also stressed that it remained unclear when the energy crisis would end.

Hard-fought negotiations on the EU budget

Commenting on the negotiations over the EU’s Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), the President described the position of the Irish Presidency as difficult, noting that the Cypriot Presidency had previously managed to secure agreement on key aspects of the budget.

He said the matter now lies in the hands of the President of the European Council and expressed the view that discussions will focus on more concrete proposals for new EU own resources.

According to him, the objective is to avoid any further reduction of the EU budget or, if this proves unavoidable, to keep it to an absolute minimum.

Asked about the reaction of some member states to the proposals for new own resources, Christodoulides said that certain countries had expressed reservations due to national priorities, but noted that some ideas had been received positively by member states.

Tough negotiations over EU budget

Commenting on negotiations over the EU’s Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), Christodoulides said the Irish Presidency faced a difficult task, noting that the Cypriot Presidency had previously secured agreement on key budget issues.

He said the matter was now in the hands of the European Council President, adding that discussions were expected to focus on more concrete proposals for new sources of EU revenue.

The aim, he said, was to avoid further cuts to the EU budget or keep them to a minimum if unavoidable.

Asked about member states’ reactions to proposals for new EU revenue sources, Christodoulides said some countries had raised concerns over national priorities, while others had responded positively to certain proposals.

World.title: Japan's first female PM says makeup and housework add hours to her working day
World.content:
Japan's first female PM says makeup and housework add hours to her working day

 

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has sparked debate over gender roles and work-life balance after saying household chores and personal grooming add three to four hours to her daily routine compared with male prime ministers.

Speaking in parliament on Wednesday, Takaichi said she prepares breakfast, cleans up and applies makeup before starting her official duties.

“In the morning, I take a bath, prepare breakfast, clean up afterwards, and then do my makeup. When you add all that up, I feel I may be spending an extra three or four hours compared with a male prime minister,” she said.

Takaichi also explained that her staff had initially struggled to accommodate the time she needed to prepare for television appearances.

World.title: New White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia on way out after only five days on job, reports say
World.content:
Zacharia, having only served five days in the role, would be the shortest-serving press secretary in White House history. It comes after a rocky debut at the press room podium and controversy surrounding her background.

New White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia is on the way out from her position, the New York Times and other US news outlets reported on Friday.

Zacharia started her new job just five days ago, taking over for Karoline Leavitt.

Earlier on Friday, President Donald Trump suggested that Zacharia might be leaving. "I told her: 'I think you're better off being happy, and I'm not sure you can ever be ​happy in this stuff.' There's nothing easy about this stuff," Trump ​told reporters.

He added: "I said to her honestly, 'If ​I ‌were you, I'd reconsider... think about it. But I would reconsider.'"

Last Friday, Trump announced Zacharia's appointment as the new press secretary. However, she became embroiled in controversy when her previous claims to be a lawyer were revealed to be false.

What do we know about Zacharia

Until last week, Zacharia was a commentator for conservative outlets Fox News and Newsmax. She also advised the Trump Media and Technology, the company behind Trump's Truth Social platform.

Zacharia has also long described herself as a lawyer, but her credentials remain unverified. Neither she nor the White House has provided evidence that she passed the bar exam in any state or in China, where she worked for a large law firm years ago.

According to her LinkedIn profile, Zacharia was an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011 to 2013. She was also a general counsel at Fix California, an advocacy group founded by Trump ally Ric Grenell, from 2024 to 2025.

Zacharia earned her law degree from Pepperdine University in 2011. While nearly all licensed US lawyers first obtain a law degree, law school graduates cannot legally practice law in the US without first being admitted to a state bar.
