We cannot do what we do without your support. Senior delegations from Poland and Ukraine’s state institutes of national remembrance have held talks in the Ukrainian city of Lviv, marking the first time the heads of the two organisations have met in eight years. The meeting, at which the two sides discussed issues including exhumations of World War Two victims and possible joint research projects, comes as Poland and Ukraine seek reconciliation over historical issues that have regularly caused tensions between two otherwise close allies. 📢 14 października 2026 r. we Lwowie delegacja Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej spotkała się z przedstawicielami ukraińskiego Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej. Było to pierwsze bezpośrednie, robocze spotkanie szefów tych instytucji od 2018 r. ➡️ Stronie polskiej przewodniczył kierujący… pic.twitter.com/qHpZwLeCEa — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) October 14, 2026 News of the meeting was announced on social media by Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), which noted that it was “the first direct, working meeting between the heads of these institutions since 2018”. The IPN is currently headed by its deputy president, Karol Polejowski, because Poland’s parliament has been unable to agree on a permanent new president. The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINR) is led by Oleksandr Alfyorov. “The first topic of discussion,” according to the IPN, was the planned reburial of 115 Polish soldiers recently exhumed in Lviv, where they died in 1939 defending the city (then part of Poland and known as Lwów) during the Nazi-German and Soviet invasions. Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of 115 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending Lviv – now in Ukraine but then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of WWII https://t.co/yQNeq2D54E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026 Their exhumation resulted from a diplomatic breakthrough last year between Warsaw and Kyiv that saw Ukraine lift a moratorium on exhumations that had been in place since 2017 in protest at the dismantling in Poland of a monument to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA). Ukraine has also allowed the exhumation on its territory of Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres, which were led by the UPA. Poland likewise recently granted permission for Ukraine to search for Ukrainian victims of a massacre led by the Polish Home Army in the village of Łasków (Laskiv in Ukrainian). At this week’s meeting, the UINR gave an update on its work in Łasków, where it has uncovered the remains of 30 people. The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance has found 30 human remains in a village in Poland where Polish partisans killed Ukrainian civilians in WW2 It thanked Poland for permission to search the site, calling it a step towards "true reconciliation" https://t.co/BeeEtl6gCa — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026 The IPN and UINR also discussed planned exhumation work in the now-depopulated village of Huta Pieniacka (Huta Peniatska in Ukrainian), where the local Polish population was massacred in 1944 by a Nazi SS regiment mainly made up of Ukrainians. There was also “willingness on both sides to restore cooperation in the field of historical scientific research”, said the IPN. “The possibility of undertaking joint educational initiatives was also discussed.” The two sides also agreed to hold another meeting in Warsaw, though no date has been set. This week’s meeting comes after a period of tension over historical issues between not only Poland and Ukraine more broadly, but also the two countries’ remembrance institutes. In February this year, the IPN criticised Alfyorov over an interview in which he initially called the Volhynia massacres “one of Poland’s state myths”, before later appearing to correct himself and saying it was “not a myth, but one of the key elements of the Polish grand narrative”. By contrast, “for most Ukrainians, this is just a local episode of history”, added Alfyorov. Referring to Poland’s recognition of the massacres as a genocide – a term Ukraine rejects – he asked if Polish massacres of around 28,000 Ukrainians during the war should also be called a genocide. In response, the IPN called Alfyorov’s remarks “outrageous” and declared that the Volhynia massacres were “not an ‘episode’, but rather one of the largest genocides against civilians in 20th-century Europe”. It also condemned Ukraine for honouring figures associated with the massacres. The UINR, for its part, criticised a law proposed by Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki (a former head of the IPN), that would criminalise the promotion of ideologies associated with World War Two Ukrainian nationalist groups. Ukraine has criticised a law proposed by Poland's president that would criminalise promotion of historical Ukrainian nationalist ideologies, equating them with Nazism and communism It warns of "retaliatory measures" if the bill is passed https://t.co/TaX2Vj5z8v — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2025 In another sign of reconciliation, in May the UINR and Poland’s Mieroszewski Centre held a historical congress in Warsaw, bringing together more than 100 historians “to discuss complex issues of the shared past and explore common approaches to their interpretation”, in the words of the Ukrainian foreign ministry. However, that same month, President Volodymyr Zelensky prompted a diplomatic crisis by approving the naming of a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted Nawrocki to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle. Since then, both sides have made efforts to reach a diplomatic solution, including a pledge by Zelensky to “grant a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”. World.title: Ukraine finds remains of 30 people in search for victims of massacre by Polish WWII partisans
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINR) has reported the discovery of 30 human remains at a site in Poland where Polish partisans killed Ukrainian civilians during World War Two. The head of the UINR, Oleksandr Alfyorov, thanked Poland for granting permission to conduct research at the location, which he said would help advance “true reconciliation” between the two countries over their difficult shared history. Ukraine has likewise recently allowed Poland to search for and exhume the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists during the war. At the end of August, the Polish authorities approved a request from Ukraine to conduct a search in the village of Łasków in southeastern Poland, around 10km from the border with Ukraine. On 10 March 1944, units of the Home Army (Armia Krajowa) and Peasant Battalions (Bataliony Chłopskie), two major Polish underground resistance movements that emerged during the Nazi-German occupation, attacked Łasków, which had a predominantly ethnic Ukrainian population. Estimates suggest that around 300 civilians were killed. Among them was a local Orthodox priest, Lev Korobchuk. On the same day, members of the Home Army also attacked the nearby village of Sahryń, where they are estimated to have killed hundreds more Ukrainians. Ukraine has also submitted an application to carry out exploratory work there. Poland has granted permission for Ukraine to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during WWII https://t.co/4JeAAhYJcY — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 2, 2026 Work began in Łasków on 6 October and, on Wednesday this week, the UINR announced that it had “discovered the remains of 30 victims…[who] died as a result of the attack of the units of the Home Army and the Peasant Battalion in March 1944″. Svyatoslav Sheremeta, the head of the Lviv-based Dolya memorial and search centre, which carried out the work on behalf of the UINR, said that they now hope to “conduct exhumation, rebury the dead, and honour their memory with dignity”. “Thank you to the Polish side for the opportunity to conduct research,” added Alfyorov. “Our common task is to ensure a worthy commemoration of all victims, regardless of their origin and nationality.” “True reconciliation begins with respect for everyone’s memory, recognition of the pain of the other side, and the common desire for understanding,” said the head of UNIP, which shared images from the search site in Łasków’s Orthodox cemetery. At the time of writing, Polish officials had not yet commented on the development. However, when search work began last week, Rafał Kościański, a spokesman for Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), told Radio Lublin that IPN staff were participating as observers. Wiesław Koman, from the Provincial Office for the Protection of Monuments, added that cooperation between Polish and Ukrainian archaeologists at the site had been “impeccable”. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s ambassador to Poland, Vasyl Bodnar, told the broadcaster that the work in Łasków was “a step towards reconciliation between our nations”. “This is happening on both sides of the border and demonstrates the openness of both sides to commemorating the victims of the past conflict,” said Bodnar. “There are differing voices from different sides of the political arena, but this is the right path, one we should have been on for a long time.” Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of 115 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending Lviv – now in Ukraine but then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of WWII https://t.co/yQNeq2D54E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026 The legacy of wartime massacres has long overshadowed relations between Poland and Ukraine, who have otherwise become close allies since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. In 2017, Ukraine imposed a ban on searches on its territory for Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian nationalists massacred around 100,000 ethnic Poles, mostly women and children. Poland has recognised those massacres as a genocide. Ukraine rejects the use of that term, and also points to anti-Ukrainian repression in the interwar Polish state and the massacres of Ukrainian civilians carried out by Polish partisans during the war. In a diplomatic breakthrough last year, Kyiv agreed to lift its moratorium on exhumations. Since then, it has granted permission for Poland to conduct searches and exhumations at a number of locations. The remains of 55 Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, around half of them children, were exhumed this summer https://t.co/4q3giZhBAL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2026 However, tensions over historical issues reemerged this year, when President Volodymyr Zelensky approved the naming of a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”, the group that led the Volhynia massacres. That prompted his Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle. However, the two sides subsequently made efforts to reach a diplomatic solution, including a pledge by Zelensky to “grant a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”. Poland’s energy ministry has signed an agreement with two state-owned companies, Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe (PEJ) and Polska Grupa Energetyczna (PGE), setting out responsibilities for preparing for the construction of Poland’s planned second nuclear power plant. “This is an investment in our security, sovereignty and economic development,” declared energy minister Miłosz Motyka. “Having our own stable energy sources strengthens Poland’s resilience to crises and reduces dependence on external suppliers.” ❗️ @ME_GOV_PL, @PEJ_PL i @Grupa_PGE podpisały dziś porozumienie określające zasady współpracy przy przygotowaniu budowy drugiej polskiej elektrowni jądrowej 🇵🇱 Polska jest 20. gospodarką świata, ale nasze ambicje sięgają wyżej. Nie będzie silnej, niezależnej gospodarki bez… pic.twitter.com/eQ7zWFEolh — Miłosz Motyka (@motykamilosz) October 13, 2026 Under the agreement, PEJ, which is also responsible for developing a first nuclear project that is already underway on Poland’s northern Baltic Sea coast, will act as the investor and coordinate the project. PGE, the country’s largest power producer, will prepare preliminary feasibility studies and analyse potential locations for the plant. However, a decision on selecting an international partner for the project is not expected to be made until next year. The potential candidates include US company Westinghouse, which is involved in the first nuclear power plant, France’s EDF, and Canada’s AtkinsRéalis. The second plant was initially envisaged as a joint project with Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP), a South Korean company, under a letter of intent signed in 2022 under Poland’s former government. However, the partnership was never formalised and fell through last year. Once the new partner has been selected, it will work with PGE to analyse potential sites. The current preferred locations are Bełchatów – home to the largest coal-fired power station in Europe, owned by PGE – and Konin, both in central Poland, because of their existing energy infrastructure and experience in electricity generation. According to the Polish government’s nuclear strategy – which was last month updated for the first time since 2020 – construction of the second plant is scheduled to begin in 2032, with its first reactor potentially entering service in 2040. That would be one year behind the previously planned schedule. The government has updated Poland's nuclear strategy for the first time in six years, with the new plan confirming that the first nuclear plant will launch three years later than previously planned, in 2036, and the second in 2040, one year behind schedule https://t.co/vgtuSXLDjZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 3, 2026 Meanwhile, Poland plans to begin construction of its first nuclear power station in 2028, with the plant beginning operation in 2036, three years later than previously planned. Together, the two plants are expected to have a combined capacity of up to 9 gigawatts. The move is part of Poland’s transition away from coal – which still generates around half of electricity, by far the highest proportion in the European Union – and towards cleaner sources of energy, particularly nuclear and renewables. Under a national energy and climate plan approved in June, Poland aims by 2040 for coal to account for only 0-5% of the energy mix. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%). World.title: Everything you need to know one year ahead of Poland’s parliamentary elections
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Daniel Tilles Poland will hold parliamentary elections a year from now. The outcome will decide who governs the country for the next four years – although, given how close the polls are, and with questions over coalition formation, it could also result in uncertainty, chaos, and even new elections being called. Below, we explain how the elections work, which parties will be standing, what kind of outcomes are possible, and which issues may animate the campaign. When will the election take place? Assuming early elections are not called, the vote must take place on a non-working day in the last 30 days before the end of the current four-year parliamentary term, which began on 13 November 2023. Because elections in Poland are held on Sundays, that gives four possible dates: 17, 24 or 31 October, or 7 November (though 1 November and 11 November, which are public holidays, are also theoretically possible). It is the president, Karol Nawrocki, who will choose the date. He must do so no later than 90 days before the end of the current parliamentary term. How does voting work? The 460 members of the more powerful lower house, the Sejm, are elected through proportional representation, meaning that seats are distributed more or less on the basis of the share of the vote parties receive (using the so-called D’Hondt method for allocating seats from electoral lists put forward by each party). However, parties must receive at least 5% of the vote nationally to enter parliament (a figure that rises to 8% for coalitions of parties who stand on a single electoral list). The 100 members of the upper-house Senate are chosen through a first-past-the-post system similar to how members of the US Congress or British House of Commons are elected, with the candidate in each district that receives the most votes winning the seat. How is a government formed? A government can only be formed if it can win a vote of confidence in the Sejm. After the elections, the president designates a prime minister, who is tasked with forming a government – which would almost certainly be made up of a coalition of parties – that must then win a vote of confidence. If they fail to do so (as happened in 2023), the Sejm votes to choose an alternative prime minister, who likewise must try to form a government that has the confidence of the Sejm. Parliament has chosen @donaldtusk as Poland's new prime minister. That paves the way for him to form a new government in the coming days, ending the eight-year rule of the national-conservative PiS party https://t.co/iZUKh2rxnP — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 11, 2023 If that fails, the president has a second chance to pick a prime minister, who must again win a confidence vote. However, whereas the previous two votes require an absolute majority (większość bezwzględna) to be carried, this time only a simple majority is needed, making it easier to form a minority government. If this third and final attempt does not work, then parliament is dissolved and new elections are called. Who is likely to form the next government? At the moment, it is incredibly difficult to say. Polls suggest an even split in support between parties generally aligned with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition – which ranges from left to centre right – and the right-wing opposition. However, the 5% electoral threshold complicates the picture. According to current polling averages compiled by Polish website eWybory and Politico Europe, Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) leads with 32%. One of its coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), is on 7%, while two others, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), are on around 3% and 1%, respectively. Another left-wing party, Together (Razem), which previously caucused with the ruling coalition but split in 2024, is on around 4%. Meanwhile, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, is on 20%. Two far-right opposition groups, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have 14% and 9%, respectively. The right-wing Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), which broke away from PiS this year, is at around 5%. If we treat those as two potential blocs, parties more or less aligned with the current government are on around 47% while the right-wing opposition is on 48%. However, PSL and Poland 2050 currently look likely to fall below the 5% threshold if they stand alone, meaning votes for them would not count. That would significantly harm Tusk’s chances of forming a new government. If Rozwój Plus stood alone and fell below the threshold, that would harm the opposition. It is therefore likely that, as the elections draw nearer, parties that seem likely to fall below 5% will seek to join forces with other groups. In 2023, PSL and Poland 2050 stood together in the so-called Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance. But they have made clear they do not intend to do that again. That leaves them with limited options. They could join forces with KO on a single electoral list, but that does not guarantee that their voters will follow them. Indeed, some may baulk at voting for Tusk’s party. The Polish People's Party's parliamentary survival is on a knife edge, and could determine whether @donaldtusk's coalition remains in power after next year's elections.@AleksSzczerbiak looks at the challenges facing PSL and how it may respond to them https://t.co/MmswSLNWJE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 30, 2026 Meanwhile, there are some wildcards in the pack. KKP, led by radical-right extremist Grzegorz Braun, is shunned by the mainstream right for its antisemitism, anti-Americanism and sympathy towards Russia. PiS’s leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, has declared that he would not allow Braun to join government. Development Plus has taken a similar position. Both parties value relations with the US and the Trump administration, whose ambassador to Poland has reportedly pushed them to rule out working with Braun. However, if KKP maintains its current level of support, it looks almost impossible for the opposition to form a parliamentary majority without it, meaning there would be a strong temptation to somehow work with Braun. Kaczyński’s determination to remove Tusk from power may outweigh his dislike of Braun and desire to keep the Americans onside. The Together party – if it manages to pass the 5% threshold – could likewise represent a challenge for Tusk when forming a coalition, given that it has criticised the government for failing to keep promises on healthcare spending, public sector pay, and liberalising the abortion law. There also remains the possibility of some elements from each camp joining the other side – either entire parties or individual MPs defecting – in order to help form a government. PiS has long sought to tempt PSL to its side (and recent reports suggest that even President Donald Trump tried to persuade PSL’s leader, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, to do so). It is conceivable that Rozwój Plus could work with parts of the current ruling camp, though its hatred of Tusk would make that very difficult. All of the difficulties outlined above mean there is a significant chance that it will not be possible for anyone to form a government, necessitating fresh elections – something that has never happened before in Poland. If that happens, it would mean uncertainty and a lack of clear leadership at a time when Poland is facing major security challenges and a worsening fiscal situation. What about the Senate? The Senate, like the Sejm, is currently controlled by the ruling coalition. Indeed, Tusk has an even larger majority there than in the lower house, making it harder for the opposition to flip. Although the Senate is much weaker than the Sejm – and control of it does not determine who forms the government – it does have some powers that make it a useful asset. It can slow down the passage of legislation, though not block it. The Senate also must approve the appointment of certain officials, such as the heads of the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) and the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), as well as the Commissioner for Human Rights (RPO). In a rare clash between Poland’s two houses of parliament, in both of which the government has a majority, the Senate has rejected a candidate chosen by the Sejm to become the new head of the state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) https://t.co/QUsqfDNh4s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2026 The upper house is also required to approve proposals by the president to hold national referendums. This year, the Senate has twice blocked moves by Nawrocki to hold a referendum on EU climate policies. In a situation where Tusk’s coalition controlled the Sejm, and was therefore still in government, but the right-wing opposition held the Senate, that would give the president a powerful tool to call referendums on policies important to him and the opposition. To that end, there have been calls for the right-wing and far-right opposition to form a so-called Senate pact, of the type that Tusk and his allies used to win control of the upper house in 2019 and 2023. What that means in practice is that the parties forming the pact agree to stand only one candidate between them in each of the 100 Senate districts, making it more likely that they will scoop up votes from supporters of all the parties in the pact and win the winner-takes-all contest. What role will Nawrocki play in all of this? Presidents are in theory expected to be non-partisan. In practice, however, they will seek to boost parties or coalitions aligned with them, and with whom it will be easier to work. Since Nawrocki was elected last year, relations and cooperation between the president and government have reached unprecedently low levels. Within just 10 months, Nawrocki had vetoed more bills than any previous president in history over their entire terms. He has made it abundantly clear that he would prefer to work with a government formed from the right-wing opposition. During his first year, President Nawrocki has transformed his office into a centre of resistance to the government and become a unifying figure for the fragmented right. But he faces new challenges moving towards the next election, writes @AleksSzczerbiak https://t.co/uNYrFOppSp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026 However, the extent to which he will be involved in the election campaign is unclear. Some figures on the right hope that Nawrocki will act as a figurehead, using his positive relations with parties across the right-wing opposition to bring them together. In practical terms, this could involve him acting as the patron of a Senate pact (something the head of Nawrocki’s cabinet recently said the president was willing to do), as well as helping right-wing parties form a coalition government after the elections. Nawrocki also continues to enjoy strong approval ratings among the conservative electorate, meaning that his presence during the election campaign could act as a boost for the opposition. What issues are likely to feature in the campaign? A major issue will be the question of sovereignty. The right-wing opposition accuses Tusk of being Brussels’ and Berlin’s lapdog, handing over ever more power to the EU and prioritising Germany’s interests over Poland’s. The ruling coalition, meanwhile, argues that PiS is too beholden to the Trump administration and warns that the opposition is pushing Poland towards “Polexit” from the EU, which would leave the country isolated and vulnerable, as well as much poorer. Those battle lines extend to security policy too, with the Tusk government shifting emphasis towards Europe as a defence partner but PiS insisting that only the US can truly guarantee Poland’s security. Poland’s desire to host a new permanent US military base has already become highly politicised. If progress stalls, the opposition will blame the government. If Washington confirms that the base will go ahead, Nawrocki will seek to take the credit, based on his good relationship with Trump. On this point, though, it is worth noting the split within the opposition. While PiS and Rozwój Plus are strongly pro-American, Confederation and, to an even greater extent, KKP, are opposed to a greater US presence in Poland. President @NawrockiKn says that a planned new permanent US military base in Poland is “confirmed” because his American counterpart, Donald Trump, is “famous for keeping his word”. He also suggested that the new facility will be called “Fort Trump” https://t.co/uGGJSBe5nr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 23, 2026 Where the right-wing opposition has been united, however, is on pushing for a tougher position towards Ukraine and Ukrainian refugees in Poland. While tensions have calmed significantly since the crisis sparked in May by President Volodymyr Zelensky naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles in World War Two, it is likely that relations with Ukraine and the large-scale presence of Ukrainians in Poland will remain important issues during the election campaign. The ruling coalition, meanwhile, will be keen to emphasise its tough overall approach to immigration, which it says was out of control under the former PiS government. It can point to the falling number of new residence permits being issued, the growing number of deportations, and tougher measures on the Belarus border, including a ban on asylum claims. Poland has forcibly removed 2,100 foreigners from the country this year, around twice as many as in 2024. The figures come after the government introduced a tougher new migration policy last year, which has included more deportations of foreign criminals https://t.co/zOBxPLipy8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 31, 2025 The economy, public finances and cost of living are also likely to be major issues. As long as the current global energy crisis sparked by the conflict around Iran continues, the opposition will seek to place the blame for record fuel prices on the government. They will also cite large deficits and the ballooning public debt as evidence that Tusk is mismanaging the economy. The ruling coalition will point to continued strong economic growth and blame Nawrocki, who has vetoed revenue-generating tax bills, for the fiscal situation. World.title: Kraków’s new mayor withdraws patronage of LGBT+ equality march
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. In one of his first policy announcements since being elected on Sunday, the new mayor of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has declared that he will withdraw official patronage of its annual LGBT+ equality march. Łukasz Gibała, who has been supportive of LGBT+ rights in the past and has previously attended the march, argues that the event has become too “partisan”. He stood for election as an independent and has pledged to depoliticise city hall. His decision does not prevent the march from taking place. But it means that it no longer has the official support of the city. Łukasz Gibała: Nie obejmę patronatem Marszu Równości. Polityka progresywna nie zawsze się sprawdza https://t.co/vIw8ZsSPQK — Radio Kraków (@RadioKrakow) October 12, 2026 Kraków’s equality march, which was first held in 2004, draws thousands of participants when it takes place each year in May. The event is used to demand greater LGBT+ rights in Poland, which is ranked as one of the worst countries in Europe for LGBT+ people. In 2021, the city’s former mayor, Jacek Majchrowski, became an honorary patron of the march. In 2024, his successor, Aleksander Miszalski, became the first mayor to attend the event, declaring that Kraków should be “a home for everyone”. However, Miszalski was removed from office earlier this year in a recall referendum, necessitating a new election, which was won by Gibała. He beat Monika Piątkowska, who, like Miszaski, is a member of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party of Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Kraków's new mayor has announced that he will attend the city’s LGBT parade next week, something his long-serving predecessor never did. "I want to build a tolerant Kraków, a home for everyone," says @OlekMiszalski, who took office this week https://t.co/ZQ9SzZiHp4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 9, 2024 The day after his victory, Gibała was asked by local broadcaster Radio Kraków if he would continue city hall’s patronage of the equality march. The new mayor, who takes office next week, declared that he would not, saying he “will avoid sponsoring events that have a partisan character”. “I have the impression that, over the past three years or so, the community that organises equality marches has simply become partisan,” said Gibała. “These are people who ran for parliament and local government on the lists of specific political parties.” Gibała did not indicate who he was referring to. However, one of the organisers of the equality march in Kraków is Magdalena Dropek, who has three times stood as a candidate for The Left (Lewica), one of the groups in Tusk’s ruling coalition, in elections to the Polish and European parliaments. Gibała emphasised that he has himself attended equality marches in the past “and does not regret it”. He was previously an MP for both KO (when it was known as Civic Platform, PO) as well as for the liberal Palikot’s Movement (Ruch Palikota), later known as Your Movement (Twój Ruch). During the recent mayoral election campaign, Gibała told broadcaster TVN that, as an MP, he had supported the introduction of same-sex civil partnerships in Poland, and said that his views had not changed. When asked if that meant that, as mayor, he would continue the city’s practice of transcribing foreign same-sex marriages into the civil registry – as Poland was ordered to do last year by the Court of Justice of the European Union – Gibała said that he would. However, he added that he was doing this as a “legalist” who respects the current legal situation. “If a different political party wins [parliamentary elections] next year and changes the law in Poland, it [recognition of foreign same-sex marriages] won’t happen,” he told Radio Kraków. In fact, although the current government supports recognition of foreign-same sex marraiges, it has not changed the law in that regard. Polish law still does not recognise any form of same-sex union. The government, aware that opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki would veto any change to the law, instead issued a regulation (which does not require presidential approval) empowering local authorities to transcribe foreign same-sex marriages into their registries. Many municipalities, especially more liberal larger cities, have begun to do so (some even did before the regulation was issued). But others, especially in more conservative places, have refused to, often arguing that there are legal doubts around the issue. Data provided to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) by the digital affairs ministry last week showed that 516 foreign same-sex marriages have so far been registered in Poland. The largest numbers were in Warsaw (209), Wrocław (73) and Kraków (46). The Polish government has granted same-sex couples who married abroad the same tax rights as other married couples It follows an EU court ruling ordering Poland to recognise such marriages even though domestic law does not allow any form of same-sex union https://t.co/3gE1PQU9AQ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 25, 2026 In the same interview this week with Radio Kraków, Gibała was asked if he would “return to your political roots” and be a “progressive mayor”. He responded by saying that, while “there are some issues where progressive policies actually work, there are others where they don’t”. Asked for an example of the latter, Gibała said that, “if we look, for example, at what’s happening in western European cities, there are entire neighbourhoods in which there is a fear of entering for people of our skin colour”. World.title: Norwegian defence firm Kongsberg to build anti-drone factory in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Norwegian defence firm Kongsberg has announced plans to build a new factory in Poland producing counter-drone systems. The firm will invest over 200 million zloty (€46 million) in the facility, creating more than 100 long-term jobs. “The new facility will support Polish industry and defence capabilities and strengthen Kongsberg’s presence in Poland,” declared CEO Eirik Lie alongside Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz at the Warsaw Security Forum, where Norway is this year serving as the official partner nation. In January, Kongsberg signed an agreement to supply a new anti-drone system to Poland in partnership with Polish state defence group PGZ. The project comes in response to growing fears over the threat of Russian drones, around 20 of which violated Polish airspace on one night in September last year. Norwegowie inwestują w Polsce. Duża inwestycja #Kongsberg na Pomorzu ogłoszona właśnie na #WSF2026. Szybka budowa fabryki i nowe miejsca pracy. pic.twitter.com/msI2FWGym8 — Beata Górka-Winter (@BeataGWinter) October 12, 2026 Kosiniak-Kamysz thanked Kongsberg for its investment and emphasised that Polish-Norwegian relations are at their highest point in history, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The announcement of the counter-drone plant came as Poland and Norway’s prime ministers, Donald Tusk and Jonas Gahr Støre, signed a declaration on strategic partnership that pledged to deepen security ties, including joint defence production and strengthening NATO’s northern and eastern flanks. While the exact location of the plant has not been revealed, Kongsberg stated that it would be in northern Poland, near the Tricity area (consisting of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Sopot) on the Baltic Sea coast. Construction of the facility is scheduled to begin this year, with production at the site scheduled to commence in the first half of 2028. Counter-drone technology has become an increasing priority for Poland following Russian airspace violations and also the growing use by Moscow of jet-powered drones to strike targets in Ukraine close to the Polish border, including recently a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw. Polish spending on drones and counter-drone systems combined rose from 100 million zloty in 2023 to 26 billion zloty in 2026, deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk announced in August, quoted by news website Interia. The summary report of this week’s Warsaw Security Forum suggested the use of counter-drone systems to create a “controlled fly-zone” over the Suwałki Gap, a strategically important choke point along the Polish-Lithuanian border that sits between the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and Russia’s ally Belarus. Poland has signed an agreement for a new anti-drone system that it claims will be the first of its kind in Europe. The network is intended to protect Poland’s eastern borders, where last year around 20 Russian drones crossed in an unprecedented incursion https://t.co/WhWhJxDwXA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 30, 2026 Poland has in recent years moved to strengthen its defence ties with countries around the Baltic Sea. In January, it was announced that Poland will manufacture missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is purchasing from South Korea. Norway has already bought Piorun air-defence systems from Poland. In 2024, Poland and Sweden signed a strategic partnership. The two countries subsequently held their first bilateral military exercises in the Baltic, and Poland this year ordered three submarines from Swedish manufacturer Saab. Saab this year also signed a strategic collaboration agreement with PGZ that will see them cooperate on naval production, servicing and technology. On Monday this week, Norway’s defence ministry announced that Poland will join an initiative recently launched by 11 European countries and Canada to cooperate more closely on security in the North Atlantic, Arctic and Baltic Sea. World.title: New Polish constitutional court judge takes oath in defiance of president
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The standoff between the government and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki over Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom Prime Minister Donald Tusk recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president. Berek is now the fifth judge to take their oath without presidential approval. The previous four have been denied entry to the TK, and speculation is rife that the government may soon take action to ensure that the excluded judges are able to take up their positions. PILNE 🚨 dr Maciej Berek złożył w Sejmie ślubowanie na sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego! pic.twitter.com/sZlzLnsL3M — Bogdan Zdrojewski (@BZdrojewski) October 14, 2026 Under Polish law, a new TK judge must swear an oath “before the president”. However, since Berek was elected to the TK by the government’s majority in parliament in early September, Nawrocki has refused to swear him in. The president claims that Berek has not presented evidence that he meets the statutory requirement of having practiced as a legal counsel for at least 10 years. Berek says he has done so. Nawrocki has also expressed his opposition to the fact that Berek has gone from serving in Tusk’s cabinet, where he was minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of policy, to becoming a TK judge. Even some members of Tusk’s ruling coalition opposed Berek’s candidacy, saying that it contradicted the government’s earlier pledges to “depoliticise” the judicial system, including by banning anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge. With no invitation from Nawrocki forthcoming, on Wednesday morning Berek instead swore his oath at a ceremony organised in parliament. He declared that he was directing the oath towards the president, despite Nawrocki not being present. The development came a day after the Venice Commission, an advisory body to the Council of Europe on constitutional law, had issued an opinion effectively supporting the government’s position on the crisis around the TK. The commission found that the Polish president should swear in TK judges chosen by parliament “without delay” and does not have the power to review their election. It added that, if the president refuses to receive a judge’s oath, they are justified in taking it without him being present. The opinion was welcomed by Tusk and his government. However, Nawrocki’s spokesman, Rafał Leśkiewicz, pointed out that the Venice Commission’s opinions are advisory and not legally binding. 1294/2026 Poland – Opinion on the powers of the President in the context of the oath-taking of the judges of the Constitutional Tribunal and of other judicial appointments.https://t.co/vcpfNeteWo — Radoslaw Szewczyk (@SzewczykRadek) October 13, 2026 Earlier this year, four other TK judges chosen by parliament similarly organised their own swearing-in ceremony in parliament after Nawrocki failed to invite them to take their oaths before him. However, when they arrived at the TK to take up their positions, they were prevented from doing so by the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government (and had previously served as a minister in that government). Święczkowski argues that the judges cannot take up their positions unless they swear an oath in the presence of Nawrocki, who was elected as president last year with the support of PiS. In May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that the four judges be accepted onto the TK. However, Święczkowski has so far refused to comply, arguing that the ECHR does not have the authority to make such a decision. In a further escalation of the crisis around Poland's constitutional court, prosecutors have charged two officials for preventing new judges from taking up their positions. Meanwhile, the chief justice has launched proceedings against three other judges https://t.co/aeKKue37oN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 24, 2026 Since replacing PiS in office in December 2023, Tusk’s government has refused to recognise the legitimacy of the TK, pointing to the fact that some of its judges were unlawfully appointed under PiS. It has ignored all rulings issued by the tribunal. Until this year, the ruling coalition refused to fill new vacancies that resulted from the expiration of judges’ nine-year terms or their retirement. However, that position changed in March, when it began filling the backlog. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its candidates in theory now have a majority on the 15-person court. However, Nawrocki has only sworn in three of those judges, with the other refused entry to the TK. Prime Minister @donaldtusk has succeeded in having Maciej Berek, whom he recently described as his “right-hand man”, elected by parliament as a constitutional court judge, staving off a rebellion from some members of his own coalition https://t.co/VAVbkGL8xS — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 4, 2026 Speculation has been rife that the government will take action to ensure that the excluded judges can gain access to the court, perhaps even using the police to force entry. Speaking to broadcaster Polsat today, justice minister Waldemar Żurek said that “the state must do everything to enable these judges to adjudicate”. He added that Berek’s swearing-in “brings us much closer to launching the tribunal’s work”. However, Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, told Polsat that today’s ceremony in parliament was “grotesque” and “a sad day for Polish democracy”. This morning has also seen some clashes between police and supporters of PiS and Nawrocki, who have been camped out outside the TK in order to defend it from any takeover by force. ❗️Policja szarpie posłów oraz zgromadzonych obywateli pod TK ❗️ pic.twitter.com/eGPRFQJnAX — Oskar Szafarowicz (@Szafarowicz2001) October 14, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Prague Christmas Markets 2026 Start in November – Dates and Locations
World.content:
Prague’s Christmas markets will return in November 2026, with the first stalls opening at Náměstí Míru on November 20.

The main markets in Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square will follow on November 28, bringing traditional Czech food, handmade decorations and a program of seasonal performances to the city center.

Náměstí Republiky follows on November 25, and Tylovo náměstí opens on November 26.



The main markets at Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square begin on November 28 and continue until January 6, 2027. The other markets close on Christmas Eve, December 24.

Here are the opening dates and hours for the main locations.

– náměstí Míru — November 20 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

– náměstí Republiky — November 25 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

– Tylovo náměsti — November 26 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

– Old Town Square — November 28 to January 6, 2027, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

– Wenceslas Square — November 28 to January 6, 2027, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

Smaller Christmas Markets Across Prague

Several markets open before the main city-center venues and offer alternatives for visitors who want to explore different neighborhoods.

Further options include the market at Anděl and Lesser Town Christmas on Kampa Island.

náměstí Jiřího z Poděbrad will host farmers’ markets during Advent, with a design market joining them every Sunday during the season. These events offer opportunities to browse locally made products and find gifts beyond the usual Christmas-market stalls.

World.title: Modeselektor to Open Spectaculare Festival at Prague’s ROXY
World.content:
Berlin electronic duo Modeselektor will open the 14th edition of Spectaculare on 3 March 2027, bringing their live show to ROXY alongside new music from their latest album, MDSLKTR

Gernot Bronsert and Sebastian Szary will perform a set combining techno, electro, hip-hop and bass music, accompanied by visual projections and lighting.

The concert comes shortly after the release of MDSLKTR, an album that revisits the sound and influences that have shaped the duo’s nearly three-decade career.



The record follows Classics Vol. 01, a project that revisited material from their early albums Hello Mom! and Happy Birthday! and drew on years of studio recordings and unfinished ideas.

With MDSLKTR, Modeselektor return to the sounds that first defined their music, drawing on Berlin rave culture, techno, electro, IDM and hip-hop while continuing to move between genres.

Since emerging from Berlin’s underground electronic scene, the duo have built an international following through their studio albums, live performances and collaborations with artists including Radiohead frontman Thom Yorke, Tommy Cash, Flohio and Blixa Bargeld.

They also formed Moderat with producer Apparat and run the independent record label Monkeytown Records.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Festival Spectaculare (@spectaculare_music)

Berlin-based multi-instrumentalist Philipp Johann Thimm will open the evening. A longtime collaborator of Apparat, Thimm has worked across electronic and acoustic music as well as audiovisual projects. His work on Apparat’s album *LP5* contributed to a Grammy-nominated project, while his solo work explores the meeting point between electronic composition and live instrumentation.

World.title: Prague’s Día de Muertos Festival Returns to Holešovice on November 5th
World.content:
Prague’s Holešovice Market will host the fifth annual Día de Muertos festival on November 5, bringing Mexican food, live music, traditional decorations and family activities.

The event, organized in cooperation with Jarritos and Nuevo Progreso, will run from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. Halls 13 and 11 will host a Mexican market and a carnival for children.

Visitors can arrive throughout the day, with the food stalls opening at lunchtime.



The selection will include Mexican and South American specialties, tortillas, grilled dishes and Jarritos soft drinks. A special beer brewed by Falcon brewery for the occasion will also be available.

The food zone will remain open until 10 p.m., giving visitors time to sample different dishes and explore the festival’s other attractions.

One of the main attractions will be a traditional ofrenda, or Day of the Dead altar, prepared by the Mexican Embassy. Decorated with photographs, flowers, candles and personal objects, the altar will introduce visitors to the traditions behind the holiday.

Día de Muertos is dedicated to remembering deceased family members and loved ones.

In Mexican tradition, the holiday celebrates their continuing place in family life and the belief that their spirits return to visit the living. Its customs differ from Halloween, combining remembrance with food, music, flowers and colorful decorations.

Hall 11 will become the PEDRO Kids’ Zone from 1 p.m. to 7 p.m., with a program designed for children and families.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Holešovická tržnice (@holesovickatrznice)

Activities will include dance workshops, Mexican music, crafts, stories about the holiday and a game in which children throw balls at illuminated skulls. Visitors will also have the opportunity to meet a Xoloitzcuintle, the Mexican hairless dog traditionally associated with guiding souls to the afterlife.

Costumes are welcome, and the organizers have divided the program into six one-hour sessions beginning at 1 p.m., 2 p.m., 3 p.m., 4 p.m., 5 p.m. and 6 p.m.

Admission costs CZK 100 per person for adults and children aged three and older. Tickets are available through GoOut and at the venue, subject to availability. Each ticket covers one hour of activities, after which visitors can explore the rest of the festival.

The program will also feature mariachi musicians, stilt walkers, colorful masks and costumes, and a festival parade. DJs will provide music throughout the day, while a screening of the animated film Coco will offer another introduction to Mexican traditions surrounding death and remembrance.

World.title: Danish-Japanese Chain Sticks’n’Sushi to Open First Prague Restaurant
World.content:
Sticks’n’Sushi will open its first Czech restaurant in central Prague on Wednesday, November 4, introducing its combination of Japanese cuisine and Danish design to the local dining scene.



The restaurant will occupy a site on Jungmannovo náměstí in Prague 1. Ahead of the official opening, guests will be able to sample the menu at half price from November 1 to 3.

Those interested in attending the preview must register online. Registered guests will then receive a link to book a table for one of the available dates.

The menu combines sushi, sashimi and salads with kushiyaki, Japanese-style grilled skewers. The restaurant will also offer set menus intended for sharing, making them suitable for groups.

Among the dishes are Beef Tataki, served with miso aïoli, truffle ponzu and crispy Jerusalem artichoke, and the Temaki Setto, which allows diners to assemble their own hand rolls with ingredients including lobster, Wagyu tartare and avocado.

Another addition is the Ebi Sando, a sandwich featuring crispy shrimp, truffle and miso aïoli. The Sticks Setto features skewers of Japanese Wagyu beef, Iberian pork, shrimp and miso-marinated black cod, served on a hot stone at the table.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Sticks’n’Sushi Czech Republic (@sticksnsushi_cz)

The drinks list includes sake, Japanese teas, cocktails and premium spirits. The restaurant will also serve a Japanese rice lager brewed for the chain by Danish brewery Mikkeller.

Zbyněk Pokorný, chief executive of Sushi Group s.r.o., which is bringing the concept to the Czech market, said the opening followed nearly two years of preparation.

“We believe that the combination of Japanese quality, Danish hospitality, and a strong focus on the overall guest experience is a perfect fit for Prague,” Pokorný said. He added that the company was looking forward to welcoming its first guests.

Reservations can be made through the company’s Czech website.

About Sticks’n’Sushi

Founded in Copenhagen in 1994, Sticks’n’Sushi was established by brothers Jens and Kim Rahbek, who have Danish and Japanese roots, and Thor Andersen. The first restaurant opened in a basement space in the Danish capital.

The business has since expanded into an international restaurant group, with locations in Denmark, Germany and the United Kingdom. Its interiors draw on Japanese and Danish influences, with individual restaurants featuring their own design elements within the brand’s overall concept.

World.title: Czechia Among Top 5 Destinations for Digital Nomads
World.content:
The Czech Republic has been ranked the fifth-best country in the world for digital nomads, outperforming popular destinations such as Portugal, France, and the United Arab Emirates.

The ranking, compiled by Global Citizen Solutions and reported by Euronews, assessed factors like visa accessibility, cost of living, and quality of life.



The study found that Europe dominates the list, with Spain taking first place, followed by the Netherlands, Uruguay, and Canada. Seven out of the top ten destinations for remote workers are in Europe, confirming the continent’s continued appeal for professionals seeking stability and mobility.

Spain secured the top position thanks to its dedicated digital nomad visa, which allows foreigners to work remotely either for international companies or for Spanish-based businesses, provided that domestic work accounts for no more than 20 percent of their total income.

From an economic perspective, Spain is described as more affordable than northern European countries, especially in smaller cities where living costs are lower but the quality of healthcare, safety, and services remains high.

The Czech Republic, meanwhile, ranked fifth globally and third within Europe, praised for its balance between affordability and high living standards. The country offers a stable environment, well-developed infrastructure, and a relatively low cost of living compared to Western Europe — qualities that continue to attract freelancers and remote professionals.

According to the report, “Many European jurisdictions offer direct paths to permanent residency and eventual citizenship, providing digital nomads with strong passports and long-term mobility. Add to that Europe’s reputation for safety, stable institutions, and cultural richness, and it’s easy to see why the continent remains such an attractive base.”

The Czech Republic was followed by Portugal, France, the UAE, Germany, and Malta rounding out the top ten. Interestingly, while Southeast Asia remains a favorite among travelers, its countries did not make it to the upper ranks of this year’s digital nomad list — a sign that security, stability, and residency options are becoming increasingly important to remote workers.

Here are the top ten countries for digital nomads in 2026:

Spain The Netherlands Uruguay Canada Czechia Portugal France United Arab Emirates Germany Malta

World.title: The Czech Republic’s Tallest Structures Have Been Torn Down
World.content:
Two 355-meter radio transmission towers in Liblice were brought down in a controlled demolition on October 15, ending nearly half a century as the country’s tallest structures.

The towers collapsed at 11:15 a.m. local time after demolition crews used approximately 4.5 kilograms of Semtex explosives to sever supporting cables, iDNES.cz reported.



Hundreds of spectators gathered to watch the demolition, some bringing binoculars and folding chairs. Several residents were visibly emotional as the towers fell.

“We’ve lost our beacon and a symbol of home,” local residents told the outlet.

The Liblice B transmitter entered service in December 1976 and was once the most powerful radio broadcasting facility in Central Europe.

Czech Radio stopped using it for medium-wave broadcasts at the end of 2021, while Country Radio continued operating there until March 2025.

Some locals had called for the towers to be preserved as part of Czechoslovakia’s engineering and broadcasting heritage. Others viewed them as obsolete structures dating from the communist era.

With the towers gone, the 347.5-meter Krašov television and radio transmitter has become the tallest structure in the Czech Republic.

Crews are expected to spend approximately 20 more days clearing the collapsed steel structures.

World.title: Brno Burger Brand Pickle Plans Up to Seven Locations in Prague
World.content:
A burger brand recently launched in Brno is preparing to expand into Prague, where it plans to open up to seven restaurants.

Pickle also has ambitions to enter other Czech and Slovak cities before expanding across Europe and eventually Asia.

The first Pickle restaurant opened in Brno in June 2026.



Co-founder Peter Szamuhel now plans to establish the brand in Prague and Bratislava before launching a franchise network. If preparations proceed as planned, the first franchise locations could open in early 2027.

The company is considering six or seven restaurants in Prague and two or three in Bratislava. Other potential locations include Ostrava, Olomouc, Hradec Králové, Liberec, Nitra and Trnava.

Pickle aims to have its franchise model ready by the end of 2026. Although prospective partners have already expressed interest, the company is not yet signing agreements.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Pickle Brno (@pickledoublecheese)

The same burgers at every location

Maintaining consistent quality will be a major challenge as Pickle expands. The company plans to use regular inspections, mystery shopping, regional managers and ongoing staff training to ensure that customers receive the same food and service at every restaurant.

Ingredient supplies are another priority. Meat, buns and other key products must match those used at the original Brno location.

The restaurant currently prepares approximately 1,000 to 1,300 burgers a day, according to Szamuhel. Expanding the chain will require a supply network capable of supporting substantially greater demand.

Global ambitions within ten years

Pickle aims to establish ten locations across Czechia and Slovakia within three years, followed by another ten restaurants in other European countries over the next five to six years.

Its longer-term goal is to operate hundreds of locations worldwide within a decade, with Asia among its eventual targets.

World.title: Do You Really Need 10,000 Steps a Day? A Doctor’s Guide to Walking in Prague
World.content:
Walking is part of daily life in Prague, but how much is enough to benefit your health?

A doctor at Charles University explains why 7,000 steps a day may be a more realistic target.

Living in Prague often means walking to the tram, crossing the city centre on foot or taking a stroll through one of its parks. But does this add up to enough physical activity to improve your health? And is reaching 10,000 steps a day really necessary?

According to research published in The Lancet Public Health in 2025, walking around 7,000 steps a day may be enough to deliver significant health benefits.



The study found that people taking approximately 7,000 steps daily had a 47% lower risk of premature death and a 25% lower risk of cardiovascular disease compared with those walking around 2,000 steps a day.

These figures represent associations rather than guarantees, but they suggest that the widely promoted 10,000-step target is not a requirement for better health.

Why walking matters

Regular walking can help strengthen the heart, improve circulation, regulate blood pressure and blood sugar levels, and support muscle and joint health.

Its benefits are not limited to physical fitness. Spending time outdoors and walking regularly can also help reduce stress, improve mood and support better sleep.

The World Health Organization recommends that adults get 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity each week. This can include brisk walking for around 30 minutes a day, five days a week, to meet the minimum recommendation.

The pace matters, too. Brisk walking should make you breathe slightly harder while still allowing you to hold a conversation comfortably.

Where to walk in Prague

Prague offers plenty of opportunities to incorporate more walking into daily life without joining a gym or travelling outside the city.

Stromovka is a good option for beginners and those looking for longer walks on relatively flat paths. The extensive park provides a break from traffic and the busy streets of the city.

For a more demanding route, Divoká Šárka offers hills and woodland trails that provide a more strenuous workout while remaining within Prague.

Vyšehrad is suitable for a shorter walk, combining gentle climbs with views of the city and the Vltava River. Its location also makes it a practical option for those who have limited time.

For a longer weekend outing, Prokopské údolí offers walking routes through valleys and green spaces away from the city centre.

How to keep walking during winter

Shorter days, cold temperatures and icy pavements can make walking less appealing during the winter months. However, the arrival of colder weather does not mean abandoning a regular routine.

Dressing in layers, wearing shoes with good grip and choosing well-lit, cleared paths can make outdoor walks safer and more comfortable.

Even a 10- to 15-minute walk during a lunch break can be worthwhile. When pavements become icy, slowing down or choosing a safer indoor alternative is advisable.

Small changes can make a difference

Building more walking into everyday life does not require a major change in routine. Getting off the tram one stop earlier, taking a walk during lunch or using the stairs when practical can all help increase daily activity.

Those who currently walk relatively little can start with 10 to 15 minutes a day and gradually increase the duration as their fitness improves.

Rather than focusing on a fixed target, people who track their steps can aim to increase their usual daily total over time.

About the author

Darren Andrew Noronha, MD, is a medical doctor and PhD candidate at Charles University in Prague, with a research focus on cardiovascular health and disease prevention.

World.title: Hungarian international footballer Milos Kerkez removed from controversial Ukrainian blacklist
World.content:
Liverpool defender Milos Kerkez has been removed from a controversial Ukrainian blacklist, weeks after an incident involving the Hungarian international sparked outrage.

Milos Kerkez, the Hungarian international footballer currently playing for Liverpool, has been removed from the Ukrainian Myrotvorets database, which publishes information about individuals it considers hostile to Ukraine. According to HVG, the player’s removal may have been secured through the intervention of the Hungarian Football Federation and the country’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade.

However, while Kerkez’s name has disappeared from the controversial website, his father remains listed.

How did the Liverpool defender end up on the list?

The controversy began following a Nations League match between Hungary and Ukraine in Budapest, when Kerkez became involved in an altercation with several Ukrainian players during the closing stages of the game.

His father subsequently shared footage of the incident on Instagram, accompanied by Russian Paradise, a song by Russian rap group AK-47. The choice of music sparked outrage in Ukraine, particularly given the ongoing war with Russia.

Shortly afterwards, both Kerkez and his father appeared on the Myrotvorets website, accused of supporting Russian aggression. His father was also described as a pro-Russian provocateur. The footballer strongly rejected the allegations, insisting that he had never supported aggression of any kind.

“I have never supported any form of aggression in my life, and I do not support it now,” Kerkez told Hungarian news outlet Telex earlier this month.

He also distanced himself from his father’s social media activity, stressing that he could not be held responsible for another person’s actions.

Kerkez explained that the confrontation on the pitch had been about defending a teammate and that he would have acted the same way regardless of the opposing team.

If you missed it: Former Budapest mayor makes striking claims about Orbán and corruption

Hungarian foreign ministry may have helped secure removal

Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán had previously condemned the inclusion of Kerkez and Fidesz politician Balázs Hidvéghi in the database, criticising what she described as the stigmatisation and intimidation of Hungarian citizens.

The incident also attracted attention because several Hungarian political figures, including former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, have appeared on the website.

Established in 2014, Myrotvorets, meaning Peacemaker, publishes personal information about people its operators consider pro-Russian or hostile to Ukraine.

Despite its name and activities, the website is not an official Ukrainian government database. Its operations have long attracted controversy, particularly over the publication of personal information and the criteria used to identify alleged enemies of Ukraine. Although Kerkez has now been removed, his father, Hidvéghi and Viktor Orbán remain listed.

The exact circumstances surrounding the Liverpool defender’s removal have not been disclosed, and it remains unclear what discussions, if any, took place between Hungarian officials and those operating the website.

World.title: Wizz Air CEO on night flights: “We’ll give passengers the minister’s phone number”
World.content:
Wizz Air CEO József Váradi has made a sarcastic remark about Hungary’s transport minister amid a dispute over night-time flights at Budapest Airport and warned of a difficult winter for European aviation.

Wizz Air CEO József Váradi has warned that efforts to restrict night-time flights at Budapest’s Ferenc Liszt International Airport could have serious consequences for passengers. Speaking at a press event on Friday, he discussed the challenges of avoiding late arrivals and made an ironic remark about Hungary’s Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy, as reported by HVG.

The government has been working with Budapest Airport, HungaroControl and Wizz Air to reduce aircraft noise during the night. A joint working group is examining how to protect residents living near the airport without unnecessarily disrupting flight operations.

Váradi acknowledged that residents’ concerns were justified, but argued that many delays are caused by circumstances beyond the airline’s control.

Wizz Air CEO’s sarcastic response to night flight restrictions

According to Váradi, a delay early in the morning can affect an aircraft’s entire daily schedule, potentially causing its final flight to arrive in Budapest during restricted night-time hours.

In such situations, the airline may have to cancel the flight or divert passengers to another airport, such as Bratislava, rather than land in Budapest.

“And we’ll give passengers the minister’s phone number so they can call him,” Váradi remarked.

He argued that government measures intended to protect consumers could sometimes have the opposite effect, leaving travellers to deal with the consequences of cancelled or diverted flights.

While Wizz Air is adjusting its schedules to minimise late-night arrivals, Váradi stressed that disruptions cannot always be prevented. He also claimed that the airline’s newer aircraft generate roughly half as much noise per flight as those of some competitors.

If you missed it: Wizz Air cancels several Eastern flights for the entire winter season

Strong growth in Hungary despite a difficult outlook

Váradi said the airline remains the market leader in Hungary with a 38% share, operating 19 aircraft from its Budapest base and serving 88 destinations from Budapest and Debrecen combined.

The company carried 2.6 million passengers in Hungary during the summer, a 30% increase compared with the previous year. It expects to transport around nine million passengers in the country by the end of 2026, exceeding its original target of 8.3 million.

“We consider ourselves Hungary’s national airline,” the CEO said, highlighting the company’s contribution to tourism and major international events. However, the CEO warned that the coming winter would be challenging for Europe’s aviation industry, as high fuel prices and supply chain disruptions continue to affect airlines.

Wizz Air believes it has an advantage over competitors, having secured 82% of its fuel requirements for the next six months at approximately half the current market price. More than three-quarters of its fleet also consists of fuel-efficient Airbus A321neo aircraft.

Despite the difficult environment, the airline is pursuing further expansion, including new bases in Madrid, Valencia, Pristina and Brașov. By 2030, Wizz Air aims to carry 127 million passengers annually, compared with fewer than 70 million in 2025, while expanding its fleet from 276 to 335 aircraft.

World.title: Former Budapest mayor makes striking claims about Orbán and corruption
World.content:
Former Budapest mayor István Tarlós has made unusually sharp remarks about Viktor Orbán’s responsibility for corruption under Fidesz. However, the veteran politician was far from complimentary about Péter Magyar’s Tisza government either.

Former Budapest mayor István Tarlós has spoken openly about corruption allegations surrounding the former Fidesz government, acknowledging that a small group of people accumulated disproportionate wealth during Viktor Orbán’s time in power. In a wide-ranging interview with Hungarian news portal 24.hu, he also criticised the new Tisza government and reflected on the reasons behind Fidesz’s defeat in April’s parliamentary election.

Tarlós questions Orbán’s responsibility for corruption

István Tarlós, who served as Budapest’s mayor between 2010 and 2019 with the backing of Orbán’s Fidesz party and was a long-standing political ally of the former prime minister, acknowledged that a relatively small group of individuals became disproportionately wealthy under Fidesz, some of whom had close ties to Orbán.

He argued that Orbán bore political responsibility for these developments, although the extent of his legal responsibility remained unclear. Tarlós also admitted that he could not determine how widespread corruption had been during the Fidesz governments.

The former mayor also pointed to growing public dissatisfaction with Fidesz and Orbán, acknowledging that some of the criticism directed at them was justified.

“Fidesz was characterised by excessive self-confidence in almost every area, which ultimately backfired,” Tarlós said.

He also criticised the party’s internal culture, arguing that “servility sometimes took precedence over professionalism”.

Despite his criticism, Tarlós defended aspects of Orbán’s political legacy, arguing that the former government had left behind a functioning and organised state. However, he expressed doubts about Orbán’s chances of returning to power, suggesting that such a comeback currently appeared unlikely.

Péter Magyar’s government also faces criticism

The former mayor was equally outspoken about Hungary’s new government, led by Prime Minister Péter Magyar, whose Tisza Party defeated Fidesz in the April election.

Tarlós suggested that Magyar was still operating in campaign mode, attempting to maintain the protest sentiment that had helped his party secure victory rather than placing sufficient emphasis on the practical challenges of governing.

He was particularly critical of the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office, an institution established under the new administration to recover assets allegedly acquired through corruption.

According to Tarlós, the office’s extensive powers and political oversight raise serious concerns about the rule of law. He questioned the way arrests and investigations were being presented to the public, arguing that some individuals were effectively being declared guilty before investigations had concluded.

Nevertheless, he acknowledged that it was still too early to judge the Tisza government as a whole, noting that he barely knew most of its ministers and had met Magyar only on a few occasions.

If you missed it: PM Magyar met Zelensky in Brussels: Here’s what they talked about

Difficult decisions ahead for the new government

Tarlós welcomed the government’s decision to reduce spending on political propaganda but argued that this alone would not be enough to address Hungary’s wider challenges.

He also warned that recovering allegedly misappropriated public funds could involve lengthy legal proceedings, potentially taking years before any money returned to the state budget.

Turning to Hungary’s relationship with the European Union, the former mayor suggested that the new administration would face difficult choices. He argued that concessions to Brussels on issues such as migration, the war in Ukraine and LGBTQ-related policies could undermine Tisza’s domestic support, while renewed confrontation with the EU could trigger negative reactions from investors.
