World.title: Orbán government spent EUR 2.2 million on a monastery in Slovakia, but it is still unusable
World.content:
A historic monastery complex in southern Slovakia, purchased with Hungarian public money under the former Orbán government, remains unusable despite HUF hundreds of millions of being spent on its renovation.

The Orbán administration paid approximately EUR 219,000 for the properties in Šahy (Ipolyság), while nearly HUF 800 million (more than EUR 2.2 million) was allocated for the restoration project. However, construction has stalled, and its future remains uncertain. According to information provided by Hungary’s Ministry of Transport and Investment, more than HUF 440 million (more than EUR 1.2 million) has already been spent on renovation work. A further substantial investment will be needed before the complex can be put to use.

How did the Orbán government acquire the monastery?

As investigative journal Átlátszó reported, the story began in December 2020, when Slovak-Hungarian politician Örs Orosz announced that his Sine Metu civic association had purchased a historic building in Šahy. The complex included a former Premonstratensian monastery, which dates back around 800 years, and a neighbouring building associated with the Jesuits. The buildings had deteriorated significantly over the years. Orosz subsequently approached Hungarian government officials to discuss financing a complete restoration.

In March 2021, Manevi SK, a Slovak subsidiary of the Hungarian state-backed Central European Heritage Preservation Foundation (KEOMA), acquired the monastery complex and surrounding properties. The ministry has since confirmed that the properties were purchased from several sellers for a combined EUR 219,000, equivalent to approximately HUF 87 million (currently around EUR 240,000) at the time. This included EUR 99,000 paid to Sine Metu for properties associated with the Jesuit monastery.

Nearly HUF 800 million allocated for renovation

Hungary’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, led by Orbán’s arguably most important minister, Péter Szijjártó, allocated HUF 774 million (more than EUR 2.1 million) for the project, officially described as the rehabilitation of the former Premonstratensian granary in Šahy. The funding agreement was signed in December 2023 by Deputy Foreign Minister Levente Magyar. The first phase of the renovation was awarded to Pesti Építő Zrt., which secured the contract for a net HUF 445.97 million (more than EUR 1.2 million) in February 2025.

The work included structural repairs, strengthening the foundations and replacing the existing asbestos-containing roof. While the roof now appears to have been completed, the wider renovation remains unfinished. The original plans envisaged a restaurant, a 13-room hotel with a small wellness area and a brewery. These visions were shown in a Facebook post on the monastery’s official page in March 2025, but to this day it is their last post on the page.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

New government yet to decide the complex’s future

The renovation has stalled, with construction workers having left the site months ago. The change of government in Hungary has added uncertainty to the project. Péter Magyar’s government dissolved KEOMA, which had acquired 41 properties outside Hungary using public funds. Responsibility for its public duties and ownership rights over its subsidiaries was transferred to the Ministry of Transport and Investment.

The ministry confirmed that funding for the second phase remains available. However, work has not resumed because the authorities are reviewing the foundation’s property portfolio and the ownership structure of its corporate group. Officials said they could not yet provide details about when reconstruction might continue or how the complex would eventually be used.

More on the Orbán government: EU court rules Hungary broke the law by the early release of 2,500 people smugglers

Questions over transparency

The circumstances surrounding the purchase and renovation have raised questions about transparency in the Orbán government’s spending on properties beyond its borders. Orosz did not respond to questions about the original purchase price paid by his association or the source of its funding before publication of the original report.

Former Hungarian MP Ákos Hadházy has criticised the project, arguing that it illustrates wider concerns about the transparency of public spending on properties and initiatives in Hungarian communities abroad. For now, the historic monastery remains an unfinished project, with HUF hundreds of millions of already spent and its eventual purpose still undecided.

World.title: PM Magyar met Zelensky in Brussels: Here’s what they talked about
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has welcomed Ukraine’s first steps towards strengthening the rights of the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia following talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky in Brussels. The meeting also raised the prospect of a landmark visit to Budapest, where Zelensky has been invited to attend commemorations marking the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Hungarian Revolution.

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar held a one-to-one meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Brussels on Friday, describing progress on minority rights as an important first step towards restoring mutual trust between the two countries.

In a statement published on Facebook, Magyar said the main focus of the talks was the situation of the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia, western Ukraine. He welcomed a political agreement between Hungary and Ukraine aimed at strengthening minority rights and praised Kyiv for beginning to implement it.

According to Magyar, Ukraine’s parliament has adopted a law on minority education under the agreement, with implementation already under way.

Hungary welcomes progress on minority rights

Magyar also thanked Ukraine’s parliament for a resolution adopted in September acknowledging that crimes had been committed against ethnic Hungarians in Transcarpathia through forced labour and mass deportations between 1944 and 1946.

The issue is a sensitive part of the two countries’ shared history and has contributed to tensions between Budapest and Kyiv. Both leaders agreed to continue bilateral consultations at ministerial level, with particular attention to improving the situation of minorities living in their respective countries.

They also agreed that resetting political and economic relations was in the interests of both nations.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Magyar offers diplomatic support for peace

Beyond bilateral relations, the Hungarian prime minister expressed solidarity with Ukraine over Russia’s nearly five-year-long war of aggression. Magyar told Zelensky that Hungary was prepared to provide assistance through all available diplomatic means to help secure an early ceasefire and lasting peace.

Zelensky invited to Budapest for 1956 Revolution anniversary

Meanwhile, Ukraine has indicated that Zelensky could visit Budapest as early as next week after receiving an invitation to commemorations marking the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Hungarian Revolution. Igor Zhovkva, deputy head of the Ukrainian president’s office, told Euronews in an exclusive interview on Friday that Zelensky had been invited to the anniversary events.

According to MTI, Zhovkva said Kyiv was optimistic about the new diplomatic opening between the two countries and viewed the event as an opportunity to turn recent progress into concrete results. He also expressed gratitude for Hungary’s support in advancing Ukraine’s EU accession negotiations.

Zhovkva added that Zelensky would welcome Magyar in Kyiv, saying the Hungarian prime minister would always be a welcome guest in the Ukrainian capital. Other locations in Ukraine could also be considered for a meeting.

World.title: Repulsive: Hungarian police officer lures teenager away and asks to kiss her – “I’ll make the case disappear”
World.content:
A 17-year-old Hungarian girl says a plain-clothes police officer promised to make her misdemeanour case disappear before taking her to a secluded street and asking whether he could kiss her. Her mother reported the incident to prosecutors the same day, and the Hungarian Helsinki Committee is providing legal representation in the criminal proceedings.

A police officer is facing allegations of abusing his position after allegedly using a 17-year-old girl’s misdemeanour case as a pretext to take her to an isolated location and make an unwanted romantic advance. The Hungarian Helsinki Committee, which represents the teenager, says criminal proceedings have been launched in connection with the case.

According to the human rights organisation, the incident took place on 1 September in a small town in Bács-Kiskun County, southern Hungary. The girl, referred to as Hajni in the organisation’s statement, had not previously met the officer and did not know his name or identification number.

‘I’ll make the case disappear’

According to Hajni’s account, a plain-clothes police officer arrived near her family home in a marked or official police vehicle and told her that she had been reported for a misdemeanour. She acknowledged the offence at the scene.

The officer then allegedly asked whether she wanted to keep the matter from her mother. He offered to take her somewhere secluded, where they could complete the paperwork and he could make the case disappear.

He reportedly told her they needed to go somewhere nobody could see them because he was putting his job at risk.

The teenager agreed to get into the vehicle. They eventually stopped on a quiet street, where the officer moved to the back seat beside her and asked her to sign several documents that appeared to be official. According to the account published by the Hungarian Helsinki Committee, she was not given copies of the paperwork.

Officer allegedly asked to kiss the teenager

After the documents had been signed, the officer allegedly asked Hajni whether she had a partner. When she said she did not, he asked whether he could kiss her.

The teenager refused. The officer then reportedly offered to take her somewhere else, but she declined that offer as well. After he left, Hajni called a friend, who came to collect her and took her home.

Her mother said the girl arrived home in tears and immediately told her what had happened. The mother filed a complaint with the Regional Investigation Prosecutor’s Office in Szeged that same day.

According to the Hungarian Helsinki Committee, a security camera belonging to a neighbour recorded the officer’s initial encounter with the teenager outside her home. The girl was subsequently given a warning in the misdemeanour proceedings against her.

Human rights group calls for thorough investigation

The Hungarian Helsinki Committee is providing legal representation to Hajni in the criminal proceedings. The organisation says the officer’s alleged conduct raises suspicions of criminal offences and raises serious concerns about the misuse of police authority.

The organisation argues that a police officer must not exploit their official position to approach a minor personally or intimately while placing them in a vulnerable situation away from their parents and without independent oversight.

World.title: Hungary joins EU countries challenging carbon tax: summit descends into 3-hour row
World.content:
Hungary has joined Italy, Poland and Czechia in demanding a delay to the EU’s planned carbon pricing scheme for heating and transport, triggering a three-hour argument at a Brussels summit. Most member states rejected the proposal, raising questions about the future of one of the bloc’s key climate policies.

What was supposed to be a discussion about tackling Europe’s soaring energy prices turned into a lengthy dispute over the EU’s climate agenda at Thursday’s European Council summit in Brussels. Hungary joined three other countries in calling for the bloc to postpone its planned carbon pricing scheme for road transport and building heating until at least 2030.

According to POLITICO, the first session of talks lasted around three hours, delaying lunch for European leaders until later in the afternoon.

Italy, Poland, Czechia and Hungary called for the EU’s Emissions Trading System 2 (ETS2) to be postponed by a further two years, while Estonia suggested scrapping the measure altogether.

However, most EU member states rejected the proposal, with several diplomats describing it as unacceptable.

What is ETS2, and why is it controversial?

ETS2 is an already-approved EU scheme designed to put a price on carbon emissions from fuels used for road transport and building heating. Under the current legislation, it is due to take effect in 2028.

The system is intended to encourage households and businesses to switch to cleaner alternatives by making fossil fuels more expensive. Critics, however, fear that it could increase household energy and transport costs, particularly for people who cannot easily afford to upgrade their heating systems or change how they travel.

If you missed it: Strasbourg court rules against Orbán: His government unlawfully restricted Hungarian teachers’ right to strike

The dispute reflects a growing divide between governments that want to protect households from rising energy costs and those determined to maintain the EU’s climate commitments.

Although Thursday’s argument focused on ETS2, the debate also touched on the bloc’s existing Emissions Trading System (ETS), which puts a price on carbon emissions from industrial facilities and power plants.

Together, the two systems are intended to play a central role in reducing greenhouse gas emissions across the European Union.

Photo: MTI

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Hungary joins a growing coalition seeking changes

Italy and Poland have emerged as leading voices calling for changes to the EU’s carbon pricing policies. Their efforts have attracted support from several other countries, including Hungary. According to POLITICO, a group of member states concerned about the existing ETS had grown from 10 countries in March to 16 by the time of a meeting led by Poland earlier this week.

The countries argue that carbon pricing places additional pressure on household bills and businesses at a time when Europe is struggling with energy costs and geopolitical uncertainty. Italy and Poland also secured support from Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary and Greece for a request to reassess ETS2 and postpone its entry into force until at least 2030.

However, that coalition struggled to win over the majority of EU leaders at Thursday’s summit.

The dispute comes as the European Commission prepares to review the existing ETS in July. Some governments want the review to lead to further easing of the system, even though the proposed reforms already envisage less stringent carbon restrictions over the coming decade to give industry more time to invest in cleaner production methods.

Have you heard? EU court rules Hungary broke the law by the early release of 2,500 people smugglers

Nordic countries, France and Germany oppose changes

Several EU diplomats told POLITICO that Nordic countries and the Netherlands strongly oppose changes to ETS2. France and Germany have also backed that position. Nevertheless, the political future of the existing ETS has become less certain as far-right parties gain support in several European countries.

In Germany, the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which opposes the ETS, has strengthened its position following strong performances in regional elections in September. In France, Marine Le Pen’s National Rally is leading in opinion polls ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

The political pressure could complicate efforts to maintain support for the EU’s climate policies, particularly if energy costs remain a major concern for voters. Jordan Bardella, a prominent National Rally politician, criticised the existing carbon pricing system in the European Parliament in May, questioning who ultimately bears its costs.

World.title: Good news: Hungarian wages rise faster than expected, inflation remains low – but there is a catch
World.content:
Hungarian wages grew faster than expected in August, with the average gross salary exceeding HUF 740,000 and real wages rising by 8.6% year on year as inflation remained low. But the median salary reveals a more modest picture of what workers actually earn.

Hungary’s average gross monthly earnings rose to HUF 740,600 (EUR 2,040) in August 2026, while average net earnings reached HUF 519,900 (EUR 1,430), according to the latest figures published by the Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH). The data point to an acceleration in wage growth after several months of weaker-than-expected increases.

Gross average earnings were 8.4% higher than in August 2025, while net earnings increased by 10%. Real net earnings, which take inflation into account, rose by 8.6% year on year.

Wage growth accelerates after a slower period

The August figures came as a positive surprise, following months in which annual wage growth had slowed to around 7%. Both the business sector and public institutions recorded faster increases.

Wages in the business sector rose by 8.1% year on year, while earnings at budgetary institutions increased by 9.2%, according to data reported by Portfolio.

The figures suggest that the slowdown in wage growth seen earlier in the year eased towards the end of the summer.

Photo: freepik.com

If you missed it: Average salaries in Hungary by profession in 2026: Which jobs pay the most?

Why are net salaries rising faster than gross wages?

The increase in take-home pay outpaced gross wage growth partly because of changes to Hungary’s tax benefits for families and mothers.

The KSH highlighted several measures behind the stronger rise in net earnings, including higher family tax allowances introduced on 1 January 2026 and personal income tax exemptions for certain groups of mothers.

These include mothers raising three children, who became eligible for the exemption in October 2025, as well as mothers under 40 raising two children, who became eligible from January 2026. Tax benefits for mothers under 30 were also expanded.

As a result, employees can take home a larger proportion of their earnings even when their gross salaries increase at a slower rate.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Median salaries show what Hungarian workers really earn

Although average earnings provide a useful overview of wage trends, they do not necessarily reflect what a typical employee takes home. High salaries can push the average upwards, even when most workers earn less.

The median offers another perspective: half of employees earn less than this amount, while the other half earn more.

In August, Hungary’s median gross monthly salary was HUF 611,400 (EUR 1,680), up 8.5% compared with the same month last year. The median net salary reached HUF 433,400 (EUR 1,195), representing an annual increase of 9.9%.

Both median figures were considerably lower than their respective averages, highlighting the gap between the typical employee’s earnings and the headline wage figures.

Low inflation boosts real wages

One of the main reasons employees’ purchasing power improved so markedly was the relatively modest rise in consumer prices.

Inflation stood at just 1.3% year on year in August. With net average earnings increasing by 10%, the result was an 8.6% rise in real wages.

In practical terms, the average net salary could buy a larger basket of goods and services in August 2026 than a year earlier. However, the actual impact varies from household to household, depending on individual earnings and spending habits, as well as how the prices of particular goods and services have changed.

Low overall inflation does not mean that everyone experiences the same improvement in their standard of living.

Can employers keep up with rising wages?

The figures also raise questions about the sustainability of wage growth from employers’ perspective. If real wages in Hungary continue to rise by more than 8% while labour productivity improves by only around 1%, businesses may struggle to absorb the additional costs, Telex noted.

Higher wages can strengthen household purchasing power, but they also increase the cost of employing staff. Unless productivity improves at a comparable pace, employers may find it increasingly difficult to finance further pay rises.

World.title: Tougher Security Response Won’t Solve Albania’s Growing Crisis: Experts
World.content:
The past three days of unrest follow several months of peaceful protests – the so-called “Flamingo Revolution” demonstrations, which began in June and combined demands for environmental protection with calls for Rama to go.

Their initial trigger was a plan to build a luxury resort in a protected area – a project connected to Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Protesters saw Rama as a facilitator of ecological destruction for profit.

However, Rama has rejected calls for him to go, arguing that the government can only be changed by elections. His Socialist Party was re-elected by a landslide last year. He has also suggested that the current unrest could hinder Albania’s progress towards European Union accession.

The Prime Minister’s Office did not respond to BIRN’s question about whether Rama had considered resigning to resolve the crisis. In a statement to Reuters on Thursday, however, he said this would be a betrayal of the voters.

“My responsibility is to listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward. The alternative would be a betrayal of the ​Albanians who gave me a strong mandate to complete negotiations on European Union membership,” Rama said.

In a video recorded on Wednesday at a fire-damaged site near the Prime Minister’s office, Rama blamed the opposition for the violence and warned that those responsible for attacks will face prosecution.

But political analysts argue that the escalation of the protests has triggered a crisis that requires a political solution rather than a tougher security response, arrests and court cases.

The Political Dialogue Forum, an initiative established by academics, experts and public figures, issued a statement arguing that if the Prime Minister fails to take significant action, the crisis risks deepening.

“The government continues to respond to the crisis by ignoring its underlying causes and producing propaganda that no one believes anymore. This propaganda is directing attention towards the side-effects of the uprising rather than its root causes,” the forum said.

The forum proposed the formation of a technical government with a limited mandate to prepare free and fair elections, continue Albania’s EU integration process, amend the electoral code and adopt a new code that reflects Albanians’ representational needs – and then hold pre-term elections before the end of the year.

“A new system must free the state from the [ruling Socialist] party and the economy from politics,” the statement concluded.

Ermal Hasimja, a political science lecturer and one of the forum’s founders, insisted that “only a political solution” will work.

“It cannot be resolved with police or PR tricks, which Rama always resorts to in an attempt to deflect crises,” he told BIRN. He was not optimistic, however: “Rama will, of course, refuse to resign, and consequently the crisis will deepen.”

In Hasimja’s view, even if Rama manages to quell the current protests, more will erupt before long because the underlying causes remain unresolved.

World.title: Serbia Channels Public Funds to Pro-Vucic Diaspora Groups
World.content:
In Serbia itself, the Directorate regularly funnels money to local organisations that claim to support the Serb diaspora in the region.

The Izrazajnost association, for example, received a total of 23,800 euros in 2023-2024 for two projects promoting the use of Cyrillic.

Izrazajnost is led by actor Milan Bosiljcic, who in 2023 was among a host of public figures who put their signatures to a statement of support for the SNS.

In 2024, the Directorate awarded 9,400 euros to an association co-founded by Bosiljcic’s daughter, Sara, called Jeremija, for the purposes of a language camp. The association’s first project, which was not funded by the Directorate, was conducted in cooperation with Solidarité Kosovo, an organisation founded by SNS member Arnaud Gouillon, who was head of the Directorate at the time.

Since 2023, the Belgrade Centre for Education and Youth Development, CEROB, has received almost 34,000 euros from the Directorate for diaspora youth camps.

In late 2023, the Centre for Investigative Journalism of Serbia, CINS, reported that SNS activists tasked with canvassing voters for their support were being paid in cash at CEROB’s Belgrade office.

A year later, CEROB representative Ognjen Kocevic was appointed by the Serbian government to the Managing Board of the Institute for the Evaluation of Education Quality.

The Directorate also awarded two grants totalling 13,600 euros to the Association of Students of Republika Srpska in Serbia.

During local elections in 2024 in Serbia’s second city of Novi Sad, members of the association were caught on camera working in an SNS call centre at the Novi Sad Fairgrounds, where party operatives used voter records to track turnout.

Last year, the Directorate gave 8,500 euros to the Association of War Veterans of Serb Lands 1990–1999, for summer youth camps. The association’s leader, Zeljko Vukelic, previously sparked public outrage for sending children aged 11 to 15 to military training camps in Russia in 2017, where children were taught to handle guns and hand grenades.

None of the associations mentioned above responded to requests for comment.

Political scientist Dusko Radosavljevic said the direction of funding reflects the SNS roots in the ultranationalist Serbian Radical Party, which Vucic was a key part of through the bloody collapse of Yugoslavia in the 1990s, right up until 2008 when he broke away and formed the SNS.

“It must not be overlooked that this regime has, from its inception, carried a distinct ideological marker – a far-right stance,” Radosavljevic said.

“This is a regime rooted in the Serbian Radical Party, one of the most abhorrent political creations in Serbia. It exerts a malignant influence fueled by disputes with neighbours, nationalism, and support for war crimes.”

World.title: Croatian Football Fans’ Pro-Nazi Chants Prompt Arrests
World.content:
Torcida fan group march before match on Thursday. Photo: Torcida Split/Facebook

Police in Split have arrested several people after members of Torcida, a group of hardcore supporters of Hajduk Split football club, marched through the city chanting antisemitic slogans, including “Trample, trample the Jews,” “Auschwitz, Auschwitz,” and “Rise, Adolf”, referencing Adolf Hitler.

The incidents are being investigated for hate speech. Further arrests are expected on Friday. All those detained are members of Torcida and already known to the police. An investigating judge will decide whether to order pre-trial detention.

The chants occurred a few hours before Hajduk’s match against Dutch club Ajax – a club seen as having a longstanding Jewish connection.

The incident has been condemned by the Croatian government, the mayor of Split, political parties and members of the public.

“We strongly condemn the unacceptable chants glorifying the Nazi regime,” the government stated on its X profile. “Such shameful behaviour represents a negation of sport and the democratic values ​​that modern Croatia upholds,” the post added.

Torcida fans are known for expressing extremist views.

A series of incidents occurred before the Conference League match, when Hajduk chanted fans marched in a column led by a VW Golf Mk1 with a coffin on its roof, on which the word “Ajax” was written.

The Israeli embassy in Zagreb also condemned the incidents.

The embassy was “deeply shocked by the grave antisemitic incident that occurred yesterday in Split and condemns it in the strongest possible terms,” ​​a statement provided to the news agency Hina said.

“We are deeply grateful to the Government of the Republic of Croatia and to Sara Lustig, Special Advisor to the Prime Minister on Holocaust Issues, for their swift response and clear condemnation of this event,” it added, expressing confidence that “authorities will act quickly and decisively regarding this matter”.

“Such incidents should be unequivocally and decisively condemned by all competent authorities at every level,” it continued.

Croatian President Zoran Milanovic said verbal condemnation was not enough.

“Words of condemnation, such as those we hear from the government, are no longer sufficient; measures and sanctions are necessary to demonstrate that there is no place in Croatia for the glorification of Nazism and Ustasha ideology,” Milanovic said in a press release, referencing Croatia’s World War II fascist movement.

The game itself was halted for 12 minutes during the second half after Hajduk fans let off various pyrotechnic devices, including flares and powerful firecrackers.

Hajduk could face a heavy fine from UEFA. Following the match, Hajduk issued an official apology.

“When situations like today’s occur, we are obligated to apologise,” it stated. The club also apologised to the management and players of Ajax, who witnessed scenes “by which we do not wish to be remembered in Europe”. It did not mention the specific events before the match or the Nazi chants.

The match ended with a 2-1 victory for Hajduk.

World.title: Albania PM Defiant as Protests Spread to Provincial Cities
World.content:
Prime Minister Edi Rama blamed the opposition and “foreign actors” on Friday for the escalation of violence during student protests in Tirana, describing the continuing unrest as an attempt to hinder Albania’s progress toward the European Union.

Speaking from a kiosk that had been burned down during the protests, Rama tried to suggest that students weren’t the ones leading the violence that has accompanied demonstrations in recent days, while accusing his political opponents of exploiting the discontent of young people for their own ends.

World.title: Serbia’s ‘Captured’ TV Screens All Tell the Same Story
World.content:
Serbia approaches October 25 elections with a deeply polarized and uneven national media ecosystem. The media environment is characterized by systemic political influence, instrumentalization, government control, the independent regulator’s paralysis and heightened security risks for independent journalists and media outlets.

These worrying trends have greatly affected the pre-election media space, which has been defined by extreme structural asymmetry. Meanwhile, traditional television, dominated by heavy regime influence and a lack of critical voices, remains the main vehicle for political communication and voter mobilization.

Traditional TV is watched in Serbia for five hours daily on average, and is the main source of political information for the older population. On the other side, websites and social networks offer diverse views and are the main source of information for people aged 15 to 30.

Paradoxically, despite more than 2,500 registered media outlets, Serbia has been placed in a group of high-risk countries concerning media pluralism because of severe deficits in political independence of the media and lack of overall market plurality, according to the Media Pluralism Monitor 2026.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Polish Man Charged With Plotting to Kill PM, Suspected Saboteurs Arrested
World.content:
Czech Army chief warns of possible Russian attack; PM still has conflicts of interest

The chief of the general staff of the Czech Army, Miroslav Hlavac, this week warned that Russia could test the cohesion of NATO by launching a partial attack against one of its members. “I want to emphasise that we are ready and we will defend the Czech Republic with what we have,” he said in an interview with the Czech News Agency. “And I say this with all the force and responsibility for the army of the Czech Republic, also warning that the country’s response to a potential foreign attack did not only rely on Czechia’s military capabilities but also on the response from the entire state apparatus, defence industry and society. “State preparedness is a never-ending process. You will never be 100 per cent prepared. It is important that the state, and any state, not just the Czech Republic, has its security system prepared in such a way that it is able to respond to the threat and subsequently mitigate and address the consequences of the crisis,” Hlavac insisted.

“Based on the assessment of the information provided by the Czech national authorities, the Commission has concluded that [Czech Prime Minister Andrej] Babis’s situation constitutes a conflict of interest,” Elizabeth Werner, head of the European Commission’s directorate general for agriculture and rural development, was quoted as saying this week by Transparency International Czechia as part of DG Agri’s response to the Czech NGO’s previous complaint. Czech and foreign anti-corruption watchdogs have for months warned that the Czech PM’s steps to distance himself from his business interests – particularly the transfer of his shares of Agrofert into a trust fund back in February – in reality did nothing to mitigate the risks and ultimately did not resolve his conflicts of interest. Babis, meanwhile, insists the EU Commission’s evaluation is “nonsense”. Talking about his former agro-chemical empire, Babis insisted: “I did much more than I had to do. If I had followed the rules for conflicts of interest with European commissioners, I would have just reported the conflict and walked out the door… I will never get [Agrofert] back and I don’t receive any profit from it.”

It was an intense week of closed-door talks as parties from across the political spectrum launched negotiations following last weekend’s municipal elections. Less than a week after the ballot, the future leadership and coalition formats appear clearer in about half of Czechia’s 13 regional cities. Having emerged first in six of the country’s larger cities, Babis’s ruling ANO party has so far been able to reach an agreement with other partners in two of them – Karlovy Vary and Pilsen. On the contrary, ANO is likely to end up in the opposition in Czechia’s two largest cities, Brno where several parties have already entered coalition talks, as well as in the capital Prague where the centre-right and victorious STAN movement promised “to present the framework of cooperation” for the future municipal leadership by next week. Post-election talks remain largely open in the cities of Ostrava, Pardubice, Jihlava, Zlin and Ceske Budejovice.

World.title: Dinamo Beats Anderlecht With 96th-Minute Penalty
World.content:
Dinamo beat Anderlecht 1-0 in the second round of the Europa League, with Dion Drena Beljo scoring the only goal from the penalty spot in the 96th minute. It was Dinamo’s first goal in this season’s Europa League, after a goalless draw with Israel’s Hapoel in the opening round.

Dinamo started strongly and pressed the visitors from the first whistle. Anderlecht soon settled, however, and there were good chances at both ends in the first half.

Luka Stojković had the first in the 15th minute. Left unmarked after a Hoxha cross, he was in an excellent position ten meters from goal, but the ball took an awkward spin off an Anderlecht defender and he could not make clean contact.

What followed was a spell in which Anderlecht could easily have scored more than once. In the 21st minute the Belgian side hit the crossbar twice in the same attack, with Dinamo goalkeeper Dominik Kotarski getting a touch to the second effort.

In the 28th minute Tristan Degreef shot from close range, unmarked, but Kotarski again reacted superbly to keep it out. Dinamo responded towards the end of the half, when Iker Almena found himself well placed from a cut-back but failed to hit the target.

Dinamo created three very good chances in the second half. The best fell to Arber Hoxha in the 81st minute, who was through on goal before Anderlecht full-back Barry got back to knock the ball away from behind him. The home side still found a winner at the death.

Substitute Dani Rodríguez struck the arm of Anderlecht left-back Oleg Reabciuk, and after a VAR review Dinamo were awarded a penalty, which Beljo sent down the middle.

The goal and the win go a long way to improving the picture for Dinamo. They are now 14th in the table, a play-off place, with six matches still to play in the league phase. For Anderlecht, it was a second defeat in this season’s Europa League.

World.title: Hero from Omiš Who Saved 60 People From a Fire Receives Bravery Award
World.content:
October the 16th, 2026 – A hero from a small coastal settlement near Omiš who saved 60 people from a massive fire has received a well-deserved bravery award.

Milan Balić, a young man from Stanići near Omiš, selflessly saved around 60 people with two boats when the fire broke out back in August. He has since received the Croatian Grand Security Award for bravery. Index reports that the ceremony in Opatija he modestly said that he simply found himself at the scene of the fire and emphasised that many other people also took part in the rescue. The recognition was presented to him as part of the 20th Conference of Croatian Security Managers at the Hotel Ambasador in Opatija.

The Croatian Association of Security Managers (HUMS) otherwise awarded prizes in 14 categories, and among the winners are also the City of Split, the State Hydro-meteorological Institute, APIS IT, the City of Zagreb and RTL Danas.

“it was sheer horror”

“What can I tell you, is that it was sheer horror. It was pure horror. Everything started from the upper side of the road and we hoped it wouldn’t cross to the lower side. But the fire passed across. People were running towards the sea, which was the most logical thing to do in that situation,” Balić said at the time.

“My house is among the first by the shoreline and I tried to save it as much as I could. Luckily, nothing happened to it. People were coming down to the beach, everyone was. Older people, young people, children. I decided then and there during the fire to take my boat and try to help them” he added. He set off on the rescue with two vessels. He tied the smaller boat to the larger one and loaded a total of 60 people onto them, among them children, elderly and injured persons. “I put the older men in the small boat, and the women, children and elderly people in the large one. There was really great panic,” Balić said.

“people were screaming from the beach”

The journey to Omiš was extremely dangerous. A strong bora was blowing, and because of the dense smoke visibility was almost non-existent. During the voyage Balić was especially afraid for the people in the smaller boat he was towing. “After we boarded, people were still shouting from the beach. I would have liked to help everyone, but there simply wasn’t any more space. While we were towing the smaller boat, I was most afraid that it wouldn’t sink, because there were also injured people in it,” he said. The drama did not end even upon arrival in Omiš. When docking in the town harbour the smaller boat capsized and people ended up in the sea.

“Everyone fell into the sea. Luckily, the army and special police were there and helped us pull them all out,” Balić said. For the bravery shown during that action he has now received the Croatian Grand Security Award in the category Brave Act in the Service of Security. At the award presentation, he modestly thanked all those gathered for the recognition, stressing that at the moment of the fire he simply found himself at that place. He emphasised that credit for the rescue also belongs to numerous other colleagues who took part in the action.

World.title: Croatia Should Never be a Cheap Destination, Claim Experts
World.content:
October the 16th, 2026 – Croatia should under no circumstances ever be permitted to be a cheap Mediterranean destination claim experts, but just how far has it gone the other way?

Poreč has become the centre of discussion on the direction of Croatian tourism, with a special emphasis placed on the role of hospitality operators in the development of the tourism sector. Boris Bilas reports for Glas Istre that the Parentium Plava Laguna hotel was the host of the 38th Congress of Hospitality Operators and Tourism Workers of the Croatian Chamber of Trades and Crafts (HOK). It gathered together a record number of crafts owners, tourism sector leaders and numerous high-ranking state officials.

istria generates a third of total croatian tourist traffic

The central themes of this year’s three-day gathering focused on preserving profitability in conditions of strong growth in input costs, the chronic shortage of qualified labour, and upcoming legislative changes. Opening the congress, HOK president Dalibor Kratohvil pointed out that 12,094 crafts currently operate actively in the Guild of Hospitality Operators and Tourism Workers, which is 140 more than last year. Nevertheless, he warned of the harsh economic reality on the ground.

“Hospitality operators are the last in the price-formation chain and do not realise any extra profits. While input costs of energy, supplies and labour are relentlessly rising, our margins are constantly falling. We have not raised prices in order to get rich, but exclusively for bare survival and the preservation of jobs,” Kratohvil said, emphasising that HOK continues to insist uncompromisingly on the introduction of the right to a full old-age pension while continuing to perform a craft activity.

The host of the meeting, president of the Chamber of Trades and Crafts of Istria County Robert Momić, proudly highlighted the role of Istria, which generates as much as one third of total Croatian tourist traffic with 29.5 million overnight stays realised in the first nine months.

“In the area of Istria we have almost 12,000 craftsmen, of whom 1,200 are directly in hospitality. Top-quality tourism does not happen here by chance; it is created, and our enogastronomy sector is a key motive for guests’ arrival. Thanks to synergy with local self-government and tourist boards, we have a clear strategy for a bright future of the profession,” Momić stated. Deputy County Prefect of Istria Jessica Acquavita addressed the far-from-easy reality of the labour shortage, emphasising that foreign workers have become an economic necessity without which the tourism system could no longer function.

language issues in istria

“We’re currently facing the complex challenges of language barriers and preserving the recognisable Istrian hospitality. In Istria County we are thinking seriously about this and have launched an initiative to establish a regional support network for foreign workers. We want these employees to become part of the local community as quickly and painlessly as possible, because by facilitating their integration we are directly investing in the stability of your business and preserving authenticity. Sustainable tourism is a balance between economic growth and social responsibility,” Deputy County Prefect Jessica Acquavita said.

tourists are spending more and more

Director of the Croatian National Tourist Board (HTZ) Kristjan Staničić stressed that the success of the season must no longer be measured exclusively by the number of arrivals and overnight stays, but by the overall economic effects on the economy. In doing so he exclusively presented the first data from the new comprehensive TOMAS survey that HTZ conducted in cooperation with the Institute for Tourism.

“The average daily expenditure of tourists in Croatia has risen to €160 per person per overnight stay, which is an increase of as much as 16 percent compared to a few years ago. Absolute record holders are guests from the USA who on average spend around €280 per day, followed by the British with €248. This justifies our strong investments in air traffic and digital promotion towards those emitting markets,” Staničić revealed. He also highlighted that as many as 68 percent of tourists choose mid-price restaurants, which means that “value for money” must remain at the centre of the offer.

The most important political message of the congress came from State Secretary in the Ministry of Tourism and Sport Monika Udovičić, who directly responded to the discontent of hospitality operators regarding complicated administrative obligations and the constant updating of price lists that was imposed on the sector this summer.

price increases remain a serious issue

“We’ve heard your voice and your opinion. The state’s intention was to prevent uncontrolled price increases that also affect you yourselves through procurement, but decisions in practice must not be unenforceable nor further stifle your business. That is precisely why those disputed rulebooks have been put out of force. New acts are being prepared and we will ensure enough time for us to discuss them together,” Udovičić announced.

She also addressed stories about Croatia’s expensiveness and prices in tourism and sent a clear message that Croatia must under no circumstances be the cheapest country on the Mediterranean.

“Croatia should not and must under no circumstances be a cheap destination on the Mediterranean. Our competition such as Italy or Greece is investing strongly and investing a lot. We must be a destination in which the price is fully justified by top quality and an authentic experience, and that is precisely what our craftsmen offer in their taverns and restaurants,” the State Secretary concluded, announcing that the new Hospitality Activity Act, which enters into force at the beginning of 2027, will bring a more effective fight against unfair competition and unregistered business, as well as simpler, digital procedures for all legal craftsmen.

istria’s 180-year-old tourism brochure

Poreč Mayor Loris Peršurić recalled a historical curiosity, a fascinating 180-year-old tourist brochure kept in the Poreč museum, proving that the tradition of hospitality across the region of Istria has some very deep roots. “Behind the success of Poreč stands not only natural beauty, but primarily local people, people who own crafts and their warm hospitality,” Peršurić concluded.

World.title: Turks to Purchase Uljanik for €12.05 Million
World.content:
October the 16th, 2026 – The Turks are set to purchase Uljanik for €12.05 million. The Kuzey Star Shipyard will now officially take over 97.13% of the shares of Brodogradnja 1856.

With the agreement on the transfer of business shares, Morski reports that the moves brings the months-long sales process to a close and opens a new chapter in the revitalisation of Pula’s shipbuilding industry.

The aforementioned Turkish company offered a purchase price for Uljanik of €12.05 million, which is higher than the initially sought €11.08 million. CERP therefore readily accepted Kuzey Star’s binding offer at the beginning of September, while the second received offer from the Luxembourg company Mira Finance Holding was not accepted because the payment of the prescribed guarantee wasn’t recorded in CERP’s account. Given that the buyer is from a country that is not within the EU, before the actual conclusion of the contract, it was also necessary to carry out a foreign investment screening procedure in order to determine whether the investment poses a risk to national security and public order.

the continuation of shipbuilding has been ensured

The key condition of the contract concerns the retention of the core shipbuilding activity, the construction, repair and overhaul of ships and floating objects, across the entire area of the maritime domain under concession. By taking over the company, the Turkish investor obtains the existing shipbuilding infrastructure and concession rights for the use of the maritime domain in the Bay of Pula, but not ownership of the entire land and sea space.

Minister of the Economy Ante Šušnjar emphasised the importance of this decision for this previously less than stable Croatian industry: “By signing this contract, Croatia is approaching the completion of the process of revitalising the shipbuilding industry in the Pula area. Through its decisions the Government has preserved the possibility of continuing shipbuilding in Pula. The further development of Uljanik will depend on the business decisions, investments and contracted work of the new investor.”

experience and existing business ties

The director of Uljanik Brodogradnja 1856, Samir Hadžić, assessed as positive the fact that the new owner comes precisely from the shipbuilding sector. The Kuzey Star group owns shipyards in the Turkish cities of Tuzla and Yalova and has extensive experience in the construction, overhaul, maintenance and conversion of ships, as well as in projects related to the energy sector.

In addition, the Turkish company is already well acquainted with the possibilities of the Pula shipyard. Namely, Kuzey Star and Uljanik are already cooperating on the project to complete Newbuilding (Novogradjna) 526 (a livestock carrier which had a hull that had stood unfinished for years), which gave the Turkish partner direct insight into the available infrastructure and the capacities of the workers. In a series of works, the Pula shipyard maintained production activity also through work on yacht hulls and the completion of a fishing vessel.

Kuzey Star is otherwise already present on the wider Croatian market, work on an additional re-gasification module intended to increase the capacity of the floating LNG terminal in Omišalj was carried out at their shipyard. In the recent period Uljanik Brodogradnja 1856 employed around 230 workers, while together with subcontractors between 250 and 300 people participated in production.

World.title: Former Croatian Roads Boss Convicted of Taking Bribes But Spared Prison
World.content:
October the 16th, 2026 – The former Croatian Roads (Hrvatske ceste) boss Josip Škorić has been convicted of taking bribes, but in expected fashion, he will be spared any prison time.

Josip Škorić has been finally convicted of taking bribes after reaching a plea agreement with USKOK. He was sentenced to 11 months in prison, which he won’t even serve given that it was replaced by community service. Morski reports that in addition, Škorić received a fine of 15,000 euros. He must also return 6,000 euros, which, according to the charges, was the value of the bribes he received.

He was convicted of accepting bribes in the form of paid dinners, plane tickets and other benefits. The verdict was handed down after the other defendants in the same corruption case were also convicted last week, likewise on the basis of plea agreements with USKOK.

he is still employed by croatian roads!

Over the past two years, Škorić found himself under USKOK investigation in two separate cases, N1 reports. First, in August 2024, he suddenly resigned as president of the Management Board of Hrvatske ceste, only to be arrested a month later on suspicion that he had favoured the company Osijek Koteks, linked to his relative Zoran Škorić, in the awarding of contracts.

A separate indictment was recently filed in that case, and (unsurprisingly) Škorić denies any guilt. The second case, the one in which he has now been convicted, was launched in June 2025, when the police and USKOK arrested him again on suspicion of taking bribes. Despite the arrests and criminal proceedings, Škorić has remained employed at Hrvatske ceste, as an adviser to the Management Board.

World.title: Hajduk Beats Ajax 2-1 at Poljud to Open Conference League Campaign!
World.content:
Hajduk opened their Conference League group stage with a 2-1 win over Ajax at Poljud on Thursday, as goals from Bamba and Šotiček saw off the four-time European champions in a match halted for 12 minutes by Torcida’s flares.

Hajduk reached the group stage of a European competition for the first time in 16 years after eight qualifying matches. Their European campaign began in the first qualifying round of the Europa League, where they knocked out Slovakia’s Žilina before going out to Cypriot side Pafos over two legs in the next round. That sent Hajduk into Conference League qualifying, where they comfortably beat Lithuania’s Žalgiris and then got past Poland’s Raków after extra time in both legs.

The draw paired Hajduk with Ajax for their opening league-phase match. The two clubs have a long history. They have met three times in friendlies and four times in competitive matches. Hajduk won all three friendlies, each played at the Stari Plac: 3-0 in 1974, 1-0 in 1977, and 4-2 in 1979, shortly before the club moved to Poljud.

Their first competitive meeting came in the first round of the 1993 Cup Winners’ Cup. With war in Croatia, Hajduk played their home leg at Ljubljana’s Bežigrad stadium and won 1-0, but Ajax won the return leg 6-0. The sides met again in the quarter-finals of the 1995 Champions League. The first leg at Poljud finished goalless, and Ajax, who went on to win the competition, took the second leg 3-0.

Hajduk have never lost to Ajax in Split, across four meetings.

Lineups

Hajduk: Silić, Hrgović, Hadžikadunić, Marešić, Acapandie, Fayad, Del Moral, Dalisson, Šotiček, Bamba, Šego

Ajax: Ter Stegen, Kehrer, Baas, Bouwman, Torrents, Amrabat, Klaassen, Brandt, Ouazane, Tsygankov, Tolu

Match report

The match got under way at Poljud with Ajax in possession and Hajduk sitting in a mid-block, looking to build their attacks down the right through Bamba.

Ajax almost scored within seven minutes. They broke quickly, and Arokodare got clear of Hadžikadunić to run through on Silić. The Hajduk goalkeeper was already on the ground, but Hadžikadunić recovered with a superb last-ditch sliding challenge to make up for his own mistake.

Hajduk began to push higher. In the 11th minute Šego sent Bamba away down the wing, but Torrents stopped his run, and from the 12th minute the home side were pressing aggressively whenever Ajax had the ball. A minute later Dalisson won possession and tried to play Bamba through on goal, but the Ajax defense reacted well.

Bamba won Hajduk’s first corner in the 17th minute, and their first shot followed straight after. Hrgović timed his run to beat the offside trap onto a Dalisson through ball and shot from a tight angle into a defender, leaving Šego frustrated that he had not crossed. By then the Poljud stands were shaking with the noise from the home supporters.

Šotiček sent in a dangerous cross in the 23rd minute, but Šego was penalized for a foul in the challenge for the ball. A minute later Dalisson beat his man with a fine dribble and shot from around 20 meters, a comfortable save for Ter Stegen.

Hajduk kept coming. In the 29th minute, Hrgović played a superb ball over the top for Šotiček, but Klaasen read it well. Ajax countered in the 35th minute, only for Arokodare to be caught offside.

Two minutes later Hajduk took a deserved lead with a deadly counter-attack. Klaassen was dispossessed, Šotiček played in Bamba, and he finished to make it 1-0 in the 37th minute! The stands erupted into a chant of “Ja te volim Hajduče”.

Ajax looked for a quick response, and in the 43rd minute Klaassen’s header from eight or nine metres was saved by Silić.



Hajduk kept up their high press after the restart, but Ajax punished them as soon as they dropped deeper. In the 53rd minute, with Hajduk sitting in front of their own penalty area, Kehrer crossed, and Klaassen timed his run to drive the ball in under the bar for 1-1.

The equalizer stood for only three minutes. In the 56th minute Hajduk won the ball back with more excellent pressing. Šego pounced on a dreadful pass from Torrents and, rather than shoot from a promising position, laid it off to Šotiček, who took a touch and scored to make it 2-1!

Šego was booked in the 60th minute. Three minutes later, Bamba beat Torrents and tried to go past Baas as well, but the defender stopped him and cleared the ball out of the box. Bamba went down, but there was never a case for a penalty.

Hajduk’s tempo dropped slightly as the hour mark passed, and García turned to his bench, bringing on Dendoncker for Del Moral in the 70th minute. A minute later, Dalisson sent in a dangerous cross, but it struck Šego and rebounded straight into Ter Stegen’s hands.

Ajax made a quadruple substitution in the 76th minute, as Leonardo, Gloukh, Rosa and Mokio replaced Cigankov, Klaassen, Ouazane and Torrents.

Two minutes later, the match was stopped. Torcida lit flares in the 78th minute, and the smoke became so thick that nothing on the pitch could be seen, so the players were taken to the dressing rooms under UEFA protocol. Even then, the fans kept letting off bangers.

In the 86th minute, the stadium announcer warned that the match was at risk of being abandoned.

Play finally resumed after a 12-minute stoppage, on the understanding that any further pyrotechnics would see the match abandoned. The clock picked up from the 78th minute.

Ajax almost made the most of it. In the 80th minute, Gloukh struck the crossbar from a cut-back, though the flag was already up for offside.

Ajax was now much more dangerous and pinning Hajduk back. In the 84th minute, García made a double change, bringing on Melnjak and Šutalo for Hrgović and goalscorer Bamba.

Hajduk defended desperately as Ajax laid siege to their goal in the closing minutes. In the 90th minute, Bouwman shot over from around ten meters. At least five minutes of stoppage time were signaled.

García used his final changes in the first minute of added time, bringing on Van Hoorenbeck and Martin for Fayad and Šego. Hajduk held firm through the remaining minutes, and at the final whistle they had beaten Ajax 2-1 to start their first league-phase campaign in 16 years with a win!

Hajduk coach Gonzalo Garcia addressed the press after the win.

“What can you say to the players after this win? First game in Europe after 16 years. The way they performed, their personality with the ball, their pressing. Everything. Ajax is an amazing team with an amazing coach. You can only be proud in this moment. We never gave up, and it showed.

Our players are brave. They want to improve every day, every game. Ajax did not underrate us tonight; they knew it was going to be a hard game. But we showed from the first moment that we wanted it. We didn’t give them space to breathe.

We worked together. We were intelligent. We controlled a big part of the game. Even when we conceded a goal, we knew how to come back and play smart. The team is increasingly mature with every game.

Even if we have bad moments, we will push, and we won’t give anything for free to anyone.”

World.title: Will Croatia Prevent Montenegro EU Accession?
World.content:
October the 15th, 2026 – Croatia has multiple conditions for entry into the bloc, but could it go as far as to block the Montenegro EU accession?

Croatia has very clearly warned neighbouring Montenegro that a series of unresolved bilateral issues could slow its planned entry into the European Union by 2028. Among the open topics are war crimes, property restitution and the definition of the border, Index reports.

This week, Zagreb sent a document to the other EU Member States listing eight demands that Montenegro must fulfil before the conclusion of accession negotiations. Montenegro is otherwise widely regarded as the front-runner among the candidate countries and hopes to become the 28th member of the Union by 2028. Nevertheless, long-standing disputes with Croatia, which mostly date from the time of the break-up of the former Yugoslavia, represent an obstacle to those plans.

blockade progress

“Croatia sincerely wishes to close this painful chapter of our shared history and to build a future-oriented relationship with Montenegro. However, mutual trust and genuine and lasting reconciliation cannot be achieved without resolving these issues,” the Croatian document states. On Monday, Montenegro advanced in its negotiations with the EU after closing the chapters on statistics, economic policy and employment. This brought the total number of closed chapters to 21 out of 33.

Croatia, however, is blocking progress in four other areas: transport, external relations, fundamental rights and internal affairs. Every member state has the right of veto over the enlargement process, which gives Zagreb significant influence over Montenegro’s path to membership. The document elaborates in detail the objections that the Croatian Ministry of Foreign Affairs already put forward back in July, which largely stem from the wars of the 1990s.

a list of croatia’s open issues

One of the most sensitive demands concerns compensation for around three hundred Croatian citizens who were detained and abused in the Morinj concentration camp in Montenegro from October 1991 to August 1992. During the conflict, Croatian civilians and prisoners of war were forcibly taken to that camp. Croatia also demands that the memorial plaque at the site of the former camp remain permanently visible. The plaque was enclosed in a metal structure after protests by Montenegrin nationalist groups. Another demand concerns the fate of 14 people who are still listed as missing from the Homeland War.

Zagreb is therefore asking Montenegro for help in locating their remains and describes this as an important humanitarian issue that has not yet been resolved. Croatia also demands that in the cases of already convicted war criminals for crimes against civilians in Morinj, command responsibility be taken into account.

long-standing disputes from the 1990s

Zagreb also expects Montenegro to resolve long-standing property disputes from the early 1990s concerning Croatian families whose property was confiscated without adequate compensation. The document notes that a 2021 law enabled the restitution of land in a region with a predominantly Albanian minority, which “raises concerns about unequal treatment in similar cases.”

Zagreb also seeks the return of the “Jadran” vessel which has been under Montenegrin control since the break-up of Yugoslavia in 1991. Finally, Croatia demands the resolution of territorial disputes over the land and maritime border in accordance with the decisions of the Arbitration Commission on Yugoslavia. Croatia itself has an unresolved border dispute with Slovenia, although that did not prevent it from joining the European Union back in 2013.

“Croatia has consistently encouraged Montenegro to resolve the open bilateral issues and at the same time has actively supported its entry into the EU. Despite Croatia’s constant efforts and constructive approach, none of the open issues has yet been resolved,” the document concludes.

World.title: How Will Croatia Actually Benefit From the €50 billion Data Centre?
World.content:
October the 15th, 2026 – In what way will Croatia actually concretely benefit from the giant €50 billion data centre in Topusko that has many deeply concerned about the environment and water?

The previously announced construction of the huge and very controversial Pantheon data centre in Topusko, whose value is estimated at as much as €50 billion, raises a series of questions about the real benefits Croatia could gain from such an investment. Vedran Salvia reports for Index that this gigantic project recently took another step towards realisation. Sisak-Moslavina County has initiated amendments to the spatial plan in order to create the conditions for the construction of the centre and the accompanying infrastructure.

Although a series of procedures and the obtaining of the necessary permits still lie ahead before construction can begin, below we provide answers to some of the key questions about the project, its possible benefits and costs. For the purposes of this text we also received an expert comment from Tomislav Vazdar, an expert in cybersecurity and artificial intelligence.

intended for large tech companies with little care for anyone else

According to Ryan Rich, executive partner of Pantheon AI, who wrote about the project for the Wall Street Journal, the centre is intended for large technology companies that need enormous computing capacity for continuous operation and the development of artificial intelligence. Rich also stated that the infrastructure would be available to European defence, intelligence and commercial users.

Pantheon representatives were asked about who specifically will use the future data centre and whether there are already agreed tenants, but we had not received a reply by the time this text was published. Project manager Mario Gudelj explained to Večernji list in July that the final value of the investment will depend on the requirements of future users, whom he described as large technology companies developing artificial intelligence. According to the announcements at the time, the first users should start using the centre’s capacities at the beginning of 2029.

Vazdar explained to us who the most common users of such data centres are. “The largest users are global cloud service providers, companies developing large artificial intelligence models, and increasingly the defence and security sector. In a centre of this scale, AI models would primarily be trained and run. Money is earned by renting out capacity, most often through long-term contracts with a few large clients,” Vazdar commented for Index.

is there any benefit to anyone outside of big tech?

Part of the investment will relate to construction works and infrastructure, and a significant part to the purchase of computer and other technological equipment. The value of the campus construction is estimated at up to €12 billion, while the total investment, including IT equipment, should exceed €50 billion. One of the possible long-term benefits is the construction of electricity infrastructure. In addition to the construction of a 500-megawatt solar power plant, for which cooperation with the international energy group Greenvolt has been announced, according to project representatives’ announcements, the construction of approximately 280 kilometres of power lines and a new substation is planned, and the investment would be financed by the investor.

The built infrastructure should then pass into the ownership of the Croatian Transmission System Operator. “The benefits won’t come by themselves; all of that has to be contracted in advance. So, a share of capacity for domestic companies, universities and the public sector, engagement of domestic contractors and investment in the network that remains with the state. Equally important is control over the data. If data is processed in Croatia but control over it remains outside the European legal framework, the state bears the risk and does not gain digital sovereignty,” Vazdar said.

are there any benefits for croatian companies?

One of the concrete opportunities for Croatian companies is linked precisely to the construction of the mentioned electricity infrastructure. At the end of April, Končar signed a non-binding letter of intent on cooperation on the Pantheon project, which envisages the participation of several companies from its group, including Dalekovod. One of the investors, entrepreneur Jako Andabak, claimed on HRT back in April that the majority of the works during the construction and equipping of the centre should be carried out by Croatian companies, using domestic knowledge and workforce.

what about new employment opportunities?

As announced at the project presentation, more than 3,000 workers should be engaged during construction, around 1,500 people employed after the centre starts operating, while the project could indirectly contribute to the creation of a further 6,000 jobs. Andabak stated that approximately half of the 1,500 permanently employed should have higher education qualifications. That would mean around 750 highly qualified jobs, primarily linked to the operation and maintenance of complex technological infrastructure.

It is not yet known how many of the employees will be from Croatia, and especially how many jobs could go to residents of Topusko and the surrounding area. “The most jobs are created during construction, and once the centre is up and running there are few permanent employees, although these are highly qualified positions. Realistic expectations should be based on signed commitments, not on announcements,” Vazdar said.

how will pantheon help croatia’s own tech sector?

One of the potentially greatest long-term benefits of the project could be the development of Croatia’s technology sector, especially companies dealing with artificial intelligence. Large computing capacities are needed for the development and training of advanced artificial intelligence models, and access to such infrastructure could open new opportunities for domestic companies, universities and research institutions.

Project manager Mario Gudelj spoke to N1 in May about the ambition for Pantheon to bring the industry of the future to Croatia and position it among the leading countries in digital transformation. Vazdar said more about the importance of Pantheon for the development of artificial intelligence and the domestic technology sector. “The significance is potentially great, but only with clear access conditions for domestic companies and scientists. Without that, the centre can operate at full capacity for foreign clients, while the domestic sector gets almost nothing from it,” he added.

how much will the state and the local community benefit financially?

In addition to employment and the engagement of domestic companies, one of the more important potential benefits of the Pantheon project relates to tax and other public revenues. The Municipality of Topusko has particularly high expectations. Its mayor Ivica Kuzmić stated on HRT in May that the realisation of the project could increase the municipality’s revenues three to four times. He emphasised that the additional funds would primarily be used to improve communal infrastructure.

However, a detailed financial projection showing how much the state and the Municipality of Topusko would earn annually from the centre’s operations has not yet been publicly presented. The amount of tax revenues will depend, among other things, on the centre’s business results, the number and salaries of employees, and the way in which the business of the companies involved in the project is organised.

will electricity prices shoot up?

One of the more important questions relates to the high consumption of electricity and water and the possible consequences for the general public, for whom a giant data centre represents little but a deep worry. As Gudelj announced, Pantheon in full operation would consume around five terawatt-hours of electricity per year, 1.5 times more than Zagreb and a little more than a quarter of Croatia’s consumption.

However, he stated that electricity would not become more expensive for citizens because of the centre. According to his announcements, the centre would primarily be supplied from renewable sources, and the investor would also finance the necessary electricity infrastructure. “A data centre of this scale consumes as much electricity as a large city, and continuously. That means great pressure on the electricity system and a risk that the cost of adapting the network will spill over onto all users if the rules are not set in advance,” Vazdar adds.

“Cooling data centres down also requires significant amounts of water, so it is necessary to transparently determine how that will affect local sources. All of this must be publicly and independently assessed before any decision,” Vazdar says.

data centres and their devastating environmental impact

The impact of Pantheon on the environment is a separate and extremely important topic that deserves an analysis of its own. We have already written about this in detail on Index, and here we will only recall that part of the public is mainly concerned about the high water consumption, noise, waste heat, interventions in the space and potential consequences for the local ecosystem.

Vazdar warns for Index that cooling a data centre requires significant amounts of water, which is why it is necessary to transparently determine the possible impact on local sources and to assess everything publicly and independently before any decision is made. Gudelj says that the final solution has not yet been chosen. Pantheon, as he emphasised, will not connect to the public water supply or use water from rivers and streams, and hydrogeological research is being carried out. Earlier, the investors claimed to Index that the impact on the environment would be negligible or non-existent. In any case, the strategic environmental impact assessment and the assessment of acceptability for the ecological network are only part of the procedures that must precede construction. Therefore it still remains to be determined what consequences the project could have for the environment and what protection measures will be necessary.

World.title: AI is coming for every company, Nvidia boss says
World.content:
Stockholm – Artificial intelligence will ultimately become a key aspect of all companies, the head of AI chip giant Nvidia said during a visit to Stockholm, where he urged Europe to ramp up its AI industry.

“Every single company will be an AI company eventually. Every single industry will be impacted by AI,” Jensen Huang told an event late Thursday, part of a European tour that includes a Nvidia-hosted conference in Berlin next week.

“The important thing for us is to recognise that Europe needs to build out the entire stack,” he said, referring to the AI technology chain from data centres to chatbots and other apps.

Speaking later to AFP, Huang said his company had invested $8 billion in Europe over the past year.

“We’ve strategically invested in different parts of that ecosystem, really high quality companies that we believe could help lift it, the whole ecosystem in Europe,” he said, citing the British data centre and AI cloud provider Nscale and the Dutch cloud provider Nebius as examples.

“In the last one year, we’ve invested $8 billion already. We have another couple of billion dollars in the pipeline,” he added. “We’re helping Europe create the AI ecosystem.”

Huang was in Stockholm for the launch of Sferical One, a Swedish supercomputer using Nvidia chips that will keep sensitive Swedish data and expertise in the country.

During his visit, Volvo Cars also announced it was expanding its partnership with Nvidia to improve safety technology in its planned self-driving vehicles.

World.title: Chelsea captain James has knee surgery
World.content:
London – Chelsea captain Reece James has undergone successful knee surgery, the Premier League club announced on Friday.

The England international has missed Chelsea’s past two league games — a 3-0 defeat by Brentford and a 5-1 win over Bournemouth.

“The 26-year-old was absent from Saturday’s 5-1 victory over Bournemouth at Stamford Bridge while medical assessments took place following the injury suffered in training,” the club said in a statement.

“Those assessments confirmed surgery would be the required course of action.

“Reece has already begun his road to recovery and will be supported by the club’s medical department at Cobham during this rehabilitation phase.”

Chelsea are sixth in the Premier League ahead of Saturday’s visit to Everton.

World.title: Asian stocks rise as tech bounces from rout, Warsh upbeat on AI
World.content:
Hong Kong – Most Asian markets bounced Friday after the previous day’s tech rout fuelled by concerns over the AI boom, which Federal Reserve boss Kevin Warsh said offered huge benefits to the global economy.

Seoul and Tokyo enjoyed healthy gains in early exchanges boosted by chipmakers SK hynix and Kioxia, after having been pummelled Thursday as investors bailed out of the once-dominant AI sector.

The selling had been fuelled by forecast-beating US inflation data that ramped up bets on Fed interest rate hikes, as well as concerns about the financial health of data centre operator CoreWeave owing to its huge debt pile.

The New Jersey firm — which has borrowed heavily to finance hefty purchases of pricey semiconductor chips from Nvidia — tanked 15.5 percent Wednesday in the US as yields on some of its bonds soared, reflecting heightened angst over its future.

That added to concerns about the whole AI-tech complex, but Nvidia chief Jensen Huang on Thursday lifted spirits by defending the company and its health.

“CoreWeave’s strength is improving every day,” he told Bloomberg. “I’m optimistic. Their cost of capital is actually decreasing.”

CoreWeave’s shares climbed almost six percent.

Huang’s “defence of CoreWeave’s financial position was enough to pull the NeoCloud complex off the floor, drag AI equities higher and give the broader market something resembling a pulse”, wrote SPI Asset Management’s Stephen Innes.

“One moment the market was pricing the possibility that the AI financing machine had started eating its own tail, the next it was listening to the high priest of the boom explain that the patient was getting stronger.

“AI Jesus had entered the trading room and, for a while at least, the machines found religion again.”

Seoul jumped more than two percent and Tokyo around 1.8 percent, though they slumped 7.6 percent and 4.9 percent respectively Thursday.

Hong Kong, Shanghai, Singapore, Taipei, Mumbai, Bangkok and Manila were also up.

Paris and Frankfurt opened higher but London fell.

Fed chief Warsh said Friday that AI was the “most consequential change” to the global economy in his lifetime, predicting its effects would be positive but the path forward “bumpy”.

At an event at the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok he said the AI investment boom would drive prices up in the short term, but “there really is, I think, a huge benefit to the global economy, to the US economy over the horizon”.

He also reiterated his previously stated belief that the technology would “make economies and countries that put it to good use more productive”.

But he added: “The path from where we are to there is likely to be a very bumpy one, bumpy in our understanding of the technology, bumpy because we really don’t know what the market structure is going to be of these new technologies.”

Shares in Jakarta tanked more than 11 percent — its heaviest loss since 1998 — after index compiler MSCI said it was “no longer appropriate” to maintain Indonesia’s emerging-market status, fuelling fears of an exodus of foreign investment.

The US firm said earlier this year that investors had raised concerns about “ongoing opacity in shareholding structures” as well as co-ordinated trading behaviour that affected price information.

Authorities said they had carried out changes but MSCI said Friday that investors had indicated the “sufficient progress has not been observed consistently across the Indonesian equity market”, adding “it considers Indonesia’s continued classification as an Emerging Market no longer appropriate”.
