World.title: If the economic narrative doesn’t improve, things could get ugly for Labor
World.content:
Labor's sprawling backbench has been a sight to behold ever since the 2025 electoral bushfire that consumed the Coalition, leaving behind a lot of empty stumps and toasted tussocks.

The view from the press gallery seats drives this home. Below the viewer sprawls the government's 94-seat majority. It dominates the green benches of the lower house, spilling across the chamber's centre line deep into what is normally opposition upholstery.

It’s the literal embodiment of political weight. All those bums on seats.

But for the first time in this parliament's life — and we're pretty much at the half-way mark — those rows upon rows of Labor MPs this week looked more like one of those forests where too much fuel has accumulated.

A lot of wood ready to ignite.

If polls are right then voters are increasingly in a mood to light the match of a political conflagration. Many of those backbenchers would become oncers. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Anecdotes galore of rattled and angry Labor MPs

If polls are right then voters are increasingly in a mood to light the match of a political conflagration. Many of those backbenchers would become oncers.

That was the underlying vibe this week in private conversations in the corridors of parliament, where there were stories and anecdotes galore of unhappy, rattled and angry Labor MPs venting their frustrations.

Some of this might be overblown, but the fact it's out there is new.

Discipline and internal unity have been a mark of the Albanese government, now in its fifth year. Yet for the first time in years, there are plenty of rumblings.

Some backbenchers have been eager to unload their feelings on journalists and several newspapers reported growing agitation across Labor ranks.

Even ministers are at it.

The whole nervous scene was bad enough for the prime minister to resurrect his old line to colleagues — he used it in the lead up to the 2022 and 2025 elections — that despite how tough it feels now, they'll all be "kicking with the wind in the fourth quarter" come election time.

As the grizzling and fretting continued, the prime minister jumped on ABC Afternoon Briefing on Tuesday to put on a brave face.

“We need to be focused not just on — with due respect here on ABC 24 — on the 24-hour media cycle. We need to make sure as well that we’re focused on where we are a year ahead, five years ahead, 10 years ahead," he told Patricia Karvelas.

“What I’m saying is that I’m not spooked by that … we act as an orderly government.”

But gnawing at the government’s storyline of competence is the ongoing effort to sort out the budget, which is now five months old.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on ABC's Afternoon Briefing. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Defeat in the jaws of victory

Legislation has been brought in to address a series of unintended consequences from the introduction of a 30 per cent tax on trusts.

The government says that was always the plan to bring on these changes later this year, given they're not slated to take effect until future years. But the whole thing is another reminder of how much unfinished and unanticipated business sits in the government's in-tray.

Then, at a dinner hosted by the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry on Tuesday night, the prime minister appeared to take all the credit for pushing the Australian Tax Office to delay its ban on credit card payments, even though the treasurer had indicated he was already moving to address that issue when it blew up late last week.

Amid talk of the prime minister throwing the treasurer under the bus, Anthony Albanese told parliament that “the whole premise of it is completely wrong”.

“The treasurer and I had a discussion last week," he said. "We convened the expenditure review committee, and we unanimously, right across the leadership of the government, agreed that the decision by the ATO to have a limited period of pause on the ban that had been imposed needed to be extended so that there would be proper consultation with small business.”

The credit card surcharge issue turned into a headache that reinforced a notion that Labor doesn't understand business or the economy. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

It's a solid explanation. And it would have normally sufficed. But with the government struggling to keep command of the political narrative, the negative headlines reinforced the sense that it keeps finding defeat in the jaws of victory.

The credit card surcharge issue was supposed to be a positive thing. Instead, it turned into a headache that reinforced a notion that Labor doesn't understand business or the economy.

Then, on Wednesday, the Senate pulled the rug out from under one of the government's bigger budget savings — the plan to wind back a rebate to over-65s for health insurance, a $3 billion measure that Health Minister Mark Butler said would be redeployed for aged care services.

Crossbench, Greens and Coalition senators joined forces to scupper the measure, which the government promptly reintroduced.

Loading

The Senate's growing hostility

There are different ways to read this clash.

The government says it shows the Coalition is not serious about finding savings, despite its rhetoric on the need for budget repair.

The Coalition reckons older Australians, pensioners in particular, shouldn't be made to pay for the broken budget.

Interestingly, Barnaby Joyce told this column on Friday that “Labor has a point” on the rebate issue.

"If that’s not where you want the savings, then where do you want to find savings?" he said.

"You've got to move away from just talking about being financially prudent and put meat on the bones."

Either way, the Senate's growing hostility to the government's agenda is worth watching closely.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

The Greens under new leader David Shoebridge have come out swinging, eager to throw sand in the government's wheels.

And some of that new mood of disruption is because all the big players are starting to focus on the next election. While not due until May 2028, its influence on political behaviour has already begun. Not least as the prime minister can always call an election early, perhaps for a year from now.

The Greens have already shown they're starting to rethink their approach. And the Liberals will have to make a threshold decision in coming months on whether they stick with Angus Taylor to lead them to the next election.

If they think he can't deliver, they'll need to give whoever they opt for time to prepare. For now he looks as safe as you'd expect of any major party leader struggling to reach a primary north of 20 per cent to be. Which will make the lead-up to Christmas a nervous time for him.

Labor will also eventually need to make strategic decisions in coming months, particularly about when and how to renew the frontbench, many of whose members have been in their portfolios since 2019.

If the economic and budget narrative doesn't improve, things could get ugly.

"Usually they're brilliant at discipline," Joyce told this column of Labor. "But we've had different views coming forward. When you see a little bit in public you know there's a lot going on behind closed doors."

Jacob Greber is political editor of ABC's 7.30 program.

World.title: Could a whale really swallow a human? A marine scientist says yes
World.content:
Just when you think it's safe to go back in the water, along comes Whalefall.

Based on Daniel Kraus's 2023 novel, the thriller follows Jay Gardiner (Austin Abrams), a young scuba diver who attempts to shake off the grief of his father's recent passing with a dive.

But his swim turns dangerous when Jay's diving gear becomes tangled with a giant squid that has been marked as lunch by a hungry sperm whale, and Jay is swallowed with his mollusc companion.

Stuck in the belly of a whale, Jay must figure out a way to escape in 60 minutes before the oxygen in his scuba tank runs out.

When the trailer for Brian Duffield's Whalefall film adaptation hit the internet this year, fans were thrilled to see Kraus's story of grief and acceptance hit cinema screens.

But a question remained: Could a human actually be swallowed by a whale and survive?

Dr Vanessa Pirotta. (Supplied: Luke Stambouliah)

Dr Vanessa Pirotta, a lecturer and whale scientist in the Marine Predator Research Group at Macquarie University, has written books on the gigantic creatures and addressed the National Press Club in 2025 on the importance of ocean research to our wider environment.

She's currently conducting Australian-led research as a part of the Sydney Offshore Megafauna Surveys to find out how many gentle giants we have in our waters.

We're talking about Whalefall. But before we dive into it, I must ask: what is your favourite whale fact?

Oh, God, where do I start? I think the one I love is that whales have belly buttons because they're mammals. They live birth.

Wow, how big is a whale belly button?

I've done many whale necropsies where I've measured a whale but I never thought to measure the actual width of the belly button. I would say, focusing on an adult whale, maybe it's like the size of a clenched fist.

One of my favourite things and most interesting things to do as a whale scientist is understanding, working with pathologists and vets, to understand why the animals died. It sounds completely morbid, but the only opportunity for me really to see and learn about whale anatomy is by investigating dead whales and it's really the most interesting thing in my life that I do.

Austin Abrams has a potentially deadly encounter with a hungry sperm whale in Whalefall. (Supplied: 20th Century Studios)

I've got to ask you the question on everybody's mind. Could a human be eaten and swallowed by a whale?

This is the billion-dollar question. So, when we're talking about Whalefall, the movie, it's a sperm whale.They're a toothed whale, as opposed to the humpback whale or toothless whales. They have baleen plates, which are hair-like strands hanging from the roof of their mouth.

They're designed not to bite down on food but to engulf lots of tiny, tiny food and water and then get rid of the water out the side of their mouth.

So, what I'm trying to say is, the biology of the whale that we're dealing with in this movie, you could potentially as a human go down the throat but whether you make it alive or not, I don't think anyone knows that.

Full disclosure: I have not yet done a sperm whale necropsy, but a human could easily fit inside their mouth and potentially be sucked into their throat.

Incredible. In the movie, Austin Abram's character is accidentally swallowed while tangled up with a giant squid, which the whale is hunting. Could this situation ever happen in real life?

This is where the movie is doing my head in. That feeding behaviour would usually happen kilometres, at least a kilometre or so, underneath the ocean, so there's huge pressure. The animal is equipped for pressure. So technically, if a sperm whale was feeding at that shallow a depth, then potentially you could. The sperm whale wouldn't use its teeth to crunch you up and bite you and chew you like what we would be doing.

They would simply use the teeth to grab onto you, like it's doing with the squid. The teeth are there to be like a fork. So, I would say that that's why it's doing my head in because, A, it's not usual to see a sperm whale feeding at this depth and, B, how has it miraculously followed a giant squid all the way to the surface? The squid would have been gone by that stage.

Humans are not part of a whale's diet, I must point out. So, these animals are not targeting humans. A human would be dead and implode by the time they get down to that depth.

Jay (Austin Abrams) is swallowed by a sperm whale while diving off the Californian coast. (Supplied: 20th Century Studios)

Abrams is also covered in the plastic and metal of his scuba gear. Would a whale not realise that was not viable sustenance?

If that did all happen at the subsurface, my assumption would be that the whale would probably bite onto the tank attached to him and instantly know that something's not right.

Humpback whale swallows and spits out kayaker Luckily, the kayaker, Adrian Simancas came out unscathed despite being fully enclosed inside the whale's mouth.

There have been other divers that have been kayaking or swimming next to humpback whales or other baleen whales with no teeth, and these animals have had these people at least touch their mouths but realise very soon after that something wasn't right and then they usually open their mouth and eject whatever it is.

Those whales with the kayakers, those kayakers are simply basically hanging out where their dinner plate is and then the whales don't give a hoot about them. So, by no means is the whale targeting the humans.

There's never been a swallowing of a human, to my understanding.

Whales just want to eat. They don't want to hurt humans. They're not aggressive animals, are they?

Not necessarily, but nor is a shark. This is the thing. Whales just want to eat their food. That's what sharks just want to do, too. That's why there's so much anthropomorphising in these movies. But as a scientist, I welcome these movies. They're getting a whole generation of people to think about and educate them about these whales and the environment that we know so little about.

If this is showing us a fantastical version of what a whale's stomach would look like, what does a whale's digestive system look like? Do whales have the same kind of digestive acids that we do?

I've looked in many whale digestive systems and I can tell you they're slimy and they're not pretty and they stink. I don't think there'd be much air in there, although the dude is on scuba.

Whalefall production built a 3.6m tall, 5.4m long whale replica to film internal scenes. (Supplied: 20th Century Studios)

Yeah, he's got 60 minutes of oxygen in his tank.

They would have acids in their stomach. Sperm whales are famous for ambergris. Yeah. Whale vomit. So there probably is a whole heap of squid beaks in that stomach that are undigested because they can't digest them.

So, if hypothetically a human does make it to the stomach but things go wrong, could a whale potentially fully digest and expel a human?

OK, I've been asked lots of questions in my lifetime. But this one …

So, given the fact that this guy is inside a whale with a scuba tank, I would say the scuba tank would probably cause this whale to die. But if this dude was sucked in the whale without a scuba tank and just as a human, then there is potential for this guy to be broken down and passed out.

So, I would say the impeding factor here is the tank. But even before a tank could even get into a stomach of a whale, a whale is not dumb and would probably be like, 'What the hell is this? I'm used to eating things that are squishy, soft'.

Bioluminescent jellyfish help light the sperm whale's dark stomach in Whalefall. (Supplied: 20th Century Studios.)

Whalefall isn't just the name of the movie, it's a real scientific term — can you explain it to us?

See, this is again another star, in my opinion, for this movie because now I get to tell you what it is.

Whalefall is essentially when a whale dies, it will float to the surface and for a period of time sharks or other animals will break it down. Then the animal will fall to the bottom of the ocean, moving a whole heap of nutrients and carbon with it. So, even in death, whales will transfer carbon from our atmosphere down to the deepest part of the oceans and lock it away.

A 3m-long minke whale fall at a depth of 5,610m in the Diamantina Zone and covered in brittle stars, scale worms, bone-eating worms and tube worms. (Supplied: Global TREnD/IDSSE)

We've got to thank whales for so much. Whales are environmentally and economically important alive and even more so environmentally important in death.

Is there a reason we're behind in knowing about whales or is there a reason we don't know more than we should?

Yes, because so much of the world is focused on what's above and not below and deep-sea research and research on whales is very expensive.

So, when it comes to learning about our deep blue, we know so little. In fact, we know more about space than we do about whales in terms of their environment, rather. Someone will eat me alive for saying that. So if anything, a nice silver lining is the fact that people learn about whalefalls and the role of whales and their ecosystem.

What do you think people should know about whales that is largely unknown at this moment?

They're so environmentally, economically important, and their whale poo drives the movement of iron — it's called the iron pump — around the ocean. So, we have whales to thank for the functioning, healthy ecosystems that we enjoy.

But also, we can do our role for whales, and especially humpback whales, making sure that we don't remove krill from the ocean because we need to keep their food there. If you're a little kid, I always say don't release your balloons at birthday parties. If you're an adult, don't buy krill oil tablets.

Our actions for these animals can be simple, but we need to have them front of mind, not out of sight. What is it? Out of sight, out of mind? In this case, it takes a very popular movie so that we can connect and learn so much, and that's what I absolutely love about Hollywood in this case.

This interview is lightly edited for clarity and brevity. Whalefall is in Australian cinemas now.

World.title: Hidden from view in bushland, one rehab centre is saving lives
World.content:
Kane Wandin's withdrawn demeanour shifts when asked if he has a favourite tattoo.

The 26-year-old pulls back the sleeve of his hoodie, straightens his posture and holds his arm stiffly in front of his chest, as if providing a shield for his own body.

Etched across his forearm, in permanent black ink, is the word Wurundjeri.

"I spent basically my whole life on drugs and on the streets," he says.

"Connecting to culture was what [gave] the most strength in helping me sort myself out and get off drugs."

The walls at Bunjilwarra are adorned with murals. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

Hidden from view, amid the rustling gums and gentle breeze from a distant coastline, the lives of young First Nations people like Mr Wandin are quietly being changed forever.

Set in an undisclosed nook of Victoria's Mornington Peninsula, Bunjilwarra is an Aboriginal community-controlled residential rehabilitation centre and healing site for people recovering from addiction.

It is perhaps the least clinical setting imaginable.

An open fireplace sits at the heart of the Bunjilwarra grounds. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

Residents are encouraged to further develop their physical and mental wellbeing. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

At the heart of the grounds, a fire crackles gently throughout the day, stoked by residents on log stools.

A nearby basketball court abuts a veggie garden. The art room windows look out to a set of footy goals.

"To feel the energy here being solely run by mob, for mob … you've got Uncle over there, you've got Auntie calling out, 'Lunch is ready, come and eat,'" says Carla Lauch, a Gunditjmara Kirrae Whurrong—Bundjalung Yaegl woman and youth mentor at Bunjilwarra.

" Honestly, it feels like home. "

Carla Lauch says Bunjilwarra feels like home for many residents. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

Staff prepare meals in the kitchen at Bunjilwarra. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

As Australia's drug consumption reaches record levels, experts say the culturally centred model offers valuable lessons for a broader community problem.

"This place gave me stability," Mr Wandin says.

"It saved my life."

Ice 'twice the problem' of cocaine

If there is hope to be found inside the walls of Bunjilwarra, there is ringing alarm to be heard outside of them.

For those working at the intersection of drugs, crime and homelessness, the unabated rise of methamphetamine in particular — or ice — in the broader community is of profound concern.

Recent wastewater analysis shows methamphetamine use continues to push to new record highs. (ABC News: Fred Hooper)

Australia has among the world's highest per capita use of ice (also referred to by authorities as methylamphetamine), with recent national drug detection data finding record levels turning up in our wastewater.

"The methylamphetamine market is the highest risk drug market in Australia. It poses the highest threat. It also causes the most harm of the illicit drugs," says Shane Neilsen, principal drug specialist at the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission (ACIC).

"Cocaine seems to get a lot of the coverage. The point I would make is that twice as much methamphetamine is consumed in Australia as cocaine.

"It's at least twice the problem."

Kane Wandin experienced homelessness from a young age. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

Mr Wandin was just 13 and living on the streets of Frankston in Melbourne's south-east when he started using ice.

"As bad as it all sounds in the news, it's worse," he says.

" Ice is everywhere at the moment. "

The ACIC estimates the street value of the drug at $11 billion over the most recent 12-month reporting period.

There are growing accounts of ice turning up in the furthest corners of the country, including remote Aboriginal communities.

Concerns have been growing about the creeping presence of ice in regional and remote communities. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

Do you have a story to share about your community? Email Jeremy Story Carter at storycarter.jeremy@abc.net.au or his secure email jstorycarter@protonmail.com.



"If anything, per capita it's more prevalent in regional and remote areas of Australia than it is in capital cities," Mr Neilsen says.

"Serious and organised crime groups have established networks that can supply local communities.

"There's a whole series of cases in which … crime groups are cynical enough to provide methylamphetamine to users and say that they can consume a portion themselves and sell the rest to pay for it.

"That way they're outsourcing the most risky part of the supply chain — the local level distribution — to people who are also using."

More young people are turning to Bunjilwarra after having used methamphetamine. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

Carla Lauch says Bunjilwarra, which is run by the Victorian Aboriginal Health Service, is seeing a "huge increase" in young people who have used methamphetamine.

"Meth is very scary," she says.

"Alcohol was bad enough for our mob and then you've got something as potent as methamphetamine … to see how it changes them and the effects that it has on their lives and their family and the community is devastating."

New analysis from the Penington Institute found Indigenous Australians were more than four times more likely to die from an unintentional drug overdose, with methamphetamine a significant contributing factor.

In NSW, The Glen has far more applications that it can cater to. (Supplied: The Glen)

On the Central Coast of New South Wales at the Aboriginal community-controlled rehabilitation treatment centre The Glen, demand for services far outstrips capacity.

"You literally couldn't even apply for a bed at The Glen a lot of the time. I'm not saying that with pride," The Glen's executive director, Joe Coyte, says.

"We don't shut applications because beds are full. We shut because beds are full and we've already got 100 people who've been assessed and another 60 or 70 in the system being assessed.

"So there's no point us taking more applications."

'We are keeping kids out of jail'

In his time as deputy director of the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, Anthony Shakeshaft investigated the benefits of Indigenous-led programs in aiding rehabilitation and combating drug harm.

He believes more centres are "absolutely" needed around the country.

There are calls for more rehabilitation centres around the country. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

"If you just think about it economically, there's no reason you wouldn't do it," says Professor Shakeshaft, now head of psychology at the University of Sunshine Coast.

"A really key feature of these programs is that they improve clients' health broadly, not just in terms of substance abuse.

"Clients that go to rehab and do a period in an Indigenous drug and alcohol service are [also] much less likely to end up back in jail."

Residents often gather at the main common area at Bunjilwarra. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

It is an argument echoed by Mel Bedford from Bunjilwarra, where six young residents at the centre are currently on bail.

"We are keeping kids out of jail here," she says.

"It's a lot cheaper for us to have a resident staying here than what it is to keep a resident in custody, and we're definitely helping their healing journey rather than being in custody."

From little things

There are only a dozen or so residents at a time at Bunjilwarra — a mere fraction of those in the wider community grappling with addiction.

That limited intake nonetheless creates fertile ground for more meaningful connection and change to occur, particularly for those experiencing intergenerational trauma.

Culture is central to the rehabilitation process at Bunjilwarra. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

On some days, that may take the form of a carpentry workshop or practical support around employment and nutrition.

It could also mean a walk with an elder through nearby bushland, or a conversation about culture and identity in the yarning circle around the fire.

A mural of Uncle Patrick Farrant Snr, who was a respected elder at Bunjilwarra. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

"Some of them are so sick culturally," Ms Lauch says.

"We talk about mental health, but if they're also culturally and spiritually disconnected, that's something that needs working on as well."

The centre only became a fully Aboriginal community-controlled service in the past year, but the site is now being visited by similar organisations looking to replicate aspects of the service interstate.

Carla Lauch remains hopeful that young people in the community will be able to turn their lives around. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

"I've seen workers in this industry who have all the qualifications in the world, but they cannot sit down and hold a conversation with a young person because they can feel the clinical energy," Ms Lauch says.

"I feel like mob just understand what mob needs, and there's that immediate trust with our young people to speak to someone who's been through it."

The words "From little things, big things grow", a reference to Kev Carmody and Paul Kelly's unofficial Australian anthem, are painted on one of the yarning circle logs.

A seat around the fire with a reference to the song From Little Things Big Things Grow. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

For Ms Lauch, whose mother and grandmother were part of the Stolen Generations, change is going to come, even if it is starting small.

"These young people that we have come through Bunjilwarra are our future elders," she says.

"We want them to be empowered to share culture, to right the wrongs of what our grandparents went through."

World.title: $2m payday for home battery owners as heatwave catches grid off guard
World.content:
On Monday evening this week, self-styled home battery boffins were buzzing with excitement on Reddit.

Deep in niche threads, they shared screenshots and boasted about how much money they'd made that afternoon on the National Energy Market (NEM).

Electricity prices in New South Wales had suddenly skyrocketed around 3:30pm (AEDT), peaking at $23,107 per megawatt hour (MWh), just shy of the market cap. Prices exceeded $5,000/MWh in 11 separate five-minute intervals.

"Rolling power spike pricing, have made $100 in an hour selling 30kw/h," one Reddit user commented.

"Solid effort!!," replied another.

Screenshots from a Reddit sub where people discuss home batteries. (Supplied)

A spring heat wave was sweeping the state, pushing temperatures into the mid-30s. At Observatory Hill in Sydney, temperatures spiked at 34.7 degrees, more than 12 degrees above the long-term monthly average.

For people with solar panels on their roofs and batteries in their garage, it was a chance to make money selling power back to the grid at much higher rates.

"Hot day shenanigans," another Reddit user posted under another earnings screenshot.

"Good for us hey!"

Tristan Edis is the CEO of Green Energy Markets, an industry analysis company. (Supplied: Green Energy Markets)

Green Energy Markets CEO Tristan Edis said the price spike was a reminder of an underlying NEM vulnerability in a rapidly warming climate as it tried to manage aging coal plants while building generation and storage.

"It's normal for electricity prices to be high when temperatures go noticeably above 30 degrees," Edis said.

" What's problematic is that doesn't normally happen in October. "

What happened?

Fuelling the extraordinary spike in prices was a confluence of factors.

As temperatures climbed, four of NSW's 12 coal-fired generating units were out of action and two were at reduced capacity.

The Eraring Power Station is scheduled to shut down in 2029. (AAP/Greenpeace)

To make matters worse, several high transmission lines were also running below capacity due to maintenance, meaning huge amounts of mostly renewable energy and storage capacity could not be delivered to Sydney just when it needed it most.

Australian energy intelligence firm GridScout said the energy was instead curtailed, or shut off at the source, because the high-voltage network could not transport more electricity.

"Technical curtailment peaked at (2,800 megawatts), with renewables and batteries in Southern NSW being the most heavily affected," the firm noted on social media.

"This was all while prices were above $10,000/MWh."

So hot temperatures drove up demand just when less electricity was available.

Amid the chaos, market watchers were also stunned by an unusual phenomenon.

Just after 3pm AEDT as demand soared, NSW spot prices on the wholesale market started whipsawing dramatically.

They jumped from about $200/MWh to more than $1,300/MWh, hit the $23,000 market ceiling minutes later, then plunged again.

And so it went for another hour.

$2m payday for batteries and EVs

Dave Smith, a wholesale power market designer, said the wild price gyrations appeared to have been driven by a new force in energy – Australia's growing fleet of household batteries.

On the national energy grid, bids are placed every five minutes for the next five minutes of power. The cheapest bid wins, and everyone who contributes gets paid at that price.

According to Smith, the squeeze in NSW on Monday drew a predictable response from the market. Prices rose sharply as supplies struggled to keep pace with demand.

The Dinawan substation is part Project EnergyConnect and will connect New South Wales, Victoria and South Australia. (Supplied: Transgrid)

Among those responding were the legions of household battery owners with software that allows them to control their batteries, all getting alerts on their phones telling them to sell their surplus power to tap into soaring prices.

But unlike most providers, these batteries sit behind the household meter, meaning the market operator has no ability to control them.

When prices spiked on Monday, household batteries injected large amounts of power into the system, only to pull back when prices fell in the next five-minute interval.

At all times, Smith said, AEMO was on the back foot and playing catch-up.

"Everyone sees that, 'Oh, the spot price is very high'," Smith explained.

"And some people with home batteries who are seeing that price are saying, 'Oh, it's a great opportunity, I can discharge my battery for five minutes'.

"The price (in NSW on Monday) was something like $20 a kilowatt hour ($20,000/MWh). You can make a lot of money."

Amber Electric co-CEO Dan Adams. (Supplied: Amber Electric)

Dan Adams, co-CEO of Amber Electric, an online energy retailer that connects and enables battery owners to trade on the NEM, said revenue on Monday was "probably" a record.

"Those 30,000 customers made $2 million in the space of two hours," he said.

"So $69 each on average, and the top earners made over $500."

AEMO expects more batteries and less transmission in the grid of tomorrow Home batteries hit 600,000 as households play big role in energy transition, but building transmission projects remains "critical", according to the latest AEMO energy plan.

While $23,000/MWh sounds like a lot to pay for power, Adams said spiking like this is normal and how the market is designed to work.

In the past, he said, only gas-fired generators would have been able to meet such demand peaks, but not anymore.

"Individual households [can too], because their batteries and EVs are providing that capacity to the market.

"It's both displacing gas from the grid and shifting value from the big generators into the hands of individual households."

The hog cycle

Smith likened the seesawing price and demand this week to a "hog cycle", an economic term for how prices and production swing wildly because they are out of sync.

In most instances, he said, there was a delay between the prices producers saw and the production that followed.

"Whenever you have a lag, you've always got this sort of whiplash problem," he said.

"I mean, if you're driving along the road and it was 10 seconds before you turned the wheel after you realised you were going in the ditch, you'd very soon be swerving from side to side, right?

"So, whenever there's a lag, there's a problem."

Transmission constraints also contributed to the lack capacity on Monday 12 October 2026. (Supplied: NSW Government)

In a statement, a spokesman for the market operator confirmed demand rose by almost 2,000 megawatts within an hour during Monday's heatwave.

"This coincided with several coal-fired generation units being offline, including two units at Eraring Power Station. In total, approximately 2,400 (megawatts) of coal-fired generation capacity was unavailable across NSW," the spokesman said.

Spring has traditionally been when coal plants do scheduled maintenance after winter and before ramping up again for summer demand, but analyst Tristan Edis said that window appeared to be narrower due to climate change.



“If we get more hot days in spring and autumn it gives us very short windows with which to maintain those coal generators,” he said.

Could batteries save us this summer?

After years of wetter, milder seasons, south-eastern Australia is facing a potentially record El Niño, a natural climate phenomenon that can bring hotter, drier conditions.

"Let's just hope that the coal generators are going to be able to get us through another summer and will be reasonably reliable," Edis said.

Why this El Niño is different The dark, red tongue spreading in the Pacific is growing at a rate not seen in living memory. The uncertainty over what is driving it has alarmed experts.

He said Australia had been slow to rebuild its electricity grid.

"We've been really living off what was probably unwise excessive investment in power plants and they're now coming to an end," Tristan Edis said.

"And we're doing it too late. Ideally, we should have been building new transmission back in the 2010s."

But cheap, quick-to-install battery storage is coming online just when Australia needs it.

"Batteries, large and small, are fundamentally changing the way energy is produced, consumed and priced," AMEO CEO Daniel Westerman told a conference this month.

Collie is home to Western Australia’s biggest State-owned battery. (ABC News: Mya Kordic )

More than 700,000 household batteries have been installed, mostly within the past year, and AEMO estimates more than two million will be installed by 2030.

Grid-scale battery capacity has more than doubled in the past year to more than 9 gigawatts and in the third quarter of 2026, Westerman said, batteries set the wholesale electricity price almost 50 per cent of the time, up from 18 per cent in the same quarter last year.

The average wholesale price in the NEM has fallen 44 per cent in the past two years, from $133/MWh in Q2 2024 to $74/MWh in Q2 2026.

However, the analysts all agree that Monday’s price whiplash shows there is work to do to make sure home batteries can be a force for stability in the grid.

Dave Smith said the ability of household batteries to move the market was growing every day as installation numbers rose, but AEMO remained largely blind to their presence and intentions.

"You're talking about thousands and thousands of small batteries," he said.

"How do you orchestrate them? How do you make them visible? So, yeah, that's where the solution lies potentially, but it's not easy."

And Tristan Edis says they’re only one part of the solution to rebuilding Australia's electricity grid.

"They're no good to us if we can't feed them with some energy to charge them up," he said.

"We've got heaps of solar and we're building more of it and that's great and that's sort of taken care of … but we also need extra wind and that needs extra transmission and it inevitably takes time."

World.title: Trump, Netanyahu and the dangerous politics of staying in power
World.content:
More often than is healthy, international news is framed in terms of the transactions of political leaders — who has come out on top on any given day — and the impact on those leaders' political fortunes at home.

This week we have seen the US president doing something different.

Donald Trump has not just been jostling with Russian president Vladamir Putin and Ukranian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He has personally gone to war with the people of Ukraine. All, it seems, to improve the political prospects of his Republican Party in the looming US mid-term elections.

Trump this week reportedly turned off intelligence to the Ukrainians and ordered the speed to be slowed of Starlink services that help warn Ukrainians of incoming missiles. That he did so is chilling.

Reuters reported on Friday that "the order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter".

"The officials said ‌leaders at the Defence Department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed.

"The officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, did not specify who in the White House made the decision or who was responsible for implementing the order."

Starlink slowdown in Ukraine Ukraine says people will die as a result of throttled Starlink services in the country. Here's how its armed forces rely on the crucial service.

In the past six days Trump has announced a deal to buy Russian diesel (long sanctioned by the US and, indeed, the subject of threats of sanctions on others who might buy it). He has told Ukraine and European allies that the US might suspend European purchases of US weapons on behalf of Ukraine and also pressured European countries to unfreeze Russian assets.

The Trump administration is also reported to be considering easing restrictions on so-called shadow fleet vessels that have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela.

So shutting off US intelligence and ordering a go-slow on the Starshield service might be just two more points of pressure being applied to Kyiv. But they weren't moves to apply financial pressure or shift the oil market to get oil prices down.

They weren't even simple abuse of another country's leader. ("I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president," Trump told Washington reporters last Saturday).

These were explicit decisions to leave a civilian population exposed to ballistic missile attacks and to shift the balance of the war in Russia's favour

Beyond the scores killed and injured in Russian attacks on civilians in recent days, an unanswered Russian strike on energy infrastructure left at least 600,000 people in Ukraine without power on Wednesday.

It is not clear how Donald Trump would react to a loss in the mid-terms. (Reuters: Callaghan O'Hare)

Mid-term predictions mount

An increasing number of analysts in the United States believe that Trump will not just lose the US House of Representatives but also the Senate. Instead of seeing that development as a harbinger of some curbs on his erratic administration, the concern is about how Trump will respond to the news.

In the American capital, there is no great confidence that Trump will respond rationally, or will feel somehow chastened and therefore constrained, to exercise power in a way which reflects the boundaries of actual laws.

That means malevolent interventions in the Russia-Ukraine conflict could continue and only spread further shock waves into a Western Europe that is desperately trying to prop Ukraine up.

There is also the question of what Trump does, or doesn't do, on Iran and whether he does, or doesn't, do something before the mid-term elections in pursuit of a similar electoral boost.

The Middle East brings more tension

The conflict with Iran continues to dominate much of the coverage out of the Middle East.

But for those in the region, a much more pressing question revolves around the Israeli election, now just 10 days away.

Regional powers observe that Israel's prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has done everything he could to provoke a regional confrontation — whether that be in Syria, Lebanon, within the West Bank or even with Jordan — in the run up to the election.

Like Trump, Netanyahu has played his international politics hard for domestic consumption.

Like the US president, he has often presented a spectacular failure as a sign of his strength: in Netanyahu's case, the intelligence failures of October 7, the lack of any clear victory in Gaza, or Lebanon, or Iran.

There was one contested report this week that he even pushed Washington to restart the Iran war before the Israeli vote.

The man who has emerged as Netanyahu's major opponent in the upcoming elections, Gadi Eisenkot, and two other party leaders — the right wing's Avigdor Liberman and the centre-left's Yair Golan — all warned this week that Netanyahu may start a war before the election in an attempt to stay in power.

Golan said Netanyahu will try to disrupt the democratic process before and on election day.

Recent polls have given Eisenkot a significantly larger number of seats than Netanyahu. Yet, like Trump, there is no confidence in the Middle East that he is about to lose power.

At best, the numbers are so close — when all the permutations of possible coalitions are done — that the current PM is likely to continue in the job for some time, at least as caretaker prime minister.

Benjamin Netanyahu, on a visit to Mount Hermon on the border between Syria and Lebanon, has kept up destabilising actions in Syria. (Israel GPO/Anadolu via Getty Images: Ma'yan Toaf)

The biggest concern is what he might do in Syria.

The wiring of the Middle East has been rapidly rerouting since the war in Iran began on February 28: the Gulf states, Turkiye, Syria, Saudi Arabia, Lebanon, Jordan and Iraq have all been having to find new voices for themselves and new ways of getting along.

Some in the region argue that the need to keep the only recently-stabilised Syria more or less in one piece is the one thing all the locals can agree upon.

There is also an unstable Syria representing the threat of an ISIS resurgency. Conflict between the Kurds and Turkiye with spill over into Iraq and the restoration of the land bridge that Syria once represented between Iran and Hezbollah. All of these would be bad for the border security of Lebanon, Jordan and Iraq, and for a possible renewed surge of millions of refugees.

Loading

Jordan watching on

For Jordan there are particular risks, including that 40 per cent of its water supply comes from Syria.

Yet Israel has kept up destabilising actions in Syria: pushing into southern Syria and even attacking an air base close to the border with Turkiye last month.

Jordan's King Abdullah — who was visiting Australia this week in search of closer defence and intelligence ties — told the UN General Assembly last month that the Israeli government's "expansionist appetite" is now a regional threat, citing Gaza, the West Bank and southern Syria.

His tiny kingdom — which boasts one of the world's most unfortunate set of surrounding neighbours — has repeatedly expressed its alarm about Israel's actions: from the threat to its water to what King Abdullah has called an existential threat seen in Israeli talk of forcing three million Palestinians into Jordan as Israel extends its annexation of the West Bank.

Jordan has never had many cards to play in its brief history. A presumption that the US would side with Israel in any conflict would seem to make its position even weaker.

But the fact that the US has had to withdraw many of its personnel and assets from the Gulf into Jordan changes the equation of its interest in keeping Jordan stable too.

And an irony of Netanyahu's recent actions is that it is the security deals with Jordan and Egypt — and thus relative border stability — that have allowed Israel to pursue its incursions into Gaza, into Lebanon and into Syria.

That Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu is now playing with Jordan, at least rhetorically, is just one more illustration of the mess he and Donald Trump are creating around the world in their determination to stay in power.

Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.

World.title: As fertility rates fall, mums of three share joy and sacrifice of big families
World.content:
Read the story in Bahasa Indonesia

Dian Winata returned to work just two weeks after the caesarean birth of her third child.

She only took one month off after the birth of her second child, who was also delivered by caesarean.

But that wasn't because Ms Winata couldn't wait to get back to her job. Financially, she didn't have a choice.

When her daughters were born, Ms Winata was not a permanent Australian resident, was not eligible for government-funded parental leave, and had used up her paid leave entitlements.

"If you ask why I could have three kids, it's because I love it," said Ms Winata, whose eldest child was born in Indonesia.

"And why could I work that much while having three kids? Because I needed to.

"My husband and I are not from a generation that inherited wealth. So we earned our own money and saved from scratch in Australia."

Dian Winata says she often felt lonely growing up with one sibling. (Supplied: Dian Winata)

Ms Winata is among the women choosing to have bigger families at a time when Australia's fertility rates are falling.

It is a decision that comes with significant trade-offs, they say.

She and her husband, Steven Halim, both work full time to cover their mortgage and everyday living expenses for their 11-year-old son and two daughters, aged six and four.

One statistic spells challenge for Australia as it ages Australia is getting much older, and it is getting older faster than previously thought.

Ms Winata works as an assistant service manager at an Adelaide childcare centre, where she receives a staff discount that helps to reduce childcare costs for her own children.

Her mother and mother-in-law travel from Indonesia to Australia every three months to help care for her children.

Before gaining permanent residency in 2024, they paid thousands of dollars for support services for their second daughter, who has autism.

They then became eligible for the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS), easing some of the financial pressure.

"What we sacrificed was the time we could have spent more with the kids, it had to be split with work," Ms Winata said.

"What used to be our rest time, we ended up spending playing with the kids instead."

Liz Allen says some people may have fewer children because their choices are constrained. (Supplied: Liz Allen)

Australia's population is "aging more quickly", according to Australia's 2026 Intergenerational Report published in September.

The total fertility rate in 2024 was 1.48 births per woman, according to data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics, which will release new figures in November.

The Intergenerational Report estimates that by 2065, the figure will fall further to 1.34 children per woman.

Australian National University demographer Liz Allen said some people might be having fewer children than they wanted because their choices were "constrained".

"Having children has become so difficult because the social, economic and cultural supports are inhospitable to having a much-wanted child," Dr Allen said.

The 'motherhood penalty'

Lauren Treweek chose to have three children because she grew up with one brother and lots of cousins, so family events were "busy and noisy" and felt "special".

Lauren Treweek always knew she wanted at least two children. (Supplied: Lauren Treweek)

Her decision was also about finding joy.

"Each child that you have not only gives you a new little person to get excited about and to learn about, but it also gives you different experiences that you yourself can find joy in as well," Ms Treweek said.

Lauren Treweek says both she and her husband need to work to support the family financially. (Supplied: Lauren Treweek)

But being a mother has also come with trade-offs.

Three children came with bigger financial pressures, such as "hideously expensive" child care, she said.

The Melbourne-based mum, who also co-hosts a parenting podcast, said motherhood had impacted her marketing career.

"Part of me is happy to sacrifice maybe not progressing as quickly as I thought I would in order to have a greater level of flexibility to do pick-ups and drop-offs, or be available for a sick day if needed," she said.

Ms Treweek said that career setbacks were "undeniable" and part of what she described as the "motherhood penalty".

The motherhood penalty refers to "the negative consequences women experience in the workplace due to being a mother", said Sandra Buchler, who holds a PhD in sociology from The University of Queensland.

Sandra Buchler says decisions on having children are shaped by many factors. (Supplied: Sandra Buchler)

Dr Buchler, a fellow at the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for Children and Families Over the Life Course, said while decisions about having children were personal and shaped by many factors, for some women, having more children could mean slower career progression.

It could also mean lower earnings and less retirement savings because of longer parental leave, part-time work or more time spent caring, she said.

Women's earnings fall by an average of 55 per cent in the first five years after becoming a parent while men's are unchanged, according to a 2023 Treasury report.

'It's a sacrifice I chose'

For Paula Gaziero, a stay-at-home mum with three sons aged five, three and four months, returning to paid work is not a priority.

Paula Gaziero says she feels "blessed" to have her children, as she knows some people struggle to conceive. (Supplied: Paula Gaziero)

"I think this is the most important work I could be doing. I am raising little humans," the 29-year-old said.

Before having children, Ms Gaziero worked in hospitality and administration and had hoped to pursue a career in accounting.

"It is a sacrifice, but it's a sacrifice I chose," she said, adding "this is not forever".

Ms Gaziero said her family did not do "very expensive things" and had to make sacrifices compared to families with two working parents.

Paula Gaziero says she wanted her children to have the same sibling companionship she had growing up. (Supplied: Paula Gaziero)

Ms Gaziero also homeschools her eldest son and said staying at home meant the family did not have childcare costs.

Her young family is fortunate to be able to live at her husband's grandmother's acreage property in Queensland, so they do not have to pay rent.

Ms Gaziero said Australia was "very blessed to have free health care", and that had been one of the biggest factors in her decision to have multiple children.

She and her husband, Ben Spiers, were yet to decide if they would expand their family to welcome a fourth child, she added.

"They're not going to want me forever," she said.

"In a blink of an eye, they will be teenagers going about their day, and then I can focus on my career.

"It's a season, and it's a beautiful season, and I want to enjoy the most of it."

World.title: Richard Morecroft’s surname yields the anagram ‘comforter’, which is only right
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

The first time I met Richard Morecroft was at the Crows Nest Hotel, a short walk from the ABC’s Gore Hill studios. This was 1986. I was mid-20s, working behind the bar. Richard was more like 30, the media star making a rare cameo for his single drink. Tongue-tied, I didn’t start a conversation. Nor did Richard recall this episode when we ended up working together some 30 years later.

Then again, why would he? Richard was a constant in our lounge room, and I was an arts grad earning travel money. He was the voice of confirmation, the emotional anchor of the Space Shuttle disaster which happened that same month. In fact, it was around this time Richard had adopted Archie, the orphaned grey-headed flying fox. For all I know, he might have smuggled the little guy into the pub. I can’t say. We never chatted. And he left soon after.

Richard Morecroft (centre) with Lily Serna and David Astle on the set of Letters and Numbers. SBS

Advance the clock, switch the setting. We meet as colleagues, along with a maths whiz called Lily Serna, the three of us co-hosts of SBS’s Letters and Numbers in 2010. If you haven’t seen the show, think parlour games dabbling with equations or anagrams. Lily aligned the numbers, while I flapped the dictionary to verify words. Sitting at the calm centre, Richard was the puzzle ambassador, with licence to play.

And he loved it, and we loved him. Everyone loved Richard, the reasons multiple. Leigh Sales, a long-time ABC friend, on marking Richard’s death last week, described him as both a gentleman, and a gentle man. Which was perfect. Gentle is the first word that sprang to my mind too. For Lily, it was grand. For both of us: generous.

World.title: Is the Pope a Catholic? Yes, but that’s where the certainty ends
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

There are many unlikely papal moments in Paolo Sorrentino’s 2016 series The Young Pope: the Pope emerges from under a pile of babies, the Pope tames a kangaroo, the Pope spies on a couple having sex in their living room. Still, none is more unbelievable in these times than the Pope insisting that his face be hidden from the public. “I do not have an image because I am no one,” says newly elected Pope Pius XIII (Jude Law). If he must appear it will be as “a dark shadow, [a] silhouette”. Pius name-checks Banksy, JD Salinger and Daft Punk – “the most important figures in their respective fields” – none of whom let themselves be seen. “The Vatican survives on hyperbole,” he says, “So we will give them hyperbole. But this time in reverse.” Jude Law and Milvia Marigliano in The Young Pope. He has a point. The Pope is famous despite, not because of, his face. Take an ordinary man, dress him in a white pellegrina and zucchetto, add a chunky pectoral cross and you have the kind of instant recognition very few living people command. We’re talking Elvis Presley or Dolly Parton-level recognition from silhouette alone. It’s this instant identification that makes the Pope such an effective vehicle for dramatic or comedic intervention. In Italian satirist Pierfrancesco Diliberto’s new film Holy Cannoli (Che Dio perdona a tutti) the protagonist, Arturo, eats so much sugar in one hit that he hallucinates the Pope (Carlos Hipólito) is in his living room. The absurdity, the wonder and the inclination to actually listen when the apparition speaks come almost entirely from the instantly identifiable costume, at least to begin with.



As the film goes on, it becomes clear that this is a fictionalised version of the late Pope Francis, but he could just as easily be an entirely invented character. His role in the film is to guide atheistic Arturo in his quest to be worthy of his devoutly Catholic girlfriend. For this, he does not need to be an actual Pope; he needs to be both a symbol of official Christianity and benign father-figure who will appeal to the audience regardless of religious belief. The actual Pope also performs that role, of course, though his perceived benignity and appeal are far from universal. They also differ fairly dramatically depending on the specifics of the man in the costume. An Economist survey in June found the current Pope Leo XIV had the highest favorability rating among all the public figures polled, coming in a whopping 54 percentage points higher than the US president. The Public Religion Research Institute points out that his predecessor, Pope Francis, had even higher ratings at the same point in his papacy, and both have been consistently seen more favourably than Pope Benedict XVI. So the Pope is a symbol, yes, but he’s also a person. The best papal fiction exploits this tension by testing what belongs to the former and what to the latter. Returning to The Young Pope, for example, we have a pontiff whose (relatively) young age of 47 quickly becomes the least of it as we discover he is also a chain-smoking, American, hard-core reactionary who has no interest in making nice with the public, his own cardinals or Vatican bureaucrats. He also happens to look distractingly like Jude Law. Loading The conceit is that one or more of these things make him an extremely unlikely choice for pontiff but in fact, every one of these (except the Jude Law thing) has been true of at least one real pope. Pontiffs younger than Law’s Pius include medieval teen Popes Benedict IX and John XII; those said to have loved a ciggie include John XXII and Benedict XVI; and the ones who battled with their own curia are probably more common than those who didn’t. (An American pope didn’t exist until 2025, well after the show finished its run, but the joke is well and truly history now.) So despite the show’s sumptuous surrealism, it, like others in the genre of pope fiction, provides a strangely realistic thought experiment in what the enormous multi-part engine of the Vatican can and cannot absorb when it comes to an individual pope’s quirks and personal qualities.



A clear answer can be found in the many retellings of the medieval legend of a female pope. The specific characteristics of the woman said to have disguised herself as a monk before rising all the way to the top job varies wildly across versions. But from Lawrence Durrell’s Pope Joan (1954) to Donna Woolfolk Cross’ 1996 version; from Caryl Churchill’s play Top Girls (1982) to my own 2024 novel Rapture, the Pope’s female body is an absolute dealbreaker for the institution. In legend, in history, and very much in real life right now, the Pope can be almost any kind of person, as long as that person is a man. Really, almost any kind of person? Let’s consider the sub-genre of pope fiction that we might call Borgia-core (after the most obvious example, Showtime’s The Borgias), which revels in the juxtaposition of holiness and horniness, piety and perversion. The thing about these salacious stories of corrupt and hedonistic popes is that they’re taken right out of the history books. (Albeit from sometimes unreliable and agenda-driven sources.) The medieval era in particular was rife with men who took to the role with the spirit of Pope Leo X (another young Pope, at 37) who is said to have declared: “God has given us the papacy; now let us enjoy it”. John Malkovich in The New Pope. In contrast, the entirely fictional pontiff depicted by John Malkovich in The New Pope (the 2020 follow-up to The Young Pope) is decidedly unwilling to make the office his own. The conclave elected him because of his centrist views and he is unwilling to disappoint them. When the actor Sharon Stone (playing herself) asks him (having presented him with her stilettos as a gift) when “the pointless taboo” of gay marriage for Catholics will end, he answers: “When the church has a brave, revolutionary, resolute Pope. Qualities none of which I possess.” A brave, resolute Pope is exactly what we find in 1968’s The Shoes of the Fisherman (adapted from Morris West’s 1963 novel) which features a Ukrainian pope who uses his knowledge of life behind the Iron Curtain to negotiate peace between the Soviet Union and the US, becoming a serious geopolitical actor who effectively stops World War III. As with The Young Pope’s American pontiff, The Shoes of the Fisherman can appear to have manifested a real one not too far down the line. Ten years after the film, Polish-born John Paul II became, like the fictional Pope Kiril, the first non-Italian Pope in more than four centuries. Like Kiril, his experience of living in the Soviet bloc led him to intervene significantly — and successfully — in the diplomatic struggle to end the Cold War. Walter F. Murphy’s The Vicar of Christ (1979) also features a politically interventionist (and American) Pope. The book’s Pope Francis (30 years before the real life one of that name) is a war hero and US Supreme Court justice before he becomes a man of the cloth. The fictional Francis is a resolutely progressive pope on questions of moral and social teaching. His opposition to war is equally uncompromising, and so effective that he is ultimately assassinated by those for whom war is an indispensable feature of the political order.



That a pope could be powerful enough to threaten a political regime is examined in Graham Greene’s story The Last Word (1988). Greene imagines a dystopian future in which “the last Pope” is an elderly man living alone in a bedsit with a contraband bible and broken crucifix. Organised religion has been eradicated in the name of one-world government and yet, still, as a general carries out the final act of executing the old man who was once its figurehead, he experiences the “strange and frightening” thought that “what this man believed may be true”. The question of which kind of pope – centrist, progressive, reactionary or non-European – the church most needs is at the heart of 2024’s Conclave. The film is, in part, a study of how the people who know the role best disagree about who should fill it. The characters argue and grapple and pray, connive and conspire, and though for some it is a matter of personal ego and power-hunger, most are driven by a desire to find the right man for the job. Ralph Fiennes as Cardinal Lawrence in Conclave. Focus Features Conclave is indisputably fiction but in real life, as the Catholic Church’s cardinals gathered to choose a new Pope after the death of Pope Francis in May 2025, POLITICO reported that some of those eminent men were watching the film for pointers. It was, according to one cardinal, “a helpful research tool at a time when so many of the conclave participants have little experience of Vatican politics and protocol”. Audiences outside the Vatican were apparently doing the same: streams of the film shot up 283 per cent in the lead-up to the real-world version and social media was flooded with memes about it. As helpful as that film may have been for explaining the process of choosing a pope, it doesn’t necessarily help when it comes to understanding how becoming one might actually feel. What is it like to be a man one moment and a monumental, instantly recognisable symbol the next? Nanni Moretti’s Habemus Papam (We Have a Pope, 2011) suggests it is a living nightmare. In the opening scenes, we are shown the prayers of the cardinals at the conclave: not me, not me, please not me, they each pray. The unlucky contender (Michel Piccoli) tries to rise to the call, but the moment before he is to address the crowd in St Peter’s Square, he screams and refuses. A psychiatrist is brought in to intervene, though given the session is conducted in the presence of the increasingly panicked cardinals, it is no surprise when the reluctant Pope bolts at the first opportunity.



One wonders if a similar impulse passed through Cardinal Ratzinger when he was elected Pope Benedict XVI in 2005. His reluctance was widely known within the Vatican: not only did he not want to be Pope, but he had asked twice in the preceding years to be released from his role as prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith only for Pope John Paul II to refuse. Benedict later said that his election “felt like a guillotine”. Jonathan Pryce as Cardinal Bergoglio, right, and Anthony Hopkins as Pope Benedict in a scene from The Two Popes. Peter Mountain/Netflix via AP A fictionalised version of Benedict features in 2019’s The Two Popes, but his unwillingness to serve is not explored. Indeed, the film portrays Ratzinger openly campaigning for the position, in contrast to his eventual predecessor who is shown as reluctant to take on the role. It’s a reminder that a real-life Pope who has been fictionalised is still, well, fiction. In Habemus Papam, when the runaway newly elected Pope is asked by a psychiatrist what he does for a living, he answers simply: “I’m an actor”. The answer reveals a lot about this particular fictional Pope who doesn’t know how to play this next role he’s been given. This is what papal fiction does: it lets us watch the role collide with the person playing it and try to figure out what the papacy actually is. What endures despite the changing person? Is it only the stunning backdrop, millennium-old ritual and fancy Swiss guards? Pierfrancesco Diliberto and Carlos Hipólito in Holy Cannoli. The Pope is supposed to be the ultimate symbol of continuity, the same white figure emerging onto the same balcony. Yet the person inside can change the meaning of the role entirely. A pope from behind the Iron Curtain once belonged to the realm of geopolitical fantasy; then a Polish cardinal walked onto the world stage. An American pope once seemed ridiculous; now a Chicagoan is on the papal balcony.

World.title: Trump’s press secretary Katie Zacharia removed after just five days
World.content:
Breaking WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Trump’s press secretary Katie Zacharia removed after just five days Michael Koziol Updated October 17, 2026 — 5:34am ,first published 4:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Washington: Donald Trump’s new press secretary Katie Zacharia has been dumped from the role after just five days, with the president lamenting that the job was “maybe … not for her” following a poor debut performance. Trump said he had encouraged Zacharia to reconsider her position and would speak to her when he returned from interstate. But a White House official confirmed to this masthead that Zacharia was “transitioning out” of the press secretary role. President Donald Trump leaves the White House with press secretary Katie Zacharia to talk to reporters on Tuesday. AP It follows a poor debut performance on Tuesday (US time) at the White House where Zacharia – a conservative media commentator – read awkwardly from a prepared script, took few questions and fumbled her responses. She was also caught up in a furore over whether she misrepresented her legal qualifications to the president, having now admitted that she never passed the bar exam despite marketing herself as a lawyer.



Trump told reporters on Friday that he urged Zacharia to rethink the job. “I just spoke to her about it. I said, ‘Katie, is this for you?’ Because she’s been treated very rough, and she’s a nice person,” he said. Related Article Analysis

Trump's White House ‘My president ... excuse me, my husband’: Trump’s new spinner gets off to a rocky start “I said to her, ‘Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider’. You think about it. But I would reconsider. She’s got a beautiful husband and family. I said, ‘You should reconsider because you don’t want to go through this’.” Trump said he would let Zacharia make the decision. However, his remarks left little possibility she could continue in the role. “Maybe it’s not for her,” he said of the high-pressure position. Minutes after Trump made the remarks while departing the White House, several US news outlets including CNN and The New York Times reported that Zacharia had been fired, citing people familiar with the matter.



Zacharia did not accompany Trump as he left the White House for a rally in Georgia on Friday. Communications director Steven Cheung was present on the South Lawn instead as the president took questions from reporters. The 41-year-old Zacharia’s first week in the highly scrutinised role included unusually combative interviews on Fox News on Thursday night and Friday morning, both of which Trump watched. Trump speaks to reporters on the South Lawn before departing for a rally in Georgia. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin Anchors Sean Hannity and Lawrence Jones separately grilled Zacharia over her legal qualifications and why she had not told Trump she never passed the bar. “Those questions weren’t asked,” she told Jones.



Zacharia also explained that she was only offered the job last Wednesday, flew to Washington and attended a meeting at the White House on Friday, flew home to California on Saturday and then back to Washington on Sunday before starting in the job on Monday and briefing the press on Tuesday morning. “What I feel is I really stepped up to the plate to do the press conference with very little prep time,” she told Hannity. “I received briefing materials in the morning of Tuesday.” Then White House press secretary Katie Zacharia at the podium on Tuesday. AP The “tough” Fox News interviews were widely seen as orchestrated tests for Zacharia and setups to justify her removal by the president. Her five-day tenure sets a record for the shortest-lived White House press secretary in US history, beating the 11 days served by Anthony Scaramucci during the first Trump administration.



“Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain,” Scaramucci posted on Friday. Related Article Analysis

Trump's White House The disappearing women of the Trump administration Zacharia replaced former press secretary Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down in August to focus on her family after giving birth to her second child in May. Leavitt had only been back in the role briefly after her maternity leave. The White House has been without a regular press secretary for months in 2026, and the role is now vacant again just weeks before the midterm elections. World.title: Put Barenaked Ladies in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, you cowards
World.content:
CultureMusicThe Verdict Opinion Put Barenaked Ladies in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, you cowards

Tom W Clarke October 17, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Lyrically nonsensical and infuriatingly catchy, with rapid-fire verses that tumble through random references to filmmaker Akira Kurosawa, manga series Sailor Moon, TV show The X-Files and Toronto’s Birchmount Stadium, Canadian pop-rockers Barenaked Ladies are most famous for their 1998 hit, One Week. These days, that iconic opening yelp of “Yiiiiit’s been” will either fill you with joy or send shivers down your spine, remembering a time when this chaotic pop-rap earworm was inescapable. One Week was huge, a global hit that went to No.1 in the United States – as it happens, for exactly one week. It’s time for ’90s rock’s frontiersmen of fun to get the respect they deserve. The Sydney Morning Herald However, their biggest commercial triumph was a gift and a curse. In achieving mainstream success, One Week became their legacy. Mentions of Barenaked Ladies typically lump them in with a certain calibre of late-’90s nostalgia – alongside The Mighty Mighty Bosstones and The Presidents of the United States of America – as punchlines, reminders of the kind of rock-adjacent silliness that presaged “the saving of rock music” by The Strokes and The White Stripes. I’m not necessarily here trying to convince you that One Week is a stream-of-consciousness masterpiece of pop absurdism, James Joyce for the MTV generation – though if you reach that conclusion on your own, I won’t disagree.



But Barenaked Ladies are not one-hit wonders. In fact, they are among the most underappreciated bands of the ’90s, brilliant songwriters with a long record of indie success, and pioneers who dared to have fun at a time when music was at its most dour. They are a treasure. Geniuses persecuted for their whimsy, whose combination of existential suburban ennui and fun-loving irreverence preceded the breakouts of Green Day, Weezer and The Offspring. Rock criticism is often an exercise in musical elitism. Goodness knows I’ve been guilty of it myself. The main reason that Barenaked Ladies were dismissed by mainstream critics, and why their legacy and talent continues to be ignored, is that they are funny. “Novelty acts” don’t make the Hall of Fame, don’t make real music, can’t be taken seriously. Ahem, “Weird Al” Yankovic would like a word. And music in the early ’90s was SO serious. Nirvana, Pearl Jam, Soundgarden. In response to the cheesiness of ’80s hair metal and new wave, grunge was heavy, raw, sludgy and just overflowing with angst. Angst for days.



And in 1992, at the very height of grunge, Barenaked Ladies released their seminal debut album, Gordon. Less than a year after Nevermind by Nirvana, months before Dirt by Alice in Chains and Core by Stone Temple Pilots, Barenaked Ladies eschewed flannel shirts and Nietzsche in favour of offbeat observations and folk-flavoured good times. When Oasis – one of the acts set to be inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame during next month’s ceremony, alongside Iron Maiden, Joy Division/New Order and Phil Collins (solo), among others – released Live Forever in 1994, Noel Gallagher called it a response to the misery of grunge. Barenaked Ladies had already beaten him to it. Yiiiiit’s been … about 30 years now: Barenaked Ladies, still going strong, singing at an NFL game last month. AP Gordon is a unique concoction of silliness and poetry, routinely hilarious and poignant in a single beat. Be My Yoko Ono is a charmingly eccentric love song. If I Had $1000000 is a quaint delight, aspirational dreaming for a generation growing up in significant economic instability; all they want is a house, a mini-fridge and to buy their love a fur coat (“but not a real fur coat, that’s cruel”). Brian Wilson is the single most underrated song of the ’90s, as pained and contemplative an exploration of creative anxiety and world-weariness as there has been in pop. They were frontiersmen of fun, punctuating real-life struggles with self-deprecation and witticism – before the pop-punk juvenilia of Green Day and Blink-182, before the geek rock of Weezer and Ben Folds Five. You didn’t need to be brooding or apathetic to express discontent. Life can be hard without being overwhelmed by darkness.



The band also presaged two major trends in 2000s pop songwriting. On Gordon, and later on songs like One Week and It’s All Been Done, they used niche pop culture references as emotional touchstones to connect with Millennial audiences through irony, fandom and nostalgia. And they were early masters of the “sad songs disguised as happy pop” movement (think Hey Ya! by OutKast or Pumped Up Kicks by Foster The People). The Old Apartment is an upbeat dissection of domestic heartbreak and bitter memory, while Pinch Me is a desperate search for meaning in the so-called suburban dream. Maybe Barenaked Ladies will forever be misunderstood, their legacy forgotten everywhere outside the Great White North. Or maybe it’s all just karmic punishment for writing the theme song to The Big Bang Theory. But if Phil Collins can get inducted into the Hall of Fame twice, anyone’s still got a shot.
