Thousands of students miss out on a spot at select-entry Mac.Robertson Girls’ High School every year. Its popularity, and that of the state’s three other selective-entry high schools, is fuelling an ongoing debate that is about to become an election issue. Principal Sue Harrap and students on the grounds at Mac.Robertson Girls’ High School. Eddie Jim There are only 1000 new spots at the four schools every year, but thousands take the entry exam in the hope of securing a coveted enrolment. While proponents argue this demand shows why Victoria needs new selective schools – as promised by the state Liberals – critics say they are fuelling social segregation.



Mac.Robertson is hemmed in by Albert Park, apartment buildings and the chaotic Kings Way, meaning its current campus has no room to grow. The lure for parents is the promise of academic results that rival those of many private schools, without the expensive price tag. An analysis of data from the education department, curriculum and exam body found it was consistently one of the top-performing schools in the state. That’s based on the percentage of individual study scores above 40. According to the 2025 data, 34.7 per cent of the cohort received a score of 40 and above, while the median study score was 37. The state average last year was 30.



In the previous year, 31.1 per cent of the school’s students received a mark of 40 and above, and their median VCE study score was 37. Its closest competitor is Ruyton Girls’ School in Kew, which had 30.9 per cent of its cohort achieve a score of 40, while its median study score was 36. Principal Sue Harrap says she must balance the school’s “VCE reputation” with the reality of running an ageing campus with space limitations. “We are tiny, we’ve got three buildings,” Harrap says. “There’s nowhere for us to expand to.” There is no outdoor recreation area so they pay to use the nearby Melbourne Sports and Aquatic Centre and athletic centre, she says.



The school is also forced to shell out to use sports fields at Fawkner Park in South Yarra, where students have their physical education and health lessons. Mac.Robertson also does not have the funds of some of the nearby private all-girls’ schools and was forced to drop its International Baccalaureate program last year due to its running cost. A Victorian auditor-general’s report, published in June, rated the school in “worn” condition. But despite these issues, Mac.Rob’s (its nickname) is still a destination of choice, with 300 pupils earning a coveted place there each year. Harrap says many new students have to adjust to not always being the best.



“There is a huge impact on the students’ identity when they come here – they’re used to being the best,” she explains. Many have perfectionist tendencies, an internal narrative that can be damaging to their self-confidence, she says. “Then they can feel like they’re not good any more,” Harrap says. Students also have to deal with the school’s reputation as a cut-throat “VCE factory” only concerned with getting the highest ATAR or study scores.



Harrap says while they value results, the reputation is overblown. “The students understand the VCE works best if you collaborate as a group and support each other to do well,” she says. “It’s not a dog-eat-dog world that people think it might be, and no one is dragging each other down. They really support each other to grow.” Mac.Robertson Girls’ High School was deemed to be in “worn” condition in a report this year. Danie Sprague Mackenzie Li did an intensive two-month study course before the entry exam to increase her chances of being accepted.



“It feels really stressful especially for a 13-year-old,” she says of the test. Now a year 11 student at the school, the 16-year-old has just returned from the US, where she did an international extension program at Yale. But for Li, it was worth the stress and study once she was accepted. “We may not have the best facilities, or … the most money to build the fanciest campus, but I think the community really makes it worth it,” she says. While the academic side of the school can be intense, she always felt supported by staff and her peers.



“If I had to do it again, I would, just because I think being in the school has, personally, given me a pathway to be the best version of myself and my future,” she says. Stories like Li’s, however, are why critics argue the system is broken. The drive for parents to get their children into the state’s four select-entry schools see many pay thousands on professional tutors. Trevor Cobbold, from the group Save Our Schools, which campaigns for education equity, previously says more select-entry schools would be the wrong move for Victoria. “More selective schools would exacerbate social segregation in the public system and increase the already high concentration of low-income and other disadvantaged students in some schools which lowers student results.”



Harrap warns if new students fixate on academic rankings, they will be let down, and the school has shifted to ensuring students work to achieve their personal best, rather than just getting top marks. Related Article Private schools We looked at staff salaries at 40 private schools. These pay the most “The irony for this school is that you have to perform well on a test to get in, but if you continue to have that performance orientation, and you’re looking to be number one, [most] … we take 300 kids in every year, and 299 of them will be disappointed.” To combat this, the school works to shift mindsets away from pure results towards emotional regulation and wellbeing – a vital transition for the incoming year 9s. They not only have to navigate that change, but often face long commutes, a new routine and their own changing identities.



“Their mindset needs to shift to ‘I’m no longer striving to be the best; I’m striving to be the best version of myself’,” Harrap says. The students realise their peers possess similar skills, and this helps, rather than hinders, their abilities. At the same time, staff work to demystify academic struggle. Miss Universe Australia winner Priya Serrao says Mac.Rob’s was a haven. Instagram “Learning is about finding out about things you don’t already know, and that requires struggle.”



For year 12s, the myth that senior year is solely about chasing a 50 study score or a perfect ATAR is equally inaccurate, she says. “There’s always an element of fun,” 18-year-old Claire says, pointing to school formals and house dress-up events alongside study sessions. “There’s obviously a fair bit of stress as well, but it’s about riding the highs and lows as you go throughout the year.” “Now the focus is pursuing growth, not just teaching information, but helping students set goals, apply skills, find help, and celebrate their vulnerability.” Japanese teacher Shungo Sawaki Her peer Suri agrees, noting the shared pressure for year 12s creates a safety net of sorts.



“You really have your people around you as a support system, friends you can count on to take a break from studying every once in a while.” This emphasis on balance reflects an evolution within the school over the past decade, says veteran teacher Shungo Sawaki who has taught at Mac.Rob’s for nearly 30 years. “I, personally, had to change my teaching methodology a lot,” Sawaki explains of the change from when he started at the school in 1999. “Now the focus is pursuing growth, not just teaching information, but helping students set goals, apply skills, find help, and celebrate their vulnerability. “Not everyone has to be a superhero.”



Japanese teacher Shungo Sawaki has taught at the school for almost 30 years. Eddie Jim Sawaki has also watched the school demographics shift alongside Australia’s migration trends. While its original students were largely from Anglo-Saxon backgrounds, this shifted to girls of Greek and Italian heritage, then Eastern and Central European families, and most recently to students of South-East Asian and Chinese descent. According to MySchool data, 88 per cent of Mac.Rob’s students speak a language other than English at home – something the school considers one of its greatest strengths. Former student, policy adviser and Miss Universe Australia winner in 2019, Priya Serrao, says her cohort included many first and second generation migrants.



“It allowed us to get access to facilities and teaching and amenities that we wouldn’t get otherwise,” she says. For her, that included studying four languages and taking part in drama studies and performances. Serrao still remembers waiting at Watergardens train station in Melbourne’s outer north-west with about 15 other girls in their Mac.Rob’s uniform to start their first day at the school. “It was just a bit of a haven for someone like me, and I didn’t even think that schools provided those types of classes, and having kids around me that are just as kind of bubbling with excitement to do all of this stuff, too, was great,” she says.



Serrao recognises she was lucky to attend the highly sought-after school. The vast majority of students who attend Mac.Rob’s (70 per cent) come from “advantaged” backgrounds, according to data about the socio-educational background of pupils. Freddo Frog inventor, philanthropist and entrepreneur Sir Macpherson Robertson. Topical Press The sentiment that education could offer young people more opportunities goes back to the school’s founding in 1905, when the co-educational Melbourne Continuation School opened in Spring Street, offering students the opportunity for education past year 8. When the boys split off in 1927 to attend what would become Melbourne High School, the girls stayed behind in a dilapidated building.



By 1930, the Spring Street building would be condemned, forcing the girls to move first to Government House, and three years later shuffled off to King Street. A landmark gift helped secure the school’s permanent home footsteps away from Albert Park. Confectionery mogul Macpherson Robertson, who invented the Cherry Ripe and Freddo Frog, donated £100,000 to mark the state’s centenary in 1934, with £40,000 earmarked for a dedicated girls’ school. It was named in his honour. Sophia Ao attended the school and now tutors other girls, like Li, hoping to gain admission. Now studying a law and commerce degree at Monash University, Ao credits the school with her success and resilience.



She notes the increase in numbers of students who want to prepare for the entrance exam, with some starting up to a year in advance. Many of those who attended Mac.Rob’s say it provided them with a life-changing experience and lifelong connections. Its alumni include Miles Franklin-shortlisted author Alice Pung, historian and writer Clare Wright, OAM, technology entrepreneur and 1998 Young Australian of the Year Tan Le and opera soprano Antoinette Halloran. Lauren Solly, president of The Palladians Association alumni group, says an unspoken connection exists between women when they find out they both attended Mac.Rob’s.



“We know how rewarding, but also how tough, it can be at times as a Mac.Rob’s student,” she explains. “As graduates we get it and can be the safe space, the supportive ear, the mentor, the coach, the guide, the words of wisdom and encouragement.” Related Article Victorian election Coalition promises new select-entry schools in shake-up for gifted students The HR professional says leadership programs at the school helped her forge a successful career, and she wanted to give back. “As much as the students are looking to alumni for inspiration for their future paths, the students are just as inspiring for us as alumni. It’s really purposeful work,” Solly says. She says the network helped to give genuine feedback and support.



“So we can all put our best selves forward and thrive based on our merits and strengths – that’s the stuff that sticks in the long run.” The future of Mac.Rob’s and the state’s other select-entry schools may hinge on the result of November’s state election. The opposition has made an election pledge to build three additional select-entry high schools in the outer suburbs and convert six more to focus on gifted students. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson says: “Thousands of students sit the select-entry school exam every year and too many of them are missing out because there are not enough places. A government I lead will expand opportunities for students and parents from across Victoria to access select-entry schools.” Education Minister Gabrielle Williams says the plan was unrealistic for the $150 million pledge.



She warned that under the Liberals’ plan, existing year 9 students at converted schools would have to leave if they didn’t pass a test. The minister did not respond to questions by The Age about whether she would consider land acquisition for MacRob’s or pledging more money to update infrastructure. World.title: Damned if you work, damned if you retire: The Baby Boomers stuck in a Catch-22
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Over the two decades from 2003 to 2023, retirement rates among 65- to 69-year-old Australians plunged significantly, with women’s numbers dropping from 86 per cent to 66 per cent and men’s falling from 73 per cent to 61 per cent, according to the University of Melbourne’s most recent Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) survey findings.

Newbegin is part of a fast-growing club of older Australians delaying retirement well beyond the expected finishing line of 67. Today, more than 760,000 Australians over 65 are in the workforce, the highest level since Australian Bureau of Statistics’ tracking began in 1995. “Twenty years ago, one in 10 men were working at age 70; today it’s one in four,” says Terry Rawnsley, director of planning and infrastructure economics at KPMG.

Between five kids, nine grandkids, and his wife Jenny – who’s still powering through full-time work as a medical receptionist at 65 – Newbegin appears to be hardwired for perpetual motion (“my dad worked ’til he was 75,” he shrugs). Forget fine dining, Pacific cruises or the latest high-tech baubles; the four motorbikes he dotes on like prized thoroughbreds are his single indulgence.

“Fixing an old hardwood roof gives you a real sense of satisfaction,” he beams. “These new radiata pine ones? You can bounce up and down on ’em.”

Clocking in at 2.30pm for an eight-hour shift at the cannery is merely the second act of Newbegin’s working day. He’s already hammered out a full morning of roofing – a trade he’s been toiling at since age 17. Amid a tradie shortage, he’s in constant demand, particularly for his repair work on old-school hardwood rafters, which he says modern materials can’t match.

Theo Newbegin cuts a wiry silhouette striding between towers of peaches and pears in the echoing vastness of the SPC canning factory in Victoria’s Shepparton. Newbegin’s weathered face and long, white beard may bear witness to his 67 years, but once he jumps behind the wheel of a forklift and whips around a labyrinth of palettes, readying them for loading onto a truck, the decades melt away. His right knee might bark at him occasionally, but his lightning-fast reflexes put younger workers to shame. “I don’t feel any different to how I was in my 40s,” he grins. “People ask if I go to the gym.”

All of which has done nothing to dent the national sport of Boomer-bashing. It kicked off a few years back when Gen Z provocateurs leveraged the catchphrase “OK, Boomer” to slap down anything they pinned as peak smugness by their elders.

For 75-year-old Brisbane-based educator Margaret Harrington, teaching has been a passion for more than 45 years – and something she continues out of a deep love for the calling rather than financial necessity. When she was made redundant from classroom teaching a decade ago, her students refused to let her go, telling her, “We know where you live and will come to you” – and she’s continuing to tutor privately from her home.

For Shane Scully, 67, renting in Sydney while raising two teenage daughters makes working a financial necessity. “I don’t have an option. I need to keep working,” he says flatly. Yet, Scully, who designs outdoor classrooms and sensory gardens for public schools and special education units, finds his work deeply rewarding: “Turning a barren space into something that brings joy to the kids ... this makes it all worthwhile.”

For Anne Drane, a property manager for a real estate agency in south-western Sydney’s Liverpool, working three days a week is necessary to cover soaring private health insurance premiums and medical costs for a lung condition. But she also loves her job, and completed a financial counselling certificate only four years ago. “I like to keep busy, and also want to be able to afford to travel,” the 78-year-old enthuses.

Marion Wales, 78, says she still works as a dental nurse as she has to support her 81-year-old husband, and “the pension isn’t covering our bills.”

For Marion Wales, a 78-year-old dental nurse in Moss Vale in NSW, it’s the fact her superannuation coffers are running low, and she has an 81-year-old husband with limited mobility to support. “I can’t retire now because the pension isn’t covering our bills, and we don’t have enough in the super kitty,” she says. “I also want to have a decent life.”

Why are Australians staying on the clock? Although many remain in the workforce seeking purpose and social connection, the underlying driver for most is just to pay the bills. Rawnsley reckons something bigger is brewing – a shift in how we actually see retirement.

If you imagine most Boomers accumulated massive super payouts by the time they reached their 60s, think again. Super didn’t even exist until July 1992, when early Boomers were already in their 40s. Even then, it kicked off at just 3 per cent of earnings before taking more than a decade to crawl up to 9 per cent (it’s now 12 per cent). Without a place to call your own or a fat super nest egg to pay the rent, retirement in a pricey capital city with no income coming in apart from the government pension can be a fast track to poverty.

While at least 66 per cent of retirees own their homes outright, HILDA reports, an increasing number of younger ones – so-called “Generation Jones” (those born between 1954 and 1965) – are more likely to be still shackled to a mortgage. Vanguard’s 2026 How Australia Retires report found 24 per cent of Baby Boomers now expect to retire with a mortgage.

The lucky generation? Sure, for the top tier of older Baby Boomers, the 20 per cent who control most of the overall wealth of their generation, but there is a vast and frequently overlooked gulf between the haves and have-nots. The Baby Boomers most at risk of financial stress are the “forever renters”, those locked out of home ownership and battling rental increases of nearly 40 per cent in real terms since the early 2000s, according to HILDA .

Boomers, so the resentment story goes, hit the historical jackpot: dirt-cheap houses, free uni degrees, careers so stable they’d bore – or bring – a young gig economy worker to tears, and plump super payouts. And to top it all off, these silver-haired fat cats retired early, slapped a “SKI” (spend the kids’ inheritance) sticker on their shiny new LandCruiser, and flipped the bird at the young-uns as they hit the open road. What a bunch of self-serving parasites, right?

Boomer-bashing has turned into a minor publishing industry in recent years: from highbrow US takedowns like A Generation of Sociopaths by Bruce Cannon Gibney, and OK Boomer, Let’s Talk: How My Generation Got Left Behind , by Jill Filipovic, to Australian Fiona Wright’s satirical novel Kill Your Boomers , published earlier this year. Comedians and influencers alike have joined the pile-on, from Tom Ballard trying to turn a comedy festival crowd into a choir of Boomer-haters back in 2019 with “When the f--- are Baby Boomers going to die?” to US YouTuber Caleb Hammer griping to podcaster Joe Rogan in June that this generation “had the best housing market, college, jobs – they were set up for everything”.

While more and more older Australians are remaining in the workforce, participation rates are still below that of countries like Sweden, Japan and New Zealand, according to the OECD. And it’s been estimated by KPMG that boosting labour-force participation among experienced older workers could increase GDP by $29 billion.

Don’t assume the Boomer-bashing doesn’t have a real-life impact. Myra Hamilton recalls that after delivering a talk in which she dismantled the myth that Boomers are universally comfortable and uncaring, an older woman approached her with tears welling in her eyes. ” ‘Thank you so much,” she said. “It hurts deeply to be branded selfish. I poured my life into raising my children, worked part-time, put everything on hold to care for my ageing parents, and I’m still pushing through work every day to cover my expenses. I love my children – yet society keeps accusing my generation of stealing their future.’ ”

Patricia Sparrow, CEO of COTA (Council on the Ageing), complains there are two deeply damaging media narratives on Boomers. “They’re either living on Easy Street or they’re frail and blocking up hospital beds. Both entirely ignore the huge social contribution Boomers are making.”

Much of the current wave of Boomer-bashing comes from young privileged commentators with no clue of what working-class life was really like in the 1960s, ’70s and ’80s. In 2023, Myra Hamilton, a Millennial, co-wrote a hard-hitting op-ed for this newspaper with her father Clive Hamilton , who recently retired from Charles Sturt University as professor of Public Ethics. “We now have a cohort of younger commentators furiously mining the data and cherry-picking the numbers to find new reasons to excoriate Baby Boomers,” the pair wrote.

The new face of the housing crisis isn’t a struggling 20-something; it’s a single woman over 55 only one rental hike away from living in her car or couch-surfing. Having poured decades of sweat in and out of the workforce raising families and then caring for ageing parents, she can wind up with only a small super nest egg. “By the time they retire, Australian women typically have around one-third less superannuation than men,” notes Myra Hamilton, a sociologist at the University of Sydney. “While the super gap has narrowed in recent years, parity for women is still decades away at current rates. A quarter of grandparents – and it’s usually grandmothers – provide care for a child in a typical week, enabling their children to stay in the workforce.”

For University of Melbourne senior research fellow Dr Kyle Peyton, who is a fresh-faced 39, the most eye-opening statistic to emerge from the HILDA survey was a doubling between 2003 and 2023 in the number of retirees who are renting, now 12 per cent and rising. “The divide between Australians who own property and those who don’t is deeply concerning – not just for financial security, but for social cohesion,” he observes. “It’s a divide that exists within generations as well as between them.”

Whitegoods? In 1975, buying a $400 fridge or a $250 fully automated washing machine meant many months of disciplined saving or a dreaded lay-by: the equivalent of forking out $3500 to $4000 today. Even a humble Victa lawnmower carried the modern equivalent of a $1200 price tag. Now, a 4-stroke model is a steal for $424 at Bunnings. (It’s easy to forget how much globalisation and supply chains shifting to Asia have brought down prices.)

Home entertainment? When colour television was launched in Australia on March 1, 1975 (“C-Day”), a Baird set (remember when the Brits manufactured TVs?) cost about $1300 – a staggering $11,667 in today’s dollars. Even the cheapest portable AWA-Thorn carried a price tag of $400, or $3700 now. TVs were so punishingly expensive that for many families, like mine, owning a TV wasn’t an option – we rented one for several years. Fast-forward to 2026: you can pick up a 55-inch LED Kogan smart TV for $449: a weekend impulse buy.

The family car? A popular vehicle like a Holden Kingswood sedan automatic would set you back about $4070, or a premium Cortina XL E, $4000, nearly two-thirds the median annual salary of the time ($6448). Contrast that with today’s family-sized SUVs: an MG ZS Vibe starts at just $22,990 – a mere third of today’s median annual salary of $74,000-78,000 – with Chinese hybrids like the Chery Tiggo 4 Urban and the BYD Atto 2 DM-1 starting at under $25,000.

But life was so much cheaper back then, and everything’s outrageous today, right? Think again. For a reality check, let’s rewind to 1975, a year when the first Baby Boomers were in their late 20s, when flared jeans were de rigueur , lava lamps set the mood for disco hits like Lady Bump , and when a household purchase at a retail stalwart like Waltons or Grace Bros meant a Seriously Big Buy.

Whitlam abolished tuition fees at universities in 1974, but it was middle-class kids, not working-class youth, who took advantage of it, insists Clive Hamilton. “The idea that Baby Boomers universally benefited from free higher education is a myth; university participation rates at that time were under 15 per cent,” he tells Good Weekend .

Growing up in the decades after World War II, Boomers lived at a time of far greater austerity than today: a more threadbare welfare net, sparse workplace protections, widespread discrimination based on gender and colour, and zero universal healthcare. Gough Whitlam’s original Medibank didn’t arrive until July 1975, only to be scaled back months later when Malcolm Fraser came to power – leaving the country to wait until 1984 for Bob Hawke to finally establish the Medicare system we now take for granted.

Groceries? Staples like milk, butter, eggs and bread cost way less now than in 1975 when adjusted for wages; chicken is much cheaper, red meat pricier, and while ice-cream and biscuits are cheaper, they’ve suffered shrinkflation (here’s looking at mini you, Chocolate Montes and Cornettos). Some items, such as washing powder, are marginally more expensive, but the prices of all plastic consumer goods (Glad Bags, Tupperware) have plummeted. Economists today may sweat over an inflation rate of 4 per cent, but in 1975, it was galloping at a wallet-shredding 15 per cent. Grocery prices were moving faster than a disco beat.

Dining out? Until the 1980s, your options were milk bars, hotel dining rooms, department-store cafeterias, tearooms and a handful of cafes in Sydney’s Potts Point or Melbourne’s St Kilda. Try asking a 1975 waiter for an oat milk piccolo whatevs, or quizzing them about the “provenance” of the sirloin or whether the peas are “hyper local” or not, and they’d most likely assume you were on a bad acid trip.

Clothing? Just about every item of casual and formal wear was far more expensive in 1975, when many garments were still manufactured locally, made to last and, in many working-class families, were passed down to younger siblings. When I recall to Anne Drane that my mother, a seamstress in a shirt factory, insisted on making most of my teenage shirts, much to my annoyance, she warms to the theme (“yes, we relied on our auntie to make all our clothes”). Today we’ve traded durable, locally made craftsmanship for “fast fashion” – a relentless tsunami of ultra-cheap, synthetic junk that winds up in landfill at the end of each season.

International travel? In 1975, a standard return economy airfare from Sydney to London on a major carrier like Qantas cost about $2300 – about a third of the median annual wage. Today, a return economy airfare on Qantas for the same trip costs much the same – starting at about $2200, less than three per cent of the median annual wage. Once largely the preserve of the well-heeled, international travel has become as mundane as booking an interstate bus trip.

Margaret Betteridge, 73, who has worked as a curator at the City of Sydney for more than 30 years, recalls her first flight overseas to London in September 1975 to do a course in museum studies. “My salary was around $3000 per annum and the airfare to London cost a bit more than that,” she recalls. “Because it was so expensive, people who flew to Europe either saved up a long time, if they were young, or if they were old, tended to be very comfortable financially.”

Today’s acquisitive lifestyle, hypercharged by the internet’s endless digital bazaar, makes 1975 look positively spartan by comparison. We’re drowning in smartphones, iPads, Fitbits, Sonos, noise-cancelling headphones, flatpack furniture, disposable threads and – ugh! – plastic plants as decor. Consumerism didn’t truly hit its stride in Australia until the ’80s and ’90s, when tariff walls were brought down, ushering in the so-called “affluenza” era of cheap imports – and a mountain of landfill.

Curator Margaret Betteridge, 73, recalls that in 1975, her first flight to London cost more than her annual salary. Brent Lewin

While financial strain is very real today, and risks getting much worse because of deteriorating international conditions, decades of lifestyle creep have turned what were once luxuries into non-negotiables. We might be skint, but do we really have to ditch our cafe breakfasts or streaming subscriptions?

Today’s great expectations were noted by many of the Boomers interviewed for this story. “This need for instant gratification – ‘We’re entitled to this now’ – didn’t exist a few decades ago,” muses Drane, who recounts a childhood in south-western Sydney’s Revesby in the 1950s marked by poverty and missed meals while her mother toiled at part-time jobs and her father struggled with post-war trauma and alcoholism.

There’s no denying, though, that Boomers were blessed with a big stroke of historical luck with housing. In 1975, a Sydney home cost about $28,000 – manageable at four times the average annual income. Today, that same dream requires $1.53 million, a suffocating 16 to 18 times the median annual salary. And yes, history has been generous to Boomers in terms of building equity in bricks-and-mortar over the decades. But this doesn’t mean they gamed the system: all they did was stay in their homes while market forces over time drove values through their roof.

Today’s housing market is brutally unfair for young people, but it’s pure piffle to imagine that getting a home loan or paying a mortgage were pieces of cake in decades past. Home loan interest rates didn’t just climb in the 1970s and ’80s – they throttled the household budget, rising from 10 per cent in 1975 to a punishing 17.5 per cent by 1990.

For my own working-class parents, both of whom worked in factories from the 1950s to the 1980s, home ownership was but a distant mirage for the entire time I was growing up. When I finally managed to help them buy a home, my monthly mortgage repayments became a high-wire act across a chasm of soaring interest rates that drove me to getting a second job until they began to fall after a year or so.

Lucky for them, they had a son: back in the 1950s, ‘60s, and ’70s, a single woman applying for a housing loan might as well have asked a bank manager for the keys to the vault. Banks routinely demanded a male “financial chaperone” – a father, brother, or partner – to sign off as guarantor, assuming the little lady would eventually resign to pop out babies anyway. Just ask Drane. When she sought to buy her first home as a 25-year-old single woman in the early 1970s, she had to jump through hoops, even though she was beginning her career in the Commonwealth Bank at the time. “To be considered, I got a second job and worked seven days a week for a year to meet their strict criteria,” she says.

It wasn’t much easier 10 years later for teacher Margaret Harrington, who applied for a loan in 1983. Even with tens of thousands of dollars in the bank from her divorce settlement, her request for a modest top-up to buy an apartment fell on deaf ears. The then 30-something had to go to five different banks before finally finding a lender willing to treat her as an independent borrower. “It was a terrible experience, made worse by bank managers making sexist remarks,” she recalls.

Back then, sexism was baked into the entire workplace. Drane recalls with absolute clarity being passed over for promotion after promotion for less-qualified males during her banking career in the 1970s. It wasn’t until the banks were deregulated in the 1980s and social attitudes began to change that those roadblocks started crashing down. By 1993, Drane didn’t just walk into a bank, hat in hand for a housing loan – she was manager of a suburban branch of the St George bank.

As a single woman the early 1970s, Anne Drane had to get a second job and work seven days a week for a year to meet a bank’s home-loan criteria. Brent Lewin

Younger Boomers and Gen Xers undoubtedly profited nicely off the Howard government’s 1999 tax perks, including capital gains cuts and boosts to negative gearing, which many economists believe unintentionally drained capital away from start-ups and innovation, a regrettable shift expertly exposed in Amy Remeikis’s recent book Where it All Went Wrong. “Howard turned housing from a place to live to a source of wealth,” she writes. But if you imagine Boomers monopolise the rentals and are to blame for your latest rent hike, sneak a peek at your landlord’s ID. ATO figures show that more than 73 per cent of landlords are Gen Xers or Millennials, with Boomers holding under 27 per cent (a number that COTA insists is now much lower, and set to crater, as older people offload investment properties and pass away).

If Gen Zers imagine they’re the first generation to face a raw deal, they may draw some comfort from the fact high home-ownership rates in Australia have been the historical exception, not the rule: from Federation until World War II, barely half the nation owned the roof over their heads. And home-ownership levels have remained pretty steady over the past 50 years (68 per cent in 1975 compared with 66 per cent today), although that may be under threat in the years to come.

And don’t fall for the line – often pushed by pro-development YIMBY cheerleaders – that senior Australians are selfish for wanting to stay in the family home, where they built their lives. Look around our suburbs, and you’ll see that all too often, Granny’s big, leafy backyard is bulldozed, not for a duplex or low-rise apartments, but for a brick-veneer mansion with a small paved courtyard. Forget the modest family cottage of 1975 – a sensible 130 to 150 square metres. Today’s typical Aussie house has bloated into a monstrous brick-veneer box of between 214 to 235 square metres, bursting with cinema rooms, multiple bathrooms, and empty bedrooms galore – all built to house tiny families that are half the size of those in the 1970s.

In our rapidly ageing nation, keeping senior Australians in the workforce, particularly in critical sectors like aged care, education and health, is no longer an option but an economic necessity. “Australia is shooting itself in the foot by treating willing and capable older workers like a financial liability rather than an economic lifeline,” argues Chris Grice, CEO of National Seniors Australia.

Championing the peak body’s “Let Pensioners Work” campaign, Grice believes the system actively discourages people over retirement age from staying in the workforce. For every dollar earned above $226 a fortnight for singles, the pension is slashed by 50 cents; for couples earning above $396 a fortnight, it reduces by 25 cents in the dollar. (Centrelink’s Work Bonus helps you keep more of your pension if you meet eligibility requirements, however.) Slapping seniors with fortnightly income reporting can also be a disincentive because of all the red tape, notes Grice.

Even finding a job when aged over 55 can be a marathon. ABS data shows it takes older jobseekers an average of 20 months to land a new role after losing one – more than double the nine months for younger applicants (15 to 54). COTA’s State of the Older Nation 2025 report reveals that 38 per cent of people over 50 have experienced some form of age discrimination and one in two recruiters show little or no openness to hiring workers 65 and over. “Ageism can be a significant deterrent for seniors trying to re-enter the workforce,” says COTA’s Sparrow.

Chris Grice says that institutional ageism remains rampant in recruitment and promotion, particularly in financial services, media and some areas of hospitality and sales. AI may be a double-edged sword, he says, enabling instant screening-out of older applicants, yet also simplifying software processes and helping seniors bridge technical skill gaps.

In a basic sense, Boomers are caught in a damned-if-you-work, damned-if-you-don’t Catch-22. Stick around in the office, and you’re a job-hoarder robbing eager young things of a career ladder; retire, and you’re a freeloading burden bleeding taxpayers dry. For many manual labourers and tradies, there isn’t even a choice: decades of hard physical toil make working past their 60s virtually impossible.

Painting Australia’s 3 million Baby Boomers as a uniform group of comfortable, home-owning Anglo-Saxons ignores a far more diverse and complex reality. It erases the waves of European migrants – 2 million in total between 1945 and 1965 – who spent decades breaking their backs in low-paid factory jobs, and the Indigenous Australians who have battled racism and job discrimination for their entire lives. “Boomers aren’t a single, homogeneous group,” says Sparrow. “The rich diversity of our broader community exists across every age bracket.”

Beneath all the anti-Boomer noise lies a fundamental truth that now seems long forgotten: these old-school trailblazers forged the very social freedoms we take for granted today. This was, after all, the generation of the counter-culture, one which transformed the rights for women, gay people and, to a degree, Indigenous Australians, as well as launching the environmental movement, says Clive Hamilton, whose 2016 book, What Do We Want? The Story of Protest in Australia, traces the grassroots history of these movements – and the high price some then-young people paid for their principles (arrests, fines, legal consequences). “Let’s be clear: only between 10 and 20 per cent of Baby Boomers were active participants, but the majority of young people supported their broader aims,” he says.

Clive Hamilton: “The idea that Baby Boomers universally benefited from free higher education is a myth.” Alex Ellinghausen

To this day, surveys consistently show Boomers outperforming Millennials and Gen Z when it comes to sustainable habits like recycling and curbing waste. The bitter irony? Many of the hard-won environmental protections and equal rights agendas that Boomers fought for are now under assault from populist demagogues – US President Donald Trump, the UK’s Reform leader Nigel Farage, One Nation’s Pauline Hanson – whose reactionary rhetoric is supercharged by social media algorithms.

A landmark University of Melbourne study recently exposed a dark rise in misogynistic attitudes in Australian classrooms: nearly a third of teenage boys believe gender equality has gone too far, with one in four agreeing violence is a fair response to feminism. It’s a sad spectre: impressionable young blokes taking life lessons from manosphere hucksters like brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate, now languishing on remand in a Miami, Florida prison, fighting extradition to the UK for charges of rape and human trafficking. (At his Miami bust, Andrew Tate looked less like a badass and more like a dancer at a Barry Manilow tribute, sporting an unbuttoned purple silk shirt, skin-tight Capri pants and pointed loafers, for which social media roasted him into oblivion.)

“If the Tate brothers had arrived in the 1960s and 1970s, they’d have been laughed off the stage,” chuckles Clive Hamilton. “The crowd would have been shouting, ‘Get off, you fools.’ The Tates are a reactionary backlash to the rights that Boomer women – and men – fought so hard to build.”

The young blokes pining for the good ol’ days of strict gender roles and “trad” wives remain amusingly blind to the crushing financial pressures placed on men of that era as sole breadwinners – and the battle-hardened grit of the women, forged by survival instincts in a man’s world (a theme vividly captured in Dorothy Hewett’s 1959 novel Bobbin Up). Had they been transplanted back to the factory floor of the 1950s and ’60s, these young keyboard warriors typing outrage from their family bedrooms would have been chewed up and spat out before smoko.

Besides, younger people can’t take much of the high ground with Boomers, when they’re about to become beneficiaries of their largesse. The country’s much-heralded, mega financial handover from Boomers to Gen Xers and Millennials is rapidly accelerating, notes KPMG’s Terry Rawnsley, as Boomers sell off larger homes, bankroll their offspring’s property ambitions and prepare to pass over a mammoth $3.5 trillion in the coming years.

Some weeks after our interview, Shane Scully messages me. He’d just been admitted to hospital for an angiogram, where doctors discovered an artery that was 95 per cent blocked. Surgeons inserted a large stent in the nick of time – dodging what cardiologists ominously call the “widowmaker”.

After the near-fatal scare, Scully was back at work within just over a week. He’s been prescribed meds and advised to walk more and adhere to a stricter diet, but the new regimen has inconveniently coincided with one of the most frantic times in his business.

For many working Boomers, the real daily grind isn’t the job itself but rather, looking after your health. “It’s a bitch getting old, I tell you,” reflects Scully.

World.title: Fetu Samoa win praise despite loss
World.content:
Fetu Samoa won praise from their Australian counterparts despite Friday night's 40-0 loss to the defending champions in their opening pool game at the Rugby League World Cup.

Despite losing the game, the Annetta Nu'ualusala captained side out on an impressive defensive show in the second half, spoiling the Jillaroos plans a number of times.

Aussie skipper Isabelle Kelly said Samoa were impressive in the second half, saying it was a tough outing.

"I would like to congratulate Samoa," she said.

Kelly said their opponents were tough in the second half and fought hard all the way.

Australia had led 28-0 at half-time but only managed to get 12 points in the second spell of 40 minutes.

Fetu Samoa captain Nu'ualusala said they knew Australia was going to be tough.

"Yeah we knew coming into this game that the Jillaroos were going to give it to us," she said post-match.

"They took it out the last few years as well as the last world cup for a reason.

"You know they the pinnacle of women's rugby league internationally, so we knew it was going to be tough."

And she thanked the fans who backed them last night.

"You know our supporters pick us up when we needed it, especially that back to back defense in that last bit," she said.

"We are really, really grateful for them."

Samoa turned their defensive game on in the second spell and thwarted a number of possible Australian tries.

Winger, 18-year-old Freedom Crichton Ropati was a star, making two big tackles late in the half to stop Australia's attacking opportunities.

Australia looked great in patches, a bit stilted in others, but clear winners in the end.

Earlier in the evening, Toa Samoa kicked off the Pacific Islands teams' appearance at the world meet with a big 78-4 win over France.

Port Moresby will host both Papua New Guinea's matches on Saturday.

The PNG Orchids will meet France in the women's competition, followed by the PNG Kumuls taking on Lebanon in the men's.

Tonga will kick off their campaign against England later Saturday night in Perth.

Fiji will be the last island teams to play in round one, with the women's Bulikula team facing New Zealand, while the Fiji Bati tackle Cook Islands.

World.title: Christopher Luxon says his government has 'certainly strengthened healthcare' - has it really?
World.content:
There's nothing like the worst flu outbreak in 10 years to test the mettle of the health system - and to test the prime minister's claim it's in better shape than three years ago.

In August, when Christopher Luxon survived his second leadership coup attempt he delivered a one minute speech including a line that the government had "certainly strengthened healthcare".

But as nurse after nurse after patient after doctor spoke out about overloaded emergency departments and general practices this winter, at the very least the "certainly" seemed like a stretch.

Ministers and health officials repeatedly talked about the winter plan they had put in place.

That included attempting to increase access to urgent care clinics, to encourage immunisation, and to get pharmacists to take on more care.

Inside hospitals it included extra beds, and staff who could pivot to where they were needed most.

But some nurses and doctors in overwhelmed EDs said they saw no sign of the plan in action as patients piled up in public corridors, some double parked, some even waiting outside the waiting rooms.

They say what would have been most helpful was an end to Health NZ's hiring go-slow, well before flu season kicked in.

In August, when Christopher Luxon survived his second leadership coup attempt he delivered a one minute speech including a line that the government had "certainly strengthened healthcare". SANELE CHADWICK / RNZ

ED claims and what the stats say

Nationally, the latest emergency department wait figures show 76.3 percent of patients were in and out of hospital emergency departments within the target of six hours.

That is five percentage points more than the last figures under Labour's reign - in 2023. A win in the big picture.

But there are two significant caveats - the figures are from March to June 2026 so do not reflect this winter's late flu outbreak; and a breakdown by region also shows huge variations, with about half of the country's hospitals going backwards year on year.

Palmerston North's hospital has repeatedly hit the headlines for its overstretched emergency department.

The statistics back that up, with just 55 percent of patients treated in the target time - a fall on the same period last year.

The Capital and Coast health district, which includes the Wellington and Hutt Valley hospitals, was second worst on 63 percent, although had improved on the previous year.

The West Coast fared the best, with 95 percent, and South Canterbury on 93 percent.

However, complex cases from both areas would likely need to go to Christchurch Hospital for more advanced trauma care. Its six-hour clearance slipped from 80 percent to 74 in a year.

Doctors and nurses there described having so many patients being treated in corridors this winter, they had to angle park beds for the first time.

In corridors, patients did not have call buttons and often did not have monitors, making it difficult to alert staff if they needed help.

It was bright, noisy and open, with no privacy and little chance to rest.

Health Minister Simeon Brown says the improvement in the overall nationwide ED clearance rate is important because it meant more people overall were being seen on time - even if better progress was needed in some areas.

The government's focus on the target of having 95 percent of people through ED in six hours was helping, he said

"And it also highlights where further work and further investment is needed to make sure that we are seeing improvements across the country," he told RNZ.

The July to September ED statistics won't be made public until well after the election.

Health Minister Simeon Brown. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

The load grows - and the GP connection

Emergency doctors and nurses have repeatedly said they are dealing with sicker patients, with more complex conditions.

That contributed to more people turning up to EDs and could mean they had to be there longer, or were more likely to need to be admitted to a ward.

The average number of people attending an emergency department each day has grown from 3156 to 3693 in the past nine years.

There is a direct connection to general practice.

Many patients say they struggle to get in to see a GP when they need to, which meant conditions could get worse, leading in some cases to the need to go to an emergency department.

Others couldn't afford to see their local doctor but still needed care - and a hospital ED is free.

Health NZ has had to walk the tricky line this winter of discouraging those who did not need urgent help to stay away from EDs, while making sure those who really needed it were not put off.

Long time GP Rawiri McKree-Jansen said it has been a tough winter for general practice but access to family doctors appeared to be improving.

It was very patchy though, he said.

"Clearly there are some clinics that are struggling to have appointments for patients in a timely way. So, we still hear patients who join this clinic who come from other clinics where they haven't been able to get an appointment for three or more weeks," he said

The growing complexity of patients, including access to primary care, has also affected the outflow from emergency departments.

Hospitals are often clogged with older, sicker patients, meaning ED patients may wait for a long time to get a bed in a ward.

That in turn meant they were taking up space in the EDs while new patients kept coming in, and were often a big factor in overcrowding.

It meant emergency nurses were having to care for patients who should be getting their care in a ward, as well as looking after all the new people coming into the ED.

Long time GP Rawiri McKree-Jansen. Supplied / Tend

The plan for general practice

As part of the government's big push for health targets, it created a new one for primary care in June.

It wants more than 80 percent of patients to be able to get an appointment with a GP within a week.

Few patients would disagree, especially in areas where the wait could be several weeks.

GPs generally want that too but some pointed out it was not that simple.

GenPro, a group representing clinic owners, said long term relationships with family doctors and face-to-face appointments must be prioritised.

Telehealth, which had grown in the past three years, was a good innovation but should complement community care, rather than be the main source, the group said.

General practices are partially funded by the government - via Health NZ - and partly funded by the fees they charge patients.

This year, after a long negotiation general practice got a $175 million funding boost.

That meant an increase of at least 6.9 percent for most clinics, but that could be as high at 13.9 percent if they met new targets relating to immunisation, cervical screening, smoking and online booking systems.

Some GPs warned it would be easier for some clinics to hit the targets, such as those with less complex patients, making the funding inequitable.

But Brown said the funding rewards "progress" towards the targets meaning every clinic could benefit, no matter where it started from.

Despite stories from desperate patients struggling to get appointments for weeks, Brown said over this government's term there were now fewer general practices with "closed books", meaning more were taking on patients.

And online GP services were a good innovation, he said.

"It's not for everybody, but it is about saying that if you can't get in as quickly as you need, there is an alternative," Brown said.

The College of GPs said the recent improvement to funding had helped the situation of general practice - but much more was needed.

Ninety percent of medical issues were managed in in primary care, with 24m "patient contacts" a year compared with 1.4m ED visits.

Strengthening GP level care would keep patients healthier and improve the whole health system, the college said.

National's Christopher Luxon (L) and Simeon Brown at a health clinic in Auckland this week. RNZ / Tuwhenuaroa Natanahira

Health and the election

Voters are getting more worried about the state of health care.

September's Ipsos Issues Monitor, which asks New Zealanders what they think are the country's biggest issues, puts healthcare and hospitals at number two. It is trumped only by the cost of living.

Forty-four percent of people listed hospitals/health as one of their top three concerns, up from 38 percent three months earlier.

Despite Christopher Luxon's assertion that his government had "certainly strengthened healthcare", key parts of the system struggled this winter, with some emergency department staff saying it was the worst it had ever been.

After the dire conditions at North Shore Hospital's emergency department were exposed in August, the Nurses Organisation held a community meeting.

World.title: Exhibition celebrates six generations of Hetet and Te Kanawa weaving whānau
World.content:
Six generations of the Hetet and Te Kanawa weaving whānau whose work helped safeguard raranga and take it to the world stage are being celebrated in a new exhibition in Hamilton.

Rīpoi Anamata, Rīpoi Inamata brings more than 180 years of that legacy together at Te Whare Taonga o Waikato Museum and Gallery, from Mere Te Rongopāmamao Aubrey to Dame Rangimārie Hetet, Diggeress Te Kanawa and their descendants.

"We grew up with flax in the house, being in the house, and busy hands ... that was a natural thing," said Ata Te Kanawa (Ngāti Maniapoto) one of Diggeress Te Kanawa's daughters and part of the working group on this exhibition.

Ata Te Kanawa said museums had always been a familiar environment for the whānau because her mother and grandmother were always exhibiting.

"Even if we didn't quite understand what they were doing at the time, as we were growing up, certainly now, it's a real stop and take heart of the work, their dedication, their commitment, their patience, and their foresight."

Photo from the Rīpoi Anamata, Rīpoi Inamata Exhibition showing some of the cloaks made by the Te Kanawa and Hetet whānau. Supplied/Te Whare Taonga o Waikato

Te Kanawa said the theme of the exhibition was to draw a correlation between portraits and kākahu.

One of the portraits features a third-and fourth-generation mokopuna wearing korowai woven for tamariki by their kuia, Dame Rangimārie Hetet.

Te Kanawa said it was based on a portrait of their kuia and her older sister at 16 and 18 years old respectively.

"Both of them [the mokopuna] go to a wharekura, both have got reo, they're very strong, they're very assertive, and we wanted to capture that. So we kind of coach them to have a resting face, to own the space, to own who they are, as opposed to portraying them to be delicate, sweet, smiling petals, of which they are not."

Photo from the Ripoi Anamata, Ripoi Inamata Exhibition showing a close up of the cloaks. Supplied/Te Whare Taonga o Waikato

There were over 25 kākahu in the exhibition from across the generations of the whānau. Ata Te Kanawa said that included one made from dingo by a niece in Australia and one gifted to opera singer Kiri Te Kanawa.

Ata Te Kanawa recalled a fundraiser at the whānau homestead to raise money for Kiri to go to London for training.

"My sister and I, we can remember hiding under the piano or near the piano with our fingers and in our ears, because no one in the room had ever experienced opera singing before. So that was kind of funny, everybody, all the nannies nodded and smiled as if they liked it, but they probably didn't."

Photo of Hautāmiro: Bound by the Winds, an installation by the Mataaho Collective. Supplied/Te Whare Taonga o Waikato

Waikato Museum curator Maree Mills (Ngāti Tūwharetoa) told RNZ the museum had a long relationship with the whānau, with the work of Rangimārie and Digeress exhibited in the past.

"They were such committed teachers, and such committed women to continuing the craft of weaving, that in their own whānau, they've got children and grandchildren, their nieces, all still weaving and teaching weaving as well. And that's also celebrated in the exhibition."

Presented alongside the exhibition is Hautāmiro: Bound by the Winds, a monumental installation by the award winning Mataaho Collective.

World.title: 'Simply unacceptable': Charities call for sustained political action on child poverty
World.content:
Charity groups are calling for sustained action on incomes and housing to fight child poverty.

The Child Poverty Action Group (CPAG) and the New Zealand Council of Christian Social Services (NZCCSS) issued a report on child poverty on Saturday morning.

CPAG's communications manager Isaac Gunson said the charity aimed to lay bare the facts of child poverty ahead of the election.

"The number one thing any of these parties can do is just get out into their communities and see the lived reality for a lot of people.

"It's so unbelievably tight for so many families right now and we cannot keep relying on individual families to stretch and stretch and stretch to make things work."

He said National and Labour-led governments had achieved reductions in poverty, but both had also overseen increases.

"Right now, close to 170,000 tamariki in our country are going without essentials on a regular basis.

"That is simply unacceptable," he said.

The report showed material hardship had grown from a low of 11 percent in 2021/22 to 14 percent in 2024/25 - a percentage point above the 2017/18 when the Child Poverty Reduction Act was passed.

He said the main driver was incomes not keeping up with inflation.

Since 2020, the number of children living in households receiving a main benefit rose by 17 percent, according to the report.

"On top of that, you add a housing crisis, you add disability allowances, which have not kept pace with inflation. All these things add up and over time they have just pushed more and more children into the toughest and most unthinkable circumstances."

He said child poverty was a "political choice".

Child Poverty Reduction Minister Louise Upston. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"When serious action is taken on incomes and on welfare to make sure that all children are living in households where they're not having to try so hard to make ends meet, we've seen child poverty rates come down.

"The evidence is really, really clear and no government should be making children suffer for the decisions that their parents make through benefit sanctions."

In August, CPAG released its manifesto, outlining steps to reduce child poverty through cross-party collaboration.

It included calls for an increase to minimum wage, more housing and better access to services such as education and healthcare.

NZCCSS also made policy recommendations, advocating for a Poverty Reduction Act, improvements to the welfare system, tackling rising food costs, and better access to housing and jobs.

Child Poverty Reduction Minister Louise Upston said: "Every child in New Zealand should go to bed safe, well and knowing how loved they are."

She said more work was needed to reduce child material hardship.

World.title: Law and order has entered the election 2026 chat
World.content:
Analysis - In a neck-and-neck election campaign there's no greater gift for a political party than an unforced error by the opposing team.

Enter the Green Party and its monumental brainfade this week to not only attend an election hui with patched gang members, but to pose for photos with them.

Mongrel Mob lifetime member Harry Tam proceeded to post the photos on social media on Tuesday afternoon, which caught the attention of the National Party and sent it into overdrive.

By Wednesday morning Te Pāti Māori MP Oriini Kaipara had also shared the photos of herself along with her colleague Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke and Greens' Hūhana Lyndon and Michel Mulipola at the whānau, health, and wellbeing election hui.

Law and order is not a feature of this election campaign - in the most recent Ipsos Issues Monitor in September it was ranked the eighth most important issue facing New Zealanders.

That's a far cry from June 2023 when Labour was last in government, and Chris Hipkins was prime minister, and fear about rising crime hit a record high - the number two issue facing voters in New Zealand.

Labour's Chris Hipkins. NZME / Dean Purcell

Law and order has long been a weak spot for Labour and a strength for National, which put a lot of time and resource into reducing youth crime and victimisations in the past three years.

The problem for National is law and order is only useful for the party when it's in a bad state and bothering enough people to warrant tackling it.

Because there currently isn't a problem, or not one big enough to be in the top five issues, there's no airtime on it for the governing party.

At least that was the case until the Greens propelled it back into the headlines this week and then co-leader Marama Davidson doubled down.

Greens co-leader Marama Davidson. RNZ / NICK MONRO

Labour doesn't want to be dragged into talking about law and order because it's not its natural home.

Cost of living and health is primarily the focus of the Opposition this election campaign and that sharp focus has been working for Labour.

In the past 48 hours it has been able to point to cancer treatment for children at Starship Hospital being delayed due to staffing shortages as evidence National isn't on top of healthcare.

The uncomfortable coverage of Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and Health Minister Simeon Brown on the election campaign in Auckland this week facing questions about young children missing out on chemotherapy because of well established gaps in the staffing roster was a bleak watch.

Never in more need of a lifeline, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori were happy to step up to the plate.

Behind the scenes some in the Green Party believe engagement with marginalised communities, including gangs, is important work but can't believe Lyndon and Mulipola didn't have the political radar to say no to photos.

While National is pushing the message that no MP should ever engage with gang members who "peddle misery" it's less about the meeting and more about the chummy photos that were circulated.

Ministers and MPs across the political divide visit prisons and come across people who have committed crimes in their day-to-day electorate work, whom they have a duty and obligation to listen to and at times offer help.

But they don't take photos smiling side-by-side giving the thumbs up and post it on the internet for all to see.

They especially don't do it three weeks out from an election that is very much on a knife-edge.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon. NZME / Dean Purcell

A large chunk of middle New Zealand have no time for gangs or any of their behaviour, but that's not where the Green and Te Pāti Māori vote largely comes from.

However, the increasing fragmentation in the political system has seen the Greens rise from a 10 percent party to a 15 percent one in the most recent 1News-Verian poll.

That extra five percent almost certainly includes some soft centre-left voters, who may have previously voted Labour, but are looking for something different in an election that is seeing the major parties bleeding votes.

There's a chance the Greens suffer as a result of the intense public scrutiny in the past week.

Equally there's a chance Labour pay the price and lose voters who can't stomach the idea of a coalition with a party like the Greens, which not only condones but doubles down on socialising with patched gang members.

It's that threat which prompted Hipkins to so swiftly rule out any Green MP holding a police or corrections ministerial warrant in a government he leads.

The National Party machine is already pushing out plenty of "don't risk it" messaging about a Labour-led government with the Greens and Te Pāti Māori calling the shots on the economy.

World.title: Recap: Rugby League World Cup: Fetū Samoa v Jillaroos
World.content:
Australia's Jillaroos have proved too strong for Fetū Samoa in the women's Rugby League World Cup.

Australia ran in seven tries for a 40-0 victory in Sydney on Friday night.

But it was not entirely one-way traffic as Fetū Samoa put up a noteworthy defensive effort.

Earlier in the night, Toa Samoa had started their campaign with a hiss and a roar, beating France 78 - 4.

World.title: Toa Samoa give France a thrashing in World Cup opener
World.content:
Samoa kicked off their 2026 Rugby League World Cup campaign with a strong 78-4 win over France at the CommBank Stadium in Sydney on Friday night.

Toa Samoa scored 14 tries in the process, four through replacement winger Sualauvi Fa'alogo, and 22 points through the boots of Stephen Crichton, who kicked 11 goals.

Toa Samoa players showed a lot of emotions as their national anthem was sung and the Siva Tau battle challenge was laid down before kick-off.

And it took them just three minutes to get on the board with Deine Mariner running untouched out wide as the French defensive pattern was left wanting.

In the end the Blues of Samoa showed their fans and the world they are serious contenders, even though France was not as strong as many would have hoped for.

Co-captain and hard running forward Junior Paulo thanked the fans after the game, adding they are the reason the players do what they do.

"It's awesome to see the way they turn up," Paulo told Seven post match.

"It means everything to us.

"This is the reason why we play for our nation. To turn up here and see the crowd it means the world to us.

"We gotta dig deep out there; they are the reason."

Head coach Ben Gardiner told the players at halftime they needed to hang on to the ball longer, after their play had dropped heading into the last 10 minutes of the first 40.

Toa Samoa led 18-0 by the 10th minute mark, with two more touchdowns through Benaiah Ioelu in the sixth minute and Jermaine McEwen, in the eighth, as the team dominated play early.

Crichton kicked all three conversions for the 18-0 lead.

In the end they ran up 13 tries, with replacement winger Sualauvi Fa'alogo claiming four on the night.

Fa'alogo replaced Mariner early in the first half after the first try-scorer of the night had to leave the field after he pulled his hamstring.

Luai, Chanel Harris-Tavita, Tabuai-Fidow, Brian To'o and Crichton combined to run hard against the French.

Up front, co-captain Paulo, Connelly Lemuelu, Jermaine McEwen and Francis Manuleleua were on fire, gaining valuable yards and territory every time they had the ball in hand.

Luai was the mastermind, with Harris-Tavita being the other option to command play.

Fa'alogo claimed his first try in Toa Samoa colours after the 10th minute before Tabuai-Fidow got his name on the score sheet.

France had their first visit into the Samoan territory in the 23rd minute but dummy-half Benjamin Garcia passed the ball forward 10 metres from the Samoan line and gave away the team's first real momentum.

But they got their first points on the board when Garcia sent the ball right close to the Samoan line, which saw Louis Grossemy finishing with a try in the corner in the 24th minute.

That was after a good defensive set inside their own 20-metre line won them a penalty and the ensuing sets saw them get a second penalty 10 metres out from the Samoan tryline.

The try seemed to have lifted the French, as they forced the Samoans into errors and put them under pressure a few times.

That also saw a drop in the Samoans' game as they dropped passes and knocked the ball on a few times.

Fa'alogo grabbed his second try in the 37th minute after some straight-up-the-middle runs by the forwards and Crichton slammed his conversion from out wide through the uprights, sending Samoa into a 34-4 lead at halftime.

The second 40

Gardiner's pep talk at halftime fired the Samoans back into action in the second spell.

He told Seven before resumption of play that the side needed to keep the ball and work on their game.

The team responded.

Crichton got Samoa's seventh try, two and half minutes after the restart, before Francis Manuleleua got his name on the board too.

Fa'alogo got Samoa's ninth try and his third for the night, running on to another Luai long pass, with 15 minutes to go, before adding his fourth some minutes later.

Warriors playmaker Tavita was on hand to touch down between the posts after another Luai show of his deft footwork, before centre Izack Tago managed to get a try to his name with eight minutes to go, with Crichton adding his ninth conversion, as Samoa went further up to 66-4.

Big forward Francis Molo, who previously played for the Cook Islands, powered his way over the French line for Samoa's 70th point in the game.

Crichton kicked his 10th conversion, and Samoa went up 72-4.

It was Ioelu who scored Samoa's 14th try in the dying seconds of the game after he jumped high to collect the ball that had bounced off the upright, from Crichton's attempted penalty kick.

World.title: Employment Court ruling over Calendar Girls sets 'important precedent' for country, dancers say
World.content:
An Employment Court decision regarding a Wellington strip club has set an important precedent for the entire country's adult entertainment industry, the dancers who pursued the case say.

This week, the Employment Court ruled that five dancers were employees of Calendar Girls when they worked at its Wellington club, not contractors.

The dancers took an employment case against the chain of adult venues after being effectively fired for challenging changes to their work conditions.

Cherida Fraser, from the Aotearoa Sex Workers Collective, told RNZ's Checkpoint the dancers had been handed a contract on a work night that reduced their proportion of fees, while also increasing the overall fees.

"They grouped together to address it and engage in good faith with the club and wrote their letter and tried to get a meeting with them," Fraser said.

"But this was denied and they were just terminated immediately, which was grossly unjust.

"They lost their livelihoods overnight when they were actually just trying to engage in good faith."

During a hearing earlier this year, the dancers argued they were effectively being treated as employees, not contractors.

In its ruling, the court highlighted the level of control Calendar Girls had over the dancers, with numerous restrictions in place.

"The way they performed and the services that were on offer, they weren't able to choose how much they charged for the services they offered on top of the baseline club fees," Fraser explained.

"Their attendance, their sick leave, they were expected to do regular shifts, they weren't able to take breaks when they wanted to."

Even the dancers' appearances were subject to scrutiny, Fraser said.

"Someone wanted to change their hair colour and that wasn't allowed.

"As well as that, they were restricted from working anywhere else. So there were significant trade restraints."

Audio player for " Power imbalance between Calendar Girls and dancers laid bare " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/1958957%2Femployment-court-ruling-over-calendar-girls-sets-important-precedent-for-country-dancers-say

Power imbalance between Calendar Girls and dancers laid bare Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

Financial penalties were in place for breaches of those restrictions. Dancers would be fined $200 if they stayed in changing rooms for too long, $100 for misuse of a cell phone, and $100 for wearing a g-string.

The "coercive threat of financial penalty" was outrageous, Fraser said.

She said the women felt energised by the Employment Court's ruling that they were employees, not contractors.

"And deservedly, this doesn't happen without personal cost to them," Fraser told RNZ's Checkpoint.

The women had shown "absolute fortitude" by putting their lives on hold to pursue the case, Fraser said.

She shared a statement from the dancers, where they said they were proud to have stuck it out and received some hard-earned closure.

"We're even more proud to have played a part in something much bigger than ourselves.

"We believe this judgment sets an important precedent for the adult entertainment industry on the whole."

Fraser said the ruling meant the dancers could now be compensated for unfair dismissal.

She said the decision would put other clubs on notice to treat their workers better.

"I think this is a very strong signal to the clubs to ensure that the contracts and the practices that go with those contracts are truly independent.

World.title: Jillaroos flex muscle in 40-point World Cup win over Samoa
World.content:
Australia's quest for a fourth consecutive Women's Rugby League World Cup has started with a bang courtesy of a 40-0 victory over Fetu Samoa.

Unbackable favourites leading into the tournament opener, the Jillaroos overcame an ill-disciplined opening 10 minutes to shut out Samoa in the seven-try rout.

Things were far from easy for Australia in the second half, but the damage was already done by half-time, with five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher and reigning Dally M medallist Tamika Upton leading the way with two try assists apiece.

Kelleher, making her Jillaroos debut, was named player of the match, where she was dangerous in attack and her kicking game troubled Samoa.

Speaking to ABC Sport, Kelleher said she had been waiting a long time for her chance to play for the Jillaroos.

"It's a dream come true," she said.

"Was in the squad last year, but got my debut jersey this year. So excited and so happy to be here."

Despite the 40-point win, it was far from a perfect performance from the reigning world champions.

"We still have a lot of things to fix from today. It wasn't perfect out there," Kelleher said.

Samoa, in their first World Cup since 2008, had several chances early but lacked the class to capitalise against their much-fancied opponents.

Gold Coast Titans star Jaime Chapman ended her three-year Jillaroos exodus by scoring Australia's first try in the 11th minute, beating opposite winger Freedom Crichton Ropati out wide.

Australia's greatest ever try-scorer, Julia Robinson, lived up to her reputation seven minutes later when she beat three would-be defenders for her 23rd Jillaroos try in 14 appearances.

Tries to back-rower Shaylee Bent and hooker Keeley Nizza followed in quick succession before lock Olivia Kernick crossed moments before halftime to seal a 28-0 lead at the break.

Kernick turned playmaker in the opening five minutes of the second period when she handed the ball off for Keilee Joseph to extend the Jillaroos' lead.

Brave defence might have turned the tide for Samoa, who ground their way to more opportunities at the Jillaroos end over the final 25 minutes.

Prop Laikha Clarke went the closest to securing some consolation points for Samoa, but was ruled to have dropped the ball over the line.

Of further concern for Samoa was a suspected knee injury in the dying stages to centre Sarina Masaga.

A try in the final two minutes from Australian centre Jessica Sergis capped the Jillaroos' victory and extended their almost three-year unbeaten run.

Samoa's men thrashed France in the opening match of the day, putting on a record score to win 78-4.

World.title: PNG Chiefs to go ahead with NRL logo launch after court decision
World.content:
New Zealand's High Court has knocked back an application for an interim injunction on the PNG Chiefs NRL franchise using its name in the country.

New Zealand Rugby (NZR) had rushed to court before the PNG team's logo and jersey reveal in Port Moresby next week.

The organisation claimed use of the Chiefs name, which is also the name of the long-standing Super Rugby Pacific outfit, would cause confusion and damage to the brand.

But a judge at today's two-hour Wellington hearing turned down the application after hearing an injunction could harm the NRL expansion outfit's efforts to attract players ahead of a 2028 debut.

"The PNG Chiefs welcome today's decision in the New Zealand High Court and look forward to the launch of our inaugural logo and supporter jersey in Port Moresby on Wednesday,," PNG Chiefs CEO Lorna McPherson said.

NZ Rugby to protect 'Chiefs' name New Zealand Rugby has sought interim and final injunctions before the NRL's Papua New Guinea team is officially launched later this month.

"As the matter remains before the court, no further comment on this matter will be provided at this time."

The dispute continues, with an application for a final injunction still before the court and legal action in Australia under consideration.

ARLC executive chairman Peter V'landys last week labelled NZR's action one of "mind-blowing hypocrisy", using the example of the Auckland Blues' arrival decades after NSW "had been the Blues".

"Today's decision is not a judgment on the strength of our case and the matter will still be heard in full," NZR boss Steve Lancaster said.

"As the trademark holder, our responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand hasn't changed. We remain open to working with the ARLC on a solution."

NZR's lawyer Earl Gray argued today that the PNG Chiefs' use of "PNG Chiefs" and "Chiefs" interchangeably created confusion for fans of both codes and that, with no clear distinction between the two, it would strip the rugby Chiefs of brand exclusivity.

He said NZR had trademark protections for the Chiefs in New Zealand that the NRL had not acknowledged.

ARLC lawyer Clive Elliot argued that the request for an urgent injunction, about a year after NZR became aware of the PNG Chiefs name, was not appropriate.

He said an injunction now would cloud the franchise's reputation ahead of a recruitment blitz once free agency opened next month.
