World.title: Surgery giving Kiwis hope of Ponga playing again in World Cup
World.content:
Kalyn Ponga will undergo surgery on his broken arm but will remain in camp, with New Zealand not giving up on the superstar fullback playing again in the Rugby League World Cup.

Ponga failed to finish his long-awaited Test debut for the Kiwis, departing in the 70th minute of the 24-22 loss after suffering the injury earlier in the second half.

Receiving clearance earlier this year to switch his allegiance to New Zealand, Ponga delivered a stand-out performance at Western Sydney Stadium as his side fell to Australia in the Thursday night thriller.

The Newcastle skipper scored two tries while running 253 metres from 16 runs, making three line breaks and five tackle breaks.

He has been booked in for surgery after breaking the radius in his left arm but Kiwis team doctor Greg Macleod sounded hopeful about the prospect of Ponga playing again through the tournament.

Australia's dominance looms over World Cup Ahead of the women's Rugby League World Cup, the dominance of the Jillaroos looms like a spectre.

"We wish Kalyn all the best with his surgery today," Macleod said in a statement.

"We'll see how that goes but for now he will remain in camp."

The 28-year-old is viewed as critical to the New Zealand's hopes of claiming their first World Cup since 2008.

Coach Stacey Jones, whose side will face the Cook Islands in Christchurch next week before wrapping up their group stages matches against Fiji, said Ponga had played through pain.

"He couldn't catch a ball or anything like that. He was in a bit of discomfort," Jones said.

Ponga was replaced by Keano Kini as he trudged off late in the match and was seen on the sidelines with his arm in a sling.

"He's obviously disappointed, but there's a bit of upbeat about him too. He really wants to still be involved," Jones said.

If New Zealand decide Ponga's tournament is over, the Kiwis have the option to ask for clearance to add an additional player to their squad.

"He's a tough guy and obviously has a lot of pride in the black and white jersey, and he doesn't want to let his teammates down," Kiwis captain James Fisher-Harris said.

"I thought he did an outstanding job. He's a freakish player, but he's also one of those tough players. We're feeling for him right now, but fingers crossed it's not too bad."

Jones said Kini would likely replace Ponga in next week's pool match.

The Kiwis' narrow loss to Australia was one that will burn Jones for a while.

Two of the Kangaroos' five tries were the result of interceptions and another two were from kicks.

The Kiwis dominated territory but lacked the polish to make Australia pay for their mistakes.

"Unfortunately, we were on the losing side, but we will learn from it, and we will get better and we will make some adjustments," Jones said.

"You go in that changing room and everyone's down, they're hurting.

"But you just bounce back and you get back into it. We know these boys, they work hard, they're professional. We'll be OK"

World.title: Carlton suspends defender over high-range drink-driving charge
World.content:
Carlton has suspended defender Wade Derksen for drink driving on an off-season trip, allegedly blowing more than three times the legal limit.

The Blues suspended Derksen for all preseason games and up to round three of the AFL season next year.

The 25-year-old was charged with high-range drink-driving in Jabiru in the Northern Territory.

Derksen failed a roadside breath test late last month, allegedly returning a reading of 0.174.

Police said his licence was suspended and his case will be heard in court in the Northern Territory next month.

Cowan suspended by AFL The AFL hands down its sanction to Lachie Cowan following an investigation into his use of an illicit substance last weekend.

"While we acknowledge the upcoming legal process will carry its own penalty, Wade's conduct falls well below the standards we expect," Carlton general manager of football Chris Davies said.

"Wade is fully aware how disappointed we are in what occurred. We will continue to support him throughout this period as he takes full responsibility for his actions."

Derksen joined Carlton at the start of the season after GWS de-listed him at the end of last year.

He played 15 games for the Blues this season.

The AFL announced earlier today that Carlton's Lachie Cowan had been suspended for two games after an investigation into his use of an illicit substance last weekend.

World.title: Tahiti police gather evidence after pro surfer suspended over alleged incident
World.content:
Police in French Polynesia are gathering evidence following an alleged incident in Tahiti that has led world surf bodies to suspend a professional surfer from competitions.

Both the International Surfing Association (ISA) and World Surf League (WSL) announced this week they had suspended a male competitor after learning of the "serious" allegations.

Neither organisation has identified the suspended surfer, and the ABC has not independently verified their identity.

The Outerknown Tahiti Pro attracts international professional surfers. (AFP: Jerome Brouillet)

The WSL said the alleged incident happened at a private gathering in Tahiti in August, which was not affiliated with the organisation.

Surfing World magazine, which reported the suspension this week, said it understood the alleged incident occurred at a party after the final day of the Outerknown Tahiti Pro surfing event.

The alleged incident involved a teenage Australian female surfer and at least three men, it reported.

"[Surfing World] understands that NSW police have been advised of the allegations and have been in contact with surfing authorities," it reported.

However, Australian and French Polynesian police appear at odds regarding who has jurisdiction over the matter.

The ABC understands law enforcement officials in Tahiti believe they do not have jurisdiction, because the alleged victim reported their complaint to police in Australia.

It is also understood that local police in French Polynesia are now gathering evidence relating to the alleged incident to have ready for Australian law enforcement, but are yet to receive a formal request for information.

The World Surf League said its discipline committee suspended the professional competitor. (AFP: Martin Bureau)

NSW Police has declined to comment on the matter, saying that French Polynesian police have jurisdiction and carriage of the investigation.

The Australian Federal Police also said enquiries should be directed to local authorities.

'Serious allegations of abuse'

The ISA on Thursday said it had decided to provisionally suspend the professional surfer from "ISA-sanctioned" events "pending further investigation and review".

"The International Surfing Association is deeply concerned by recent reports of serious allegations of abuse within the surfing community," it said in a written statement on Thursday.

"This precautionary decision has been taken in the interest of athlete safety and welfare, and does not constitute a determination of wrongdoing.

"The ISA remains committed to respecting due process, confidentiality, and the rights of all individuals concerned.

" The ISA firmly believes that all athletes have the right to participate in sport in a safe and respectful environment, free from harassment, violence and abuse of any kind. "

The WSL, which was first to suspend the surfer, on Sunday said it had suspended a surfer on the 2026 Men's Championship Tour after it was made aware of "allegations of a deeply serious nature involving the competitor".

It said it had offered to assist relevant authorities.

World.title: Teen killed in cricketing tragedy 'died by misadventure', coroner finds
World.content:
The grieving family of a 17-year-old boy who died in a cricketing tragedy say they are relieved a coroner will not recommend changes to the rules of the game their son loved.

Ben Austin was hit in the neck by a ball thrown with a side arm device while practising in the nets at Wally Tew Reserve in Ferntree Gully, in Melbourne's outer east, in October last year.

Cricket authorities confirmed at the time he was wearing a helmet but not a stem guard, which protects the neck.

Ben later died at the Monash Children's Hospital.

Coroner Simon McGregor on Friday confirmed the 17-year-old died as a result of misadventure by well-meaning young people using proper equipment at a "caring, well-run club".

Ben's parents Tracey and Jace wiped away tears as the facts were read at a directions hearing in the Coroners Court of Victoria, with legal teams for Cricket Australia and Cricket Victoria also present.

Jace and Tracey Austin speak to media outside the Coroners Court of Victoria. (ABC News)

The coroner confirmed no adverse comments would be made about anyone's behaviour and "no individuals or organisations contributed to the cause of Ben's death".

He added that no recommendations or comments about rule changes would be made, paving the way for the summer cricket season to continue "in the normal way".

The coroner proposed commending the fact that some clubs and leagues had made safety changes without waiting to be told, with one bringing in neck guards and another banning the use of side arms.

But he said there was still some misunderstanding about individual clubs' ability to make safety changes, with some under the mistaken impression authorities would tell them what to do in response to safety issues.

The coroner is considering making a comment about the governance structure and how safety and best practice messages are conveyed.

The teenager's death shocked Ferntree Gully and the wider Melbourne cricket community. (ABC News)

Speaking after the hearing, Jace Austin said the lack of adverse findings and rule changes were exactly what Ben would have wanted.

"There's no way we want to change this great game," he said.

"But on the other hand, we don't want another Benny or Phil [Hughes, who died in similar circumstances in 2014].

"From what we've heard, it's exactly what we wanted."

With the anniversary of Ben's death nearing, he said the family would be coming together to reflect.

"Every day's tough, but when this comes to an end, this will be Benny's full stop, so you sort of want it to drag out."

"Every day's brutal to be honest."

Tracey Austin wore a necklace bearing her son's name.

"I've got him close to my heart," she said.

Jace and Tracey Austin say their family will be coming together to reflect on Ben's death. (ABC News: Wayne Hammond)

Cricket Victoria's Nick Cummins said the organisation would work through the coroner's initial comments and later findings.

"What we didn't want to do is go out and start finding solutions before we understood the coroner's findings," he said.

"Cricket is a safe sport. It's always been a safe sport. We have measures in place to make sure that's the case.

"But it's always important to have an open inquiry around incidents like this."

Cricket Victoria chief executive Nick Cummins attended the hearing on Friday. (ABC News)

He said the cricketing community had come together after Ben's death, with the Austin family raising $180,000 at a fundraiser last week.

"It's been incredibly heartening to see how cricket brings people together," he said.

The coroner's formal findings will be handed down before Christmas.

World.title: Cowan handed AFL suspension following illicit substance investigation
World.content:
The AFL has suspended Carlton's Lachie Cowan for two matches following an investigation into his use of an illicit substance last weekend.

The league said "the circumstances in which the matter subsequently became public" were also the subject of the investigation.

Cowan was found guilty of conduct unbecoming.

He will be suspended for the first two home-and-away matches of the 2027 season and issued with a $5,000 fine.

Two Carlton AFL players hospitalised in Melbourne The club has confirmed Lachie Cowan and Will Hayward have been admitted to hospital under separate circumstances.

No action was taken against Cowan's Blues teammate Will Hayward, who was also admitted to hospital on Sunday due to a separate incident.

Cowan's sanction was handed down as the AFL confirmed its new illicit drugs policy would come into effect in January.

The league said all players would be hair tested upon their return to training in January, "with readings going as far back as three to six months prior".

Cown said he should not have put himself "in such a vulnerable situation".

"I want to apologise for the impact my actions have had on my family and the football club," Cowan said in a Carlton statement.

"I also want to thank the medical professionals who helped me on the night, the football club for their ongoing support and everyone who took the time to reach out and make sure I was okay.

"This is a wake-up call and I am just so grateful to now be in a position to learn from this."

The AFL Players' Association (AFLPA) released a statement in the wake of the AFL handing down its suspension.

"This has become a public matter because private information regarding players seeking medical treatment has been shared," AFLPA chief executive James Gallagher said in the statement.

"That is unacceptable."

Gallagher said Cowan's suspension could discourage players from seeking emergency medical assistance.

"We don't want players using illicit substances and that is why the [AFL's] illicit drugs policy is so important, with its overarching purpose to change behaviour and minimise harm," he said.

"However, it is contrary to this health and wellbeing model to sanction players after they have sought medical treatment, particularly in an emergency.

"As an industry, we need to encourage help-seeking behaviour, not penalise or disincentivise it."

The Blues said Cowan's wellbeing remained the club's priority.

"Most importantly we are thankful that Lachie is okay and received the medical attention he needed," Carlton general manager of football Chris Davies said.

"We have been in regular contact with Lachie this week and he has taken ownership of his mistake.

"Lachie understands that it is his responsibility to ensure he makes better decisions moving forward."

Lachie Cowan issued an apology via the Carlton Football Club. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

Cowan will be required to undertake further education above the current mandated training on illicit substances and their effects.

The league said the matter would "constitute a notifiable adverse finding under the AFL's illicit drugs policy".

"AFL players have a responsibility to themselves and their professional careers to uphold community expectations," AFL chief operating officer Tom Harley said in a league statement.

"They are well-educated when it comes to the harms associated with the use of illicit substances.

"Lachlan admitted his mistake and understands he must be accountable for his actions."

World.title: Supercars to return to Phillip Island, plugging hole left by MotoGP exit
World.content:
Supercars will return to Phillip Island next year, helping plug an economic gap left by MotoGP's move to Adelaide.

Victorian Major Events Minister Anthony Carbines today announced a five-year deal to host a Supercars Championship final series round.

It will be the first time since 2019 that the island has hosted Supercars.

"We know Supercars fans are wrapped with this news. We know our drivers are wrapped because they love Phillip Island, they love the circuit and they can't wait," Mr Carbines said.

"It was critical that we got back out there and made sure we locked in something that was going to make a big difference to the community of Phillip Island and the vast coast, but also to bring Supercars back to the Island."

Phillip Island will host its final MotoGP from October 23 to 25.

The track has hosted the event since 1989, but lost it to South Australia after the Victorian government rejected a request to move it from Phillip Island to Melbourne's Albert Park.

It later lost the Australian round of the FIM Superbike World Championships, which will be held on Phillip Island for the last time in 2027.

The loss of the two events has created anxiety in the local business community, which relies heavily on event-driven tourism.

Local tourism body Destination Phillip Island says racing is worth $80 million to the local economy.

Phillip Island will host a Festival of Motoring in March next year, with Labor and the Coalition both promising to back the event.

Opposition major events spokesperson David Southwick today said the Coalition would provide $100,000 to fund the event if it wins November's state election.

Victorian opposition major events spokesperson David Southwick and Bass Liberal candidate Rochelle Halstead say the Coalition will back a motoring festival on Phillip Island. (ABC Gippsland: Madeleine Stuchbery)

"We know the government has announced supercars today from Federation Square," Mr Southwick said on Phillip Island.

"They don't care about Bass Coast, they don't care about the island.

"We're here today because we care and we know it all starts with homegrown events."

Motorsport central to Phillip Island

President of the Association of Motoring Clubs Keith Mortimer said motoring culture connected many people to Phillip Island.

He said the goal for the next 12 months was to ensure the first motoring festival's success and make sure the event "is here to stay".

He said motorsport, whether it's bikes, classic cars, or Supercars, connected many visitors to the island.

Keith Mortimer says motorsport connects many visitors to Phillip Island. (ABC Gippsland: Madeleine Stuchbery)

"There are some wonderful things to see here, around Churchill Island, around the chocolate factories, around the local produce," Mr Mortimer said.

"It really does have something for everyone."

Destination Phillip Island chief executive Kim Storey said one in four jobs on the island were connected to the visitor economy.

She said the five-year commitment will boost confidence in local accommodation, hospitality, retail and tourism.

"Supercars represents meaningful progress towards rebuilding major event visitation," she said.

"There is still important work ahead to replace lost demand across the year and support the broader economic transition facing Phillip Island and San Remo."

Tech.title: Why Apple is finally making its own smart home devices
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

For more than a decade, Apple has told other companies to build smart home devices for its platform. This week, Apple launched its own. The Apple Home Collection is a lineup of cameras, thermostats, sensors, a smart door lock, and a video doorbell, all codeveloped with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. They arrive alongside HomeView, Apple’s first smart display.

Even after 12 years of HomeKit, Apple’s smart home ecosystem still feels underdeveloped, especially compared to the competition. Amazon’s and Google’s ecosystems support more products, and both have popular in-house brands: Ring and Nest. Apple had nothing of its own to point customers to as an Apple experience — and now it does.

But why now? And does Apple actually add anything new here, or is this mostly packaging? At Apple’s “Welcome home” event in New York this week, I spoke with Kaiann Drance, vice president of product marketing for home at Apple, about the company’s new approach to the smart home and what this means for Apple’s commitment to Matter, the interoperable open smart home standard it helped found.

Apple’s HomeView is viewed as a gateway to bring people into the smart home. Photo by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Why now?

Drance says the big reason was the development of the right technologies. The first was Matter, which provided the ecosystem. The second was AI, which brought a more conversational Siri voice assistant. Both were necessary to create a dedicated home device in HomeView. “With the magic of Siri AI, it comes together in a way that we haven’t been able to deliver before,” Drance says. “That’s been a really critical piece of bringing this all together.”

The bigger play is HomeView as a gateway to the smart home.

The bigger play here is HomeView as a gateway to the smart home for Apple’s users. Buy one for playing music, guided cooking recipes, and checking your calendar, and you might soon want a camera or smart lock to go with it. Drance says they’ve seen that once people try a single smart device and find it easier than they expected, it “unlocks this delightful understanding of what’s possible once you bring these products into the home.” She argues that most people just don’t know what a smart home can do.

She’s not wrong. The biggest barrier to buying smart devices is that people don’t see any value in the products, according to research from Parks Associates. Privacy and security concerns and complexity also rank high, along with cost. While Apple isn’t addressing the cost concern here — the products start at $200 — the other elements are part of its pitch: one-tap setup, your data stays yours, one app to run it all. Apple’s stamp of approval also carries a lot of weight. “People who own Apple products are very, very loyal, and there is a large user base,” says Elizabeth Parks, president and CMO at Parks Associates.

Several Apple Home Collection products: LG smart door lock, indoor camera and video doorbell, and a Schneider Electric thermostat.

From a choose-your-own adventure to a tailored solution

Until now, Apple Home has been a bit like a buffet: You can pick from any brand that supports HomeKit or Matter and hope it all goes together. The Home Collection is more like the chef’s choice, a short list of dishes Apple promises will pair well. Drance says that’s what some customers were asking for. “There is a lot of choice with Matter, and there’s a lot of great products out there,” she says. “But sometimes we do get asked, ‘Hey, what product should I put in the home?’”

“Sometimes we do get asked, ‘Hey, what product should I put in the home?’” — Kaiann Drance, Apple

Rather than build devices itself, Apple chose to codevelop the lineup with partners that “have their own expertise in the home.” Both have a global footprint and home experience, she says, “LG more so in consumer products, Schneider through home build and home installations.” Drance says it was a ground-up collaboration with Apple bringing “the design aesthetic that would be suitable for the home and suitable to go with our family of products.” The company is also partnering with ADT through Apple retail stores to help people install the devices.

Drance says setup and ease of use were a big focus. “The one-tap setup was really important to make it so easy, having no need for a separate account, no need for a separate app,” she says. “We just wanted that simplicity to be at its core, and of course, the privacy that we’ve developed together with our partners.” She says everything integrates through Apple Home; you don’t need to create an LG or Schneider account, and all data is end-to-end encrypted, so only you can access it.

Drance was clear that the Apple Home Collection isn’t replacing the buffet — the hardware ecosystem that has grown up around Apple Home. “We still have this incredible ecosystem with Matter, and with Works with Apple Home, that is going to remain,” she says. “We know that homes are not a one-size-fits-all solution, so our customers will continue to have that choice, and we remain committed to building that ecosystem as well.”

The hardware mostly backs that up. The lock, thermostats, and sensors are Matter-compatible; the lock supports Aliro and works entirely locally, and every device supports Thread. The exception is the cameras, which use Apple’s HomeKit Secure Video, not Matter. That’s the biggest lock-in. I was surprised Apple didn’t announce Matter camera support. But the Thread radios suggest the hardware might be Matter-ready, and Apple may be waiting for the Matter camera standard to support encrypted uploads, something HKSV already does.

So, what’s the benefit?

Does the Home Collection do anything other Apple Home devices can’t? In theory, no; in practice, yes. “What we’ve done with Apple Home Collection is we’ve added another layer on top of that, that deeper integration,” says Drance. There aren’t features exclusive to the Home Collection; it’s more that Apple is saying all the features will be here. It’s a bit like Google making a Pixel phone to show Android developers what Android can do: Apple’s products come with the full suite of capabilities the platform offers. At least that’s the promise. We’ll have to test these devices to see how well they deliver.

“The one-tap setup was really important to make it so easy, having no need for a separate account, no need for a separate app.” — Kaiann Drance, Apple

According to Apple, setup is as simple as tapping your iPhone to the device, like pairing AirPods, with no extra account or app needed and no scanning required. Every device uses Thread to stay connected if Wi-Fi drops, and Apple says each can update its own network credentials when you change your Wi-Fi. This could address the offline-device problems that plague Apple Home. Everything is end-to-end encrypted, and the cameras keep recording to onboard storage if your Wi-Fi drops.

The devices also support Apple Home features other manufacturers have been slow to adopt. The LG lock is only the third to offer hands-free Home Key unlocking over UWB, and both thermostats work with Apple’s Clean Energy Guidance and Adaptive Temperature, which adjusts around your location and sleep schedule.

The LG door lock and video doorbell pair in the Apple Home app so you can unlock the door when you see who is at the door.

A curated garden path

Together, Apple’s new devices form a polished, cohesive starter kit for the smart home — albeit an expensive one. The cameras, lock, and thermostats cost $200 to $400, and camera history requires an iCloud Plus plan. As Drance said, the smart home isn’t a one-size-fits-all solution, so this won’t work for everybody. If you already have a Ring doorbell or Google Nest Hub, this probably isn’t for you. Instead, Apple is trying to guide its existing customers who haven’t bought a video doorbell or smart lock yet down a curated path into the smart home.

However, Apple faces a tougher challenge in the broader market: It’s arriving late. The smart display category is already mature; millions of homes have Echo and Google smart displays. Millions more have Ring or Nest doorbells, neither of which will work with HomeView at launch.

As a smart home platform, Apple Home ranks third in adoption, behind Google, with Amazon holding a big lead, according to Parks Associates research. But customer loyalty to those platforms isn’t guaranteed. Four in five smart-home households would consider switching, Parks says, especially if another platform lets them control everything in one place. “Interoperability will be critical, but the bigger prize is owning the consumer relationship,” she says.

With its Home Collection, Apple isn’t reinventing the smart home; it’s trying to make it easier to get into one.

Tech.title: The new Apple TV 4K just got its first (very small) discount
Tech.content:
Earlier this week, Apple announced its new Apple TV 4K, which costs nearly twice as much as the 2022 model did at launch. Amazon is now offering the first discount on the forthcoming streaming box (coming out on November 13th), just days after discounting Apple’s new smart display for the first time. Right now, you can preorder the latest Apple TV 4K ahead of its November 13th release date for $289.99 ($9 off) at Amazon. Yes, it’s a tiny discount, but every little bit helps given the higher price tag.

Powered by the new A19 chip, Apple’s latest streaming device now features support for Siri AI out of the box, which is coming to older Apple TV 4K models via a software update. Unlike its predecessors, though, the new model features far-field microphones so you can quickly make hands-free requests. You can, for example, ask for recommendations, like nature documentaries available on Apple TV, or ask questions about what you’re watching. Siri AI can also understand personal context, too, so long as you have an iPhone or iPad connected to your account that supports Apple Intelligence.

Apple has made a few other welcome upgrades, though — as my colleague John Higgins points out — not as many as some may have expected. While Apple skipped features we’d hope to see on a $300 streamer, like audio passthrough and support for 120fps output, it’s nice that the Siri Remote now supports Find My precision tracking, so you can make it ring when it goes missing or use the Find My app on your iPhone to pinpoint its location. The new Apple TV 4K also supports a more expansive surround-sound setup, allowing you to pair up to four compatible HomePod speakers instead of just two.

Tech.title: Apple’s HomeView has an app problem
Tech.content:
It’s been a couple of days since Apple’s big smart home announcement, and we have some more information — and a bunch of new questions — about the Apple HomeView. The device has plenty of computing oomph, is always connected to power, and looks like a perfect place to run a bunch of apps. And yet the HomeView is relying almost entirely on CarPlay. What gives here?

On this episode of The Vergecast, David and Nilay try to make sense of the HomeView’s app situation, and why Apple would choose not to make its home hub into its own app platform. After that, they talk about the latest Gemini model and whether building the best model matters if you can’t build the best products around it. They then debate the merits of returning to X, why none of the supposed Twitter replacements worked, the latest in Brendan Carr nonsense, and much more.

In case you missed it this week: We also talked about the rest of the HomeView launch news, the first big AI slop case, and how to live in a world filled with recording devices. And we want to hear all your thoughts about all of it! Call the Vergecast Hotline at 866-VERGE11, send us an email at vergecast@theverge.com, and tell us everything that’s on your mind. And make sure you subscribe so you don’t miss an episode!

Tech.title: Analogue is re-releasing its SNES and Genesis consoles with some nice upgrades
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Analogue announced new versions of its Super Nt and Mega Sg retro consoles today with a “reworked industrial design” and built-in wireless connectivity for controllers and accessories. Like the original versions, the new Super Nt Plus and Mega Sg Plus are able to play Nintendo and Sega Genesis cartridges using an FPGA processor that perfectly recreates the functionality of Nintendo and Sega’s 16-bit consoles without the need for emulation.

Although neither of the new consoles allows SNES or Genesis titles to be played in 4K like the Analogue 3D does with Nintendo 64 titles, the 1080p Super Nt and Mega Sg Plus add a USB-C port so you can power them with the cables you already use with your phone and mobile devices, and an additional USB-A port for other peripherals. Both consoles also introduce a built-in Bluetooth or a low-latency 2.4Ghz wireless connection for connecting to gamepads without requiring an additional controller port dongle.

Despite their redesigns, both upgraded consoles look very similar to the original versions that launched in 2017 and 2018. Image: Analogue

Wired controllers are still an option, and the upgraded consoles can both be powered up remotely using whatever gamepad is connected as the primary controller. Analogue also says game cartridges can now be hot swapped without having to completely power down either console after quitting the game through a menu.

Both the Super Nt Plus and Mega Sg Plus will be available for preorder starting on October 19th at 9AM PT/11AM ET for $219.99 with shipping expected to start sometime in December, later this year.

Tech.title: A fake WhatsApp clone is showing up before the real version on the Play Store
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

After a Chrome clone was spotted on the Play Store earlier this week, a user on Reddit says they’re seeing a fake version of WhatsApp in a “sponsored” slot above the real version. As reported earlier by Android Authority, the WhatsApp dupe has racked up over 500,000 downloads and, at the time of writing, its Play Store listing is still live.

Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The WhatsApp clone is from a developer going by “Agment Assets sallu” who doesn’t currently have anything else listed on the Play Store. Their listing for the WhatsApp impostor has the same icon, screenshots, and text as the real version, but the real WhatsApp has over 10 billion downloads, an “editor’s choice” badge, and over 246 million reviews. Android Authority points out that the WhatsApp clone may be using Google Play’s Early Access program to disable public user reviews, which could have helped users warn people against downloading the app.

Tech.title: A week with RTX Spark: everything we’ve learned using Nvidia’s new laptops
Tech.content:
Nvidia’s RTX Spark N1X processor is finally here, and we’ve been collectively testing a small fortune’s worth of powerful laptops sporting this new “superchip.” RTX Spark is designed to be a high-performing Arm-based SoC for laptops and small desktop computers, rivaling the best from Apple, Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm. It has loads of cores, Nvidia RTX Blackwell graphics, and enough power and unified memory to run sizable local AI models.

The flagship placement is inside Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra with a staggering 128GB of unified memory, which our own Tom Warren fully reviewed. Sean Hollister has been testing a 64GB version of the Asus ProArt P16, which I’ve also been testing in its top-spec 128GB config. Since I’m the most spoiled of the lot, I also have a 64GB Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 and a 32GB HP OmniBook Ultra in for testing.

All of these laptops have the same N1X chip with 20 CPU cores and 6,144 GPU CUDA cores, and they’re all wildly expensive — ranging from the HP OmniBook at $3,199.99 to the Asus ProArt’s $6,999.99. There’s an 18-core / 5,120 CUDA N1X chip in lower cost configs, but that only gets as cheap as $2,599.99 for a Surface Laptop Ultra or a smaller Asus ProArt P14 with 24GB of RAM.

These are big and expensive laptops built on new chips. They’re meant for developers, coders, and content creators who might also want the ability to use local AI and even play games using the latest Nvidia tech like DLSS 5. There’s a lot to test, and we have not had a ton of time to test it all. So below you won’t find an exhaustive scored review of any one laptop, but instead our impressions and thoughts from three writers using five laptops for a week.

Is Nvidia’s “superchip” really all that super? Are Apple, Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm officially on notice? Have any of us gotten any sleep?

Does it just work?

A laptop costing $7,000 better just work, and work well. Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

Antonio Di Benedetto: Windows on Arm is no longer a wholly subpar experience like it was a few years ago. Thanks in large part to the push around Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X chips, lots of development has been put into native Arm-based apps for Windows. And many x86 apps work fine via Microsoft’s Prism emulation layer.

Adobe has had native Arm versions of Photoshop and Premiere for some time now, and even though my precious Lightroom Classic is still an x86-based app I don’t notice any issues using it on Arm. At this point, you’ve gotta be relying on specialized software that’s exclusively x86 based for Windows on Arm to be a non-starter — or you want to freely play any games out there without any worry of incompatibilities.

Sean Hollister: Every so often, there’s that moment when an app takes longer to load than it should, and I wonder whether it’ll load at all. Even then, it typically loads. Occasionally, it takes more than one try. My Evernote notes disappeared a few times one day when I alt-tabbed away, but a force refresh fixed that. And apps don’t seem to respect my system preference for dark mode.

But I largely agree with Antonio. I made an RTX Spark my daily driver, with all my typical work and personal apps — Signal, Discord, Audacity, CapCut and Evernote, Irfanview, Slack, ScreenToGif and more — and nothing has failed me so far. I never once needed to think whether I was running an Arm or an x86 app. The real hitches came with gaming and AI, as you’ll read below.

Tom Warren: I’ve been using a Windows on Arm laptop with a Qualcomm chip daily for the past two years and things have improved to the point that I can’t tell if an app is native or not anymore. That’s the same story on the RTX Spark laptops, and I feel like Nvidia’s entry into this category will only improve the story for creative apps and gaming.

Can it game?

Gears of War: E-Day running on the Surface Laptop Ultra during a Microsoft demo. Photo: Meron Menghistab

TW: Windows on Arm never looked like a serious gaming platform before now. While there still aren’t many native Arm games, Nvidia’s GPU helps bruteforce through the emulation layer. Your mileage in gaming is going to vary depending on the title, but for the most part I’ve found that medium settings, running at 1440p and DLSS performance, will get you to a stable 60fps in most games.

I mostly game on my desktop, where I’m spoiled by using an RTX 5090 on a 32-inch 4K screen every day with maxed-out game settings, but I didn’t mind the look of medium settings on a 15-inch display. I was able to run Black Myth: Wukong at 70fps on average at native resolution (3270 x 2180) with medium settings and DLSS performance mode enabled. I ran the same medium settings and DLSS performance in Cyberpunk 2077 and averaged 66fps, and Forza Horizon 6 managed an average of 57fps.

In some titles you may need to drop the resolution or settings lower, though. This definitely isn’t as good as a dedicated gaming laptop, but for something that’s roughly on the level of a MacBook Pro it’s more than good enough for gaming on the go.

SH: Like Tom says, the GPU power is there — but the CPU might hold back some of your games. I had plenty of power for a smooth 60fps in Returnal (at 1440p with high settings), Expedition 33 (at a DLSS “Performance” upscaled 1200p with high settings), Jedi Survivor (DLSS “Performance” upscaled 1200p with medium settings), and Shadow of the Tomb Raider (at native 1800p and highest spec).

But when I fired up Helldivers 2, even dipping down to a DLSS-upscaled 1080p was no guarantee of 60fps in the highest difficulty missions. There are just too many enemies on screen for the Spark to keep up. Star Wars Zero Company is even more CPU-bound — the Spark didn’t care whether I was maximizing or minimizing the graphics and screen resolution. No matter what I tried, I typically saw my framerate capped between 37fps and 39fps in battle.

Even ancient and low-powered games can have quirks. I tried the 2003 title Max Payne 2 and saw situations where framerate dipped to 50fps. I even saw a few hitches in the excellent UFO 50, a collection of 2D games, though a couple other 2D games ran great.

I’m also not sure if RTX Spark is suitable for VR yet. The excellent Titanfall 2 VR mod worked, and it seemed to run fine at first, but lost a little stability after a few minutes. That could be my Wi-Fi, because the driver for Valve’s Steam Frame wireless adapter wouldn’t install on the Spark. Neither did Steam’s streaming audio solution, so the audio came out of the Nvidia laptop instead of the headset.

Just so we’re clear, all of this is assuming you want a laptop maxing out its fans and positively dumping heat on your desk or lap. That’s not unusual for thin gaming notebooks, but it’s way louder and hotter than a good desktop or handheld.

2560x1600 2560x1600 2560x1600 2560x1600 Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark (20-core, 6144 CUDA, 128GB RAM) HP OmniBook Ultra RTX Spark (20-core, 6144 CUDA, 32GB RAM) Framework Laptop 16 5070 (2025, 8GB VRAM) MacBook Pro M5 Max Black Myth: Wukong TSR 27 27 28 Not compatible Black Myth: Wukong DLSS 41 44 45 Not compatible Black Myth: Wukong DLSS FG 53 59 71 Not compatible Cyberpunk 2077 Ultra 41 46 57 56 Cyberpunk 2077 Ultra RT & DLSS quality 30 35 44 42 (MetalFX Quality) Cyberpunk 2077 Ultra RT & DLSS Frame Gen x2 53 56 68 75 (MetalFX Quality, FSR 3.1 FG) Cyberpunk 2077 Ultra RT & DLSS Frame Gen x4 92 103 Not tested Not compatible Average FPS results in gaming benchmarks we ran on the Asus ProArt P16 and HP OmniBook Ultra, against an RTX 5070 Laptop GPU and M5 Max MacBook Pro.

AD: I’ve wanted a MacBook Pro-like laptop with full PC gaming chops for as long as I can remember, so I was hyped for these laptops to deliver the goods in graphics. The first night, I set up the Asus ProArt P16, with all 128GB of its ridiculously large pool of memory, and when I booted up Big Walk for my planned online evening with some friends my first thought was, “Well, that looks okay. I guess.” I know Big Walk isn’t some triple-A graphical titan, but it has some fairly demanding graphics for the “friend slop” genre. I expected the N1X to max it out, or at least get close, but not really.

I had to bump the P16’s 4K display down to 2560 x 1600, and instead of Big Walk’s Highest or Very high graphics presets, I brought it down to High to maintain a decently solid 60-ish fps. Does any of that really matter for this silly co-op game about solving puzzles with your buddies? Of course not. It looked fine, after all. But it was a sobering reminder that this “superchip” is no graphical magician.

As Tom and Sean point out, RTX Spark can do some decent gaming, but temper your expectations for medium or even low settings in some cases, and be ready to rely on DLSS and frame gen. There’s no denying that cheaper desktops and even laptops with discrete Nvidia graphics cards can easily beat out an N1X. Nvidia claims it’s like having an RTX 5070 Laptop GPU in an SoC, but in my testing it was somewhere between that and an RTX 5060 Laptop GPU — not a slouch, for sure, but if you’re a gamer first your money goes much further with traditional Nvidia graphics cards.

How’s the battery life?

Sadly, only Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra has that slick magnetic USB-C charging. Photo: Meron Menghistab

SH: Nvidia’s partners saw fit to equip their first wave of RTX Spark laptops with some of the biggest batteries you can bring on an airplane with no questions asked — but even with a 99.9 watt-hour pack like the one in my Asus ProArt P16, these laptops won’t be winning awards for longevity. While Tom and Antonio spent their days testing every use case under the sun, I made the P16 my daily driver for normal work while watching the battery meter like a hawk. That mostly means writing stories in a web browser, and it’s not quite lasting the day.

My best run was 5 hours and 40 minutes of real-world work at 50 percent brightness, including an hour-long video call with Tom and Antonio to strategize our RTX Spark coverage plan. The next day, I got only about 5 hours from a full charge because I spent two of them editing this video in Capcut. The third time I drained the battery, it took 5 hours, too.

With web work, I’m typically seeing 13-17 watt battery drain on the laptop’s default settings, but that climbs to 20-30 watts with light video work, up to 50 watts during the (brief) Capcut video export, and I made it jump all the way to 120 watts playing Indiana Jones and the Great Circle. The battery couldn’t keep feeding at that rate — it slowly went down, and at 30 percent charge I saw a big performance hit as it dropped dramatically to 60 watts.

The good news is the Asus charges fast from a 140W USB-C PD power source. It took 20 minutes to go from dead to 50 percent battery, another 15 minutes to get to 70 percent, and a total of 1 hour, 15 minutes to reach 95 percent charge.

AD: I’ve had to run lots of benchmarks while plugged in, so I haven’t been able to spend as much time testing battery life as I’d normally like. Anecdotally, in lots of fits and starts, battery life seems solid. As Sean saw, you’re unlikely to get through a full eight hour work day unless you’re going out of your way to be efficient. And if you fire up anything heavy, like a local AI model (more on that in a minute), you won’t even make it to lunch. I’ll eventually do more thorough battery testing as I continue using these laptops, including our usual rundown tests for a bit of 1:1 comparisons.

Does local AI seem useful?

A local AI model running on a Surface Laptop Ultra. Photo: Meron Menghistab

TW: Not yet. It all feels like a beta aimed at developers right now: from the install experience of AI agents flashing up command prompts and Visual Studio, to the fans blasting away for the most basic of queries.

I struggled to come up with many compelling use cases for the power of these chips for local AI work. A lot of tasks could simply be done far more quickly and without the laptop fans spinning up by using a free cloud model. The power here is really in leaving the agent running at full throttle to build something overnight, running tasks that developers would favor.

It’s also nice to have this all on a local device, without having to share emails and files with a cloud service and worry about the privacy aspects. Still, I would regularly close OpenClaw or Hermes and not let them run in the background all day, especially if I had given them permissions to access local files. I’m just not ready to trust AI fully, local or not.

Microsoft and Nvidia both envision a future where AI agents automate things on your PC, but I’m still not fully convinced. While there are some mundane tasks I could certainly automate, I like using my PC to edit photos or videos, write, and play games. I don’t want to sit there and watch a robot do all of that for me. That’s part of the joy of computing to me.

SH: I walked out of Nvidia’s Editor’s Day thinking I might finally have a reason to fire up local AI. I asked Hermes, running Qwen3.8-27B, to build me a daily news briefing much like the one in Nvidia’s on-stage demo. It took 10 minutes, and 10 percent of my entire 99.9 watt-hour battery, to finally produce a list of stories that took the cloud-based Claude (Opus 5.5) half as long — while utterly monopolizing my GPU and dramatically heating up the Spark laptop. The laptop stayed hot and a little sluggish as long as I kept Hermes open.

Claude also produced better results, with more detail and better sourcing. I guess I got the local AI tokens for “free,” I wouldn’t trust Claude with my email, and I probably could have used a smaller, lighter model. But I went with what the program recommended, and that was the result. I tried a clean reinstall of Hermes to make sure it wasn’t a misconfiguration, but this time, the prompt took even longer and used 60 percent of my battery. Ouch.

Previous Next

1 / 2 Seems easy enough to get these product images edited by a local model, right?

AD: I’m still early in my journey of learning to use local AI, and these RTX Spark laptops are obviously a viable — albeit, expensive — option. But even if you have 128GB of memory to use some chunky models, it’s still not a user-friendly experience for beginners. Microsoft’s Get Started intro in Windows 11 gives you easy one-click installs for Hermes Agent, OpenClaw, and Perplexity. (Which all have ESRB ratings for some reason?) But after that, you’re kind of on your own. I stuck with Hermes, since that’s what I was already using on the Mac Studio, but if you’re using it on a system with 32GB of RAM or less it just tells you there isn’t enough memory for its recommended local Qwen models — either routing you towards the cloud or fully relying on you to go fetch a smaller model on your own.

Using local AI has major privacy advantages over cloud models, but it’s definitely less convenient since local LLMs are much slower to process and more taxing on your system. Churning a local model through your laptop’s memory tears through any of these laptops’ large batteries, and the results from LLMs are still mixed. I burned through 30 percent of the Lenovo Yoga 9n’s battery in 36 minutes to get a Qwen 3.8 27B model to resize and add a white background to five product images in PNG format — and it cropped the images wrong and cut off the products. I got it to do it right after a couple follow-up prompts, and grabbing the power cable to prevent Hermes from killing the laptop in the process.

Is the hardware truly great?

Previous Next













1 / 8 The HP is a little hefty, but boy does it look and feel fantastic. Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

AD: These laptops are very expensive, but that also means the manufacturers are mostly bringing their A-games. Across the Asus, HP, Lenovo, and what I gathered from Tom’s thoughts on the Surface, the RTX Spark line is awash in great-to-excellent haptic trackpads, keyboards, screens, and speakers. The metal builds of the three I’m testing feel great to the touch. The OLED displays all look fantastic. And each of these are decently thin for the kind of workstation-class laptops that they are.

If I had to pick one for myself based on hardware alone I’d probably choose the Asus ProArt. It ticks the most boxes for me with its three USB-C ports, super bright display, superior inverted-T arrow cluster, and full SD card slot. The HP actually feels the nicest, with an impressively rock-solid chassis, but at nearly five pounds it’s the heaviest of the bunch, and its microSD card slot is much less useful to me.

As for the Lenovo, it’s actually been my sleeper favorite. It’s the only 2-in-1 in this crop I’ve been testing, and that just makes it more flexible (pun intended) and fun. You can use its large stylus on either the screen or the large trackpad, giving it lots more potential for graphics and design work. And tent mode with a large 16-inch 120Hz OLED is a delight for the occasional gaming session or watching shows and movies — it’s just not as bright as the Asus.

SH: I’ve only truly driven the Asus P16 so far, but I was impressed with the build quality of the whole spectrum of RTX Spark launch laptops at Nvidia’s Editor’s Day. The Asus P16 probably wouldn’t be my pick personally because of its extra glossy screen and oversensitive touchpad. I like to use my laptops in rooms with lots of ambient light, and find I have to crank up the brightness of this machine’s otherwise excellent calibrated OLED screen. Meanwhile, my palms keep tapping my mouse cursor on things I didn’t mean to tap, just because they accidentally brush the touchpad while typing.

The speakers and webcam also leave something to be desired, but the Windows Hello face login and proximity sensing are excellent. As soon as I walk away, the screen dims, and I’m logged right back in just by looking at my laptop. Despite the heat, Asus’ fans aren’t shrill — they’re very loud and noticeable while gaming, but at least it’s whoosh rather than whine.

TW: While I ran into some weird bugs with the Surface Laptop Ultra during testing, I can’t fault the hardware. The look and feel is very similar to a MacBook Pro, and the magnetic USB-C port really feels like something Apple should have done — it’s that good. The large haptic trackpad carries on the tradition of great Surface trackpads, with the added benefit of subtle haptic feedback when you move windows around or align objects in apps like PowerPoint.

I would have preferred an OLED display on the Laptop Ultra, but I found switching away from the default “Vivid” color option to “Enhanced” improved the contrast on the mini-LED panel. I also really appreciate the port section on the Laptop Ultra, especially that there’s a full SD card reader and even a USB-A port. Check out my full review for more thoughts.

Is it fast? Does it hang with Apple M-series chips?

AD: Yes, the RTX Spark N1X is a powerful chip. These high-end laptop configurations we’ve been testing with lots of unified memory are meant to compete with the Pro and Max chips in Apple’s MacBook Pros. And while they can hang in some GPU performance tests, like tying the top spec M5 Max in a Blender render, Apple’s CPUs are much more powerful.

Apple has put lots of development into its in-house processors and the extra-fast “super cores” of its M6, M5 Pro, and M5 Max chips. And, frankly, nothing competes with those chips in single core performance — not even Nvidia’s “superchip.” (Seriously, can we stop with the word super?) But the part that stings most about the RTX Spark’s 20-core CPU is that even a lowly 12-core M6 Mac Mini competes with it in multicore performance — and a Mac Mini starts at just $900.

It’s awesome to see this kind of graphics performance without the need for a discrete GPU, allowing for thinner system designs with less noisy fans. I’m into it, just as I was with AMD’s Strix Halo APU — but like Strix Halo, Nvidia’s RTX Spark is a pricey part. And there’s no denying that Apple’s offerings are more well-rounded performers, so long as you don’t care as much about games.

TW: It’s definitely up there, but I think Qualcomm comes closer to Apple’s M-series chips on the CPU side. Qualcomm also had years of experimentation with Windows on Arm before it acquired Nuvia and managed to create a competitive chip with the Snapdragon X series.

I think Nvidia will need a similar amount of work to catch up on the CPU side for future RTX Spark chips. The development of the RTX Spark took at least three years, and I had heard from sources familiar with Nvidia’s plans that the chips were supposed to launch last year. So work has been ongoing, but the CPU side is still a little disappointing.

Nvidia picked MediaTek for its Arm-based CPU, a chipmaker that is better known for the Wi-Fi hardware in laptops, not the CPUs. I sure hope the next-generation is more powerful. The whole time I’ve been testing the Surface Laptop Ultra I couldn’t help but think the forbidden dream would be a combination of a Qualcomm CPU and Nvidia GPU. I can’t see that ever happening in reality, but it would certainly be interesting to see.

So what’s our take on RTX Spark so far?

A chip this powerful in a 2-in-1 this large, with a stylus? Nifty. Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

TW: I think it will elevate interest in Windows on Arm for creative and gaming tasks, simply because we haven’t had Arm-based Windows laptops that are really capable of running games until now. Nvidia is targeting creators and developers with its first round of RTX Spark laptops, but there’s definitely a gap here for a more affordable version focused on gaming. Perhaps that’s the N1 chips we’ve heard rumors about.

SH: Nice, but too pricey. Too hot and loud when you’re doing the things that would theoretically justify that price. I care what they stand for, and the direction they’re pointed, far more than I care to own one.

AD: I love that there is now even more competition in the laptop space, but the super high prices makes RTX Spark laptops mostly unattainable. I want to see lower cost options come around, as well as an eventual second generation with higher CPU performance to hopefully close the gap further with Apple. I also hope this helps push development for Arm-based and Arm-compatible games forward. Maybe it could even one day mean easier porting of games to macOS. Wouldn’t that be a fun outcome?

As cool as it will be to keep testing these super high-end RTX Spark models, I’m most hyped to get my hands on a base Surface Laptop Ultra or Asus ProArt P14 with 24GB of RAM and see how they stack up to the entry-level 14-inch M5 MacBook Pro. That’s my personal sweet spot for Apple’s lineup — the people’s MacBook Pro. (Well, okay, less these days now that it starts at two-grand.)

It’s an exciting time in computing when it comes to chip choice, but it’s also an absolutely cursed time thanks to RAMageddon and sky high prices. I’m constantly wondering what laptops like these RTX Sparks or even Googlebooks might have cost if AI demands didn’t drive up the prices of RAM and storage. I have no idea who is going to spend up to $7,000 on these laptops when PC sales as a whole seem on a downward trend, but it’s cool they exist.

Tech.title: The incredible flying Tesla Roadster is just for show
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Last night, Elon Musk gave the people what they want: a car driving vertically up a multi-story ramp, launching off the edge, executing a mid-air “kickflip” over a lineup of Teslas, and landing via cold-gas thrusters.

That’s what the people want, right? “We were promised flying cars,” sure, but isn’t the operative word in that statement “we”? Because as far as I can tell, everything we saw last night — while extremely cool and incredibly impressive — won’t result in a real, production-ready car you can park, or, I guess, land in your driveway.

Tesla’s late-night demonstration in Waco, Texas, certainly gave some corners of the internet what it wants. And the gushing praise and wide-eyed reactions on X, a platform already predisposed to absolving Musk of all his sins, were hard to avoid.

Previous Next









1 / 6 Image: Tesla

Taken purely as a stunt, the demo was jaw-dropping. Equipping an electric supercar with 600 liters of compressed air, 10 directional cold-gas thruster nozzles, and a 2G suction-fan system directly inspired by SpaceX is undeniably rad. Seeing a 0-to-60 mph launch in under a second pushes the absolute outer limits of physics — even if it could lead to a detached retina or two.

Yet, calling this a “car reveal” or even viewing the flying Roadster as a real product, in the sense that it can be purchased by an unaffiliated third-party for private ownership, stretches the definition beyond recognition. Tesla says the “Rocket” configuration of the Roadster, the one we saw doing all the cool shit, will be “invite only.” But even that strains credulity. That version of the Roadster removes the passenger seat to make room for the ultra-high-pressure gas tanks, and trades road practicality for short bursts of thruster-powered levitation. But where you can take your flying Tesla remains a mystery, because the company admits it won’t be approved for “public road use.”

Taken purely as a stunt, the demo was jaw-dropping.

Even for the wealthy supercar shoppers, the event offered almost nothing of substance. Tesla skipped basic commercial details like pricing or battery range specs. The Roadster’s range estimate was downgraded from 600 miles to 300 miles. And Musk casually pushed the production window out to 2028 — more than a decade after early adopters handed over $50,000 deposits.

Musk himself has acknowledged the Roadster is a “small potato” project that won’t move the needle financially compared to mass-market models like the Model Y. He also called it “the last best driver’s car,” in a nod to his belief that autonomous driving will define Tesla’s future.

Some analysts are already theorizing that the Roadster’s re-release is an attempt to set the stage for a rumored Tesla-SpaceX merger. Musk’s fans on X are practically begging for it — even though it would likely result in the dilution of their own equity. But that’s just table stakes in Musk’s quest to consolidate control of his companies.

In some sense, the car had to fly in order to make the preceding decade of missed deadlines feel worth it. Tesla has already been lapped several times in the electric hypercar market. Even some of the Roadster’s most impressive tricks have already been done. There are cars that can drive upside down, cars that can jump in the air, and cars that can accelerate very, very fast.

BYD’s Yangwang U9 Extreme uses four electric motors (one more than the Roadster) to produce an insane 3,000 horsepower for a top speed of 308mph in testing — beating Rimac’s Nevera 268mph record. And the McMurtry Spéirling single-seater holds the record for quickest acceleration from 0 to 60 mph in 1.35 seconds. The Roadster could best it, but we’ll need to wait for independent testing to confirm.

But no one puts on a show quite like Elon Musk. So if the goal is to score a PR victory, dominate social media feeds, and cement Tesla’s brand as a frontier tech pioneer, then I would say the Roadster demo was a success. Competitors like Rimac, Porsche, and BYD will continue shipping real, track-ready hypercars while Tesla spends another few years refining its rocket-boosted prototype.

It’s completely useless as a viable product. But as a 30-minute flex of engineering muscle, it was truly a sight to behold.

Tech.title: Meta’s new terms may allow it to train AI on news sites for free
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta’s new terms appear to give it permission to crawl and scrape websites “associated” with the businesses that use its platforms — including online publishers, according to a report from Nieman Lab. The new terms, which go into effect on October 30th, say Meta can use this outside content to “develop, improve, research,” and “train” its AI products.

While Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts says that the company is just “consolidating” its commercial and self-serve ad terms, legal experts tell Nieman Lab that this could allow Meta “to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions,” like a site’s robots.txt file. That could potentially allow Meta to bypass a licensing agreement and freely train its AI models on content posted by online publishers.

The new policy applies to business accounts that promote their content across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger:

You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.

Roberts pushes back on Nieman Lab’s reporting, saying “There is no change to how Meta uses web crawlers; any suggestion to the contrary is false… Content owners can still use robots.txt flags to indicate their preferences, as we clearly explain in our developer documentation.” Meta has followed OpenAI in striking AI licensing deals with CNN, Fox News, USA Today, and People Inc., but these terms could give the company access to a much broader swath of content.

“For news publishers, this clearly represents permission to Meta to train AI on any content from their sites and possibly to deploy some of that content, even in competition with the publishers themselves,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell, tells Nieman Lab.

Andy Stone, Meta’s vice president of communications, writes in a post on X that this change isn’t meant to target news sites. “This update is designed to make sure we’re able to pull accurate information about products for sale on third-party websites when making on-platform ad and content recommendations, not about scraping news sites.”

Businesses that don’t agree to Meta’s new policies “may stop all access or use of our Products for business or commercial purposes,” the terms say. Last month, Meta launched a new Meta One subscription that requires businesses and creators to pay to include links in posts and reels. “Put another way, Meta has begun charging users to post links to the same content that it will be permitted to crawl for free,” Nieman Lab says.

Update, October 16th: Added a statement from Meta and legal commentary.

Tech.title: India becomes the latest country to report rogue AI agent activity
Tech.content:
AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday.

The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it had received “multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers” whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, “had reached the live systems of Indian organizations.”

The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles, and their actions “exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks.”

This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal.

At Hugging Face, OpenAI’s agents started the same way but then found and exploited software flaws to run code on the company’s servers. CERT-In described no such hacking in India, where the agents appear to have simply used the access left lying around.

Still, the Indian cases appear to be worse in one respect, which is what the agents saw: In Australia, OpenAI said it found no evidence its agents touched individuals’ medical or criminal records, even after they wrote files inside a Medicare statistics system, while in India, agents read personal data and confidential business records. And unlike earlier incidents, each disclosed by a single lab, India’s case involved agents from multiple providers.

CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations, or say whether the agents altered any systems. TechCrunch has reached out to CERT-In for more information.

For now, the closest parallel seems to be Anthropic’s July disclosure of Claude breaking into three companies’ systems during testing using basic techniques like weak passwords.

In India, as in Anthropic’s cases, the affected organizations had not detected the intrusions on their own. The disclosures have left governments relying on AI companies causing these breaches to voluntarily disclose rogue AI agent activity.

Tech.title: An Nvidia insider-turned-VC on why robotics hasn’t hit its ChatGPT moment, yet
Tech.content:
Loading the player…

Amulya Vishwanath, who spent seven years leading product marketing for NVIDIA’s robotics platforms, says robotics is currently in its “Lego era,” with the basic building blocks like actuators, robotic hands, software, and safety standards still being rebuilt.

This view runs counter to those who believe that robotics, powered by a general foundation model, is about to have its “ChatGPT moment” — that day when the shockingly capable chatbot was launched in late 2022. (General Intuition CEO Pim de Witte told Equity earlier this year that a single general foundation model would make much of today’s specialized robotics work redundant, and be that moment.)

On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Dominic-Madori Davis caught up with Vishwanath to discuss where she’s writing first checks as the founder and managing partner of Techable VC. They also talked about what she’s learned as one of the first women executives to spin out of Nvidia and launch her own early-stage firm investing in physical AI across robotics, materials science, and life sciences.
